meta.textbook: Potter & Perry, Fundamentals of Nursing, 12th ed.
meta.notes: Exam 3 practice questions for Iggy chapters 16, 19, 31, 27, 29, 30, 32, 45, 58 and 59, Potter chapter 46, Enteral Nutrition, plus the Cardiac Assessment and Infusion Therapy skills. Built from the lecture PowerPoints and the skill course, with readings as support. Questions marked "new": true are the newest additions (addedBatch 11): written so every PowerPoint concept in each chapter or chapter group has a question, all application level clinical judgment items with a "cjmm" field. Questions that revisit a covered topic are hard (difficulty "difficult"). NGN style items (matrix, cloze, highlight, bowtie, ordered response) are kept near 15% of each section. Stems were trimmed (trimmedBatch 12) so client scenario details appear only where the question needs them.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate absolutes
optionStrategies.cue: always, never, all, none, only, every
optionStrategies.note: Absolutes are usually wrong because medicine rarely deals in certainties.

optionStrategies.name: Favor qualifiers
optionStrategies.cue: usually, generally, often, may, approximately, most
optionStrategies.note: Qualifiers make a statement realistic. Not automatically right, but worth a second look against an absolute.

optionStrategies.name: Opposite pair, look closely
optionStrategies.cue: increase vs decrease, before vs after
optionStrategies.note: Often one of the pair is correct. Sometimes both are distractors, so treat it as a flag for attention.

optionStrategies.name: Global or umbrella option
optionStrategies.cue: one option covers two or more others
optionStrategies.note: If one option encompasses the others it is often the most complete answer.

optionStrategies.name: Patient centered option
optionStrategies.cue: asks, involves, or respects the patient
optionStrategies.note: Options that involve the patient beat options that decide for them.

optionStrategies.name: Duplicate facts
optionStrategies.cue: a wrong fact shared by two or more options
optionStrategies.note: One shared wrong fact eliminates several options at once.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
optionStrategies.cue: don't worry, it's nothing, most people are fine
optionStrategies.note: Therapeutic communication reflects feelings and invites more.

optionStrategies.name: Odd man wins
optionStrategies.cue: three options share an idea, one stands apart
optionStrategies.note: When most options point one way, the different one is often correct.

optionStrategies.name: Negative polarity
optionStrategies.cue: avoid, except, not, least, contraindicated, requires further teaching
optionStrategies.note: You are hunting the wrong option. Identify polarity before reading the choices.

optionStrategies.name: Priority key word
optionStrategies.cue: priority, immediate, first, best, most, least
optionStrategies.note: More than one option may be true. The key word decides how to choose among them.

optionStrategies.name: Apply the ABCs
optionStrategies.note: In ordering and priority questions, airway, breathing, and circulation come first, then safety, then comfort.

optionStrategies.name: Assessment before intervention
optionStrategies.cue: assess, check, determine versus administer, apply, notify
optionStrategies.note: When the stem asks what comes first and an assessment option is present, assessment usually precedes action.

optionStrategies.name: Treat each option as true or false
optionStrategies.note: Work each option independently. Partial credit means a wrong selection costs you, so only select what the scenario supports.

questions.stem: A client had a laceration on the left forearm closed with sutures 6 hours ago. The wound edges are warm, with redness 0.5 cm from the wound and slight swelling. The client rates the pain 4 of 10 and makes a full fist with the left hand. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C. The client's partner says, "Please do something before this turns into an infection." Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document the findings and report them to the provider now as an early wound infection
options.rationale: Documenting is right, but the label is wrong. Warmth, redness, swelling, and pain 6 hours after closure do not establish infection.

options.text: Recheck the left forearm on a schedule and hold the documentation until a change appears
options.rationale: Rechecking is right, but the first set of findings is the baseline. Without it there is nothing to compare a change against.

options.text: Document the redness size, pain rating, and hand function with the time, then recheck on a schedule
options.rationale: These are the expected early findings of inflammation. Measured findings with a time give the baseline that later checks are compared with.

options.text: Document the findings and tell the partner that redness this soon means healing has been delayed
options.rationale: Redness this soon is expected. Vessels dilate and blood flow increases in the vascular response.

questions.takeaway: Early warmth, redness, swelling, and pain at a wound are expected. Record measured findings with the time so that later findings can be compared with baseline.
questions.strategy: Every option documents or rechecks, so read the second half of each one. Only one sets a measured baseline without adding a wrong label or a wrong delay.

steps.detail: Four cardinal signs, 6 hours after closure, function intact.
"As infection," "hold the documentation," and "healing delayed" are each one thing off.
Measured findings with a time, then a scheduled recheck.

elimination.verdict: Document measured findings with the time and recheck on a schedule.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

questions.nursesNote:
Yesterday 0800, day 1 after closure of a left forearm laceration: wound edges warm, redness 0.5 cm from wound edge, swelling limited to the wound edges, pain 4 of 10, makes a full fist with left hand, oral temperature 36.7 °C.

Today 0800: Wound edges are warm. Redness is 0.3 cm from wound edge. Swelling extends to the left wrist. Pain is 4 of 10. Unable to make a full fist with left hand. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow-up.

segments.text: Wound edges are warm
segments.rationale: Warmth is a cardinal sign and matches yesterday's entry.

segments.text: Redness is 0.3 cm from wound edge
segments.rationale: Redness was 0.5 cm yesterday. It is smaller, which is not a worsening finding.

segments.text: Swelling extends to the left wrist
segments.rationale: Yesterday the swelling was limited to the wound edges. It has spread, and a worsening sign is followed up.

segments.text: Pain is 4 of 10
segments.rationale: Pain is a cardinal sign and the rating is unchanged from yesterday.

segments.text: Unable to make a full fist with left hand
segments.rationale: Yesterday the client made a full fist. Decreased function is a cardinal sign, and a loss from baseline is followed up.

segments.text: Oral temperature is 36.8 °C
segments.rationale: This reading is close to yesterday's 36.7 °C and does not change the plan. The local findings are judged against their own baseline.

questions.takeaway: A cardinal sign that matches baseline is expected. A cardinal sign that is worse than baseline is followed up, and function counts as much as redness.
questions.strategy: Do not highlight a finding because it is a sign of inflammation. Line up each of today's findings with yesterday's entry and highlight only what is worse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Six findings in each entry.

steps.action: Mark what changed for the worse
steps.detail: Swelling has spread and the fist is lost.

steps.action: Leave what matches or is better
steps.detail: Warmth, pain, and temperature match. Redness is smaller.

questions.objective: Identify the five cardinal signs of inflammation

questions.stem: A client had a laceration on the left forearm closed with sutures 3 days ago. Yesterday at 0800 the nurse marked the edge of the redness at 0.3 cm from the wound. The client rated pain 4 of 10, swelling reached the left wrist, and the client was unable to make a full fist. Today at 0800 the redness is 1 cm from the wound, past the marked line, and pain is 5 of 10. Swelling is back to the wound edges and the client makes a full fist. Oral temperature is 36.9 °C. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Report the wider redness and higher pain now, and include that swelling and hand function are better
options.rationale: Redness has crossed the marked line and pain has risen. Worsening findings are reported, and the report gives the whole picture, including what is better.

options.text: Document all four changes and recheck at 2000, because swelling and hand function are better
options.rationale: Two findings are better, but two are worse. Improvement in one sign does not cancel worsening in another.

options.text: Report the wider redness and higher pain now as a wound infection that needs treatment
options.rationale: Reporting is right, but the label goes beyond the findings. Redness and pain alone do not establish infection.

options.text: Redraw the line at 1 cm and use today's redness and pain as the baseline from now on
options.rationale: A new mark helps later checks, but resetting the baseline without reporting hides the change just found.

questions.takeaway: Compare every sign with baseline. Worsening in any sign is reported, even when other signs are better, and the report states findings without naming a cause.
questions.strategy: The trend is mixed, which makes waiting look reasonable. The deciding cue is that redness has passed the marked line and pain is up: two signs moved the wrong way. Then choose the report that does not add a diagnosis.

steps.detail: Redness and pain are worse. Swelling and function are better.
Worsening symptoms are reported. Better signs do not cancel them.
One states findings. One adds "infection," which the findings do not establish.
Moving the baseline hides the change.

elimination.verdict: Report the wider redness and higher pain, with the improved swelling and function.

questions.objective: Identify the five cardinal signs of inflammation

questions.stem: A client had a deep laceration of the left forearm that extended into the muscle. It was sutured 3 weeks ago and has healed with a firm scar. The client says, "The scar feels tight and my left grip is weaker than my right. Did the healing fail?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "It did not fail. Once the scar matures, the muscle under it will work as it did before."
options.rationale: The first sentence is right. The promise is not: scar tissue does not work like the tissue it replaced.

options.text: "The scar shows that the repair stage did not finish, so the weak grip should be reported."
options.rationale: Scar formation is part of tissue repair. It does not show that the stage was left unfinished.

options.text: "It did not fail. A scar means that new muscle cells have replaced the damaged ones."
options.rationale: Replacement with new cells is regeneration. A scar is the other way tissue repairs.

options.text: "It did not fail. Scar is one way tissue repairs, and it may not work like the tissue it replaced."
options.rationale: Tissue repair happens by regeneration, scar formation, or both. The area returns toward normal function, and scar tissue does not function like the original tissue.

questions.takeaway: Tissue repair is regeneration, scar formation, or both. The area returns toward normal function, and scar does not work like the tissue it replaced.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options reassure the client that healing did not fail. Compare what each one says about the scar: full return, new muscle cells, or a repair that may not work like the original.

steps.action: Drop the option that calls repair unfinished
steps.detail: A scar is repair.
One promises full return and one describes regeneration.
"May not work like the tissue it replaced."

elimination.verdict: It did not fail, and scar may not work like the tissue it replaced.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

questions.stem: A client with no immunity to an infectious disease was exposed to it this morning, and immune globulin is ordered. The client says, "I would rather have the vaccine. I heard it lasts longer." Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "The vaccine does last longer, so it is the better choice for the exposure you had today."
options.rationale: Longer lasting is true, but active immunity takes time to develop, so it cannot be counted on alone for protection right now.

options.text: "Immune globulin protects you now but fades. A vaccine takes time but builds your own protection."
options.rationale: Passive immunity is immediate and temporary. Active immunity takes time, creates memory, and often lasts longer. Both halves are true and they explain the order.

options.text: "Immune globulin protects you now, and it also teaches your body to remember this disease."
options.rationale: The first half is right. The second is not: passive immunity does not create personal immune memory.

options.text: "The vaccine protects you now, and immune globulin is added later to make that protection last."
options.rationale: This reverses the two. The vaccine takes time, and immune globulin is the one that acts immediately.

questions.takeaway: Passive immunity is immediate but temporary with no personal memory. Active immunity takes time to develop, creates memory, and often lasts longer.
questions.strategy: The client is right that a vaccine lasts longer, which makes the first option tempting. The stem's cue is timing: the exposure was this morning.

steps.detail: Exposed this morning, no immunity.

steps.action: Test each half of each option
steps.detail: Two options pair a true half with a false half, and one reverses both.

steps.action: Keep the option with two true halves
steps.detail: Now but fades, versus slow but the client's own.

elimination.verdict: Immune globulin protects now but fades. A vaccine takes time but builds the client's own protection.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: A client received immune globulin after an exposure and asks, "What kind of protection did that shot give me, and is it enough?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "This is artificial active immunity. It protects you now, and a vaccine when the provider advises gives longer protection."
options.rationale: Artificial active immunity follows vaccination, when the body makes its own response and the response takes time to develop. Immune globulin supplies antibodies made by another source, so the type is wrong.

options.text: "This is artificial passive immunity. It protects you now and keeps protecting you, so a vaccine is not needed."
options.rationale: The type is right, but passive protection is temporary and creates no personal immune memory. Immune globulin does not remove the need for the client's own response.

options.text: "This is natural passive immunity. It protects you now and keeps protecting you, so a vaccine is not needed."
options.rationale: This has two errors. Natural passive immunity is maternal antibodies passed through the placenta or breast milk, and immune globulin is a health care product, so it is artificial. Passive protection is also temporary, so the client still needs a vaccine for lasting protection.

options.text: "This is artificial passive immunity. It protects you now, and a vaccine when the provider advises gives longer protection."
options.rationale: Antibodies from another source given as a product are artificial passive immunity: immediate but temporary, with no personal memory. A vaccine produces active immunity, which creates memory and often lasts longer.

questions.takeaway: Immune globulin gives artificial passive immunity: immediate, temporary, and without personal memory. Lasting protection needs active immunity, such as a vaccine.
questions.strategy: Each option has two claims: the type of immunity and whether a vaccine is still needed. Judge each claim on its own; a wrong option can miss one or both.

steps.detail: Another source made the antibodies and they were given as a product: artificial passive. This removes A (active) and C (natural).
Passive protection is immediate but temporary, so a vaccine is still needed. This removes B and also C.
D names the right type and the need for the client's own response.

elimination.verdict: D. Artificial passive immunity protects now but fades; a vaccine builds the client's own lasting protection.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: A client is breastfeeding a 4 month old infant. The client had chickenpox as a child. The infant had chickenpox at 2 months of age and recovered. The nurse teaches the client about the infant's protection against chickenpox. After teaching, which statement by the client shows correct understanding?

options.text: "Getting over chickenpox gave my baby its own immunity, with memory. My milk's antibodies add temporary protection."
options.rationale: Recovering from a natural infection produces natural active immunity: the infant's own response, with memory and often long lasting protection. Antibodies in breast milk are natural passive immunity, which is immediate but temporary.

options.text: "My milk passes my chickenpox antibodies to my baby, and that is the main reason my baby will stay protected."
options.rationale: Breast milk does carry maternal antibodies, but that protection is passive and temporary with no memory. The infant recovered from chickenpox and made its own response, which is what lasts.

options.text: "My baby got chickenpox antibodies across the placenta before birth, and those will protect my baby for years."
options.rationale: Antibodies across the placenta are natural passive immunity, which is temporary. They also did not prevent the infant's chickenpox at 2 months.

options.text: "Getting over chickenpox gave my baby passive immunity, so the protection will fade within the next few months."
options.rationale: Recovering from a natural infection is active immunity, not passive. The infant made its own response.

questions.takeaway: Recovery from a natural infection is natural active immunity, with memory and longer protection. Maternal antibodies through the placenta or breast milk are natural passive immunity: immediate but temporary.
questions.strategy: A and B both describe real protection, and breastfeeding pulls toward B. The cue that decides is "the infant had chickenpox at 2 months of age and recovered": the infant made its own response, and that is the lasting one.

steps.detail: Chickenpox at 2 months, then recovery.
Natural active: own response, memory, longer lasting.
Natural passive: immediate, temporary, no memory.

steps.action: Reject the placenta and passive claims
steps.detail: Placental antibodies are temporary; recovery is active, not passive.

elimination.verdict: Recovery made the infant's own immunity with memory; milk antibodies add temporary protection.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: A client with no prior immunity to a disease received immune globulin after an exposure 3 months ago. The client received the first dose of the vaccine against the same disease 2 days ago. Today the client reports a new close exposure to the disease this morning and says, "I have had both, so I am covered." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "The immune globulin from 3 months ago is still working, so nothing more is needed today."
options.rationale: Passive protection is temporary. The nurse cannot assume it is still present 3 months later.

options.text: "The vaccine from 2 days ago covers you, because vaccines create immune memory."
options.rationale: Vaccines do create memory, but active immunity takes time to develop. Two days is too soon to count on it.

options.text: "Neither can be counted on today. One is temporary and the other needs time. I will report this exposure."
options.rationale: Passive protection fades and active protection has not had time to form. The client may be unprotected, so the nurse reports the exposure for a decision about protection now.

options.text: "Neither can be counted on today, so I will give you another dose of immune globulin now."
options.rationale: The reasoning is right and the product may be what is needed, but the nurse does not give it without an order. The exposure is reported first.

questions.takeaway: Passive immunity is temporary and active immunity takes time to develop. A client can sit in the gap between the two.
questions.strategy: Each product sounds like it should cover the client, and two options lean on one of them. The deciding cues are the two time points: 3 months since the temporary product and 2 days since the slow one.

steps.detail: Immune globulin: immediate but temporary. Vaccine: lasting but slow.
3 months is long for a temporary product, and 2 days is too early for the other.
One acts without an order. One reports so that a decision can be made.

elimination.verdict: Neither can be counted on today, so the exposure is reported.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: A client twisted an ankle 1 hour ago, has never injured it before, and it is already warm and swollen. The client asks how the body can react this fast. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "This is your body's built in response. It starts right away because cells matched to this injury were ready."
options.rationale: Built in and immediate are right. The reason is not: cells matched to one specific target belong to adaptive immunity.

options.text: "This is your body's built in response. It starts right away and needs no earlier exposure."
options.rationale: Inflammation is part of innate immunity: present at birth, rapid, broad, and ready without prior exposure.

options.text: "This is a targeted response. It starts right away because antibodies are already present."
options.rationale: A targeted response with antibodies describes adaptive immunity, which develops through exposure to antigens.

options.text: "This is your body's built in response. It will be faster next time because it creates memory."
options.rationale: Creating memory for a faster response next time is a feature of adaptive immunity, not of inflammation.

questions.takeaway: Inflammation is part of innate immunity: present at birth, rapid, broad, and needing no prior exposure. Memory and targeting belong to adaptive immunity.
questions.strategy: Three options begin the same way. The difference is the reason each gives, and only one reason belongs to the innate system.

steps.detail: One hour, first injury, already warm and swollen.
Matched cells, antibodies, and memory are all adaptive.
Needs no earlier exposure.

elimination.verdict: A built in response that needs no earlier exposure.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.scenario: A client twisted the right ankle 2 days ago. At 0800 today the nurse documented: right ankle warm, warmth limited to the ankle; redness 4 cm across over the outer ankle, edge marked with pen; right ankle circumference 26 cm, swelling limited to the ankle; pain 4 of 10 at rest; bears weight on the right leg with a limp. The nurse reassesses at 1600.
questions.stem: For each 1600 finding, indicate whether it is expected with inflammation or requires follow up.

rows.text: Right ankle warm to the touch, warmth limited to the ankle
rows.rationale: Warmth is a cardinal sign of inflammation, and it is limited to the ankle, as at 0800.

rows.text: Redness over the outer right ankle 4 cm across, its edge on the line marked at 0800
rows.rationale: The redness reaches the marked line but does not pass it. It is the same 4 cm as at 0800, so it has not spread.

rows.text: Right ankle circumference 28 cm, swelling still limited to the ankle
rows.rationale: Swelling is still limited to the ankle, but the measurement is 2 cm larger than the 26 cm at 0800. Worsening swelling is documented and reported.

rows.text: Pain 6 of 10 at rest
rows.rationale: Pain at rest was 4 of 10 at 0800. A rise in a cardinal sign is a worsening finding to report.

rows.text: Bears weight on the right leg with a limp
rows.rationale: Decreased function is a cardinal sign, and this is the same function as at 0800.

questions.takeaway: Cardinal signs that match the 0800 baseline are expected with inflammation. A measured increase in a sign, even one that still looks limited to the ankle, is a change over time that is reported.
questions.strategy: Two rows are traps. Redness that reaches the line has not passed it, and swelling still limited to the ankle has grown by 2 cm. Compare each number with the 0800 entry instead of the description.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warmth, redness, swelling, pain, and function.

steps.action: Check the redness against the line
steps.detail: On the line, 4 cm, so unchanged.
28 cm now, 26 cm at 0800, so the swelling grew.
Pain rose from 4 to 6 of 10; weight bearing is unchanged.

elimination.verdict: Rows 3 and 4 require follow up. Rows 1, 2, and 5 are expected with inflammation.

questions.objective: Identify the five cardinal signs of inflammation

questions.stem: A client fell onto an outstretched right hand 4 hours ago. Imaging shows no fracture. The client has deeply pigmented skin. The nurse assesses both wrists and compares the right with the left. Which findings does the nurse document as cardinal signs of inflammation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Skin over the right wrist is warmer to the touch than the left wrist
options.rationale: Local warmth at the injured site, compared with the other wrist, is a cardinal sign of inflammation.

options.text: Skin over the right wrist is darker than skin over the left wrist
options.rationale: In deeply pigmented skin, the redness of inflammation can appear as a darker color. A color change at the site is the cardinal sign of redness.

options.text: Right wrist circumference is 2 cm larger than the left wrist
options.rationale: A larger circumference on the injured side is measured swelling, a cardinal sign.

options.text: Client is unable to turn a doorknob with the right hand
options.rationale: Decreased function is the fifth cardinal sign and the one most often left out. Losing a task the hand can normally do counts.

options.text: Oral temperature is 37.0 °C
options.rationale: Warmth as a cardinal sign is local, felt at the site. A core temperature within the reference range is not one of the five signs.

options.text: Capillary refill in the right fingers is 2 seconds
options.rationale: This checks circulation beyond the injury and is within the reference range. It is not one of the five cardinal signs.

questions.takeaway: The five cardinal signs are warmth, redness, swelling, pain, and decreased function, all found at the site. In deeply pigmented skin, redness can show as a darker color, and lost function counts as fully as swelling.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Recite the five signs and match each option to one of them. Warmth means warmth at the site, not core temperature, and a color change is the redness sign even when it does not look red.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warmth, redness, swelling, pain, decreased function.
Warmer right wrist, darker right wrist, larger right wrist, lost doorknob task.

steps.action: Reject the systemic and circulation checks
steps.detail: Oral temperature and capillary refill are not among the five, and both are within reference ranges.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Identify the five cardinal signs of inflammation

questions.stem: A client touched a hot pan with the left palm 1 hour ago. The palm is warm, red, and swollen, and the skin is intact. The client asks what the body is doing to heal the burn. Place the events of the inflammatory response in the order in which they occur.

options.text: White blood cells move through the blood vessel walls into the burned area
options.rationale: This begins the cellular response, the second stage. Cells arrive after the vascular response has opened the way.

options.text: Blood vessels in the left palm dilate and blood flow to the area increases
options.rationale: Vessel dilation starts the vascular response, the first stage. Histamine released at the site causes this dilation, which produces the warmth and redness.

options.text: The area heals by new cells, scar, or both and returns toward normal function
options.rationale: Tissue repair is the third stage. Damaged tissue heals by regeneration, scar formation, or both.

options.text: Fluid moves out of the vessels into the tissue and the palm swells
options.rationale: Still in the vascular response: fluid leaves the dilated vessels, causing swelling and helping deliver immune cells.

options.text: Neutrophils and macrophages engulf dead cells and harmful material
options.rationale: Once in the area, white blood cells remove harmful material and dead cells by phagocytosis, completing the cellular response.

options.text: Mast cells and basophils in the left palm release histamine
options.rationale: Mast cells and basophils release histamine and other substances that promote inflammation. Histamine release comes first because it is what dilates the vessels in the vascular response.

questions.takeaway: Inflammation runs in three stages: vascular (histamine release, dilation, then fluid shift and swelling), cellular (white cells migrate in, then engulf), and tissue repair (regeneration, scar, or both).
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort the six events into the three stages first, then order the two events inside each stage. Within a stage, something has to arrive before it can act.

steps.detail: Histamine release, dilation, and fluid shift are vascular. Migration and engulfing are cellular. Healing is repair.
Histamine release comes first; it is what dilates the vessels.
Vessels dilate before fluid can leave them.
White cells must move into the area before they can engulf anything.
The area returns toward normal function at the end.

elimination.verdict: Histamine release, dilation, fluid shift and swelling, white cell migration, engulfing, tissue repair.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

questions.stem: A nurse at a clinic reviews the immunity history of six clients. Each client has antibodies against the disease named. Which clients have active immunity? Select all that apply.

options.text: A client who has measles antibodies 10 years after recovering from measles
options.rationale: Recovering from a natural infection is natural active immunity. The client made the antibodies and has memory.

options.text: A client who received an antitoxin 1 hour ago and now has antibodies against the toxin
options.rationale: An antitoxin is artificial passive immunity. The antibodies came from another source, so the protection is immediate and temporary.

options.text: A 13 month old who received a measles vaccination at 12 months of age
options.rationale: A vaccine stimulates the body to produce its own response. This is artificial active immunity, even in a young child.

options.text: A 3 month old who has measles antibodies that crossed the placenta from a parent who had measles
options.rationale: The parent has natural active immunity, but the infant received the parent's antibodies. For the infant this is natural passive immunity.

options.text: A client who received a vaccine containing a weakened virus 3 weeks ago and has made antibodies against it
options.rationale: A vaccine with a weakened pathogen stimulates the client's own response. This is artificial active immunity.

options.text: A client who has antibodies 2 days after receiving immune globulin, with no vaccination or illness
options.rationale: Immune globulin is artificial passive immunity. The antibodies came from another source and do not create personal memory.

questions.takeaway: Active immunity means the person produced the response, after a natural infection or a vaccine. Passive immunity means antibodies came from another source: immune globulin, antitoxins, the placenta, or breast milk.
questions.strategy: Every client here has antibodies, so the presence of antibodies decides nothing. For each one ask who made them: the client's own body, or another source.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Who produced the antibodies?
Recovery from measles and two vaccinations.

steps.action: Reject the antibodies from another source
steps.detail: Antitoxin, immune globulin, and the placenta.
The parent's immunity was active; the infant's is passive.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: A client had a splinter in the left index finger 1 year ago; within 1 hour the fingertip was warm, red, and swollen. Yesterday the client got a splinter in the same finger, and within 1 hour the fingertip was again warm, red, and swollen, with the same size of swelling as the first time. The client asks, "Did my body remember the first splinter?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "No. That reaction is your inborn, broad response. It starts fast every time and does not build memory, so it was the same both times."
options.rationale: Inflammation is part of innate immunity: present at birth, rapid and broad, and needing no prior exposure. It does not create memory, which fits a second reaction that matched the first in speed and size.

options.text: "Yes. Your body formed memory after the first splinter, so the second reaction was targeted to that finger and started within the hour."
options.rationale: Adaptive immunity does create memory, but memory produces a faster, stronger response on the next exposure. The stem says the second reaction was the same speed and size as the first.

options.text: "No. That reaction is a targeted response aimed at splinters, and targeted responses form memory only after a vaccine is given."
options.rationale: Inflammation is broad, not targeted. Adaptive immunity also forms memory after natural exposure, not only after vaccination.

options.text: "Partly. Your inborn response builds some memory, but only for injuries to the same finger, so it began faster this time."
options.rationale: Innate immunity does not create immune memory, and the stem says the second reaction began within the same hour as the first.

questions.takeaway: Innate immunity is rapid and broad and has no memory, so it looks the same each time. Adaptive immunity creates memory, so a second exposure brings a faster, stronger response.
questions.strategy: A and B both sound reasonable, because memory is real. The cue that decides is "the same size of swelling as the first time": memory would have made the second response faster and stronger.

steps.detail: Warmth, redness, and swelling within an hour is inflammation, part of innate immunity.
It makes the next response faster and stronger.
Same timing and same size, so no memory effect.
Innate immunity builds no memory, and adaptive memory is not limited to vaccines.

elimination.verdict: No; the inborn response is fast and broad every time and builds no memory.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: A nurse at a clinic reviews four client histories while preparing for possible measles exposures over the coming year. Which client is most likely to have a fast, specific immune response if exposed to measles 1 year from now?

options.text: A client who received immune globulin containing measles antibodies yesterday
options.rationale: This client has measles specific protection now, but passive protection is temporary and creates no personal memory, so it will not last a year.

options.text: A client whose skin becomes red and swollen within hours of every minor cut
options.rationale: A fast local reaction is inflammation, part of innate immunity. It is rapid but broad, not specific to measles, and creates no memory.

options.text: A client who received a measles vaccine 1 year ago and has had no measles exposure since then
options.rationale: Vaccination gives artificial active immunity. The client produced the response and has memory for measles, which supports a faster, stronger response on future exposure.

options.text: A 2 month old infant who received measles antibodies across the placenta from a parent who had measles as a child
options.rationale: Antibodies across the placenta give natural passive immunity: immediate but temporary, and the infant forms no memory of its own.

questions.takeaway: Passive immunity protects at once but fades and leaves no memory. Inflammation is fast but broad. Only active immunity creates the memory that gives a fast, specific response on a later exposure.
questions.strategy: Two options give measles specific protection. The deciding cue is 1 year from now: immune globulin protects at once but is temporary and leaves no memory, so only the vaccinated client will make a fast, specific response then.

steps.action: Reject the fast but broad response
steps.detail: Inflammation is innate and not specific.
Antibodies from another source fade and leave no memory.
The vaccinated client made their own response and has memory cells.

elimination.verdict: The client vaccinated against measles 1 year ago.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: A nurse reviews immune events described in six client records. Which events are part of innate immunity? Select all that apply.

options.text: Swelling around a scrape on the right knee within 1 hour, as fast and as large as after the client's earlier scrapes
options.rationale: Inflammation is part of innate immunity. A response that is the same speed and size each time shows no memory, which fits innate immunity.

options.text: Antibodies that bind only the measles virus, found 3 weeks after a measles vaccination
options.rationale: Antibodies that bind one specific antigen and appear weeks after a vaccine are an adaptive, humoral response.

options.text: Redness and warmth at a vaccine injection site in the left upper arm 4 hours after the injection
options.rationale: The vaccine is meant to start an adaptive response, but local redness and warmth within hours is inflammation, which is innate.

options.text: A faster, stronger response to a virus the second time the client is exposed to the same virus
options.rationale: A faster, stronger response on a later exposure comes from memory cells, a feature of adaptive immunity.

options.text: Neutrophils engulfing bacteria at a new cut on the left hand of a 2 day old newborn
options.rationale: Innate immunity is present at birth and needs no prior exposure. Neutrophils engulfing bacteria is phagocytosis, an innate defense.

options.text: Antibodies from an immune globulin injection binding a virus within 1 hour of the injection
options.rationale: This protection is fast, but it is passive: the antibodies came from another source. Antibodies bind specific antigens, which belongs to adaptive immunity, not innate immunity.

questions.takeaway: Innate immunity is present at birth, rapid, broad, and the same each time; it includes inflammation and phagocytosis. Specific antibodies and faster responses on reexposure belong to adaptive immunity, even when they arrive quickly from another source.
questions.strategy: Two traps run through this item. Speed alone does not make a response innate (immune globulin is fast), and a vaccine setting does not make every response adaptive (the injection site still inflames). Ask whether the event is specific or shows memory.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Present at birth, rapid, broad, no prior exposure, no memory.
Scrape swelling, injection site redness, neutrophils in a newborn.
Measles antibodies after a vaccine, faster response on second exposure.
Immune globulin antibodies are passive and specific, not innate.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: A client scraped the right knee on gravel 4 days ago. On the day of the injury the knee was warm, red, and swollen, with redness 2 cm around the scrape. Today new pink skin covers the edges of the scrape, the redness is 0.5 cm around it, the swelling is gone, and the client bends the right knee fully. The client asks, "Which stage is my knee in, and what comes next?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Your knee is in the cellular response now. The next stage is tissue repair, when new cells or scar replace the damaged tissue."
options.rationale: The order of the stages is right, but the stage named is not. New pink skin and the return of full bending show damaged tissue being replaced and function returning, which is tissue repair.

options.text: "Your knee is in tissue repair, the last stage. New cells replace damaged tissue, and the knee keeps returning toward normal function."
options.rationale: Tissue repair is the third and last stage, so no stage follows it: damaged tissue heals through regeneration and/or scar, and the area gradually returns toward normal function. New pink skin at the edges and full bending of the knee show this stage.

options.text: "Your knee is in the vascular response now. The next stage is the cellular response, when white cells move into the knee to engulf debris."
options.rationale: The vascular response, with dilated vessels, warmth, redness, and swelling, fits the day of the injury. Today the swelling is gone and new skin is forming.

options.text: "Your knee is in tissue repair now. The next stage is the cellular response, when white cells clear the remaining debris from the knee."
options.rationale: The stage named is right, but the order is wrong. The stages run vascular, then cellular, then tissue repair, so the cellular response does not follow repair.

questions.takeaway: The stages run in order: vascular response, cellular response, then tissue repair. New tissue at the wound edges and returning function mark tissue repair, the last stage.
questions.strategy: A has the right order and D has the right stage, so both look defensible. The cue that decides is "new pink skin covers the edges" with full bending: that is regeneration and returning function, and repair is the last stage, so nothing follows it.

steps.detail: Vascular, then cellular, then tissue repair.
New pink skin at the edges, smaller redness, no swelling, full bending.
Regeneration with return toward normal function is tissue repair.
Repair is last, so A and D both fail on one point.

elimination.verdict: Tissue repair; the knee keeps returning toward normal function.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

questions.stem: A client with a swollen, newly sprained ankle asks, "Isn't the swelling just more damage?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "The swelling is damage from the injury itself. Your body starts its healing response once the swelling goes down."
options.rationale: Swelling is part of the body's response, not a separate injury, and the response does not wait for the swelling to resolve.

options.text: "Widened vessels let white blood cells crowd into the ankle tissue, and those cells are what make up the swelling."
options.rationale: White blood cells do migrate into the area in the cellular response, but the swelling comes from fluid moving out of the vessels.

options.text: "Widened vessels bring extra blood into the ankle, and the extra blood inside the vessels is what makes it swell."
options.rationale: Blood flow does increase, but that causes warmth and redness. The swelling is fluid that has moved out of the vessels into the tissue.

options.text: "Widened vessels let fluid move into the ankle tissue. The fluid causes the swelling and brings in immune cells."
options.rationale: In the vascular response, vessels dilate and fluid moves into the tissue, causing swelling and helping deliver immune cells to the injury.

questions.takeaway: In the vascular response, vessels dilate and fluid moves from the vessels into the tissue. The fluid causes swelling and helps deliver immune cells to the injury.
questions.strategy: Three options start with widened vessels. Ask what actually makes up the swelling: fluid in the tissue, blood in the vessels, or cells.

steps.detail: A new sprain with swelling: the vascular response.
More blood flow explains warmth and redness, not swelling.
Swelling is part of the response, not a separate injury.

steps.action: Compare the remaining widened vessel options
steps.detail: Swelling is fluid in the tissue, not white blood cells.

elimination.verdict: Fluid from dilated vessels causes the swelling and helps bring immune cells in.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

questions.stem: A client takes an immunosuppressant daily after a kidney transplant. The client has a 2 cm abrasion on the right shin from a fall 2 days ago. Findings: redness 0.2 cm from the wound edge, no swelling, pain 1 of 10, walks without a limp, oral temperature 36.9 °C. The client says, "It barely looks irritated, so I can stop the daily wound checks you taught me." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Your medication can hide signs of infection. Check the wound daily and report new or spreading redness, drainage, or pain, even without fever."
options.rationale: An immunosuppressant affects immune function, so the signs of inflammation and infection can be muted, and infection can be present without fever when immunity is decreased. Daily checks continue, and worsening local findings are reported.

options.text: "Keep checking the wound every day, and call the clinic if your temperature rises above 37.2 °C, since fever is the clearest sign of infection."
options.rationale: Daily checks are right, but this plan waits for fever. Infection can be present without fever, especially when immunity is decreased, as it is with this client's medication.

options.text: "These findings are mild and your temperature is in the reference range, so you can stop the checks once the redness fades."
options.rationale: For a client with a typical immune response, mild signs with a temperature in range are reassuring. This client's medication means mild signs cannot be taken at face value.

options.text: "Your medication lowers your immune response, so these mild findings mean an infection has already started in the wound."
options.rationale: The first half is right. Mild findings do not establish infection, and the nurse does not label a cause from these findings.

questions.takeaway: Medications that suppress immunity can blunt the cardinal signs, and infection can be present without fever when immunity is decreased. Teach daily checks and reporting of new or spreading local findings, not waiting for fever.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options keep the daily checks. The deciding cue is the immunosuppressant: infection can be present without fever, so a plan that waits for fever can miss it.

steps.detail: Daily immunosuppressant after a transplant.
Mild findings are not reassuring when the immune response is muted.
Mild findings do not prove infection has started.

steps.action: Compare the two daily check plans
steps.detail: One waits for fever; the other reports local changes even without fever.

elimination.verdict: Check daily and report local changes even without fever.

questions.objective: Identify the five cardinal signs of inflammation

questions.stem: During the cellular response to bacteria in a wound, white blood cells have crossed into the tissue and a neutrophil has recognized the bacteria as harmful. Which event occurs next?

options.text: The neutrophil ingests the bacteria it has identified
options.rationale: Ingesting is the core of phagocytosis, which makes it tempting. It comes after the cell has surrounded the material.

options.text: More white blood cells cross into the finger tissue
options.rationale: Migration into the tissue comes first in the cellular response, and the stem states that it has already happened. A cell must arrive before it can act.

options.text: The bacteria are broken down inside the neutrophil
options.rationale: Breakdown is the last step of phagocytosis. It removes microbes and damaged tissue, but only after the material has been ingested.

options.text: The neutrophil surrounds the bacteria it has identified
options.rationale: Phagocytosis follows a fixed order: recognize, surround, ingest, and break down. Once the cell has recognized the material as harmful, it surrounds it.

questions.takeaway: In the cellular response, white blood cells migrate into the tissue first. Phagocytosis then follows a fixed order: recognize, surround, ingest, and break down the material.
questions.strategy: Ingesting is the step everyone remembers, so it pulls first. Ask what each step needs before it can happen: a cell cannot take in material it has not first wrapped.

steps.detail: Migration and recognition are done. The question asks for the step that follows recognition.
Crossing into the tissue happens before recognition.
Ingesting needs the material surrounded first, and breakdown needs it ingested.
Surrounding follows recognition.

elimination.verdict: D. The neutrophil surrounds the bacteria; ingestion and breakdown follow.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

questions.stem: A client recovering from a viral illness asks how the body fights a specific germ. The nurse explains adaptive immunity. Which statements by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: "B lymphocytes become plasma cells, and plasma cells make antibodies."
options.rationale: When activated by an antigen, B lymphocytes differentiate into antibody producing plasma cells. This is antibody mediated (humoral) immunity.

options.text: "Antibodies bind to one specific antigen and neutralize or remove it."
options.rationale: Antibodies, also called immunoglobulins, bind specific antigens and neutralize or remove foreign material.

options.text: "T lymphocytes make the antibodies that destroy infected body cells."
options.rationale: T lymphocytes do target infected cells, but they do not make antibodies. Antibodies come from plasma cells, which develop from B lymphocytes.

options.text: "T lymphocytes target infected or abnormal body cells and help coordinate the response."
options.rationale: Cell mediated immunity uses T lymphocytes to target infected or abnormal cells, and T lymphocytes help coordinate immune responses.

options.text: "If the same germ returns, memory cells make the response faster and stronger."
options.rationale: Adaptive immunity creates memory cells that enable faster, stronger responses on a future exposure.

options.text: "If the same germ returns, the response starts over, because the antibodies from the first illness are gone."
options.rationale: Even when antibody levels fall, memory cells remain. The second response is faster and stronger, not a fresh start.

questions.takeaway: Adaptive immunity uses B lymphocytes (plasma cells making antibodies that bind specific antigens) and T lymphocytes (targeting infected or abnormal cells and coordinating the response), and it creates memory for a faster, stronger second response.
questions.strategy: Check each statement for which cell does what, then apply memory. Only the B cell line makes antibodies, and a returning germ meets memory cells, not a blank slate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: B cells through plasma cells, not T cells.
Target infected or abnormal cells and coordinate the response.
A second exposure brings a faster, stronger response.
Memory cells remain even when antibodies from the first illness are gone.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, E.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: A client recovered from a cold 2 months ago. Testing at the time identified the virus that caused it. This week a coworker has a cold, and testing shows it is caused by the same virus. The client asks, "Am I going to catch this cold again?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Your body made its own immunity to that virus, but immunity from an illness fades within weeks, so you can still get sick this week."
options.rationale: The client did make an active response, but active immunity creates memory and often gives longer lasting protection. Protection that fades within weeks describes passive immunity, not recovery from an illness 2 months ago.

options.text: "Your body made its own immunity to that virus. Memory cells can respond faster and stronger, so you may not get sick this time."
options.rationale: Recovering from a common cold is natural active immunity to that specific virus. Memory cells allow faster, stronger responses on a future exposure, and the stem says this is the same virus.

options.text: "Your immunity came from antibodies from another source during the cold, so it has most likely faded by now."
options.rationale: The client recovered from a natural infection, so the client made the response. Antibodies from another source describe passive immunity.

options.text: "Your body made its own immunity to that virus, but this kind of immunity has no memory, so your response will start over."
options.rationale: Active immunity creates immune memory. Lack of memory describes passive immunity.

questions.takeaway: Natural active immunity is specific to the organism that caused it and carries memory, so the same virus meets a faster, stronger response. A different virus would not.
questions.strategy: A and B both start from the client's own immunity. The cues that decide are "recovered 2 months ago" and "caused by the same virus": active immunity has memory and lasts, so fading within weeks does not fit, and memory applies to that virus.

steps.detail: Recovery from a cold is natural active immunity.
Specific to that virus, with memory.
Same virus, so memory applies.

steps.action: Reject the fading and no memory options
steps.detail: Active immunity has memory and lasts longer; fading within weeks and no memory describe passive immunity.

elimination.verdict: Own immunity with memory to that virus, so the client may not get sick.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: At a wellness visit, a 78 year old client with no wounds says, "I had all my tetanus shots as a child more than 60 years ago, and vaccines create memory, so I am protected for life." Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Those shots created memory cells, so if you ever get a deep wound, they will respond fast enough that you need no further dose."
options.rationale: Vaccines do create memory, but vaccine immunity needs booster doses to stay in place, and in older adults antibody duration is reduced further. Memory from 60 years ago cannot be counted on.

options.text: "Your protection has likely faded, so an injection of tetanus antibodies today will protect you for many years."
options.rationale: Fading protection is the right concern, but antibodies from another source give passive immunity: immediate, temporary, and with no memory. The client has no wound, so the goal is lasting protection.

options.text: "Your protection has likely faded, so a tetanus booster today will prompt your body to make its own antibodies again."
options.rationale: Vaccine immunity needs boosters, and at 78 antibody duration is reduced. A booster gives active immunity: the client makes the response again and memory is renewed, which suits a client seeking lasting protection.

options.text: "Your protection has faded because childhood shots give antibodies from another source, which the body clears over time."
options.rationale: Childhood vaccines give artificial active immunity: the client made the response. Antibodies from another source describe passive immunity.

questions.takeaway: Vaccination gives artificial active immunity with memory, and it needs boosters to stay in place; older adults have reduced antibody duration. When the goal is lasting protection rather than immediate cover, the client's own response is renewed with a booster, not with passive antibodies.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: B and C both restore protection. The deciding cue is that the client has no wound: the goal is lasting protection, and antibodies from another source give only immediate, short term protection with no memory.

steps.detail: Childhood tetanus shots: vaccination, artificial active immunity.
Vaccine immunity needs boosters, and at 78 antibody duration is shorter still.
Memory from 60 years ago cannot be counted on without a booster.
Antibodies from another source fade and leave no memory, and there is no wound calling for immediate cover.
Childhood shots made the client's own response.

elimination.verdict: A tetanus booster so the client makes antibodies again.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: A client received a kidney from a deceased donor 1 week ago and takes an immunosuppressant daily. The client asks, "My immune system never attacked my own kidneys. Why would it attack this one?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "The donor kidney has no HLA on its cells, so your immune cells cannot identify it and attack it."
options.rationale: HLA are found on most body cells, including the donor's. The problem is not that HLA are missing but that the donor's HLA are not the client's.

options.text: "Antibodies left over from the disease that damaged your own kidneys will attack any new kidney."
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem describes such antibodies. The immune response to a transplant starts because the organ's cells are recognized as foreign.

options.text: "Self tolerance protects a transplanted kidney, so the medicine is there to prevent infection instead."
options.rationale: Self tolerance prevents attacks on the client's own healthy tissue. The donor kidney is not self, so self tolerance does not protect it.

options.text: "The donor kidney's cells carry HLA that differ from yours, so your immune cells recognize it as non self."
options.rationale: HLA help identify the body's own cells, and each person's HLA are their own. Foreign HLA on the donor cells are recognized as non self, which starts an immune response that the immunosuppressant is meant to dampen.

questions.takeaway: The immune system tolerates cells that carry the person's own HLA and responds to cells that carry different HLA. A transplanted organ carries the donor's HLA, so it is recognized as non self.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A and D both name HLA. Read what each says about the donor cells: A says the markers are missing, D says they are different. HLA are on most body cells, so different is the accurate word.

steps.detail: They help the immune system identify the body's own cells.

steps.action: Apply it to the donor kidney
steps.detail: The donor's cells carry the donor's HLA, not the client's.
Self tolerance protects self tissue; the donor kidney is not self.
No antibodies from earlier disease are described in the stem.

elimination.verdict: The donor kidney carries different HLA and is recognized as non self.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: A client takes an immunosuppressant after a kidney transplant 3 months ago. The client was taught that the medication lowers the function of T lymphocytes. The client asks, "Which part of my protection does that weaken?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "T lymphocytes target body cells infected with a virus, so clearing those infected cells may be slower."
options.rationale: Cell mediated immunity uses T lymphocytes to target infected or abnormal cells. Lower T lymphocyte function slows that targeted response.

options.text: "T lymphocytes make your antibodies, so the vaccines you received will stop protecting you right away."
options.rationale: B lymphocytes become plasma cells, and plasma cells make antibodies. The claim that protection stops right away also goes beyond anything in the stem.

options.text: "T lymphocytes are the first cells to engulf bacteria at a cut, so a new cut will no longer swell."
options.rationale: Neutrophils are the first responders that engulf bacteria, and swelling comes from the vascular response. Both belong to innate immunity, not T lymphocytes.

options.text: "T lymphocytes place HLA on your cells, so your body will start attacking its own healthy tissue."
options.rationale: HLA are surface proteins on the body's cells; T lymphocytes do not place them. Self tolerance is what prevents attacks on healthy tissue.

questions.takeaway: T lymphocytes run cell mediated immunity: they target infected or abnormal cells and help coordinate the response. Antibodies come from B lymphocytes through plasma cells.
questions.strategy: Each option gives T lymphocytes a job. Only one job belongs to them. Match the cell to its slide function before reading the consequence.

steps.detail: Target infected or abnormal cells and coordinate the response.
Plasma cells from B lymphocytes make antibodies.
Neutrophils engulf bacteria; swelling is the vascular response.
HLA are the body's own markers; self tolerance protects healthy tissue.

elimination.verdict: T lymphocytes target virus infected cells, so clearing them may be slower.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: A client returned 4 weeks ago from a camping trip during which the client drank untreated stream water. The client reports loose stools for 3 weeks and a weight loss of 2 kg. The client has a history of seasonal allergies and today has no sneezing, itching, rash, or wheezing. White blood cell count is 7800 per mm3, neutrophils are 58%, and eosinophils are 14%. Oral temperature is 36.9 °C. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: The eosinophil rise most likely reflects the seasonal allergies, since eosinophils mediate allergic responses
options.rationale: Eosinophils do rise with allergic responses, and the client has an allergy history. But today there is no sneezing, itching, rash, or wheezing, so nothing shows an active allergic response.

options.text: The eosinophil rise points to a bacterial infection from the stream water, since eosinophils engulf bacteria
options.rationale: Neutrophils are the first responders that engulf bacteria. Eosinophils defend against parasites and mediate allergic responses.

options.text: The results show no immune response, since the white blood cell count and neutrophils are at expected levels
options.rationale: The total count and neutrophils (55 to 70%) are in range, but eosinophils at 14% are well above 1 to 4%. One cell type can rise while the total stays in range.

options.text: The eosinophil rise most likely reflects a parasite from the stream water, since eosinophils fight parasites
options.rationale: Eosinophils at 14% are well above the reference range of 1 to 4%. Eosinophils defend against parasites, and the untreated water, weeks of loose stools, and weight loss fit a parasitic cause (eosinophils rise most with parasitic worms) better than an allergy with no active signs.

questions.takeaway: Eosinophils rise for two reasons: parasites and allergic responses. The history and current findings decide which one fits.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A and D both link eosinophils to a correct function. The cue that decides is in the stem: today there is no sneezing, itching, rash, or wheezing, while the stream water and weeks of loose stools point to a parasite.

steps.detail: Eosinophils 14%; the total count and neutrophils are in range.
Parasites and allergic responses.

steps.action: Test the allergy option against the stem
steps.detail: No sneezing, itching, rash, or wheezing today.

steps.action: Test the parasite option against the stem
steps.detail: Untreated stream water, loose stools for 3 weeks, 2 kg weight loss.
Neutrophils, not eosinophils, engulf bacteria.

elimination.verdict: A parasite from the stream water; eosinophils defend against parasites.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: A client with a splinter wound asks how the body clears the bacteria that entered it. Which statements by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: "Neutrophils arrive early and engulf and destroy the bacteria in your thumb."
options.rationale: Neutrophils are first responders that engulf and destroy harmful bacteria.

options.text: "Macrophages remove bacteria, dead cells, and debris from the wound."
options.rationale: Macrophages remove microbes, debris, and dead cells from the affected area.

options.text: "Complement is a group of proteins that strengthens the defense and helps remove the bacteria."
options.rationale: Activated complement strengthens immune defense and supports the removal of invaders.

options.text: "Cytokines are proteins that surround the bacteria and digest them inside the wound."
options.rationale: Cytokines are signaling proteins. Surrounding and digesting material is phagocytosis, done by neutrophils and macrophages.

options.text: "Eosinophils are the main cells that engulf the bacteria in your thumb."
options.rationale: Eosinophils defend against parasites and mediate allergic responses. Neutrophils and macrophages perform phagocytosis.

options.text: "Cytokines carry signals between immune cells and help coordinate the inflammation."
options.rationale: Cytokines are signaling proteins that help immune cells communicate and coordinate inflammation and immune responses.

questions.takeaway: Neutrophils and macrophages do the engulfing. Complement strengthens the defense and supports removal of invaders, and cytokines are the signals that coordinate the response.
questions.strategy: Options D and F both describe cytokines, and only one can be right. Signaling proteins carry messages; they do not engulf. Then check each named cell against its slide function.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Neutrophils and macrophages engulf and remove material.
Proteins that strengthen defense and support removal of invaders.
Signaling proteins that coordinate; they do not digest bacteria.
Eosinophils defend against parasites and mediate allergic responses.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, F.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client has red, warm, swollen, itchy patches on the backs of both hands 1 day after starting a new hand cream. The skin is intact. The client rates the pain 3 of 10 and cannot fully close either hand. Oral temperature is 36.7 °C.

The findings on both hands are best explained by [[1]].

The cells that release histamine and promote this response are [[2]].

The client's inability to fully close either hand is documented as [[3]].

options.text: an adaptive response that produces memory cells within 1 day
options.rationale: Inflammation is part of innate immunity, a rapid, broad response. Adaptive responses take time to develop.

options.text: inflammation caused by microorganisms carried in the cream
options.rationale: Inflammation is the right idea, but nothing in the stem shows microorganisms entering the intact skin.

options.text: infection, because redness and swelling are present on both hands
options.rationale: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection. Inflammation can occur without infection.

options.text: inflammation without infection, triggered by an irritant
options.rationale: Inflammation can occur after exposure to an irritant, and it can occur without infection. Intact skin and a clear trigger fit this.

options.text: neutrophils and macrophages
options.rationale: Neutrophils and macrophages are phagocytes that engulf and remove material. They are not the histamine releasing cells.

options.text: basophils and mast cells
options.rationale: Basophils and mast cells release histamine and other substances that promote inflammation.

options.text: B lymphocytes and plasma cells
options.rationale: B lymphocytes and plasma cells produce antibodies in humoral immunity. They do not release histamine.

options.text: eosinophils and neutrophils
options.rationale: Neutrophils are phagocytes and do not release histamine. Basophils and mast cells are the cells the lecture names as releasing histamine to promote inflammation.

options.text: a finding unrelated to the inflammation on the hands
options.rationale: Decreased function is one of the five cardinal signs, so it is part of the inflammatory picture.

options.text: evidence that an infection has developed in both hands
options.rationale: Decreased function is a sign of inflammation, and inflammation can occur without infection.

options.text: decreased function, a cardinal sign of inflammation
options.rationale: The five cardinal signs are warmth, redness, swelling, pain, and decreased function. Not being able to close the hands is decreased function.

options.text: swelling, a cardinal sign of inflammation
options.rationale: Swelling is a separate cardinal sign. Being unable to close the hand is a loss of function, which is documented as decreased function.

questions.takeaway: An irritant can trigger inflammation without infection. Basophils and mast cells release histamine that promotes it, and decreased function is one of the five cardinal signs.
questions.strategy: The trap in blank 1 is reading redness and swelling as infection. Name the trigger first: a new cream on intact skin is an irritant, not an invasion by microorganisms.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A new hand cream on intact skin: an irritant.

steps.action: Match the chemical to the cell
steps.detail: Histamine comes from basophils and mast cells.
Warmth, redness, swelling, pain, decreased function.
Cannot fully close the hands is decreased function.

elimination.verdict: Inflammation without infection, triggered by an irritant; basophils and mast cells; decreased function, a cardinal sign of inflammation.

questions.objective: Identify the five cardinal signs of inflammation

questions.stem: A client has had three bacterial skin infections in the past year. Testing shows that the client has low levels of complement. White blood cell counts and cytokine levels have been in the expected range at each visit. The client asks, "What does complement do, and why would having less of it matter?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Complement carries signals between your immune cells, and cytokines help clear bacteria, so with less complement your cells are slower to coordinate."
options.rationale: This swaps the two. Cytokines are the signaling proteins that help immune cells communicate; complement is the group of proteins that strengthens defense and supports removal of invaders.

options.text: "Complement is made by plasma cells after an exposure, and cytokines are a type of antibody, so your protection builds only after each infection."
options.rationale: Plasma cells make antibodies in humoral immunity. Complement and cytokines are proteins of the innate response, and cytokines are signaling proteins, not antibodies.

options.text: "Complement helps clear bacteria, and cytokines carry signals between immune cells, so with less complement bacteria are cleared more slowly."
options.rationale: Complement is a group of proteins that strengthens immune defense, and activated complement supports the removal of invaders. With less complement, bacteria are removed less efficiently, which fits repeated bacterial infections. Cytokines, which coordinate the response, are in the expected range.

options.text: "Complement helps clear bacteria, and cytokines carry signals between immune cells, so with less complement your cells cannot signal each other."
options.rationale: Both definitions are right, but the consequence is wrong. Signaling between immune cells is the job of cytokines, and the stem states the cytokine levels are in the expected range.

questions.takeaway: Complement is a group of proteins that strengthens defense and supports removal of invaders. Cytokines are signaling proteins that help immune cells communicate and coordinate inflammation. A low complement level weakens removal of bacteria, not signaling.
questions.strategy: C and D share the same two definitions and differ only in the consequence. Match the consequence to the protein that is low: complement removes invaders, cytokines carry signals.

steps.detail: Complement strengthens defense and supports removal of invaders; cytokines are signaling proteins.
A gives complement the cytokine job.
Plasma cells make antibodies; cytokines are not antibodies.
Low complement slows removal of bacteria; signaling depends on cytokines, which are in range.

elimination.verdict: Complement helps clear bacteria, so with less complement bacteria are cleared more slowly.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: A client has an inherited condition in which B lymphocytes cannot develop into plasma cells. The client's T lymphocytes, neutrophils, and macrophages work as expected. The nurse reviews the client's immune function with a new nurse. Which statements by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: "The client makes few antibodies, so fewer antigens are neutralized or removed by antibody binding."
options.rationale: B lymphocytes become antibody producing plasma cells when activated by antigens. Without plasma cells, few antibodies are made, so antibody binding that neutralizes or removes foreign material is reduced.

options.text: "A vaccine may not lead to protective antibodies, because making them depends on plasma cells."
options.rationale: Artificial active immunity depends on the body producing its own response. If B lymphocytes cannot become plasma cells, the client may not make protective antibodies after a vaccine.

options.text: "Immune globulin can supply antibodies from another source for immediate, temporary protection."
options.rationale: Immune globulin is artificial passive immunity: antibodies come from another source, give immediate protection, and do not depend on the client's plasma cells. The protection is temporary.

options.text: "The client's neutrophils cannot engulf bacteria, because phagocytosis depends on antibodies."
options.rationale: Neutrophils and macrophages perform phagocytosis as part of innate immunity, which the stem says works as expected. Phagocytosis does not require the client's own antibodies to occur.

options.text: "The client's T lymphocytes will make the antibodies instead, so antibody levels stay the same."
options.rationale: T lymphocytes run cell mediated immunity: they target infected or abnormal cells and help coordinate the response. Antibodies come from plasma cells, which develop from B lymphocytes.

options.text: "Each antibody the client does make binds many kinds of antigen, so the response is broad."
options.rationale: Antibodies bind to specific antigens. Broad responses belong to innate immunity, not to antibodies.

questions.takeaway: Humoral immunity runs from B lymphocytes to plasma cells to antibodies, and each antibody binds a specific antigen to neutralize or remove it. Without plasma cells the client's own antibody response fails, but antibodies from another source can still give temporary protection.
questions.strategy: Trace the chain named in the stem: B lymphocytes, then plasma cells, then antibodies. Any option that hands the antibody job to another cell, or blames the innate cells the stem says work, is false.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: B lymphocytes become plasma cells; plasma cells make antibodies that bind specific antigens.

steps.action: Apply the break in the chain
steps.detail: Few antibodies, and a vaccine may not produce protective antibodies.
Immune globulin brings antibodies from another source.
T lymphocytes do not make antibodies; neutrophils still engulf.
Antibodies are specific, not broad.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: Testing shows that a client's own immune cells are attacking the healthy tissue that lines both knee joints. Cultures of fluid from both knees grew no microorganisms, and the client has had no recent injury. The client asks, "Why would my immune system go after my own knees?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Your knees were injured, and your immune cells are clearing damaged tissue, which is the expected response."
options.rationale: Inflammation does follow injury and helps remove damaged tissue, so this sounds right. But the stem states the client has had no recent injury, and the tissue under attack is healthy, not damaged.

options.text: "Swelling in your knees means an infection is present, and your immune cells are fighting it off."
options.rationale: Inflammation can occur without infection, and the cultures grew no microorganisms. Swelling alone does not establish infection.

options.text: "Your immune cells found foreign material in your knees, and attacking it is the expected response."
options.rationale: Recognition of foreign material does start an immune response, so this sounds right. But the stem states the cells are attacking healthy tissue and the cultures grew nothing, so there is no foreign target. The tissue under attack is self.

options.text: "Self tolerance usually stops attacks on healthy tissue, and here your cells treat it as non self."
options.rationale: The immune system normally distinguishes the body's cells from foreign substances, and self tolerance prevents attacks against healthy tissue. An attack on healthy joint tissue with no microorganism present means the client's own tissue is being treated as non self.

questions.takeaway: The immune system separates self from non self, and self tolerance keeps it from attacking healthy tissue. When immune cells attack healthy tissue and no foreign material is found, self tolerance has failed and self is being treated as non self.
