options.rationale: Before a stress test the client may have a light meal 2 hours before, avoids smoking, alcohol, and caffeine on the day of the test, and follows the cardiologist's direction on cardiac drugs, here holding the beta blocker so the heart rate can rise.

questions.takeaway: Before an exercise stress test: rest the night before, a light meal up to 2 hours before, no smoking, alcohol, or caffeine that day, and cardiac drugs such as beta blockers held only as the cardiologist directs. Avoid a hot shower for 1 to 2 hours afterward.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options share the meal and caffeine instructions. Decide on the second half: holding the beta blocker follows the order, while a hot shower after the test risks hypotension.

steps.detail: The order says hold the beta blocker, so taking it is wrong.
Fasting after midnight and bed rest belong to catheterization.
Both give the right meal and caffeine teaching. Only one keeps the drug order; the other adds a hot shower, which is avoided.

elimination.verdict: Light meal by 1100, no coffee or smoking, and skip the beta blocker that morning.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: A client, 24 years old, is seen for a physical before joining a running club. The client runs 5 km three times each week and reports no shortness of breath, chest pain, or swelling. Heart rate 58 beats per minute and regular, blood pressure 114/70 mm Hg in the right arm, lungs clear in all fields. With the bell at the apex, the nurse hears a soft, low pitched extra sound just after S2, during rapid ventricular filling. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: Record an S3 that may be a normal finding at this age, and complete the assessment
options.rationale: An S3 is heard during rapid ventricular filling and may be normal in clients younger than 35 years. At 24 years, with no symptoms and clear lungs, the nurse records it and finishes the assessment.

options.text: Report an S3 to the provider now, because it may signal decreased ventricular compliance
options.rationale: This is the right meaning of an S3 in an older adult. The client's age of 24 years is the cue that changes the interpretation: under 35 years an S3 may be normal.

options.text: Record an S4 caused by a stiff ventricle from regular endurance running
options.rationale: An S4 is heard during atrial contraction, just before S1. This sound falls just after S2, during ventricular filling, so it is an S3.

options.text: Report a pericardial friction rub, because it is often transient and may be missed later
options.rationale: A friction rub is a scratchy sound from an inflamed pericardium. This is a soft, low pitched sound tied to ventricular filling, not a rub.

questions.takeaway: An S3 occurs during rapid ventricular filling, just after S2. It may be normal in clients younger than 35 years; in older adults it may indicate decreased ventricular compliance or heart failure.
questions.strategy: Name the sound by its timing first: just after S2 is S3, just before S1 is S4. Then let the age decide what the S3 means.

steps.detail: Just after S2, during rapid filling, is an S3. The S4 and rub options are out.
One records it, one reports it as decreased compliance.
At 24 years with no symptoms and clear lungs, an S3 may be normal, so the nurse records it.

elimination.verdict: A. Record an S3 that may be normal at this age and complete the assessment.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client, 68 years old, had rheumatic fever as a child. With the client turned toward the left side, the nurse hears a low pitched rumbling sound at the apex that begins after S2 and continues until just before the next S1. The sound is not heard in the neck or the left axilla. The nurse identifies this as [[1]].

The sound is produced by [[2]].

In the record, the nurse describes the sound by [[3]].

options.text: An S3 gallop from rapid ventricular filling
options.rationale: An S3 is a single short sound just after S2. This sound lasts through the interval from S2 to the next S1, which makes it a murmur.

options.text: A diastolic murmur
options.rationale: A murmur heard between S2 and S1 is diastolic. The sound continues across that whole interval, so it is a murmur rather than a single extra sound.

options.text: A systolic murmur
options.rationale: A systolic murmur falls between S1 and S2. This sound begins after S2 and ends before S1.

options.text: A pericardial friction rub
options.rationale: A rub is a scratchy sound from an inflamed pericardium. This sound is a low pitched rumble at the apex.

options.text: Movement of an inflamed pericardium against the heart
options.rationale: That produces a pericardial friction rub, which is scratchy and often transient.

options.text: Blood filling a stiff ventricle during atrial contraction
options.rationale: That produces an S4, a brief sound just before S1, not a sound lasting across diastole.

options.text: Turbulent blood flow in or near the heart
options.rationale: Murmurs are whooshing or swishing sounds from turbulent flow in or near the heart.

options.text: Closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves
options.rationale: Closure of the semilunar valves produces S2. The murmur starts after S2.

options.text: Location, timing, radiation, and quality
options.rationale: Murmurs are described by location, timing, radiation, and quality. Here: apex, diastolic, no radiation to the neck or axilla, low pitched rumble.

options.text: Location, timing, and a grade from I to VI
options.rationale: Grading is done by the provider; the nurse is not expected to grade murmurs. Radiation and quality are also left out.

options.text: Rate, rhythm, location, and pulse deficit
options.rationale: These describe the heart rate and rhythm, not a murmur. Timing, radiation, and quality are missing.

options.text: Timing and radiation only, since location is always the apex
options.rationale: Murmurs can be loudest at any valve area, so location is always part of the description.

questions.takeaway: A murmur between S2 and S1 is diastolic; between S1 and S2 it is systolic. Murmurs come from turbulent flow and are described by location, timing, radiation, and quality.
questions.strategy: A single extra sound and a murmur can sit in the same part of the cycle. Duration decides: a murmur fills the interval, a gallop is one brief sound.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: After S2 until the next S1 is diastole.
The sound continues across the interval, so it is a murmur, not an S3.
Turbulent flow produces murmurs.
Location, timing, radiation, and quality.

elimination.verdict: 1: a diastolic murmur. 2: turbulent blood flow in or near the heart. 3: location, timing, radiation, and quality.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A client, 72 years old, with heart failure received 2 L of intravenous fluid between 0800 and 1200 for dehydration. At 0800 blood pressure was 118/72 mm Hg and the lungs were clear. At 1200 blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg, heart rate is 114 beats per minute, an S3 is heard at the apex, and crackles are heard in both lung bases. Which explanation of the change in blood pressure is accurate?

options.text: Preload rose, so the stretched fibers contracted harder, and the pressure fell from vessel dilation
options.rationale: Within limits, more filling does make the muscle contract more forcefully. The cue is the failing heart that now has crackles and an S3: the filling has gone past that limit, and the pressure fell because output fell.

options.text: Preload fell, because fluid moved into the lungs and less blood returned to the left ventricle
options.rationale: Crackles show fluid backing up behind the left ventricle, which means the ventricle is overfilled, not underfilled.

options.text: Preload rose past the point where stretch helps, so the overfilled ventricle ejected less blood
options.rationale: Preload is the fiber stretch at the end of diastole. Within limits, more stretch raises stroke volume, but excessive filling in a failing heart lowers cardiac output, so blood pressure falls and the heart rate rises.

options.text: Afterload rose, because the extra fluid narrowed the arteries and raised resistance to ejection
options.rationale: Afterload is the resistance the ventricle pumps against. Added fluid volume acts on filling, which is preload, and the blood pressure fell rather than rose.

questions.takeaway: Preload is the stretch of the ventricular fibers at the end of diastole. Within limits, more filling strengthens contraction; excessive filling, especially in a failing heart, lowers cardiac output.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options agree that preload rose. Decide whether the stretch still helps: a falling blood pressure with new crackles and an S3 in heart failure says the ventricle is overfilled.

steps.detail: Added fluid volume changes filling, which is preload. The afterload option is out.
Crackles mean blood is backing up, so preload rose. The falling preload option is out.
In a failing heart with crackles and an S3, the extra stretch no longer helps; output and pressure fell.

elimination.verdict: C. Preload rose past the point where stretch helps, so the overfilled ventricle ejected less blood.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.stem: A client, 66 years old, returns to the unit at 1030 after a transesophageal echocardiogram. The throat was sprayed with a local anesthetic before the probe was passed. The client is alert and oriented, blood pressure 128/78 mm Hg and heart rate 76 beats per minute, the same as before the test, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. The client says, "My mouth is so dry. Can I have some water now?" Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: Check the gag and swallow reflexes before giving any water
options.rationale: The anesthetic spray numbs the throat, so the gag and swallow reflexes may not have returned. Fluids before they return can be aspirated, so the nurse checks them first.

options.text: Give small sips of water, because the client is alert and vital signs are unchanged
options.rationale: Alertness and unchanged vital signs show the sedation has worn off. The throat spray is the cue: the gag reflex may still be absent even in an alert client.

options.text: Give ice chips instead of water, because they melt slowly and are safer
options.rationale: Ice chips melt into water and carry the same aspiration risk while the throat is numb.

options.text: Keep the client on nothing by mouth until the provider writes a diet order
options.rationale: Recovery of the gag reflex, not a new order, determines when oral intake can resume after the procedure.

questions.takeaway: After a transesophageal echocardiogram, care is like that after an upper endoscopy. The throat is numbed, so the nurse confirms the gag and swallow reflexes have returned before any oral intake.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: An alert client with normal vital signs looks ready to drink. Ask what the procedure did to the throat: the local anesthetic is the cue.

steps.detail: The anesthetic spray suppresses the gag reflex, which creates an aspiration risk.

steps.action: Compare water and the reflex check
steps.detail: Alertness rules out sedation as a barrier, but not a numb throat.
Assess the gag and swallow reflexes before any fluid.

elimination.verdict: A. Check the gag and swallow reflexes before giving any water.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: A client, 70 years old, is scheduled for a cardiac MRI at 1400 to evaluate ventricular function. The client had a permanent pacemaker placed in the left upper chest 6 years ago, reports feeling anxious in small spaces, and is wearing a wedding ring and a wristwatch. Which action by the nurse is most important before the scan?

options.text: Ask the provider for a prescribed antianxiety drug, since the client feels anxious in small spaces
options.rationale: Anxiety in small spaces is a real concern during a 15 to 60 minute scan, and the nurse can address it. It does not threaten the client's heart rhythm.

options.text: Remove the wedding ring and the wristwatch, and check for metal fasteners on the clothing
options.rationale: All metal objects are removed before an MRI, so this is part of the preparation. It is not the most important step for this client.

options.text: Report the pacemaker to the provider and the MRI team to confirm the device is compatible
options.rationale: The magnetic field can deactivate a pacemaker. Some newer machines allow scanning, but the team must confirm this before the client enters the scanner.

options.text: Explain that the scan is painless and that the client must lie still while it is in progress
options.rationale: Teaching about the scan is appropriate, but it does not address the device in the left upper chest.

questions.takeaway: Before an MRI the nurse removes all metal objects and screens for implanted devices. A pacemaker or implanted defibrillator can be deactivated by the magnetic field, so the team must confirm the device is compatible.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Several options are correct preparation. Rank them by harm: a device that keeps the heart beating outranks jewelry and anxiety.

steps.detail: Pacemaker, anxiety in small spaces, ring and watch.
A deactivated pacemaker can stop effective heart rhythm; jewelry and anxiety cannot.
Report the pacemaker so compatibility is confirmed before the scan.

elimination.verdict: C. Report the pacemaker to confirm the device is compatible with the MRI.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: A client, 68 years old, has a clot in a vein of the right forearm around an old intravenous site. At 1400 the client suddenly reports sharp chest pain, the respiratory rate is 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. Speech, vision, and strength in all four limbs are unchanged from 0800. The family asks why a clot from the arm went to the lungs and not to the brain. Place the structures in the order the clot passed through from the arm to the lungs.

options.text: Right ventricle
options.rationale: Fourth. The right ventricle receives blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve and pumps it toward the lungs.

options.text: Superior vena cava
options.rationale: First. Venous blood from the upper body, including the arm, returns to the heart through the superior vena cava. The inferior vena cava drains the lower body.

options.text: Pulmonic valve
options.rationale: Fifth. The pulmonic valve is the semilunar valve that lets blood leave the right ventricle for the pulmonary arteries.

options.text: Right atrium
options.rationale: Second. The venae cavae empty into the right atrium.

options.text: Pulmonary artery
options.rationale: Sixth. The right and left pulmonary arteries carry unoxygenated blood to the lungs, where the clot lodges. Blood reaches the arteries of the head only after it returns from the lungs to the left side of the heart and leaves through the aortic valve.

options.text: Tricuspid valve
options.rationale: Third. The tricuspid valve is the atrioventricular valve between the right atrium and the right ventricle.

questions.takeaway: Venous blood from the upper body enters the superior vena cava and blood from the lower body enters the inferior vena cava. Both empty into the right atrium, cross the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, and leave through the pulmonic valve into the pulmonary arteries to the lungs. A clot in a vein meets the lungs before it could reach the left side of the heart and the arteries of the head.
questions.strategy: Start where the clot starts. An arm vein drains to the superior vena cava, and the right side of the heart always sends venous blood to the lungs before any of it reaches the brain.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The clot is in the arm, so it enters through the superior vena cava, not the inferior vena cava.
Right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonic valve.
The pulmonary artery carries the clot to the lungs; the brain is reached only after the left side of the heart.

elimination.verdict: Superior vena cava, right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonic valve, pulmonary artery.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: During a right and left heart catheterization, blood samples are drawn from four sites to measure oxygen saturation. Which site does the nurse identify as carrying the most oxygen?

options.text: The pulmonary artery, which carries blood from the right ventricle
options.rationale: The pulmonary arteries carry unoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. They are arteries because they carry blood away from the heart, not because the blood is oxygenated.

options.text: The superior vena cava, which returns blood from the upper body
options.rationale: The superior vena cava returns unoxygenated venous blood from the upper body to the right atrium, so its saturation is low.

options.text: The left atrium, which receives blood from the pulmonary veins
options.rationale: Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. Of these four sites, it is the only one holding oxygenated blood.

options.text: The right ventricle, which pumps blood toward the pulmonic valve
options.rationale: The right ventricle holds unoxygenated venous blood from the right atrium and pumps it through the pulmonic valve to the lungs.

questions.takeaway: The right atrium receives unoxygenated blood from the superior and inferior venae cavae, and the right side of the heart pumps it through the pulmonary arteries to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium.
questions.strategy: Do not let the word artery decide. Ask whether each site comes before or after the lungs; only blood that has passed through the lungs carries a high oxygen load.

steps.detail: Superior vena cava, right ventricle, and pulmonary artery all sit before the lungs.
The pulmonary artery carries unoxygenated blood to the lungs.
The left atrium is the only site after the lungs.

elimination.verdict: C. The left atrium.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: A client's mitral valve does not close completely. When in the cardiac cycle, and in which direction, does the nurse expect blood to leak backward through this valve?

options.text: During ventricular filling, from the left atrium back into the pulmonary veins
options.rationale: During ventricular filling the mitral valve is open and blood moves forward from the left atrium into the left ventricle. An incomplete closure does not cause a leak at this time.

options.text: During ventricular filling, from the left ventricle back into the left atrium
options.rationale: The direction is right, but the timing is wrong. During filling the mitral valve is supposed to be open, and the ventricle is not yet pushing blood.

options.text: Beginning with the QRS, from the left ventricle back into the left atrium
options.rationale: The mitral valve is an atrioventricular valve. It closes as the QRS appears, making S1, and stays closed while the ventricle contracts. If it cannot close, the contracting ventricle pushes blood back into the left atrium.

options.text: Beginning with the QRS, from the aorta back into the left ventricle
options.rationale: Backflow from the aorta into the ventricle is a leak of the aortic valve, a semilunar valve, and it happens after S2 when the ventricle relaxes.

questions.takeaway: With the QRS, the mitral and tricuspid (atrioventricular) valves close, making S1, and the ventricles contract with all valves closed until pressure opens the aortic and pulmonic (semilunar) valves. A mitral valve that cannot close leaks blood back into the left atrium every time the ventricle contracts.
questions.strategy: Ask when the valve is supposed to be closed. A valve leaks only during the part of the cycle when it should be shut.

steps.detail: The mitral valve is atrioventricular; it closes at the QRS with S1.
It must stay closed while the ventricle contracts, so the leak starts with the QRS.
A contracting left ventricle pushes the leak back into the left atrium.

elimination.verdict: C. Beginning with the QRS, from the left ventricle into the left atrium.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: A client, 74 years old, has had a cardiac output of 2.8 L/min for 2 days after a large myocardial infarction. Blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg. Serum creatinine is 2.3 mg/dL, was 0.9 mg/dL 2 days ago, and BUN is 48 mg/dL. Urine output is 20 mL per hour. Both legs have no edema, and the lungs are clear. The family asks why the kidney tests keep rising. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Less blood is reaching the kidneys, so the wastes it carries are not removed
options.rationale: The vascular system carries cellular wastes to the excretory organs, such as the kidneys. With low output and pressure, less blood reaches the kidneys, so creatinine and BUN build up and urine output falls.

options.text: Tissue fluid is not draining back into the circulation through the lymph vessels
options.rationale: Poor lymphatic drainage causes swelling in the tissues. Neither leg has edema, and lymph flow does not explain rising creatinine and BUN.

options.text: Blood is not returning from the capillaries to the right side of the heart
options.rationale: Poor venous return shows as swelling and pooling in the limbs. The legs have no edema, and this does not explain why kidney wastes are rising.

options.text: The injured heart muscle is releasing wastes that the kidneys cannot clear
options.rationale: Injured heart muscle releases the cardiac enzymes troponin T and I, not creatinine or BUN. The kidney values rise because too little blood reaches the kidneys to remove the wastes.

questions.takeaway: One job of the vascular system is to carry cellular wastes to the excretory organs. When cardiac output and blood pressure fall, less blood reaches the kidneys, so wastes such as creatinine and BUN accumulate and urine output drops.
questions.strategy: Link the finding to a function. Rising kidney wastes with low output points to wastes not being delivered for removal, not to lymph or venous problems the stem rules out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No edema in either leg and clear lungs.

steps.action: Rule out the heart releasing it
steps.detail: Heart injury releases troponin, not creatinine.
Low output means less blood carries wastes to the kidneys.

elimination.verdict: A. Less blood reaches the kidneys.

questions.objective: Describe the basic functions of the arterial and venous systems.

questions.stem: A client, 45 years old, arrives at the emergency department 30 minutes after a deep cut to the left thigh with heavy bleeding. Blood pressure is 96/62 mm Hg in the right arm; it was 128/80 mm Hg at a clinic visit last month. Which findings does the nurse expect as the body works to raise the blood pressure? Select all that apply.

options.text: Heart rate 52 beats per minute
options.rationale: Vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation slows the heart and lowers output. With blood loss the sympathetic system is stimulated, so the rate rises.

options.text: Heart rate 118 beats per minute
options.rationale: Stretch receptors and baroreceptors sense the lower volume and pressure, and the sympathetic nervous system and circulating catecholamines raise the heart rate.

options.text: Skin on both hands cool and pale
options.rationale: Sympathetic stimulation constricts the peripheral blood vessels, shifting blood away from the skin toward the vital organs.

options.text: Skin on both hands flushed and warm
options.rationale: Dilated vessels would lower the pressure further. The compensating response is vasoconstriction, which makes the skin cool and pale.

options.text: Urine output 300 mL over the past hour
options.rationale: Releasing fluid would lower the blood volume further. The kidneys respond to low flow by holding sodium and water.

options.text: Urine output 15 mL over the past hour
options.rationale: The kidneys sense less blood flow and activate the renin angiotensin aldosterone mechanism, and antidiuretic hormone is released. Sodium and water are retained, so urine output falls.

questions.takeaway: Three systems regulate blood pressure. The autonomic nervous system responds to baroreceptors and stretch receptors by raising heart rate and constricting vessels, the endocrine system releases catecholamines, and the kidneys activate the renin angiotensin aldosterone mechanism to retain sodium and water.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask of each finding whether it would raise the pressure or lower it. Compensation always pushes the pressure up: faster rate, tighter vessels, and less fluid lost in the urine.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A faster rate raises output; vagal slowing lowers it.
Vasoconstriction makes cool, pale skin; dilation would drop the pressure.
Retaining sodium and water lowers urine output.

elimination.verdict: B, C, F.

questions.objective: Describe the basic functions of the arterial and venous systems.

questions.stem: A client, 81 years old, is seen in the clinic. Blood pressure is 172/70 mm Hg in the right arm on two readings taken 5 minutes apart; a year ago it was 148/72 mm Hg. The client walks daily and reports no symptoms. The client says, "My provider told me blood vessels get stiff with age, so this must be normal for me." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Stiff arteries are expected at your age, so we will recheck it at next year's visit."
options.rationale: The stiffening is an expected change, but the higher systolic pressure it causes is still hypertension. Waiting a year leaves the organs exposed to the high pressure.

options.text: "Your bottom number is low, so the stiff arteries are not straining your heart at all."
options.rationale: With stiff arteries the left ventricle pumps against more resistance, which leads to thickening of the ventricle. A diastolic pressure of 70 mm Hg does not remove that strain.

options.text: "The reading is high from the stress of the visit, so a home reading is all you need."
options.rationale: Two readings 5 minutes apart, a rise from last year, and no reported stress point to a real change, not a stress response.

options.text: "Stiff arteries raise the top number, and that still needs treatment to protect you."
options.rationale: With age the aorta and large arteries stiffen, so systolic pressure rises and the pulse pressure widens. The resulting hypertension must still be treated to avoid damage to the heart, brain, and kidneys.

questions.takeaway: With aging, the aorta and other large arteries thicken and stiffen. Systolic pressure and pulse pressure rise, the left ventricle pumps against greater resistance and can hypertrophy, and the resulting hypertension must be treated to avoid target organ damage.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: An expected aging change is not the same as a finding that needs no action. Ask what the change does to the body, then choose the response that protects against it.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stiff large arteries raise systolic pressure and widen the pulse pressure.
The left ventricle pumps against more resistance.
Hypertension from stiff arteries still needs treatment.

elimination.verdict: D. It still needs treatment.

questions.objective: Identify important cardiovascular changes associated with aging.

questions.stem: A client, 66 years old, with heart failure is readmitted after gaining 3 kg over 5 days. The client says, "I do not cook. My adult child does all the shopping and cooking for the house." The adult child visits each evening. Which plan for the nutrition history is best?

options.text: Give the client a printed list of high sodium foods before the client goes home
options.rationale: Teaching before the history skips assessment. The nurse does not yet know what the client eats or who chooses it.

options.text: Do a 24 hour recall of food, fluid, and alcohol with the client and the adult child
options.rationale: A nutrition history includes a 24 hour recall of food and fluid intake, diet restrictions, and alcohol use. The person who shops and cooks should be part of it, and the adult child visits each evening.

options.text: Ask the client which foods are favorites, and build the diet teaching around them
options.rationale: Preferences matter, but the client does not choose or prepare the food. A list of favorites leaves out what is actually served and the fluid and alcohol intake.

options.text: Refer the client to the dietitian, who will take the whole nutrition history
options.rationale: The dietitian may review the sodium, sugar, fat, and fiber content of the foods chosen, but the nurse obtains the nutrition history as part of the cardiovascular assessment.

questions.takeaway: A cardiovascular nutrition history covers a 24 hour recall of food and fluid, self imposed or prescribed restrictions and supplements, and the amount and type of alcohol. Include the family member who shops and cooks, and consider culture, cost, and access to food.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Assess before you teach, and assess the person who controls the food. The cue is who does the shopping and cooking.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A printed list comes before anyone knows the intake.
The dietitian reviews the foods; the nurse takes the history.
The adult child shops and cooks, so the recall includes the adult child.

elimination.verdict: B. A 24 hour recall with the client and the adult child.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: During the history of current health problems, a client with fatigue makes these statements. Which statements suggest a cardiac cause and need follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I get heartburn after spicy meals, and it goes away when I take an antacid."
options.rationale: Burning pain after food that is relieved by an antacid points to an esophageal or gastric source.

options.text: "I wake up about 2 hours after I fall asleep, gasping, and sit on the edge of the bed for about 20 minutes."
options.rationale: This is paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Lying down shifts blood from the legs back to the heart, and a failing heart cannot pump the extra volume, so the lungs congest.

options.text: "My chest hurts in one spot when I take a deep breath, right where I bumped it on a door last week."
options.rationale: Pain in one spot that worsens with a deep breath after an injury points to the chest wall or pleura, not the heart.

options.text: "I need 3 pillows to sleep now; 6 months ago I used 1."
options.rationale: This is orthopnea, dyspnea when lying flat. The number of pillows needed is a measure of its severity, and the increase shows it is worsening.

options.text: "I get short of breath climbing one flight of stairs; last year I could climb three."
options.rationale: Dyspnea on exertion is often an early symptom of heart failure. The drop from three flights to one shows a real decline.

options.text: "I feel tired after a 5 km walk, and it passes after I sit and rest."
options.rationale: Tiredness after a long walk that resolves with rest is an expected response to exertion.

questions.takeaway: Ask what brings dyspnea on, what relieves it, and the body position when it occurs. Dyspnea on exertion is often an early heart failure symptom, orthopnea is graded by the number of pillows, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea wakes the client hours after lying down.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: For each statement, ask what brings the symptom on and what relieves it. Breathlessness tied to lying flat, sleep, or less exertion than before points to the heart.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Waking gasping, more pillows, and fewer stairs all point to the heart.
Relief with an antacid is gastric; pain at an injury that worsens with a breath is the chest wall.
Tiredness after a long walk that passes with rest is expected.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A client, 63 years old, is scheduled for a coronary CT angiography with intravenous contrast at 1400. During the history, the client says, "I had a balloon procedure and a stent put in a heart artery 3 years ago." Serum creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL, and heart rate is 64 beats per minute. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: Hold all oral fluids until after the scan to lower the risk from the contrast
options.rationale: Contrast can damage the kidneys, so hydration is encouraged, not withheld. Oral fluids are encouraged after the test.

options.text: Report the stent to the provider, because a stent can make this scan less reliable
options.rationale: Previous treatment for cardiovascular disease is part of the history. A coronary stent can make coronary CT angiography less reliable, so the provider needs to know before the scan.

options.text: Give a beta blocker before the scan, because the heart rate must be slower for it
options.rationale: A low resting rate is needed, and a beta blocker may be prescribed to slow it. The rate is already 64 beats per minute, and the nurse does not give a drug that has not been prescribed.

options.text: Record the stent as past history only, since it was placed more than 1 year ago
options.rationale: Past procedures are recorded, but this one bears directly on the test being done today. Recording it without telling the provider leaves the problem in place.

questions.takeaway: Ask about previous treatment for cardiovascular disease, including diagnostic procedures and invasive treatment. For coronary CT angiography, a stent makes the scan less reliable, the heart rate must be slow, and the contrast calls for checking kidney function and keeping the client hydrated.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Connect the history to the test. The cue is a stent in the same arteries the scan is meant to show.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Contrast calls for hydration, not restriction.
The rate is 64 beats per minute and there is no prescription.
A stent can make the scan less reliable, so report it before the scan.

elimination.verdict: B. Report the stent before the scan.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.scenario: A nurse on a cardiac unit prepares several clients for diagnostic tests ordered for today: a chest x ray, a resting 12 lead ECG, an echocardiogram, and a coronary CT angiography with intravenous contrast.
questions.stem: For each nursing action, indicate the test it belongs to.

rows.text: Check kidney function before the test and encourage oral fluids afterward
rows.rationale: Intravenous iodinated contrast can damage the kidneys, so renal function is checked before and after and hydration is encouraged.

rows.text: Position the client on the left side with the head raised 15 to 20 degrees
rows.rationale: For echocardiography the client lies quietly on the left side with the head raised 15 to 20 degrees.

rows.text: Ask the client to lie still and breathe normally while electrodes are placed on the chest, arms, and legs
rows.rationale: A resting ECG records electrical activity through electrodes on the chest and limbs. It shows dysrhythmias, ischemia, infarction, hypertrophy, and electrolyte effects.

rows.text: Explain that the test uses sound waves, takes 30 to 60 minutes, and needs no special preparation
rows.rationale: Echocardiography uses ultrasound, is painless and risk free, and needs no special preparation.

rows.text: Ask the client to stand, take a deep breath, and hold it while a picture of the heart and lungs is taken
rows.rationale: A chest x ray is taken with a held deep breath and shows heart size and fluid in the lungs, with no needle or dye.

rows.text: Expect a prescribed drug to slow the heart rate before the images are taken
rows.rationale: Cardiac CT images are timed to the cycle and need a low resting heart rate, so a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker may be given.

questions.takeaway: Match the preparation to how the test works: contrast means kidney checks and fluids, ultrasound means left side positioning and no preparation, electrodes mean lying still for the ECG, and a chest x ray needs only a held breath.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask what each test puts into or onto the body: dye, sound waves, electrodes, or radiation alone. The preparation follows from that.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Kidney checks, fluids, and a slow heart rate go with coronary CT angiography.
Left side positioning and no special preparation go with echocardiography.
Electrodes on chest and limbs are the ECG; a held breath for a picture is the chest x ray.

elimination.verdict: Coronary CT angiography, echocardiography, resting 12 lead ECG, echocardiography, chest x ray, coronary CT angiography.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: A nurse begins the physical assessment of a client, 80 years old, with chronic heart failure. General appearance: thin build, which the client says has been the same for 2 years; sitting upright on 2 pillows, as at every visit; speaking in full sentences; skin on both hands warm and pink. The client is slow to answer and unsure of the date; at 0800 the client answered quickly and was oriented. Blood pressure is 78/46 mm Hg in the right arm, was 118/70 mm Hg at 0800. Which finding is the priority for follow up?

options.text: The slow answers and confusion about the date, both new since 0800
options.rationale: The mean arterial pressure is now about 57 mm Hg, was about 86 mm Hg at 0800. A mean arterial pressure of 60 to 70 mm Hg is necessary to perfuse the major organs, so the brain is likely underperfused, which explains the new confusion and slow answers.

options.text: The thin build, which may reflect malnutrition from long term heart failure
options.rationale: Chronic heart failure can leave a client thin and cachectic, but the build has not changed in 2 years. It needs a plan, not urgent follow up.

options.text: Sitting upright on 2 pillows, which may reflect trouble breathing when lying flat
options.rationale: Breathing trouble when flat is common in heart failure, but this position matches every visit and the client speaks in full sentences.

options.text: The warm and pink skin on both hands, which may hide poor perfusion
options.rationale: Skin color and temperature are part of the assessment, and warm, pink skin on both hands is an expected finding. It is not the finding that changed today.

questions.takeaway: Physical assessment begins with general appearance: build, skin color, distress level, level of consciousness, shortness of breath, position, and verbal responses. Mean arterial pressure equals the systolic pressure plus twice the diastolic, divided by 3, and 60 to 70 mm Hg is needed to perfuse the major organs. A new change in level of consciousness with a mean arterial pressure below that level signals poor perfusion of the brain.
questions.strategy: Separate chronic from new, then link the new finding to the numbers. Build, position, and skin match baseline; the mental status and the pressure both changed since 0800.

steps.detail: Build, position, and skin match prior visits.
Slow answers and confusion are new since 0800.
A mean arterial pressure of about 57 mm Hg is below the 60 to 70 mm Hg needed to perfuse the brain.

elimination.verdict: A. The new slow answers and confusion.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A client, 70 years old, is assessed with the head of the bed raised to 45 degrees. The nurse sees distended neck veins on both sides. With the bell over the left carotid artery while the client holds a breath, the nurse hears a swishing sound; none is heard over the right carotid artery. Which interpretations by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: The distended neck veins suggest raised volume and pressure on the right side of the heart
options.rationale: Neck vein pulsations reflect blood volume and central venous pressure. Distention means the filling volume and pressure on the right side of the heart are increased.

options.text: The swishing sound suggests turbulent flow through a narrowed left carotid artery
options.rationale: A bruit is a swishing sound from turbulent flow in a narrowed or atherosclerotic artery. An artery with uninterrupted flow makes no sound.

options.text: A loud swishing sound shows that the left carotid artery is almost fully blocked
options.rationale: A bruit may appear when the vessel is narrowed by half or more, but its loudness does not show how severe the disease is.

options.text: If the swishing sound is gone next month, the narrowing has resolved
options.rationale: Once a vessel is blocked 90% or more, the bruit often cannot be heard. A bruit that disappears can mean the narrowing has worsened.

options.text: Fluid volume overload is one possible cause of the distended neck veins
options.rationale: Jugular venous distention is usually caused by fluid volume overload or right ventricular failure.

options.text: The distended neck veins reflect increased flow through the carotid arteries
options.rationale: The neck veins show venous pressure returning to the right heart, not arterial flow in the carotids.

questions.takeaway: Neck vein distention reflects increased volume and pressure on the right side of the heart, most often from fluid overload or right ventricular failure. A carotid bruit reflects turbulent flow in a narrowed artery, but its loudness does not show severity, and it can vanish when the artery is nearly closed.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Keep the veins and the arteries apart. The neck veins tell about volume returning to the right heart; the carotid sound tells about flow through a narrowed artery.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Distention means more volume and pressure on the right side, often from fluid overload.
A bruit means turbulent flow through narrowing.
Loudness does not show severity, and a lost bruit can mean near blockage.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A client, 76 years old, has a systolic murmur at the right second intercostal space that was recorded at the last visit as faint but recognizable. Today the nurse hears the murmur loudly in the same place and, with the palm flat over that area, feels a vibration with each beat. The client reports no new symptoms. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: Record the murmur as unchanged, because its timing and location are the same
options.rationale: Timing and location match, but loudness has changed and a thrill is now present. Murmurs are categorized by loudness as well as timing.

options.text: Grade the murmur as grade III in the record, because it is loud and the client has no new symptoms
options.rationale: A loud murmur with a palpable thrill is grade IV or higher; grade III is loud without a thrill. Assigning a grade also does not communicate that the murmur has changed since the last visit.

options.text: Record a pericardial friction rub, because a vibration is felt over the chest
options.rationale: A friction rub is a scratchy sound from an inflamed pericardium. A vibration felt over the area of a loud murmur is a thrill.

options.text: Describe the louder sound and the palpable thrill in the record, and report the change
options.rationale: The murmur has become louder and is now accompanied by a thrill, which reflects more turbulent flow. The nurse describes location, timing, radiation, and quality, notes the thrill, and reports the change.

questions.takeaway: Murmurs are categorized by timing, clinical nature, and loudness, and they are described by location, timing, radiation, and quality. Same timing and location does not mean unchanged: a murmur that has grown louder has changed, so the nurse describes it and reports the change.
questions.strategy: Compare today with the last visit on every category, not just timing and location. The cue is the change in loudness, and the trap is an option that labels the sound without reporting that it changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Faint before, loud with a thrill now.
A grade in the record does not tell anyone the murmur changed.
Describe the murmur and thrill and report it.

elimination.verdict: D. Describe the change and report it.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: Which findings in a client with heart failure indicate right sided heart failure? Select all that apply.

options.text: Neck veins distended with the head of the bed raised to 45 degrees
options.rationale: Jugular venous distention reflects systemic venous congestion. When the right ventricle fails, blood backs up into the systemic veins.

options.text: Sleeps on 3 pillows and becomes short of breath within minutes of lying flat
options.rationale: Orthopnea comes from pulmonary congestion. Blood backs up into the lungs when the left ventricle fails, so this is a left sided finding.

options.text: New confusion, with cool hands and feet bilaterally
options.rationale: Confusion and cool extremities reflect decreased cardiac output and decreased perfusion, a left sided pattern.

options.text: Reports no appetite and nausea at meals, with a liver edge palpable below the right costal margin
options.rationale: Anorexia, nausea, and hepatomegaly come from systemic venous congestion of the liver and gut, a right sided pattern.

options.text: Abdominal girth up 4 cm in 3 days with a distended, tight abdomen
options.rationale: Ascites and abdominal distention reflect systemic venous congestion, a right sided pattern.

options.text: Urine output 22 mL per hour for 3 hours
options.rationale: Lower urine output is a decreased cardiac output finding. The failing left ventricle sends less blood to the kidneys.

questions.takeaway: Left sided failure backs blood into the lungs and lowers output: dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, cough, fatigue, tachycardia, confusion, cool extremities, lower urine output. Right sided failure backs blood into the systemic veins: dependent edema, JVD, weight gain, ascites, hepatomegaly, anorexia and nausea.
questions.strategy: Ask where the blood is backing up. Lungs or low output points left. Neck veins, belly, liver, and legs point right.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Distended neck veins, ascites, and the liver and gut findings are systemic congestion: right. Orthopnea is lung congestion: left.
Low urine output, confusion, and cool extremities come from decreased cardiac output: left.
Nausea and poor appetite sound like low perfusion of the gut, but they come from venous congestion: right.

elimination.verdict: A, D, E.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.nursesNote: Client admitted with heart failure. Reports shortness of breath walking to the bathroom and waking at night gasping for air. Coughing frequently. Heart rate 112 beats per minute. Respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. Blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg. SpO2 91% on room air. Crackles in both lung bases. Abdomen soft, not distended. No edema in either ankle. Neck veins flat with the head of the bed at 45 degrees.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that indicate left sided heart failure.

segments.text: waking at night gasping for air
segments.rationale: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea is a pulmonary congestion finding of left sided failure.

segments.text: Coughing frequently
segments.rationale: Cough is a pulmonary congestion finding of left sided failure.

segments.text: Blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg
segments.rationale: Above 120/80 mm Hg, but elevated blood pressure is a cause of heart failure, not one of the pulmonary congestion or decreased cardiac output findings of left sided failure.

segments.text: Heart rate 112 beats per minute
segments.rationale: Tachycardia above 100 beats per minute is a decreased cardiac output finding of left sided failure.

segments.text: SpO2 91% on room air
segments.rationale: Below 95 to 100%. Fluid in the lungs impairs gas exchange.

segments.text: Crackles in both lung bases
segments.rationale: Crackles are a pulmonary congestion finding of left sided failure.

segments.text: Abdomen soft, not distended
segments.rationale: No ascites or abdominal distention, so no sign of systemic venous congestion here.

segments.text: Neck veins flat with the head of the bed at 45 degrees
segments.rationale: No jugular venous distention. This is an expected finding.

questions.takeaway: This client shows left sided failure: paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, cough, crackles, and low SpO2 from pulmonary congestion, plus tachycardia from decreased cardiac output. The absence of edema, ascites, and JVD argues against right sided involvement.
questions.strategy: An abnormal value is not automatically a left sided finding. For each abnormal finding, ask whether it shows blood backing into the lungs or low output, or whether it is a cause of heart failure instead.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Night gasping, cough, crackles, and SpO2 91% all point to fluid in the lungs.
Heart rate 112 beats per minute.

steps.action: Abnormal but not a finding of left sided failure
steps.detail: Blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg is a cause of heart failure.
Soft abdomen, flat neck veins.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure is newly confused at 1000 after being oriented at 0700. Blood pressure 94/60 mm Hg, heart rate 108 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 97% on room air. Hands and feet are cool bilaterally. Urine output was 60 mL over the last 3 hours. Fine crackles are heard in both lung bases. Which explanation best accounts for the confusion?

options.text: Decreased cerebral perfusion from low cardiac output
options.rationale: Correct. The low blood pressure, tachycardia, cool extremities, and urine output of 20 mL per hour all show low output, and the brain is underperfused the same way the kidneys are.

options.text: Hypoxemia from fluid in the lungs
options.rationale: Crackles in the bases show some pulmonary congestion, so this is the right idea, but SpO2 97% on room air is inside 95 to 100%. The brain is getting oxygenated blood; it is not getting enough of it.

options.text: Systemic venous congestion from right sided failure
options.rationale: Systemic venous congestion produces edema, JVD, ascites, and liver findings, none of which are described. It does not explain confusion.

options.text: Fluid volume deficit from excess fluid removal
options.rationale: Low urine output and low blood pressure can fit a deficit, but crackles show the client still has fluid in the lungs, which argues against a deficit.

questions.takeaway: Confusion in heart failure can come from decreased cardiac output or from hypoxemia. Check the SpO2: when it is in range and the output findings (low blood pressure, tachycardia, cool extremities, low urine output) cluster, the cause is perfusion, not oxygenation.
questions.strategy: Hypoxemia and low output both cause confusion, and crackles make hypoxemia tempting. The deciding cue is SpO2 97% on room air.

steps.detail: Low output and hypoxemia both explain confusion.
SpO2 97% on room air is inside 95 to 100%, so hypoxemia is out.
Blood pressure 94/60 mm Hg, heart rate 108, cool hands and feet, 20 mL per hour of urine: low output.
No systemic congestion findings; crackles argue against a deficit.

elimination.verdict: Decreased cerebral perfusion from low cardiac output.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.stem: A client is admitted with worsening heart failure. Which actions belong in the nurse's ongoing assessment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Auscultate lung sounds and note how far up the crackles are heard
options.rationale: Lung sounds are a core heart failure assessment and show whether pulmonary congestion is spreading or clearing.

options.text: Weigh the client daily at the same time, on the same scale, in similar clothing
options.rationale: Daily weight with a consistent technique tracks fluid gained or lost.

options.text: Record intake and output each shift
options.rationale: Intake and output show whether fluid is being retained or removed.

options.text: Assess the apical heart rate and rhythm
options.rationale: Heart rate and rhythm are part of the nursing assessment; tachycardia is a low output finding.

options.text: Delegate auscultation of lung sounds to assistive personnel at each vital sign check
options.rationale: Assistive personnel can measure vital signs, but auscultating and interpreting lung sounds is a nursing assessment and is not delegated.

options.text: Weigh the client once a week on the same scale to limit day to day variation
options.rationale: Same scale is right, but heart failure weights are daily. A weekly weight misses a gain of 2 to 3 lb in 24 hours.

questions.takeaway: Heart failure assessment: respiratory status and SpO2, lung sounds, heart rate and rhythm, JVD and edema, activity tolerance, intake and output, and daily weight at the same time, on the same scale, in similar clothing.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option keeps one correct detail (lung sounds, same scale) and breaks another (who assesses, how often).

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Belongs, and the level of crackles matters.

steps.action: Weight, intake and output, heart rate and rhythm
steps.detail: All belong.
Auscultating and interpreting lung sounds stays with the nurse.
Heart failure weights are daily; weekly misses a 24 hour gain.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with dyspnea and 2+ edema in both ankles has a B type natriuretic peptide (BNP) of 860 pg/mL. An echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 35%, and the chest x ray shows an enlarged heart. Which interpretation of these results is correct?

options.text: The BNP reflects ventricular stretch, the ejection fraction shows a relaxation problem, and the film confirms the ejection fraction
options.rationale: Two errors. An ejection fraction of 35% is reduced, which is a contraction problem; a relaxation problem is heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Ejection fraction comes from the echocardiogram, not the chest x ray.

options.text: The BNP reflects heart muscle damage, the ejection fraction shows a contraction problem, and the film confirms the ejection fraction
options.rationale: Two errors. Troponin is the marker of heart muscle damage, while a BNP of 860 pg/mL reflects ventricular stretch. Ejection fraction comes from the echocardiogram, not the chest x ray.

options.text: The BNP reflects ventricular stretch, the ejection fraction shows a contraction problem, and the film may show congestion
options.rationale: BNP rises with ventricular stretch from fluid overload. An ejection fraction of 35% is heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, a contraction problem. The chest x ray in heart failure shows cardiomegaly and congestion.

options.text: The BNP reflects heart muscle damage, the ejection fraction shows a relaxation problem, and the film may show congestion
options.rationale: Two errors. A BNP of 860 pg/mL reflects ventricular stretch, not muscle damage, which troponin marks. An ejection fraction of 35% is reduced, a contraction problem.

questions.takeaway: BNP rises with ventricular stretch and fluid overload. The echocardiogram shows structure and ejection fraction: HFrEF is a contraction problem with an EF typically below 40%; HFpEF is a relaxation problem with a relatively preserved EF. The chest x ray shows cardiomegaly and congestion.
questions.strategy: Match each test to the question it answers: how stretched (BNP), how well it squeezes (echocardiogram), how big and how wet (chest x ray). Judge each part on its own; the key is the only option with all three parts right.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 860 pg/mL reflects stretch and fluid overload, not muscle damage. Eliminate B and D.
Reduced: a contraction problem. Eliminate A.
Cardiomegaly and congestion; ejection fraction comes from the echocardiogram. C remains.

elimination.verdict: C. Ventricular stretch, a contraction problem, and congestion on the film.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure has received a diuretic for 2 days. Today: weight 2 lb lower than yesterday on the same scale, urine output 1900 mL in 24 hours with intake of 1400 mL, crackles now heard only at the right base, SpO2 95% on 2 L nasal cannula, heart rate 88 beats per minute. Which finding best shows that the diuretic is achieving its purpose?

options.text: SpO2 95% on 2 L of oxygen by nasal cannula
options.rationale: SpO2 is in range, but it is measured on supplemental oxygen, so it reflects the oxygen as much as the fluid removal.

options.text: Heart rate of 88 beats per minute at rest
options.rationale: A rate in range is welcome, but many things affect heart rate. It does not directly show fluid removal.

options.text: Crackles now heard only at the right lung base
options.rationale: Fewer crackles do suggest less lung fluid, but crackles are one location on one exam. The weight and output measure the fluid removed.

options.text: Weight down 2 lb and output 500 mL above intake
options.rationale: A diuretic removes excess fluid. Weight down on the same scale and output exceeding intake measure that removal directly.

questions.takeaway: Diuretics remove excess fluid. The most direct evidence is a falling daily weight and output exceeding intake; fewer crackles, less dyspnea, and better SpO2 support it.
questions.strategy: Several options are good news. The key word is best: pick the finding that measures what the drug does.

steps.detail: Remove excess fluid.
Weight and the output to intake balance.
Fewer crackles is supportive, not a measure of volume.
SpO2 on oxygen and heart rate are influenced by other factors.

elimination.verdict: A 2 lb weight loss with output above intake.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A nurse receives report on four clients with heart failure. Client 1 reports new chest pain at rest, 6 of 10, with SpO2 96% on room air. Client 2 asks how much sodium is in canned soup before lunch. Client 3 has SpO2 86% on room air, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and crackles halfway up both lungs. Client 4 has a weight up 3 lb since yesterday on the same scale, with ankle edema now 2+ from 1+. In which order does the nurse see the clients, from first to last?

options.text: Client 1, client 3, client 2, client 4
options.rationale: Two errors. Client 3 has a breathing problem with severe hypoxemia and spreading crackles and comes before chest pain with SpO2 in range, and a weight gain with more edema comes before a teaching question.

options.text: Client 3, client 1, client 4, client 2
options.rationale: Severe hypoxemia with crackles halfway up both lungs is a breathing problem and comes first. Chest pain at rest may be ischemia and comes next. The weight gain with more edema must be addressed today but is not an emergency. The teaching question is last.

options.text: Client 3, client 4, client 1, client 2
options.rationale: Client 3 is first, but chest pain at rest outranks a weight gain with more edema, which shows worsening heart failure without a breathing or circulation emergency.

options.text: Client 3, client 1, client 2, client 4
options.rationale: The first two are right, but a gain of 3 lb in 24 hours with more edema is a physiologic change and comes before a teaching question.

questions.takeaway: Prioritize by ABCs: severe hypoxemia with spreading crackles first, chest pain at rest next, a reportable weight gain with more edema next, and a teaching question last.
questions.strategy: Apply the ABCs, then separate an emergency from a finding that is reportable but not immediately dangerous. A physiologic change always outranks a teaching need.

steps.detail: SpO2 86% with crackles halfway up both lungs: first. Eliminate A.
Chest pain at rest: second. Eliminate C.
3 lb in 24 hours with more edema before the sodium question. Eliminate D.

elimination.verdict: B. Client 3, client 1, client 4, client 2.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.scenario: A client with heart failure is sitting in a chair at 1400. At 0800, crackles were heard only in both lung bases, SpO2 was 94% on room air, and respiratory rate was 20 breaths per minute. Over the past 20 minutes the client has become more short of breath. Now: respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 158/94 mm Hg, SpO2 86% on room air, oral temperature 37.8 °C. Crackles are heard halfway up both lungs, and the client is coughing frothy, pink tinged sputum. A prescription reads oxygen by nasal cannula or mask, titrated to keep the SpO2 at 92% or higher. The nurse will monitor the response over the next 30 minutes.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Obtain a sputum specimen for culture before oxygen is started
options.rationale: The temperature of 37.8 °C makes a culture tempting, but collecting it first delays oxygen for an SpO2 of 86% and the sputum points to fluid, not infection.

options.text: Recline the chair and raise the legs to rest the client
options.rationale: Reclining and raising the legs return more blood to the congested lungs, and the blood pressure of 158/94 mm Hg gives no reason to raise them.

options.text: Place the client in high Fowler's position
options.rationale: High Fowler's eases dyspnea and lets the lungs expand.

options.text: Apply oxygen and titrate the flow to the prescribed SpO2 target
options.rationale: Oxygen treats the hypoxemia, and titrating to the prescription keeps the SpO2 at 92% or higher.

options.text: Apply oxygen at 2 L per minute by nasal cannula and recheck the SpO2 at the next vital sign check
options.rationale: Oxygen is right, but a fixed low flow with a recheck hours later does not titrate to the prescribed target of 92% while the SpO2 is 86%.

options.text: Worsening right sided heart failure
options.rationale: Right sided failure backs blood into the systemic veins, causing edema, JVD, and ascites. These findings are in the lungs.

options.text: Acute pulmonary edema
options.rationale: Sudden dyspnea, SpO2 86%, crackles that rose from the bases to halfway up both lungs since 0800, and frothy, pink tinged sputum indicate pulmonary edema from left sided failure.

options.text: Pneumonia
options.rationale: The low grade temperature and cough make this tempting, but pneumonia does not develop in 20 minutes, and frothy, pink tinged sputum with crackles rising evenly in both lungs fits fluid, not infection.

options.text: Gradual worsening of chronic left sided heart failure over several days
options.rationale: The findings are left sided, but the change came over 20 minutes, not several days. That speed, with crackles rising from the bases to halfway up both lungs and frothy, pink tinged sputum, marks acute pulmonary edema, an emergency.

options.text: Oral temperature
options.rationale: The temperature is worth rechecking later, but it does not show whether oxygen and positioning are relieving the fluid in the lungs over the next 30 minutes.

options.text: SpO2
options.rationale: Shows whether oxygen therapy is bringing the SpO2 up to the prescribed target.

options.text: Abdominal girth
options.rationale: Measures ascites from systemic congestion, which is not the current problem.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: Daily weight tracks fluid over days. It cannot show a change within 30 minutes.

options.text: Lung sounds, including how far up the crackles are heard
options.rationale: The level of the crackles shows whether pulmonary congestion is spreading or clearing.

questions.takeaway: Rapid onset, crackles rising from the bases, and frothy, pink tinged sputum mean acute pulmonary edema, even with a low grade temperature. Sit the client up, titrate oxygen to the prescription, and watch the SpO2 and the level of the crackles.
questions.strategy: Name the problem from the time course first: a change over 20 minutes is not pneumonia. Then pick actions that relieve breathing now at the prescribed target, and parameters that change within the 30 minutes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A change over 20 minutes, crackles from the bases to halfway up, and frothy, pink tinged sputum: acute pulmonary edema.
37.8 °C does not explain a 20 minute change or the sputum.
High Fowler's, and oxygen titrated to the prescribed target.
A fixed low flow with a late recheck, a culture before oxygen, and reclining with the legs up.
SpO2 and the level of the crackles change within 30 minutes; weight and temperature do not track the response.

elimination.verdict: High Fowler's and titrated oxygen; acute pulmonary edema; SpO2 and lung sounds.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure takes digoxin and a diuretic. The client reports poor appetite and blurred vision for 2 days. Apical pulse 58 beats per minute and irregular; it was regular at the last visit. Serum potassium 3.1 mEq/L. Serum creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. How does the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: Expected digoxin effect, because the drug slows the heart rate
options.rationale: Digoxin does slow the rate, but a new irregular rhythm with appetite and vision changes is not an expected effect.

options.text: Worsening right sided failure, because congestion of the gut causes poor appetite
options.rationale: Congestion can cause anorexia, but it does not explain blurred vision, a new irregular rhythm, or bradycardia.

options.text: Possible digoxin toxicity, made more likely by the low potassium
options.rationale: Anorexia, blurred vision, bradycardia, and a change from a regular to an irregular rhythm are signs of digoxin toxicity, and hypokalemia increases the risk.

options.text: Low potassium from the diuretic, which digoxin helps protect against
options.rationale: The potassium is low, but digoxin does not protect against hypokalemia. Hypokalemia makes digoxin toxicity more likely.

questions.takeaway: Digoxin toxicity: anorexia, fatigue, blurred vision, mental status changes, bradycardia, and new rhythm changes. Low potassium makes toxicity more likely, so check potassium along with the digoxin level.
questions.strategy: Read the cluster together. One option explains the appetite, one explains the slow rate, and one explains the potassium; only one explains all of them.

steps.detail: Anorexia, blurred vision, rate 58 beats per minute, new irregular rhythm.
Potassium 3.1 mEq/L is below 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L.

steps.action: Choose the explanation that covers all of them
steps.detail: Digoxin toxicity potentiated by hypokalemia.
Each other option explains one cue.

elimination.verdict: Possible digoxin toxicity, made more likely by the low potassium.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure receives the first dose of a newly prescribed ACE inhibitor. Blood pressure before the dose 112/70 mm Hg. Serum potassium 4.6 mEq/L. Which actions by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor the blood pressure every hour for several hours after the dose
options.rationale: The first dose may cause a rapid drop in blood pressure, so blood pressure is checked hourly for several hours.

options.text: Teach the client to change positions slowly, especially from lying to sitting
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors can cause orthostatic hypotension.

options.text: Teach the client to report a cough or dizziness
options.rationale: A nagging dry cough and dizziness are reportable effects of ACE inhibitors.

options.text: Suggest a salt substitute to make the low sodium diet easier
options.rationale: Salt substitutes usually contain potassium, and ACE inhibitors can cause potassium retention. Potassium and renal status must be checked before using them.

options.text: Teach the client to stop the drug if a cough develops
options.rationale: Reporting a cough is correct, but the client does not stop the drug alone. The provider decides whether to switch, for example to an ARB.

options.text: Report a systolic blood pressure of 104 mm Hg one hour after the dose
options.rationale: A fall from 112 to 104 mm Hg is small and the client has no symptoms. The report threshold after an ACE inhibitor dose is a systolic pressure below 90 mm Hg, or the protocol level.

questions.takeaway: After the first dose of an ACE inhibitor, check blood pressure hourly for several hours and report a systolic pressure below 90 mm Hg. Teach slow position changes, report cough and dizziness, and avoid salt substitutes without a potassium and renal check.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each wrong option starts from a correct idea: flavor the low sodium diet, report the cough, watch the blood pressure. Check each for the one detail that makes it unsafe or premature.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hourly blood pressure for several hours: yes.
Slow position changes, report cough and dizziness: yes.
Contains potassium; ACE inhibitors retain potassium.
Report, do not stop.
Above 90 mm Hg: not the report threshold.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure is on a sodium restricted diet. No fluid restriction is prescribed. Weight today is the same as yesterday on the same scale. SpO2 96% on room air, and the lungs are clear. The client asks for a second cup of water with lunch. Which response by the nurse is appropriate?

options.text: "Let me check with your provider first, because extra fluid can make heart failure worse."
options.rationale: Sounds cautious, but there is no restriction to clarify and no finding of worsening congestion. Holding the water to make a call imposes a restriction nobody ordered.

options.text: "I'll bring it, and I'll add it to your intake record."
options.rationale: No fluid restriction is prescribed, the weight is unchanged, and the lungs are clear, so the client may drink. Recording it supports intake and output monitoring.

options.text: "I'll bring it, but let's keep you to 1 liter a day to protect your heart."
options.rationale: The nurse does not set a fluid limit without a prescription.

options.text: "Have ice chips instead, since they count as less fluid."
options.rationale: Ice chips are recorded as fluid intake, and nothing here calls for limiting fluid.

questions.takeaway: Sodium restriction is part of heart failure treatment. Fluid restriction is used when prescribed, not automatically. Record intake for every client on intake and output monitoring.
questions.strategy: Two options sound protective. The deciding cue is the order: sodium restricted, no fluid restriction, with unchanged weight and clear lungs.

steps.detail: Sodium restricted; no fluid restriction.
Weight unchanged, SpO2 96%, lungs clear: no worsening congestion to report.
A call to hold the water, a 1 liter limit, and ice chips in place of water all restrict fluid without an order.
Provide the water and record it.

elimination.verdict: Bring the water and record it on the intake record.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a client with heart failure about home monitoring before discharge. Discharge weight 176 lb. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I'll weigh myself every morning on the same scale, in my nightclothes."
options.rationale: Correct technique: same time, same scale, similar clothing.

options.text: "I'll call if I can't walk as far as usual for a couple of days, even if my weight hasn't changed."
options.rationale: Reduced activity tolerance is reportable on its own.

options.text: "I'll call if I weigh 181 pounds by the end of this week."
options.rationale: 181 lb is 5 lb above 176 lb within a week, which is reportable.

options.text: "If I weigh 179 pounds tomorrow, I'll wait to see if it reaches 181 before I call."
options.rationale: 179 lb is a 3 lb gain in 24 hours, which is reported that day. Waiting for 5 lb applies the weekly threshold to a one day gain.

questions.takeaway: Teach daily weights at the same time, on the same scale, in similar clothing. Report a gain of 2 to 3 lb in 24 hours or 5 lb in 1 week, more edema, worsening dyspnea, reduced activity tolerance, and new dyspnea or chest pain at rest.
questions.strategy: Two statements use numbers. Subtract each from 176 lb and match the gain to its time frame: 2 to 3 lb in 24 hours, 5 lb in 1 week.

steps.detail: Need for further teaching: find the incorrect statement.
Same scale, same time, similar clothing: correct.
Reduced activity tolerance reported on its own: correct.
181 lb by the end of the week is 5 lb in a week: correct. 179 lb tomorrow is 3 lb in 24 hours: report that day, so waiting is wrong.

elimination.verdict: Waiting for 181 pounds after a 3 pound gain in one day.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure calls the clinic. The client weighed 176 lb yesterday morning in nightclothes on the home scale. This morning the client weighed 179 lb at a pharmacy scale while wearing street clothes, shoes, and a winter jacket. The client reports no change in breathing, sleeps on 1 pillow as usual, and says the ankles look the same as yesterday. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "A 3 pound gain in 24 hours means you should call your provider about it this morning."
options.rationale: A gain of 2 to 3 lb in 24 hours is reportable, so this sounds right. But the two weights were taken on different scales in different clothing, so they cannot be compared.

options.text: "That is under 5 pounds, so keep checking your weight each morning for the rest of this week."
options.rationale: The 5 lb threshold belongs to 1 week. If the gain were real, 3 lb in 24 hours would already be reportable.

options.text: "Weigh again now at home in your nightclothes, and call back if you weigh 178 pounds or more."
options.rationale: Daily weights are compared on the same scale in similar clothing. A repeat home weight shows whether the gain is real; 178 lb would be a 2 lb gain over 176 lb in 24 hours. No symptoms have changed.

options.text: "Take an extra dose of your diuretic today to help your body get rid of the extra fluid."
options.rationale: Medications are taken as prescribed. The nurse does not direct an extra dose, and the gain has not been confirmed.

questions.takeaway: A weight is only meaningful when taken at the same time, on the same scale, in similar clothing. When two weights cannot be compared and no symptoms have changed, get a valid weight before acting on the number.
questions.strategy: The 3 lb number points to calling the provider. The deciding cue is the different scale and clothing: the gain has not been measured yet.

steps.action: Check how the weights were taken
steps.detail: Home scale in nightclothes versus pharmacy scale in shoes and a jacket.
Breathing, pillows, and ankles unchanged.
Get a valid weight with the same technique, with a clear threshold to call back.
Reporting an unconfirmed number, waiting a week, and an extra dose without a prescription.

elimination.verdict: Reweigh on the home scale in nightclothes and call back if 178 lb or more.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure calls the clinic 1 week after discharge. For the past 3 days the client has had to stop and rest halfway through the usual walk to the mailbox, which the client finished without stopping on each of the first 4 days at home. Weight on the home scale is 2 lb above the discharge weight, a gain that has come gradually over 5 days.
