Breathing at rest is unchanged, the client sleeps on 1 pillow as usual, and the ankles look the same as at discharge. Which response by the nurse is appropriate?

options.text: "Being able to do less than you could after discharge needs to be reported to your provider today."
options.rationale: Reduced activity tolerance is a reportable finding by itself. It has lasted 3 days and is a decline from what the client did after discharge, so it is reported even though the weight is under the limits.

options.text: "Your weight gain is under the amounts we talked about, so keep weighing daily and call if you gain 5 lb this week."
options.rationale: The weight is correctly read as under both limits, but weight is only one reportable finding. This answer lets a separate reportable change go unreported.

options.text: "Balance activity with rest by splitting the walk into two shorter trips, and call if your weight starts to rise faster."
options.rationale: Balancing activity with rest is part of the teaching, but it treats a 3 day decline as a pacing problem. A new drop in activity tolerance is reported, not just managed at home.

options.text: "Since your breathing at rest is unchanged, mention it at your follow up visit next month."
options.rationale: Breathing at rest is only one finding to watch. Waiting a month delays a reportable change.

questions.takeaway: Any one reportable finding is enough: weight gain of 2 to 3 lb in 24 hours or 5 lb in 1 week, more edema, worsening dyspnea, reduced activity tolerance, or new dyspnea or chest pain at rest. A weight under the limits does not cancel a decline in activity tolerance.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options sound like good teaching: one checks the weight against the limits, one balances activity with rest. The deciding cue is a decline lasting 3 days from what the client could do after discharge, which is reportable without any weight trigger.

steps.detail: 2 lb over 5 days: under both limits, so weight is not the trigger.
Needing to rest halfway for 3 days, after 4 days of finishing: reduced activity tolerance.
Reduced activity tolerance is reportable on its own.
Pacing the walk or waiting for a weight trigger leaves a reportable change unreported.

elimination.verdict: Report the drop in activity tolerance to the provider today.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure has had increasing dyspnea over the last hour. Respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 150/90 mm Hg, SpO2 91% on 2 L nasal cannula. Crackles are heard in both lung bases. The client is now coughing up pink, frothy sputum. A dose of the prescribed diuretic is due in 3 hours. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Call the provider to request that the prescribed diuretic dose be given now instead of in 3 hours
options.rationale: Fluid removal is the right idea for worsening congestion, and without the sputum finding this could be the best choice. Pink, frothy sputum signals pulmonary edema, and a phone request for an early dose leaves the hypoxemia untreated while the client deteriorates.

options.text: Raise to high Fowler's, increase oxygen as prescribed, and call the rapid response team
options.rationale: Pink, frothy sputum may indicate pulmonary edema, an emergency. Upright positioning and oxygen treat the dyspnea and hypoxemia now, and the team brings help.

options.text: Obtain a sputum specimen for culture, then recheck the oral temperature and lung sounds
options.rationale: A productive cough suggests infection, but no temperature is given and the sputum is pink and frothy, which points to fluid, not infection.

options.text: Encourage coughing and deep breathing exercises, then reassess the lung sounds in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Coughing and deep breathing help clear secretions, but 30 minutes is too long to wait with pulmonary edema.

questions.takeaway: Worsening dyspnea and crackles in heart failure can be managed with the plan of care, but pink, frothy sputum may indicate pulmonary edema. That turns the situation into an emergency: position upright, give oxygen, and get help.
questions.strategy: Two options treat worsening congestion. The deciding cue is pink, frothy sputum, which changes worsening heart failure into a likely emergency.

steps.detail: Pink, frothy sputum.
Possible pulmonary edema, a breathing emergency.
An early diuretic dose is right in direction but leaves the hypoxemia untreated now.
No fever is given, and 30 minutes is too long.

elimination.verdict: Raise to high Fowler's, increase oxygen as prescribed, and call the rapid response team.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure asks, "If my heart is weak, why are my pulse and blood pressure so high?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Your body speeds the heart, tightens vessels, and holds salt and water to keep blood moving. That helps for now but adds to your heart's work."
options.rationale: This matches the compensation in heart failure. Sympathetic activation raises the heart rate and causes vasoconstriction, and the renin angiotensin aldosterone system retains sodium and water. These responses help temporarily but increase workload and worsen the failure.

options.text: "The fast pulse and higher pressure show that your heart is getting stronger again, so the failure is starting to recover."
options.rationale: A faster rate and higher pressure are compensation for low output, not signs of recovery. The cool hands and feet and the weight gain show the heart is still not meeting the body's needs.

options.text: "Your body speeds the heart, tightens vessels, and holds salt and water to keep blood moving. Over time, that lowers the work your heart must do."
options.rationale: The mechanisms are named correctly, but the effect is reversed. Vasoconstriction and fluid retention add to the work of the heart, which is why these responses worsen heart failure over time.

options.text: "The high pressure comes from salt in your meals, and the fast pulse comes from worry about being in the hospital."
options.rationale: Diet and anxiety can raise these values, but this answer misses the body's own response to low output. It also misses why the weight is rising.

questions.takeaway: In heart failure, sympathetic activation raises the heart rate and constricts vessels, and the renin angiotensin aldosterone system retains sodium and water. These compensations help at first but increase the workload and worsen the failure.
questions.strategy: Two options name the same mechanisms. Read to the end of each and check which way the effect on the heart's workload goes.

steps.detail: Faster rate and vasoconstriction from sympathetic activation; sodium and water retention from the renin angiotensin aldosterone system.
The fast pulse and high pressure the client asks about are those compensations at work.
Both name the mechanisms; only one says they raise the workload.
Recovery and diet or worry do not explain a pattern of compensation.

elimination.verdict: The body compensates, and the compensation adds to the heart's work.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews findings documented for several clients admitted with heart failure.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate the mechanism of heart failure that best explains it.

rows.text: Sleeps sitting up in a recliner because lying flat causes shortness of breath
rows.rationale: Orthopnea comes from blood backing into the lungs in left sided failure. Lying flat shifts more fluid into the lungs.

rows.text: Urine output 90 mL over the past 4 hours
rows.rationale: Low output reduces blood flow to the kidneys, so urine output falls. This is a left sided finding of decreased cardiac output.

rows.text: Coughing up pink, frothy sputum
rows.rationale: Pink, frothy sputum may indicate pulmonary edema, the most severe form of fluid backing into the lungs.

rows.text: At 1400, oriented to person only; at 0800, was oriented to person, place, and time
rows.rationale: New confusion reflects reduced blood flow to the brain from low cardiac output.

rows.text: 2+ pitting edema over the sacrum after 2 days on bed rest
rows.rationale: Dependent edema forms where gravity pulls fluid. In a client in bed, the sacrum is the dependent area, and the backup is in the systemic veins.

rows.text: Ate 2 bites of each meal for 2 days because of nausea
rows.rationale: Anorexia and nausea come from congestion of the liver and gut as blood backs up into the systemic circulation in right sided failure.

questions.takeaway: Left sided failure shows two patterns: fluid in the lungs (orthopnea, frothy sputum, crackles) and low output (low urine output, confusion, cool extremities). Right sided failure shows systemic venous congestion (dependent edema, anorexia, nausea, ascites, JVD).
questions.strategy: Ask where each finding comes from: fluid in the lungs, too little blood reaching an organ, or blood pooling in the body's veins. Watch the kidney and gut findings, which are easy to misplace.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Orthopnea and pink, frothy sputum come from pulmonary congestion.
Low urine output and new confusion come from decreased cardiac output.
Sacral edema in a client in bed comes from systemic venous congestion.
Nausea and poor intake come from congestion of the liver and gut.

elimination.verdict: Pulmonary congestion; decreased cardiac output; pulmonary congestion; decreased cardiac output; systemic venous congestion; systemic venous congestion.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.stem: A client, 70 years old, has had severe chronic lung disease for 15 years and has slept on 3 pillows for the past 5 years because of it, with no change. Today: neck veins distended with the head of the bed at 45 degrees, 3+ pitting edema in both ankles, weight up 4 lb in 1 week, a distended abdomen, and nausea at meals. Breath sounds are diminished in both bases with no crackles. SpO2 89% on 2 L nasal cannula, the same as at the last 3 clinic visits. Which interpretation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: Left sided failure, because the low SpO2 and the 3 pillows show that blood has backed up into the lungs
options.rationale: Orthopnea and a low SpO2 can come from pulmonary congestion, but both have been unchanged for years and fit the lung disease. Backup into the lungs would add crackles, and there are none.

options.text: Failure of both sides, because the 3 pillows show pulmonary congestion along with the systemic findings
options.rationale: This is the tempting choice, since orthopnea is a left sided finding. The 3 pillows have been unchanged for 5 years, before any of the new findings, and the lungs have no crackles, so nothing new points to the left side.

options.text: Right sided failure, with blood backing up from the right ventricle into the lungs
options.rationale: Right sided failure is correct, but the direction is wrong. Blood that the right ventricle cannot move backs up into the systemic veins, not the lungs.

options.text: Right sided failure from the lung disease, with blood backing up into the systemic veins
options.rationale: Severe lung disease is a listed cause of heart failure and strains the right ventricle. Neck vein distention, ankle edema, weight gain, a distended abdomen, and nausea are systemic venous congestion findings, and they are the only new findings.

questions.takeaway: Right sided failure backs blood into the systemic circulation: JVD, dependent edema, weight gain, ascites, and anorexia or nausea. In a client with lung disease, judge left sided failure by what is new in the lungs, such as crackles, not by an orthopnea or SpO2 that has been the same for years.
questions.strategy: Two options agree on the systemic findings and differ only on whether the left side has failed too. Ask which lung findings are new. The 3 pillows and the SpO2 have not changed for years.

steps.detail: Neck veins, both ankles, abdomen, weight, and nausea: the systemic circulation.
3 pillows for 5 years and the same SpO2 at 3 visits: the lung disease, not new congestion.
None, so nothing new points to the left side.
Right sided backup goes to the systemic veins, not the lungs.

elimination.verdict: Right sided failure from the lung disease, with systemic backup.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.stem: A client, 74 years old, has dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, crackles in both lung bases, and 1+ pitting edema in both ankles. B type natriuretic peptide 640 pg/mL. Echocardiogram: ejection fraction 60%, with a thick, stiff left ventricle that fills slowly. The client's adult child says, "The heart is pumping out a normal amount, so this can't be heart failure." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "The pumping is normal and this is still heart failure, but the symptoms will be milder than with a weak heart."
options.rationale: The first half is right: heart failure can occur with a preserved ejection fraction. The second half is not. Both types produce similar symptoms, and this client already has orthopnea and crackles.

options.text: "This is heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction, because the ventricle cannot squeeze its blood out."
options.rationale: A contraction problem with an ejection fraction typically below 40% describes reduced ejection fraction. This ejection fraction is 60%, so the squeeze is not the problem.

options.text: "A normal pumping amount rules out heart failure, so the provider will look at the lungs as the cause."
options.rationale: This agrees with the misconception. A preserved ejection fraction does not rule out heart failure, and the high BNP points to ventricular stretch.

options.text: "It squeezes normally but is too stiff to fill well. That is heart failure, with similar symptoms."
options.rationale: The deciding cue is the stiff left ventricle that fills slowly with an ejection fraction of 60%. This is heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, a problem with relaxation and filling, and it produces symptoms similar to reduced ejection fraction.

questions.takeaway: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is a contraction problem, typically below 40%. Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction is a filling problem from a stiff ventricle, with the ejection fraction relatively preserved. Both produce similar symptoms.
questions.strategy: Two options correctly say this is heart failure with a normal ejection fraction. The stem's echocardiogram cue, a stiff ventricle that fills slowly, and the fact that both types share symptoms decide between them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Ejection fraction 60% with a thick, stiff left ventricle that fills slowly.
Preserved ejection fraction: a relaxation and filling problem.
It is heart failure, but symptoms are similar to reduced ejection fraction, not milder.
Reduced ejection fraction needs a contraction problem; a normal ejection fraction does not rule out failure.

elimination.verdict: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: a stiff ventricle with similar symptoms.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a client with chronic heart failure before discharge. Prescriptions include a diuretic, a beta blocker, and a 2 g sodium diet. Which statements by the client indicate understanding? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I'll read food labels and buy fewer canned foods to keep my sodium down."
options.rationale: A 2 g sodium diet means reading labels for sodium content and using few canned or prepared foods.

options.text: "I'll stop the beta blocker on any day my pulse feels slow."
options.rationale: Checking the pulse is right, but a beta blocker should not be stopped abruptly, because this raises the risk of worsening heart failure. A slow pulse is reported to the provider.

options.text: "I'll sit and rest after making the bed before I take my shower."
options.rationale: Balancing activity with rest reduces the heart's workload and keeps the client able to finish daily tasks.

options.text: "I'll skip the water pill on days my ankles look normal."
options.rationale: Medications are taken as prescribed. Normal looking ankles do not mean the excess fluid is gone, and skipped doses lead to fluid buildup.

options.text: "I'll call if I start waking up gasping for air or need more pillows to breathe."
options.rationale: New paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea or worsening orthopnea is a worsening symptom to report.

options.text: "I'll weigh myself every morning on the same scale, after I urinate and before I eat."
options.rationale: Daily weight at the same time, on the same scale, in similar clothing detects fluid gain early. A gain of 2 to 3 lb in 24 hours or 5 lb in 1 week is reported.

questions.takeaway: Heart failure teaching: limit sodium by reading labels and avoiding canned foods and added salt, including salt added at the table, weigh daily on the same scale, take every medication as prescribed without stopping or skipping, balance activity with rest, and report worsening symptoms such as new night dyspnea or more pillows to breathe.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Judge each statement on its own, without counting how many you have picked. Watch for the half right one: checking a pulse is a good idea paired with an unsafe action.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Labels and fewer canned foods meet the limit.
Every morning, same scale, after urinating and before eating.
Do not stop the beta blocker or skip the diuretic on your own.
Rest between tasks.
New night gasping or more pillows means worsening failure.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with hypertension for 20 years and a myocardial infarction 2 years ago is newly diagnosed with heart failure. The client asks, "Failure means my heart is going to stop. How did this happen?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Heart failure means one side of your heart has stopped working, so the other side now does all of the pumping."
options.rationale: Neither side has stopped. Heart failure means the heart cannot pump effectively enough to meet the body's needs; one or both sides can be affected.

options.text: "Your heart still beats but cannot pump enough to meet your body's needs. Years of high pressure and the heart attack both strained or damaged the muscle."
options.rationale: This defines heart failure correctly and names two of its listed causes: hypertension makes the heart pump against high resistance for years, and the infarction damaged part of the muscle.

options.text: "Your heart still beats but cannot pump enough to meet your body's needs. The heart attack caused it, since high pressure harms only the blood vessels."
options.rationale: The definition is correct, but hypertension is itself a leading cause of heart failure. Persistent high pressure leads to left ventricular hypertrophy and heart failure, not only vessel damage.

options.text: "Heart failure means fluid has built up in your lungs and legs, and it is caused by eating too much salt and drinking too much."
options.rationale: Fluid congestion is a result of heart failure, not its definition, and diet is not the cause named for this client. The history points to hypertension and the infarction.

questions.takeaway: Heart failure means the heart cannot pump effectively enough to meet the body's needs. Causes include hypertension, coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction, valve disease, cardiomyopathy, dysrhythmias, diabetes, obesity, and severe lung disease.
questions.strategy: Two options share the correct definition. Read on to the cause, and check it against both conditions in the history.

steps.detail: Heart failure is a pump that cannot meet the body's needs, not a heart that has stopped.
Neither side stops working in heart failure.

steps.action: Reject the result as the definition
steps.detail: Fluid buildup is a consequence, and diet is not the cause in this history.
Hypertension and the infarction are both causes; only one option keeps both.

elimination.verdict: The pump cannot meet the body's needs, and both hypertension and the infarction contributed.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.stem: A client with chronic heart failure started carvedilol 2 weeks ago and calls the clinic: "I have taken it every day for 2 weeks and I do not feel any better, so I am going to stop it." Which response by the nurse is appropriate?

options.text: "Stop it for now, and your provider can restart it at a lower dose when you come in next month."
options.rationale: Stopping a beta blocker abruptly raises the risk of decompensation, and only the prescriber changes the regimen.

options.text: "Take it only on days when your heart rate is above 70 beats per minute, so it does not slow you down."
options.rationale: The client's readings show no reason to hold it, and skipping doses by a self chosen rule breaks adherence and the steady blockade the drug depends on.

options.text: "Keep taking it as prescribed. Its benefit builds over months, and stopping it suddenly can worsen the failure."
options.rationale: In heart failure, beta blockers reverse the harm of long sympathetic stimulation, and the benefit appears over a long period rather than immediately. They are not stopped abruptly.

options.text: "Keep taking it as prescribed, and ask your provider to double the dose so that you start to feel the benefit sooner."
options.rationale: Continuing is right, but the dose is raised slowly by the provider, starting from a very low dose. Doubling it to speed the benefit risks bradycardia and hypotension.

questions.takeaway: Beta blockers for heart failure start at a very low dose, are raised slowly, take months to show benefit, and are never stopped abruptly. Monitor heart rate, blood pressure, and dizziness on standing.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options keep the drug going. The difference is who changes the dose and how fast; not feeling better yet is not a reason to change it.

steps.detail: Feeling no better at 2 weeks is expected; it is not an adverse effect to act on.
Abrupt stopping or self chosen skipping risks decompensation.
Both continue the drug; doubling the dose is not how beta blockers are titrated.
The benefit builds over months.

elimination.verdict: Keep taking it as prescribed; the benefit takes time, and it is not stopped suddenly.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure reports shortness of breath while lying with the head of the bed at 30 degrees. Respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 136/84 mm Hg, SpO2 95% on room air. Crackles are heard in both lung bases. Oxygen by nasal cannula is prescribed as needed for SpO2 below 92%. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to high Fowler's position and reassess the breathing
options.rationale: High Fowler's is the intervention for dyspnea in heart failure. Sitting upright lets the diaphragm descend, eases breathing, and reduces the blood returning to the congested lungs.

options.text: Apply oxygen at 2 L per minute by nasal cannula, because the client is short of breath
options.rationale: Oxygen in heart failure is for hypoxemia. The SpO2 is 95%, above the prescribed threshold of 92%, so the prescription does not apply now.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed flat so the client can rest and slow the breathing
options.rationale: Lying flat shifts more blood into the lungs and worsens the dyspnea; this is why clients with heart failure have orthopnea.

options.text: Elevate both legs on pillows while keeping the head of the bed at 30 degrees
options.rationale: Raising the legs returns more blood to the heart and lungs, which adds to the congestion, and it does nothing for the dyspnea.

questions.takeaway: In heart failure, high Fowler's position is for dyspnea and oxygen is for hypoxemia. A short of breath client with SpO2 above the prescribed threshold needs positioning, not oxygen.
questions.strategy: Match each treatment to the finding it treats. The SpO2 decides whether the oxygen prescription applies; the dyspnea decides the position.

steps.detail: 95%, above the prescribed threshold of 92%: the oxygen prescription does not apply.
High Fowler's position.
Lying flat worsens pulmonary congestion.
More venous return adds to the congestion.

elimination.verdict: Raise the client to high Fowler's position.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure reports nausea and has eaten half of each meal for 1 week. The client takes no digoxin. Neck veins are distended with the head of the bed at 45 degrees, and there is 2+ pitting edema in both ankles. Abdominal girth is 102 cm, was 96 cm 1 week ago, and the liver edge is felt below the right rib margin. Hands and feet are warm bilaterally, and urine output was 1500 mL over the last 24 hours. Blood pressure 132/80 mm Hg, heart rate 84 beats per minute. Which explanation of the nausea is most accurate?

options.text: Blood backing up into the systemic veins is congesting the liver and gut, causing the nausea and poor appetite.
options.rationale: The neck vein distention, ankle edema, growing girth, and enlarged liver are systemic venous congestion. Congestion of the liver and gut causes anorexia and nausea in right sided failure. Warm hands and feet and 1500 mL of urine show that blood flow to the organs is holding up.

options.text: Low cardiac output is reducing blood flow to the stomach and bowel, which causes the nausea and poor appetite.
options.rationale: Decreased cardiac output is a real cause of organ dysfunction in heart failure, which makes this tempting. Here the perfusion findings argue against it: hands and feet are warm and urine output is 1500 mL in 24 hours.

options.text: Fluid in the lungs is lowering the oxygen that reaches the stomach, which causes the nausea and poor appetite.
options.rationale: Pulmonary congestion produces dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, and cough. The stem describes no lung findings, and the gut findings follow the systemic veins.

options.text: The sodium restriction is making food taste bland, which is the main reason the client eats less.
options.rationale: A bland diet may lower appetite, but it does not explain a growing girth, an enlarged liver, and distended neck veins, which point to venous congestion.

questions.takeaway: In right sided failure, blood backs up into the systemic veins: neck vein distention, dependent edema, ascites, an enlarged liver, and anorexia and nausea from liver and gut congestion. Low output shows up as cool extremities, low urine output, and confusion.
questions.strategy: Two options blame the heart for the nausea. Check the perfusion findings: warm hands and feet and a normal urine output mean blood is reaching the organs, so the cause is congestion, not low output.

steps.detail: Neck veins, ankle edema, girth, and liver all point to systemic venous congestion.
Warm hands and feet and 1500 mL of urine in 24 hours argue against low cardiac output.
No lung findings are described.
Diet does not explain the liver and girth changes.

elimination.verdict: Liver and gut congestion from right sided failure; perfusion findings are intact.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure has received a prescribed intravenous diuretic for 3 days. Weight is 6 lb lower than on admission on the same scale. Crackles are no longer heard in either lung base, and there is no edema in either ankle. Serum creatinine is 2.1 mg/dL today, was 1.1 mg/dL on admission. Blood urea nitrogen is 48 mg/dL today, was 22 mg/dL on admission. The next diuretic dose is due at 1000. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Documents that the diuretic is meeting its goal of removing fluid, and gives the 1000 dose as prescribed.
options.rationale: Clear lungs, no ankle edema, and 6 lb of weight loss do show that congestion has been relieved, which makes this tempting. It ignores the creatinine, which has nearly doubled since admission.

options.text: Requests a larger diuretic dose, because rising creatinine and blood urea nitrogen show fluid overload is worsening.
options.rationale: Every congestion finding has resolved, so fluid overload is not worsening. A larger dose would remove more fluid and reduce kidney perfusion further.

options.text: Reports the creatinine and blood urea nitrogen trend to the provider before giving the 1000 dose.
options.rationale: The deciding cue is the creatinine, 2.1 mg/dL now and 1.1 mg/dL on admission, with a rising blood urea nitrogen. Impaired kidney perfusion raises both values. With the congestion already relieved, the provider needs this before more fluid is removed.

options.text: Encourages 3 L of oral fluid today to protect the kidneys, and gives the 1000 dose as prescribed.
options.rationale: Pushing fluids in a client with heart failure is not an independent nursing decision and works against the treatment plan. The rising values need to reach the provider.

questions.takeaway: Electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, and creatinine are monitored in heart failure. Poor kidney perfusion raises blood urea nitrogen and creatinine, so a rising creatinine during diuresis is reported even when the lungs and ankles are clear.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options read the trend: one sees the clear lungs and gives the dose, the other sees the creatinine. A value that nearly doubled since admission decides it.

steps.detail: Clear lungs, no edema, and weight loss show the fluid goal has been met.
Creatinine rose from 1.1 to 2.1 mg/dL and blood urea nitrogen from 22 to 48 mg/dL since admission.
Overload is not worsening; more fluid removal lowers kidney perfusion.
This is not an independent action in heart failure.

elimination.verdict: Report the rising creatinine and blood urea nitrogen before the next dose.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: The nurse takes a health history from a client with new signs of heart failure. Which conditions in the history can lead to heart failure? Select all that apply.

options.text: A narrowed aortic valve found on an echocardiogram 2 years ago
options.rationale: Valvular disease makes the ventricle pump against a narrowed outlet, which overloads the heart and can lead to heart failure.

options.text: Osteoarthritis of both knees for 10 years
options.rationale: Osteoarthritis limits activity but is not a cause of heart failure.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation for 5 years
options.rationale: Dysrhythmias reduce effective filling and pumping and are a cause of heart failure.

options.text: Type 2 diabetes for 12 years
options.rationale: Diabetes damages the heart muscle and vessels over time and is a cause of heart failure.

options.text: Seasonal allergies treated with a nasal spray
options.rationale: Seasonal allergies do not strain or damage the heart.

options.text: Body mass index 38 kg/m2
options.rationale: Obesity increases the heart's workload and is a cause of heart failure.

questions.takeaway: Causes of heart failure include hypertension, coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, dysrhythmias, diabetes, obesity and severe lung disease. Heart failure is a common cause of hospitalization in older adults, so the history looks for these conditions.
questions.strategy: Ask of each condition whether it overloads, damages or disturbs the rhythm of the heart. If it does none of these, it does not lead to heart failure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A narrowed valve and obesity raise the heart's work.
Diabetes damages the muscle; atrial fibrillation disturbs filling and pumping.
Osteoarthritis and seasonal allergies do not affect the heart.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, F.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure reports getting up 3 times each night to urinate for 2 weeks and denies waking short of breath. The client takes a diuretic at 0800. Lungs are clear in both bases. There is 2+ pitting edema in both ankles, the neck veins are distended with the head of the bed at 45 degrees, and weight is up 3 lb in 1 week on the same scale. Daytime urine output is 600 mL over 12 hours. Which interpretation of the night urination is correct?

options.text: Decreased cardiac output from left sided failure lowering kidney blood flow
options.rationale: Decreased cardiac output in left sided failure lowers urine output; it does not cause frequent urination at night. It is the right idea of reduced kidney flow applied to the wrong finding.

options.text: Pulmonary congestion from left sided failure waking the client at night
options.rationale: Pulmonary congestion wakes clients with paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. This client denies waking short of breath, and the lungs are clear.

options.text: An expected effect of the 0800 diuretic that needs no further follow up
options.rationale: A diuretic removes excess fluid, but a dose at 0800 does not explain waking 3 times a night. Treating nocturia as expected would miss a sign of congestion.

options.text: A finding of systemic venous congestion, like the edema and neck veins
options.rationale: Nocturia is a right sided finding of systemic venous congestion, along with dependent edema, neck vein distention and weight gain. All of these are present.

questions.takeaway: Right sided failure backs blood into the systemic circulation: peripheral and dependent edema, neck vein distention, weight gain, ascites, hepatomegaly, anorexia and nausea, and nocturia. Left sided failure causes pulmonary congestion and decreased cardiac output. Fluid that pools in the legs by day returns to the circulation when the client lies down, which is why the urine comes at night.
questions.strategy: Group the findings first. The edema, neck veins and weight gain make a right sided cluster, and nocturia belongs with them.

steps.detail: No waking short of breath; lungs clear.
The diuretic is taken at 0800.
Edema, neck vein distention and weight gain are systemic venous congestion, and so is nocturia.

elimination.verdict: D. Systemic venous congestion.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.stem: A client with hypertension eats canned soup or takeout most days and asks, "How can salt make my blood pressure go up?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Sodium makes your body hold on to water, so blood volume rises and your heart pushes out more blood with each beat."
options.rationale: Sodium and water retention raise blood volume. More volume raises the amount pumped with each beat, so cardiac output and blood pressure rise.

options.text: "Sodium tightens the walls of your small arteries, so resistance rises while the amount of blood in your vessels stays the same."
options.rationale: Resistance is a real part of the equation, but the sodium mechanism is sodium and water retention, which raises volume. Volume does not stay the same.

options.text: "Sodium triggers the pressure sensors in your neck, and they answer by speeding up your heart and tightening your vessels."
options.rationale: The baroreceptors sense changes in arterial pressure. They do not respond to sodium, and they do not cause the rise.

options.text: "Sodium speeds up your heart rate, so your cardiac output rises even though your blood volume does not change."
options.rationale: Heart rate is part of cardiac output, but sodium retention works through volume, not through heart rate.

questions.takeaway: Blood pressure equals cardiac output times peripheral vascular resistance, and cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume. Sodium and water retention raise blood volume, and more volume raises the pressure.
questions.strategy: Run every option through the equation. Anything that raises heart rate, stroke volume, resistance or volume raises pressure. Anything that lowers them lowers pressure.

steps.detail: The sodium mechanism is sodium and water retention, which raises volume.
It names a real part of the equation, but it is not the sodium mechanism, and it says volume stays the same.
Sodium retention works through volume, not through heart rate.
Baroreceptors sense pressure changes. They do not cause the rise.

elimination.verdict: Sodium makes the body keep water, which raises blood volume and the output of each beat.

questions.objective: Explain the basic mechanisms that regulate blood pressure and contribute to hypertension.

questions.stem: A client with newly diagnosed hypertension asks how the body controls blood pressure. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: Pressure equals cardiac output times peripheral vascular resistance; the renin angiotensin aldosterone system constricts vessels without changing sodium and water balance; baroreceptors keep organ flow steady
options.rationale: Two errors. The renin angiotensin aldosterone system also makes the body keep sodium and water, and keeping organ flow steady is vascular autoregulation, not the baroreceptors.

options.text: Pressure equals cardiac output times stroke volume; the renin angiotensin aldosterone system constricts vessels and holds sodium and water; baroreceptors keep organ flow steady
options.rationale: Two errors. Stroke volume sits inside cardiac output; the second term of the pressure equation is peripheral vascular resistance. Keeping organ flow steady is vascular autoregulation, not the baroreceptors.

options.text: Pressure equals cardiac output times peripheral vascular resistance; the renin angiotensin aldosterone system constricts vessels and holds sodium and water; baroreceptors sense changes in arterial pressure
options.rationale: Blood pressure equals cardiac output times peripheral vascular resistance. The renin angiotensin aldosterone system raises pressure two ways, by vasoconstriction and by sodium and water retention. Baroreceptors sense changes in arterial pressure.

options.text: Pressure equals cardiac output times stroke volume; the renin angiotensin aldosterone system constricts vessels without changing sodium and water balance; baroreceptors sense changes in arterial pressure
options.rationale: Two errors. Stroke volume sits inside cardiac output; the second term is peripheral vascular resistance. The renin angiotensin aldosterone system also makes the body keep sodium and water.

questions.takeaway: Four systems regulate blood pressure: baroreceptors sense changes in arterial pressure, fluid volume regulation raises pressure through sodium and water retention, the renin angiotensin aldosterone system causes vasoconstriction plus sodium and water retention, and vascular autoregulation maintains tissue perfusion.
questions.strategy: Each distractor borrows a real term from a different control system or from the cardiac output equation. Read each option in three parts and judge each part on its own.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cardiac output times resistance. Stroke volume sits inside cardiac output. Eliminate B and D.
Constriction plus retention. Eliminate A, which keeps only half.
Sensing pressure is the baroreceptors; steady organ flow is autoregulation. C remains.

elimination.verdict: C. Cardiac output times peripheral vascular resistance; constriction plus sodium and water retention; baroreceptors sense changes in arterial pressure.

questions.objective: Explain the basic mechanisms that regulate blood pressure and contribute to hypertension.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the records of six clients who were newly found to have hypertension at a clinic. None of the clients takes a diuretic. Which clients have findings that point to secondary hypertension? Select all that apply.

options.text: Blood pressure 146/92 mm Hg, smokes 1 pack a day, a parent with hypertension, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL
options.rationale: Smoking and family history are risk factors for primary hypertension, and the labs within range show no sign of another disease.

options.text: Blood pressure 158/96 mm Hg, age 44 years, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, potassium 3.0 mEq/L
options.rationale: High pressure with low potassium and no diuretic, even with a creatinine in range, suggests primary aldosteronism, a secondary cause. The word primary in its name refers to the adrenal problem, not to the type of hypertension.

options.text: Episodes of blood pressure 172/104 mm Hg with a heart rate of 128 beats per minute, sweating and pallor
options.rationale: Fast heart rate, sweating and pallor with high pressure suggest a pheochromocytoma, an adrenal tumor that releases catecholamines.

options.text: Blood pressure 150/94 mm Hg, body mass index 33 kg/m2, a high stress job, urinalysis negative for protein and red blood cells
options.rationale: Obesity and stress are risk factors for primary hypertension. The negative urinalysis gives no sign of kidney disease.

options.text: Blood pressure 168/100 mm Hg, age 38 years, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, a bruit heard over the abdomen
options.rationale: The potassium is in range, but an abdominal bruit is typical of renal artery stenosis, a kidney cause of secondary hypertension.

options.text: Blood pressure 144/90 mm Hg, age 66 years, eats processed food daily, potassium 4.4 mEq/L, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL
options.rationale: Increasing age and high sodium intake are risk factors for primary hypertension, and the labs are within range.

questions.takeaway: Primary hypertension has risk factors but no causing disease. High pressure with low potassium, an abdominal bruit, or a fast pulse with sweating and pallor points to a secondary cause: primary aldosteronism, renal artery stenosis or pheochromocytoma.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Risk factors with labs inside the reference ranges point to primary hypertension. A finding that points to a disease process points to secondary hypertension. Do not let the word primary in primary aldosteronism decide the option.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Smoking, family history, obesity, stress, age and sodium with no finding of another disease: primary.
Low potassium, abdominal bruit, fast pulse with sweating and pallor: secondary.
Primary aldosteronism causes secondary hypertension.

elimination.verdict: B, C, E.

questions.objective: Differentiate primary and secondary hypertension and identify major risk factors.

questions.stem: A client, 34 years old, has blood pressure 150/96 mm Hg in the right arm and 148/94 mm Hg in the left arm at two clinic visits 1 week apart. At an annual visit 1 year ago, it was 116/74 mm Hg. A parent has hypertension. Body mass index is 23 kg/m2. The client does not smoke and walks daily. Three months ago, a provider started a daily oral glucocorticoid for an inflammatory bowel condition. Which statement by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: "Your glucocorticoid may be raising your pressure, so your provider may review it before adding a blood pressure drug."
options.rationale: Glucocorticoids are a drug cause of secondary hypertension. The rise began after the drug was started, and a drug that causes hypertension is stopped or changed to reverse it.

options.text: "A parent with hypertension makes primary hypertension the likely cause, so lifestyle change and a first line drug are the usual next steps."
options.rationale: Family history is a real risk factor, but it does not explain a normal reading 1 year ago followed by a rise after a new drug.

options.text: "A new rise at your age can come from kidney disease, so a urine test for protein is the first step in finding the cause."
options.rationale: Kidney disease is a common secondary cause, but the stem gives no kidney finding, while it does give a new drug that raises pressure.

options.text: "Pressure often runs higher at clinic visits, so home readings should come before anyone looks for a cause."
options.rationale: Visit anxiety can raise a reading, but the stem gives no anxiety cue, and anxiety does not explain a rise that began after a new drug.

questions.takeaway: Secondary hypertension is caused by another condition or a medication, and glucocorticoids are one of those medications. When pressure rises soon after such a drug is started, think secondary first, because stopping or changing the drug can reverse it.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Both the family history and the drug are real, but only one explains the timing. Ask what changed between the normal reading 1 year ago and today.

steps.detail: Normal 1 year ago, a new glucocorticoid 3 months ago, high now.
A real risk factor, but it does not explain a new rise after a new drug.
No kidney finding is given.
No anxiety cue is given, and anxiety does not explain a rise that began after a new drug.

elimination.verdict: The glucocorticoid is a likely secondary cause, and the drug may be reviewed first.

questions.objective: Differentiate primary and secondary hypertension and identify major risk factors.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the risk factors of a client with elevated blood pressure. Which risk factors can the nurse target with teaching because the client can change them? Select all that apply.

options.text: Smoking 1 pack of cigarettes a day
options.rationale: Smoking is a modifiable risk factor.

options.text: Drinking 4 beers most evenings
options.rationale: Excessive alcohol is a modifiable risk factor.

options.text: Low density lipoprotein level of 172 mg/dL
options.rationale: Hyperlipidemia is a modifiable risk factor. The level is above the reference of below 100 mg/dL.

options.text: Constant stress from caregiving
options.rationale: Chronic stress is a modifiable risk factor that stress management can address.

options.text: Population related risk for hypertension
options.rationale: Population related risk is a nonmodifiable risk factor. Lifestyle change lowers overall risk but does not change this one.

options.text: Hypertension in a parent and a sibling
options.rationale: Family history is a nonmodifiable risk factor.

questions.takeaway: Modifiable risk factors are high sodium intake, overweight or obesity, physical inactivity, smoking, excessive alcohol, chronic stress and hyperlipidemia. Family history, increasing age and population related risks cannot be changed.
questions.strategy: Ask of each option whether the client could change it starting today. Population related risk sounds like lifestyle, but it cannot be changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Smoking and alcohol: modifiable.

steps.action: Check the lab and the stressor
steps.detail: Hyperlipidemia and chronic stress: modifiable.
Family history and population related risk: nonmodifiable.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Differentiate primary and secondary hypertension and identify major risk factors.

questions.nursesNote: 0915. Client, 58 years old, at a first clinic visit for hypertension screening. Seated 5 minutes with feet flat. Blood pressure 152/96 mm Hg in the right arm using a standard adult cuff; right upper arm circumference 42 cm, above the cuff's labeled range. Left arm not measured. One reading recorded for the visit. Heart rate 78 beats per minute. Reports blurred vision in both eyes for 2 days. Denies headache. Takes an over the counter drug for allergies daily but cannot name it. Normal blood pressure reference: below 120/80 mm Hg.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow up by the nurse.

segments.text: Seated 5 minutes with feet flat
segments.rationale: Resting seated before the reading is correct technique.

segments.text: using a standard adult cuff; right upper arm circumference 42 cm, above the cuff's labeled range
segments.rationale: Accurate measurement requires the correct cuff size. A cuff too small for the arm gives an inaccurate reading, so the reading must be repeated with a larger cuff.

segments.text: Left arm not measured
segments.rationale: Blood pressure is compared in both arms at the first visit.

segments.text: One reading recorded for the visit
segments.rationale: Repeat readings are part of accurate measurement. One reading is not enough.

segments.text: Heart rate 78 beats per minute
segments.rationale: The heart rate is within the reference range of 60 to 100 beats per minute.

segments.text: Reports blurred vision in both eyes for 2 days
segments.rationale: Blurred vision can occur with significantly elevated pressure and needs follow up.

segments.text: Denies headache
segments.rationale: Most clients with hypertension have no symptoms. The absence of headache needs no action, though it does not mean the pressure is controlled.

segments.text: Takes an over the counter drug for allergies daily but cannot name it
segments.rationale: Reviewing medications is a priority assessment, because certain medications can cause secondary hypertension. The drug must be identified.

questions.takeaway: Accurate measurement means the correct cuff size, repeat readings, and both arms compared at the first visit. Review every medication, including over the counter drugs, and follow up on symptoms such as blurred vision.
questions.strategy: Read each line against two checklists: how the pressure was measured, and what the history must include. Highlight what breaks a rule or signals a symptom.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Seated rest is right. The cuff too small for the arm, one arm only and one reading are not.
Blurred vision needs follow up. No headache does not.
An unnamed daily drug must be identified.

questions.objective: Recognize common manifestations, complications, and priority nursing assessments for hypertension.

questions.stem: A client, 74 years old, started an antihypertensive drug 2 days ago. The nurse measures orthostatic blood pressure. Lying: 134/82 mm Hg with a heart rate of 72 beats per minute. Standing, 3 minutes later: 110/76 mm Hg with a heart rate of 88 beats per minute. The client says, "I feel a little lightheaded." Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document an expected effect of starting a new antihypertensive and teach the client to rise slowly
options.rationale: Orthostatic drops do occur with new antihypertensives, and rising slowly is good teaching. But a systolic fall of 24 mm Hg, more than 20 mm Hg, with lightheadedness is reported, not just taught.

options.text: Keep the client standing 2 more minutes, then recheck to confirm the drop
options.rationale: The drop is already confirmed, and keeping a lightheaded client standing risks a fall.

options.text: Help the client sit down, stay at the bedside, and report the orthostatic drop
options.rationale: A systolic drop of 24 mm Hg is orthostatic hypotension. The client is lightheaded, so safety comes first, and the finding is reported.

options.text: Have the client lie down and recheck lying and standing pressures in 15 minutes before reporting
options.rationale: Lying down is safe, but the drop is already measured and meets the criterion. Delaying the report adds nothing.

questions.takeaway: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop of 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic on standing, measured at least 3 minutes after the client stands. Antihypertensives can cause it, so protect the client from a fall and report it.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Calculate both drops before reading the options: systolic 24 mm Hg, diastolic 6 mm Hg. The criterion is either one, not both.

steps.detail: 134 minus 110 is 24 mm Hg systolic.
20 mm Hg systolic alone is enough.
A drop after a new drug that is more than 20 mm Hg systolic and causes symptoms is reported, not just taught.
A lightheaded client sits down before anything else.

elimination.verdict: Help the client sit, stay at the bedside, and report the orthostatic drop.

questions.objective: Recognize common manifestations, complications, and priority nursing assessments for hypertension.

questions.stem: A client, 47 years old, is at a fourth clinic visit for possible hypertension. Both arms were compared at the first visit and differed by 2 mm Hg. Today, after 5 minutes of seated rest and with a cuff sized to the arm, two readings in the right arm are 152/96 and 150/94 mm Hg. Readings at the first three visits were in the same range. The client says, "My heart races every time I come here," and shows a log of home readings from the past 2 weeks averaging 122/76 mm Hg. At the second visit, the home monitor read within 2 mm Hg of the clinic device. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: Repeat the reading in both arms now, after 5 more minutes of quiet rest
options.rationale: Repeat readings and comparing arms are correct technique, but both have already been done. Another clinic reading under the same conditions cannot resolve a clinic and home difference.

options.text: Teach that four visits of high readings confirm hypertension, and review the first line drug classes
options.rationale: The clinic readings are consistent, but home readings from a device checked against the clinic device run lower, and that difference has not been resolved.

options.text: Tell the client the home readings are normal, and continue home monitoring
options.rationale: An average of 122/76 mm Hg is not normal. Normal is below 120/80 mm Hg, so the home log does not settle the question.

options.text: Recommend 24 hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring
options.rationale: Clinic readings stay high while verified home readings run lower, and the client reports anxiety at visits. A 24 hour ambulatory monitor shows the true pressure throughout the day.

questions.takeaway: When clinic readings stay high but home readings run lower, anxiety at the visit may be raising the pressure. A 24 hour ambulatory monitor, reading every 15 to 30 minutes during daily activity, gives the true picture.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Four visits of high clinic readings make confirming hypertension tempting. The deciding cue is that home readings from a device checked against the clinic device average 122/76 mm Hg.

steps.detail: Both arms compared, two readings today, a verified home monitor.
Clinic high, home lower, anxiety at visits.
122/76 mm Hg is above normal, so reassurance is wrong.
An ambulatory monitor answers the clinic and home question.

elimination.verdict: Recommend 24 hour ambulatory monitoring.

questions.objective: Recognize common manifestations, complications, and priority nursing assessments for hypertension.

questions.stem: After lifestyle teaching for hypertension, which statements by the client indicate understanding? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I will choose lower sodium foods in place of the takeout I eat most nights."
options.rationale: Reducing sodium is a core lifestyle change.

options.text: "I will eat more fruits, vegetables and low fat dairy foods."
options.rationale: This describes DASH style eating: fruits, vegetables and low fat dairy.

options.text: "Eating fewer calories and moving more can bring my weight and my pressure down."
options.rationale: Weight reduction combines fewer calories with more activity, and the body mass index of 31 kg/m2 makes it indicated.

options.text: "I am switching from cigarettes to chewing tobacco so I still get the nicotine."
options.rationale: Stopping smoking is right, but the goal is to stop all tobacco, not to change the form.

options.text: "I will cut out dairy foods completely to lower my fat intake."
options.rationale: DASH style eating includes low fat dairy. Cutting out dairy removes a food group the plan keeps.

options.text: "I will practice a relaxation exercise when my work gets stressful."
options.rationale: Managing stress is one of the lifestyle changes.

questions.takeaway: Lifestyle changes for hypertension: reduce sodium, DASH style eating, weight reduction if indicated, more activity, stop smoking, limit alcohol and manage stress. They continue for life.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Look for statements that have the right goal with one thing off, such as switching tobacco forms or cutting out a food group the DASH plan keeps.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lower sodium and DASH style eating are correct.
Fewer calories plus activity, and relaxation: correct.
Chewing tobacco is still tobacco.
DASH keeps low fat dairy. Cutting it out is an error.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, F.

questions.objective: Describe lifestyle changes and common medication classes used to manage hypertension.

questions.stem: A client with hypertension is due for a scheduled dose of lisinopril at 0900. At 0845, the blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg in the right arm and 94/56 mm Hg in the left arm, and the heart rate is 82 beats per minute. The client reports no dizziness. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the dose as scheduled, because the client has no dizziness and the heart rate is in range
options.rationale: The absence of dizziness does not make the dose safe. The decision for an ACE inhibitor rests on the systolic pressure, and it is below 100 mm Hg.

options.text: Hold the dose and check with the provider before giving it, because the systolic is below 100 mm Hg
options.rationale: An ACE inhibitor is not given without checking with the provider when the systolic pressure is below 100 mm Hg, because the drug causes vasodilation and lowers pressure further.

options.text: Give the dose and recheck the pressure in 1 hour, because lisinopril does not slow the heart rate
options.rationale: Rechecking after a dose is reasonable practice, but the systolic pressure is already below 100 mm Hg, so the dose needs the provider's input first.

options.text: Hold the dose, document it as held, and recheck the pressure before the next scheduled dose
options.rationale: Holding is right, but holding without telling the provider leaves the plan unchanged. The guideline is to check with the provider.

questions.takeaway: Before an ACE inhibitor such as lisinopril, check the blood pressure. If the systolic is below 100 mm Hg, check with the provider before giving it. Also monitor orthostatic pressures and potassium.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options hold the dose and two give it. Of the two that hold, pick the one that brings in the provider rather than managing the dose alone.

steps.detail: Systolic 96 and 94 mm Hg, both below 100 mm Hg.
No dizziness and a normal heart rate do not override the pressure.
Holding without telling the provider leaves the plan unchanged. The guideline is to check with the provider.

elimination.verdict: Hold the dose and check with the provider.

questions.objective: Describe lifestyle changes and common medication classes used to manage hypertension.

questions.stem: A client, 58 years old, has taken a thiazide diuretic for hypertension for 3 months. The pharmacy refill record and today's pill count show every dose taken. Home readings in the right arm average 144/90 mm Hg with a cuff sized to the arm, and the clinic device reads within 2 mm Hg of the home monitor. Lying and standing pressures differ by 4 mm Hg, potassium is 4.0 mEq/L, and the client reports no dizziness. The provider adds an ACE inhibitor. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: Before teaching about the new drug, ask the client to bring all pill bottles to the next visit so adherence can be checked
options.rationale: Checking adherence before adding a drug is a sound habit, but the refill record and today's pill count already show every dose taken. Checking again delays teaching for the prescribed plan while the pressure stays above goal.

options.text: Reinforce that many clients need 2 or more drugs, and teach the client to take both as prescribed and keep the log
options.rationale: Adherence is confirmed and the readings are accurate, so the regimen itself needs a second drug. Many clients need 2 or more drugs, and the nurse reinforces adherence and ongoing monitoring.

options.text: Teach the client that the diuretic has not worked and will be stopped now that the ACE inhibitor is added
options.rationale: The provider added a drug; nothing in the stem stops the diuretic. Two drugs that act by different mechanisms are often used together.

options.text: Teach the client to take the ACE inhibitor only on days when the home reading is above goal
options.rationale: Antihypertensives are taken as prescribed every day. Dosing by a single reading breaks adherence and lets the pressure swing.

questions.takeaway: Nursing care for antihypertensives: monitor the pressure and orthostatic changes, assess each drug's adverse effects, and reinforce adherence. When adherence and accurate measurement are confirmed and the pressure is still above goal, a second drug is expected, since many clients need 2 or more.
questions.strategy: Two options are good nursing instincts: confirm adherence first, or support the new drug. The deciding cue is that adherence is already confirmed by the refill record and pill count.

steps.detail: Refill record and pill count show every dose: confirmed, so checking again delays the prescribed plan.
Cuff sized to the arm, home and clinic devices within 2 mm Hg: the readings are real.
No orthostatic drop, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, no dizziness: nothing to hold for.
Reinforce the 2 drug regimen and home monitoring; reject delay, stopping the diuretic, and dosing by readings.

elimination.verdict: B. Reinforce that 2 or more drugs are often needed and teach adherence to both.

questions.objective: Describe lifestyle changes and common medication classes used to manage hypertension.

questions.scenario: A client, 58 years old, comes to an urgent care clinic with a severe headache, 8 of 10, and blurred vision. The client stopped all blood pressure drugs 2 weeks ago because of cost. Blood pressure 206/124 mm Hg in the right arm and 202/122 mm Hg in the left arm, heart rate 104 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 91% on room air. The client is alert and oriented, hand grasps are equal, and speech is clear.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Give a prescribed intravenous antihypertensive as a rapid push to reach 140/90 mm Hg
options.rationale: Intravenous antihypertensives are a priority, but a rapid drop lowers the pressure too fast and can cause cerebral ischemia, myocardial infarction or kidney injury.

options.text: Give the stopped oral drug to bring the pressure below 130/80 mm Hg within 1 hour
options.rationale: The pressure must be lowered gradually. Too rapid lowering can decrease perfusion and cause cerebral ischemia, myocardial infarction or kidney injury.

options.text: Apply oxygen as indicated by the saturation
options.rationale: Oxygen is given as indicated. The saturation of 91% is below the reference of 95 to 100%.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids to protect blood flow to the kidneys
options.rationale: More fluid raises blood volume, which raises pressure. Kidney perfusion is protected by gradual lowering, not by fluids.

options.text: Measure the blood pressure at frequent intervals
options.rationale: Frequent blood pressure monitoring is a priority in hypertensive crisis.

options.text: Hypertensive crisis
options.rationale: A pressure of 180/120 mm Hg or higher with severe headache and blurred vision is a hypertensive crisis.

options.text: Orthostatic hypotension
options.rationale: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in pressure on standing. This pressure is extremely high.

options.text: Stage 2 hypertension
options.rationale: Stage 2 starts at 140/90 mm Hg, but this client's pressure is above 180/120 mm Hg and the client has symptoms.

options.text: Acute stroke
options.rationale: Stroke is a complication to watch for, but the client is alert and oriented, with equal grasps and clear speech.

options.text: Neurologic status, such as limb weakness, numbness or speech changes
options.rationale: Neurologic changes can signal a stroke, a target organ complication of the crisis.

options.text: Blood glucose before each meal
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem points to a glucose problem.

options.text: Weight each morning
options.rationale: Daily weight tracks fluid over days. It does not catch the acute complications of a crisis.

options.text: Chest pain and heart rhythm
options.rationale: Cardiovascular status is assessed because the heart is a target organ.

options.text: Capillary refill in the toes
options.rationale: This is a peripheral perfusion check. The crisis threatens the brain, heart and kidneys.

questions.takeaway: Hypertensive crisis is a pressure of 180/120 mm Hg or higher, often with severe headache, blurred vision, dyspnea, chest pain or neurologic changes. Priorities: frequent pressure checks, neurologic and cardiovascular assessment, oxygen as indicated, and prescribed intravenous antihypertensives that lower the pressure gradually.
questions.strategy: Separate what treats the crisis now from what belongs to a routine visit. Any option that lowers the pressure fast is the trap, because gradual lowering protects perfusion.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 206/124 mm Hg with severe headache and blurred vision.
Oxygen for 91% and frequent pressure checks.
Below 130/80 mm Hg in 1 hour is too fast.
Neurologic and cardiovascular status for target organ damage.

elimination.verdict: Oxygen and frequent pressure checks; hypertensive crisis; neurologic status and chest pain with heart rhythm.

questions.objective: Recognize common manifestations, complications, and priority nursing assessments for hypertension.

questions.stem: A client in critical care with hypertensive crisis has a blood pressure of 220/124 mm Hg when a prescribed intravenous antihypertensive is started at 1000. The client has no condition that requires faster lowering. The nurse measures the blood pressure every 5 to 15 minutes. Which reading at 1100 shows the systolic pressure lowered within the recommended limit for the first hour?

options.text: 150/96 mm Hg
options.rationale: Systolic fell 70 mm Hg, about 32%. That is more than 25% in the first hour and risks cerebral ischemia, myocardial infarction and kidney injury.
Systolic fell 52 mm Hg, about 24%. That stays within the limit of no more than 25% in the first hour.
160/100 mm Hg is the target for the next 2 to 6 hours, not the first hour. From 220 mm Hg, it is a drop of about 27%, more than 25%.

options.text: 140/90 mm Hg
options.rationale: Systolic fell 80 mm Hg, about 36%. Lowering this fast decreases perfusion to organs used to a high pressure.

questions.takeaway: In hypertensive crisis, lower the systolic pressure by no more than 25% in the first hour, then to about 160/100 mm Hg over the next 2 to 6 hours, then cautiously to normal over the next 24 to 48 hours. Too rapid lowering can cause cerebral ischemia, myocardial infarction and kidney injury.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The familiar number 160/100 mm Hg pulls you, but it belongs to hours 2 to 6. The cue is first hour: calculate 25% of the starting systolic.

steps.detail: 25% of 220 is 55, so systolic should not fall below 165 mm Hg in the first hour.
Above 165 mm Hg: within the limit.
Below 165 mm Hg: the right number at the wrong time.
150 and 140 mm Hg are far too fast.

questions.objective: Recognize common manifestations, complications, and priority nursing assessments for hypertension.

questions.stem: A client, 59 years old, has type 2 diabetes and smokes 1 pack a day. Coronary CT angiography shows a fibrous plaque narrowing one coronary artery. The client walks 3 km each morning with no chest pressure, dyspnea or fatigue. During an exercise stress test, the client reaches the target heart rate of 142 beats per minute with no chest pressure and no ECG signs of ischemia. The client asks how far the disease has progressed. Which description by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Endothelial injury from diabetes and smoking has begun, but no plaque has formed in the wall yet
options.rationale: Diabetes and smoking do injure the endothelium, but the scan already shows a fibrous plaque, so the process is past the first step.

options.text: A fatty streak has formed in the wall but has not yet become a fibrous plaque that narrows the artery
options.rationale: The fatty streak comes before the fibrous plaque. The scan shows a fibrous plaque that already narrows the artery, so this stage has passed.

options.text: The plaque narrows the artery, but supply still meets demand at peak exertion, so there is no ischemia
options.rationale: Narrowing restricts flow, but ischemia begins only when oxygen delivery falls short of demand. Reaching the target heart rate with no chest pressure and no ECG signs of ischemia shows the narrowed artery still meets demand.

options.text: Silent ischemia is present, since some clients have ischemia with no chest pressure or any other symptoms
options.rationale: Silent ischemia is real, and diabetes makes it tempting here. But the stress test found no ECG signs of ischemia at the target heart rate, so there is no ischemia, silent or otherwise, to explain.

questions.takeaway: Atherosclerosis moves through endothelial injury, plaque formation (fatty streak, then fibrous plaque), coronary narrowing, and then ischemia when reduced oxygen delivery falls short of the heart's demand. A plaque can narrow an artery before it causes ischemia; ischemia is defined by the shortfall, not by the plaque.
questions.strategy: Two later stages are defensible: narrowing, and silent ischemia. Silent ischemia is possible in any client, so look for the finding that tests the shortfall directly: the stress test at peak exertion.

steps.detail: A fibrous plaque that narrows the artery: past injury and past the fatty streak. Eliminate A and B.
No symptoms alone would not rule it out.
At the target heart rate of 142 beats per minute, no ECG signs of ischemia: supply still meets demand.
Narrowing without ischemia.

elimination.verdict: C. The plaque narrows the artery, but supply still meets demand, so ischemia has not developed.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: A client, 66 years old, has had chest pressure only after climbing 4 flights of stairs for 2 years, always relieved within 5 minutes of rest. Over the past 3 days, the pressure comes on after half a flight and takes 15 minutes of rest to ease. The client has had no pressure while at rest. Blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg in the left arm, heart rate 84 beats per minute, pain 0 of 10 now. Which change in the coronary artery best explains the new pattern?

options.text: The plaque has slowly grown and narrowed the artery further, so less exertion now outstrips the supply
options.rationale: Plaque growth does lower the exertion needed to cause ischemia, which makes this defensible. But growth is gradual over months, and this change came over 3 days after 2 years of the same pattern.

options.text: Ischemia has become infarction, so part of the heart muscle can no longer use the oxygen it gets
options.rationale: Infarction is muscle death from prolonged severe ischemia. Pressure that eases with rest and is 0 of 10 now shows reversible ischemia, not a pattern explained by dead muscle.

options.text: The blood pressure of 138/84 mm Hg has raised the heart's demand above what the artery supplies
options.rationale: Higher pressure adds to the heart's work, but this reading does not explain a sudden drop from 4 flights to half a flight in 3 days.

options.text: A plaque has likely ruptured and a partial clot narrows the artery, so less exertion causes pressure
options.rationale: Plaque rupture with thrombosis can cause an acute coronary syndrome. A clot that partly blocks flow narrows the artery within days, so angina that is suddenly worse, with less exertion and longer to ease, fits rupture even without pressure at rest.

questions.takeaway: Plaque rupture and thrombosis turn chronic coronary narrowing into an acute coronary syndrome. Unstable angina is new, worsening, or at rest, so angina that suddenly needs much less exertion and takes longer to ease is unstable even before any pressure at rest appears, and it needs urgent evaluation.
questions.strategy: Two options explain why less exertion now causes pressure: further plaque growth, or a partial clot on a ruptured plaque. Both narrow the artery. Let the speed decide: 2 years unchanged, then much worse in 3 days.

steps.detail: 4 flights and 5 minutes of rest for 2 years; half a flight and 15 minutes of rest over the past 3 days.
Pressure ends with rest, so not infarction. A reading of 138/84 mm Hg does not explain a change this sudden.
Growth and a partial clot both narrow the artery; growth takes months.
Worse within 3 days points to rupture with a clot, even without pressure at rest.

elimination.verdict: D. A ruptured plaque with a partial clot.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: A client with no history of hypertension has correctly measured readings averaging 126/84 mm Hg over 3 clinic visits. The client says, "My top number is under 130, so I only have elevated blood pressure, right?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Your bottom number places you in stage 1 hypertension, because either number can set the category."
options.rationale: Stage 1 is a systolic of 130 to 139 or a diastolic of 80 to 89 mm Hg. A diastolic of 84 mm Hg meets stage 1 even though the systolic of 126 mm Hg alone would not.

options.text: "Yes, a top number under 130 means elevated blood pressure, so the plan is a yearly recheck."
options.rationale: Elevated blood pressure is a systolic of 120 to 129 mm Hg and a diastolic below 80 mm Hg. Both conditions must be met, and a diastolic of 84 mm Hg rules it out.

options.text: "Your average falls in stage 2 hypertension, because both numbers are above the goal for adults."
options.rationale: Both numbers are above the goal of below 130/80 mm Hg, but stage 2 starts at a systolic of 140 or a diastolic of 90 mm Hg. Neither value reaches stage 2.

options.text: "Yes, the top number sets the category, and the bottom number counts only once it reaches stage 2."
options.rationale: Every category above normal is defined by the systolic or the diastolic. The higher category reached by either number is the one that applies.

questions.takeaway: Blood pressure categories use "or" above the elevated level: the higher category reached by either the systolic or the diastolic number is the one that applies. Elevated blood pressure requires a diastolic below 80 mm Hg.
questions.strategy: The client anchors on the systolic. Check the diastolic of 84 mm Hg separately before accepting the client's label.

steps.detail: Systolic 126 mm Hg alone would be elevated; diastolic 84 mm Hg alone is stage 1.
The higher category reached by either number wins, so stage 1.
B and D both say the top number decides.
Neither 126 nor 84 mm Hg reaches stage 2, so C is out.

elimination.verdict: Stage 1 hypertension, set by the diastolic of 84 mm Hg.

questions.objective: Recognize common manifestations, complications, and priority nursing assessments for hypertension.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client, 70 years old, has had vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days and has no history of kidney disease or hypertension. Lying blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg in the right arm with heart rate 80 beats per minute. Within 30 seconds of standing, blood pressure is 94/60 mm Hg and heart rate is 106 beats per minute. Urine output is 20 mL per hour for the past 4 hours, was 60 mL per hour yesterday. Serum creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL, the same as at a clinic visit 1 month ago. The rise in heart rate within 30 seconds of standing is driven mainly by [[1]].

The low urine output is best explained by [[2]].

Of the mechanisms named, the one that raises blood pressure by increasing both peripheral vascular resistance and blood volume is [[3]].

options.text: The renin angiotensin aldosterone system responding to the fluid loss
options.rationale: The fluid loss does activate this system, but its effects come through hormones over minutes to hours. A heart rate rise within 30 seconds of standing is a reflex.

options.text: Arterial baroreceptors sensing the fall in pressure on standing
options.rationale: Baroreceptors sense changes in arterial pressure and respond within seconds, speeding the heart and constricting vessels. The 30 second timing is the cue.

options.text: Vascular autoregulation in the body tissues
options.rationale: Autoregulation adjusts local flow to keep each tissue perfused. It does not sense arterial pressure and drive the heart rate.

options.text: Chemoreceptors sensing the oxygen level of the blood
options.rationale: Chemoreceptors respond to oxygen and carbon dioxide levels. Nothing in the stem describes a change in oxygenation.

options.text: Kidney damage from long standing high blood pressure
