options.rationale: Symptoms and their onset are part of the history in an infection assessment.

options.text: Ask whether anyone the client lives or works with has been ill recently
options.rationale: Exposures are part of the history and can point to the source.

options.text: Ask whether any devices are in place, such as a urinary catheter used at home
options.rationale: Devices are part of the history. They bypass natural barriers and can be a source of infection.

options.text: Ask the family member how the client's alertness and activity compare with usual
options.rationale: Findings are compared with the client's baseline. Changes in behavior and function matter, and the family member knows what is usual.

options.text: Obtain a sputum specimen for culture before finishing the history, so the organism is identified quickly
options.rationale: The nurse obtains ordered specimens. No culture has been ordered, and the history is part of the assessment, not a step to cut short.

options.text: Record the oxygen saturation of 93% as expected for a client who is 78 years old
options.rationale: 93% is below the reference range of 95 to 100%. Decreased oxygen saturation is a concerning cue, and age does not make it expected.

questions.takeaway: The infection assessment gathers symptoms, onset, exposures, recent treatment, and devices; assesses overall appearance, the likely site, and respiratory status; and compares every finding with baseline. Do not rely on fever alone.
questions.strategy: The two wrong options each sound like good practice: one rushes to identify the organism, and one explains a low value by age. Ask whether the specimen was ordered and whether the value is inside its reference range.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Onset, exposures, and devices all belong.
Comparing with usual alertness and activity belongs.
No culture was ordered, and the history is not cut short.
93% is below 95 to 100%, whatever the age.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Assess for infection and recognize clinical deterioration

questions.stem: On day 2 of an intravenous antimicrobial for a wound infection, the susceptibility report shows that the organism is resistant to the drug. The next dose is due in 1 hour. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the next dose on time, because a missed dose lowers the drug level, then report
options.rationale: On time dosing matters, but this drug may not treat the organism. The provider needs the report before the dose so the order can change.

options.text: Hold the next dose and wait for the provider to see the report on rounds
options.rationale: Questioning the dose is right, but holding it without reporting leaves the client with no treatment and no new plan.

options.text: Report the susceptibility result to the provider before the next dose is due
options.rationale: The culture and susceptibility test identifies the organism and guides the drug choice. The nurse supports appropriate antimicrobial use by following culture results, and the provider needs this result to change the treatment.

options.text: Check the complete blood count with differential to decide whether the drug is working
options.rationale: The blood count adds information about the immune response, read together with the assessment. It does not answer which drug the organism responds to.

questions.takeaway: Culture and susceptibility identifies the organism and guides the antimicrobial choice. The complete blood count with differential adds information about the immune response. Read every result together with the assessment, and act on a susceptibility report that does not match the drug being given.
questions.strategy: Match each test to the question it answers: which organism and which drug, or how the body is responding. Then look for the choice that both protects the client from an ineffective drug and gets a new plan.

steps.detail: Susceptibility answers which drug works. The blood count answers how the body is responding.
Giving the dose first and holding it silently both leave the client without an effective plan.

steps.action: Choose the action that changes the plan
steps.detail: Report before the dose is due.

elimination.verdict: C. Report the susceptibility result to the provider before the next dose is due.

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.stem: A client admitted with a urinary tract infection was alert at 0700 and is confused at 0900. Oral temperature 38.6 °C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg. At 0915 the provider examines the client, documents probable sepsis without shock, and orders blood cultures and an intravenous antimicrobial. Facility policy states that laboratory staff draw blood cultures, and they report that they can reach the unit at 1115. The antimicrobial arrives at 0930, and the intravenous access works. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the antimicrobial at 1115 right after the laboratory staff draw the blood cultures
options.rationale: Specimens are obtained before the antimicrobial when that causes no delay, and 1115 is within 3 hours. The 3 hour window is for possible sepsis without shock. Probable sepsis calls for the antimicrobial immediately, ideally within 1 hour, and waiting for cultures until 1115 delays it 2 hours.

options.text: Hold the antimicrobial, recheck vital signs every 30 minutes, and give it if the blood pressure falls
options.rationale: Rechecking vital signs is right, but waiting for a falling blood pressure waits for shock. The provider has documented probable sepsis, which calls for the antimicrobial now.

options.text: Draw blood for culture from the existing intravenous line, then give the antimicrobial now
options.rationale: Getting the specimen first is the right idea, but facility policy assigns blood cultures to laboratory staff, and the existing line is not the way the specimen is obtained.

options.text: Give the antimicrobial now, and have the blood cultures drawn when the laboratory staff arrive
options.rationale: For probable sepsis the antimicrobial is given immediately, ideally within 1 hour. Cultures come first only when drawing them delays the antimicrobial by no more than 45 minutes; here the delay would be 2 hours.

questions.takeaway: Probable or definite sepsis, or septic shock: give the antimicrobial immediately, ideally within 1 hour. Possible sepsis without shock: investigate rapidly and begin treatment within 3 hours if concern persists. Obtain cultures first only when that does not delay the antimicrobial.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: "Without shock" and the culture first habit both point toward waiting until 1115, which is still inside 3 hours. The deciding cue is the provider's word probable: the 3 hour window belongs only to possible sepsis without shock.

steps.detail: The provider documented probable sepsis, not possible sepsis.
Probable sepsis: antimicrobial immediately, ideally within 1 hour.
Cultures first is right only when it causes no delay. A 2 hour wait is a delay.
A falling blood pressure is not required to act.
Policy assigns blood cultures to laboratory staff.

elimination.verdict: Give the antimicrobial now and draw cultures when the laboratory staff arrive.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.stem: A client admitted for a planned replacement of the right hip has a nasal swab screening result that is positive for MRSA. The client has no redness, swelling, or drainage anywhere on the body. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C, and the white blood cell count is 7000 per mm3. Which statement by the nurse to the team is accurate?

options.text: "The client is colonized, so the nose is not a reservoir until an infection develops."
options.rationale: Colonization is correct, but the organism is still present and can still leave the client and reach others. A colonized client is a reservoir.

options.text: "The client is colonized, and the nose can spread MRSA mainly by droplets."
options.rationale: Colonization is correct, but MRSA spreads by contact, on hands and shared equipment, not mainly by droplets.

options.text: "The client has an MRSA infection that has not yet caused a fever."
options.rationale: The nurse does not rely on fever alone, but this client has no signs at any site and a white blood cell count within range. Nothing shows the organism invading and growing.

options.text: "The client is colonized, and the nose can be a source that hands or equipment carry."
options.rationale: Colonization differs from infection: the organism is present without symptomatic disease. A reservoir is where the agent lives, so hands and shared equipment can carry it to the next client.

questions.takeaway: Colonization means the organism is present without disease. A colonized client is still a reservoir, and an infection that develops during care can come from the client's own organisms or an outside source.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Separate carrying an organism from being infected by it, then follow the organism: where it lives and how it leaves. Three options agree on colonization, so the decision rests on the reservoir and the route.

steps.detail: Positive screen, no signs at any site, white blood cell count in range: colonization. This removes the infection option.
Colonized still means a reservoir, which removes the option that says it is not one.
MRSA travels by contact on hands and equipment, which removes the droplet option.

elimination.verdict: D. The client is colonized, and the nose can be a source that hands or equipment carry.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.stem: A client who had a stroke coughs, and the voice sounds wet, each time thin liquids are swallowed. Which portal of entry does this finding place at risk?

options.text: Respiratory tract, because the swallowed liquid is entering the airway
options.rationale: Coughing and a wet voice with thin liquids mean the liquid is going into the airway. Aspiration leads to respiratory infection such as pneumonia.

options.text: Gastrointestinal tract, because the client is swallowing the liquids
options.rationale: The liquid is swallowed, but the cough and wet voice show it is not staying in the gastrointestinal tract. Ask where the organism actually gets in.

options.text: Damaged mucous membrane, because repeated coughing injures the throat
options.rationale: Damaged mucous membranes in the throat do allow entry, but nothing in the stem shows a damaged membrane. The finding points to the airway.

options.text: Respiratory tract, because the stroke has weakened the immune response
options.rationale: The portal is right, but the reason is not. The stem shows liquid entering the airway, not a change in immunity.

questions.takeaway: Infections enter through the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts, through broken skin or damaged mucous membranes, and through vascular access and other invasive devices that bypass natural barriers.
questions.strategy: Ask where the organism would actually get in, not which body part is named first. A swallow that ends in a cough enters the airway.

steps.detail: A wet cough with thin liquids is aspiration, so respiratory tract.
Swallowing names the gastrointestinal tract, but the liquid is not staying there.
Two options name the respiratory tract; only one gives the reason the stem supports.

elimination.verdict: A. Respiratory tract, because the swallowed liquid is entering the airway.

questions.objective: Identify patient factors that increase infection risk

questions.stem: For a client with no diagnosed infection, the nurse will empty a wound drain, irrigate an incision, count a radial pulse, and give a subcutaneous injection. Which actions follow standard precautions? Select all that apply.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene before touching the client and after care is finished
options.rationale: Hand hygiene before and after client contact is part of standard precautions for every client.

options.text: Wear a gown and gloves to empty the drain, because drainage may splash onto clothing
options.rationale: Equipment is chosen for the exposure expected. Gloves protect from body fluids, and a gown is worn when drainage may reach clothing or skin.

options.text: Wear gloves to count the radial pulse at the intact right wrist
options.rationale: Gloves are right for body fluids and broken skin, but counting a pulse on intact skin carries no expected exposure.

options.text: Place the used needle in the sharps container without recapping it
options.rationale: Sharps are handled safely: needles are not recapped and go into a puncture resistant container.

options.text: Skip eye protection while irrigating the incision, because no infection has been diagnosed
options.rationale: Standard precautions apply whether or not an infection has been diagnosed. Irrigation can splash, so eye protection is worn.

options.text: Clean the hands with alcohol based sanitizer after removing gloves if drainage soiled the hands
options.rationale: Cleaning the hands after removing gloves is right, but visibly soiled hands are washed with soap and water.

questions.takeaway: Standard precautions apply to every client: hand hygiene before and after contact, protective equipment matched to the expected exposure, safe sharps handling, and soap and water when hands are visibly soiled.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: For each task, ask what exposure is expected, not what the client is diagnosed with. More equipment is not safer when no exposure is expected, and a missing diagnosis never lowers the precautions.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Drain: gown and gloves. Irrigation: eye protection. Pulse on intact skin: no gloves needed.
No recapping, into the container.
Soiled hands need soap and water, even after gloves.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: A nurse receives report at 0700 on four clients with infections. Which client does the nurse assess first?

options.text: Urinary tract infection, day 1: heart rate 98 beats per minute and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, were 74 and 14 at 0300; oral temperature 37.0 °C; alert
options.rationale: Every value is still inside its range, but the heart rate rose 24 beats per minute and the respiratory rate rose 6 breaths per minute in 4 hours. A trend away from baseline is the earliest sign of deterioration.

options.text: Pneumonia, day 3: oral temperature 38.3 °C, the same at each check since admission; heart rate 96 beats per minute; alert and oriented as on admission
options.rationale: This is the only fever, but it has not changed since admission, and mental status matches baseline. The nurse does not rank clients by fever alone.

options.text: Cellulitis of the left leg, day 2: heart rate 106 beats per minute, between 104 and 108 at every check since admission; respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute; alert
options.rationale: The heart rate is above range, but it has not moved since admission. Compared with baseline, nothing has changed.

options.text: Infected abdominal wound, day 4: pain 3 of 10, was 6 of 10 at 0300 before a prescribed analgesic; oral temperature 37.4 °C, was 37.6 °C at 0300
options.rationale: Pain and temperature are both moving toward baseline after treatment.

questions.takeaway: Compare every finding with the client's baseline and look at the trend. Values that are moving away from baseline over hours outrank values that are out of range but unchanged.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The fever in the pneumonia client and the heart rate above range in the cellulitis client look most abnormal. The deciding cue is the 0300 values: only one client's findings have moved away from baseline in 4 hours.

steps.action: Mark what is out of range
steps.detail: Fever in the pneumonia client, heart rate in the cellulitis client, a temperature slightly above range in the wound client.
Only the urinary tract infection client has worsened since 0300.
Pain and temperature are both falling.
A worsening trend comes before an abnormal value that has not changed.

elimination.verdict: The client with the urinary tract infection whose heart rate and respiratory rate rose since 0300.

questions.objective: Assess for infection and recognize clinical deterioration

questions.scenario: A nurse cares for two clients in adjacent rooms. One client, 70 years old, has a draining wound on the right leg whose culture grew MRSA. The other client receives immunosuppressive treatment, has a closed abdominal incision with no drainage, and has a central venous catheter in the right chest.
questions.stem: For each nursing action, indicate the link in the chain of infection that the action interrupts.

rows.text: Covering the draining MRSA wound on the right leg with an intact dressing
rows.rationale: This wound holds the organism, so the dressing contains drainage at the point where organisms leave the reservoir. The same action on a clean wound would protect entry instead.

rows.text: Covering the closed abdominal incision of the client on immunosuppressive treatment with a sterile dressing
rows.rationale: This incision holds no known organism. The dressing protects a break in the skin where organisms could get in, so it acts on entry, not exit.

rows.text: Performing hand hygiene before touching the central venous catheter in the right chest
rows.rationale: Hands carry organisms from one person or surface to the next. Clean hands remove the vehicle before it reaches the catheter, so the action works on transmission.

rows.text: Using sterile technique and placing a sterile dressing over the central venous catheter insertion site in the right chest
rows.rationale: The catheter is a direct pathway into the bloodstream. A sterile dressing at the insertion site protects the entry point itself, not what carries organisms to it.

rows.text: Giving the prescribed antimicrobial to the client with the MRSA wound on the right leg
rows.rationale: Treatment acts on the organism where it lives, in the wound of the client who is the reservoir.

rows.text: Offering the client with the MRSA wound, 70 years old, a recommended vaccine before discharge
rows.rationale: This client is the reservoir for MRSA, but the vaccine does nothing to that organism. It lowers this client's risk for the infections the vaccine covers, so it acts on the client as a host.

questions.takeaway: The same action can break different links. A dressing over a wound that holds the organism blocks the exit; over a clean wound it protects the entry. Hand hygiene stops the carrier; a sterile dressing at the insertion site protects the entry. A vaccine always acts on the host, even in a client who is also a reservoir.
questions.strategy: For each row, ask whether the action works on the organism's source, on what carries it, or on the place it would get in. The cue is in the row: does the wound hold the organism, and does the action clean the carrier or protect the entry point?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The MRSA wound holds the organism: portal of exit. The clean incision on an immunosuppressed client: portal of entry.
Hand hygiene cleans the carrier: method of transmission. A sterile dressing at the insertion site protects the entry: portal of entry.

steps.action: Place the antimicrobial and the vaccine
steps.detail: The antimicrobial acts on the agent in its reservoir. The vaccine changes the person's susceptibility: susceptible host.

elimination.verdict: Portal of exit; portal of entry; method of transmission; portal of entry; agent and reservoir; susceptible host.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.stem: A nurse gives a subcutaneous injection and, while placing the uncapped needle in the sharps container at the bedside, sticks the left index finger with it. The client's record lists no known bloodborne infection. Two other clients have oral medications due now. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Finish giving the oral medications that are due now, then report the injury to the supervisor
options.rationale: Reporting is right, but needlestick injuries are reported immediately. Delaying the report for routine medications delays evaluation and follow up care.

options.text: Report the injury to the supervisor, and skip the exposure protocol because no infection is known
options.rationale: Reporting at once is right, but the record lists no known infection, which does not mean no infection. The facility exposure protocol is followed for every needlestick.

options.text: Report the injury to the supervisor now, and follow the facility exposure protocol for evaluation
options.rationale: Needlestick injuries and blood exposures are reported to supervisors immediately, documented at the scene, and followed through the facility exposure protocol for evaluation and follow up care. First aid is washing the site with soap and water; the report follows at once.

options.text: Ask the client to consent to blood testing first, so the report to the supervisor is complete
options.rationale: The nurse does not hold the report while collecting more information. The exposure protocol directs evaluation, and the report comes first.

questions.takeaway: Report a needlestick injury or blood exposure to the supervisor immediately, document it at the scene, and follow the facility exposure protocol whatever the client's known history.
questions.strategy: Two options report at once. The difference is whether the client's record changes the protocol. A record with no known infection never cancels the exposure protocol.

steps.detail: Finishing medications first puts routine work ahead of an exposure.
Waiting for the client's blood test is another delay.

steps.action: Compare the two that report now
steps.detail: No known infection is not the same as no infection, so the protocol still applies.

elimination.verdict: Report the injury to the supervisor now, and follow the facility exposure protocol.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: A client who is 81 years old and has diabetes mellitus is on day 3 of admission for an infected pressure injury over the sacrum. At 0200 the client was alert and oriented, with a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute. At 0600 the client is lethargic, the respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute, the heart rate is 114 beats per minute, the oral temperature is 35.8 °C, the skin is cool and clammy, and sacral pain is 2 of 10, the same as at 0200. Blood cultures drawn on admission showed no growth. The nurse suspects sepsis. Which statements by the nurse about this client are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sepsis can be present even though the admission blood cultures showed no growth
options.rationale: An organism does not need to be found in the bloodstream for sepsis to be present. The diagnosis is clinical, based on signs of organ dysfunction.

options.text: The temperature of 35.8 °C makes sepsis less likely, because sepsis causes a fever
options.rationale: Temperature changes are common early signs, and they include feeling cold and clammy as well as fever. A low temperature with cool, clammy skin is a cue, not reassurance.

options.text: Blood vessels that dilate and leak can lower blood flow and oxygen delivery to the tissues
options.rationale: In sepsis the widespread response makes vessels dilate and become more permeable, so circulation and oxygen delivery to tissues may fall, and organ dysfunction may follow.

options.text: New lethargy, compared with alert and oriented at 0200, can be a sign of organ dysfunction
options.rationale: A sudden change in mental status from baseline is an early cue. New confusion or decreased alertness is evidence of organ dysfunction.

options.text: These findings fit an infection that is still confined to the pressure injury over the sacrum
options.rationale: The wound is the likely source, but new lethargy, a respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute, and cool, clammy skin show a response affecting the whole body.

options.text: The respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute is explained by the sacral pain of 2 of 10
options.rationale: A respiratory rate above 20 breaths per minute is concerning. The pain has not changed since 0200, while the respiratory rate rose from 18 breaths per minute, so pain does not explain it.

questions.takeaway: Sepsis is a clinical diagnosis based on organ dysfunction. It does not need a positive blood culture or a fever, and new changes in mentation and breathing from baseline are early cues.
questions.strategy: Test each statement against the client's own baseline. Anything that waits for a fever or a positive blood culture, or explains a new change with a finding that has not changed, is false.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No growth in the blood does not rule out sepsis: true.
Cold and clammy is a sepsis cue: false.
Dilated, leaky vessels lower tissue perfusion: true.
Lethargy is new: true. Pain is unchanged, so it cannot explain the new respiratory rate: false. A whole body response is not a confined infection: false.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: A client who is 81 years old is on day 3 of admission for an infected pressure injury over the sacrum. At 0200 the client was alert and oriented, with a heart rate of 90 beats per minute, a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, and urine output of 50 mL per hour. At 0600 the client is lethargic, the heart rate is 114 beats per minute, the respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute, urine output is 20 mL per hour, and the oral temperature is 35.8 °C. The nurse activates the rapid response process. Which statement best begins the nurse's report to the team?

options.text: "Infected sacral pressure injury. Heart rate 114 beats per minute, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, temperature 35.8 °C, urine 20 mL per hour. Please assess."
options.rationale: The current values are accurate, but without the 0200 values the team cannot see the change, the new lethargy is left out, and no concern is stated.

options.text: "Infected sacral pressure injury. The client is lethargic with low urine output but has no fever, so I think the infection is likely not spreading beyond the wound."
options.rationale: The findings are right, but the conclusion is wrong. The nurse does not rely on fever alone, and the change from baseline points toward sepsis.

options.text: "The client looks septic and needs antimicrobials and fluids right away. Please come to the room as soon as you can, because this is urgent and cannot wait."
options.rationale: The concern is right, but the statement gives no findings. The team needs the changes that led the nurse to escalate.

options.text: "Infected sacral pressure injury. Since 0200: alert to lethargic, heart rate 90 to 114 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 to 26 breaths per minute. I suspect sepsis."
options.rationale: This names the likely source, gives the change from baseline in mentation and vital signs, and states the concern. Trends from baseline make the deterioration clear.

questions.takeaway: When escalating care, give the likely source, the change from the client's baseline in breathing, mentation, circulation, and urine output, and the concern itself.
questions.strategy: Every option names something true. Pick the one that lets the team see the trend: current values alone hide how far the client has moved from baseline.

steps.detail: No fever does not mean the infection is not spreading.
Urgency without findings gives the team nothing to act on.
Current values alone versus values with their 0200 baseline: the trend shows the deterioration.

elimination.verdict: The report that gives the source, the change since 0200, and the concern for sepsis.

questions.objective: Assess for infection and recognize clinical deterioration

questions.stem: At 0930 a nurse has intravenous antimicrobial doses ready for four clients and can start only one at a time. Each order states to give the dose now. Which client does the nurse give the antimicrobial to first?

options.text: Urinary tract infection: the provider documented possible sepsis without shock at 0900; blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg, heart rate 108 beats per minute; alert
options.rationale: This client was documented first and has the lower blood pressure, but possible sepsis without shock calls for rapid investigation and treatment within 3 hours if concern persists. That window allows this dose to follow the client who needs it within 1 hour.

options.text: Pneumonia: the provider documented infection without signs of sepsis at 0850; oral temperature 38.9 °C, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute; alert
options.rationale: This is the highest temperature, but the provider found no sepsis. The nurse does not rank clients by fever alone.

options.text: Cellulitis of the right leg: the provider documented probable sepsis at 0920; blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg, heart rate 102 beats per minute; alert
options.rationale: For probable or definite sepsis, the antimicrobial is given immediately, ideally within 1 hour. The provider's category, not the blood pressure, sets the time limit, so this client is first.

options.text: Infected left foot wound: day 3 of treatment, dose due at 0930; oral temperature 37.4 °C, heart rate 88 beats per minute; alert
options.rationale: A dose on time matters, but this client shows no sepsis and is on day 3 of treatment. It can follow the clients who have a sepsis time limit.

questions.takeaway: The Hour 1 bundle sets the time limit by category: septic shock or probable or definite sepsis gets the antimicrobial immediately, ideally within 1 hour; possible sepsis without shock is investigated rapidly and treated within 3 hours if concern persists.
questions.strategy: The urinary tract infection client looks sicker and was documented first. The deciding cue is the provider's category: possible sepsis without shock versus probable sepsis, which carries the shorter time limit.

steps.detail: Pneumonia without sepsis and the day 3 foot wound have no sepsis time limit.
One has possible sepsis without shock, the other probable sepsis.
Probable sepsis: within 1 hour. Possible sepsis without shock: within 3 hours if concern persists. A lower blood pressure that is not shock does not change the category.

elimination.verdict: The client with cellulitis and probable sepsis documented at 0920.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.stem: A client, 79 years old, is admitted for dehydration. The lips are dry and cracked, there is a skin tear on the left forearm, and an indwelling urinary catheter was placed in the emergency department. The record shows none of the recommended vaccines. Which nursing actions use the body's defenses or prevent exposure to lower this client's infection risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Giving mouth care and moistening the lips so the oral mucous membranes stay intact
options.rationale: Intact skin and mucous membranes form barriers. Cracked lips and a dry mouth are breaks in that barrier, and mouth care helps restore it.

options.text: Covering the skin tear on the left forearm and protecting the skin from further tears
options.rationale: Broken skin gives organisms direct access. Covering the tear and preventing new ones protects the skin barrier.

options.text: Performing hand hygiene before and after handling the urinary catheter or drainage bag
options.rationale: Hand hygiene and care of invasive devices help prevent exposure. The catheter bypasses natural barriers, so clean hands at every contact matter.

options.text: Offering the recommended vaccines before discharge, following facility protocol
options.rationale: Vaccination reduces risk for the infections covered by recommended vaccines. It strengthens the host's own defenses.

options.text: Asking the provider for an antibiotic now so that an infection does not develop
options.rationale: No infection has been identified. Antibiotics given without an indication do not strengthen defenses, and unnecessary use contributes to resistance.

options.text: Using alcohol based sanitizer on hands that are visibly soiled with the client's stool
options.rationale: Hand hygiene is right, but hands that are visibly soiled need soap and water. Alcohol based sanitizer is preferred only when hands are not visibly soiled.

questions.takeaway: The body defends itself with intact skin and mucous membranes and with inflammation and immune responses. Nurses support those defenses, offer recommended vaccines, and prevent exposure with hand hygiene and device care.
questions.strategy: For each action, ask whether it protects a barrier, strengthens the host, or blocks exposure. An action that only looks protective, or uses the wrong hand hygiene method, is false.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cracked lips and a skin tear are broken barriers: mouth care and covering the tear are true.
Hand hygiene around the catheter prevents exposure: true.
Recommended vaccines lower risk: true.
An antibiotic with no infection is not prevention; visibly soiled hands need soap and water: false, false.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.stem: A nurse receives report on four clients. Which client does the nurse identify as having the highest risk for developing sepsis?

options.text: Age 84 years, cellulitis of the left leg on day 3 of antimicrobials, redness now inside the border marked on admission, no invasive devices
options.rationale: Older age is a risk factor, but this infection is shrinking on treatment and there are no devices. A worsening infection, not an older age alone, is the stronger warning.

options.text: Age 61 years, on chemotherapy for cancer, a central venous port in the right chest, urinary tract infection with new flank pain since 0800
options.rationale: This client combines reduced immune function, an invasive device, chronic illness, and an infection that is getting worse. Each is a listed risk factor for sepsis, and together they make this client the highest risk.

options.text: Age 35 years, nasal swab positive for MRSA, admitted for an elective procedure, no signs of infection and no invasive devices
options.rationale: A resistant organism sounds dangerous, but this is colonization, not infection. Sepsis is a response to an infection, and none is present.

options.text: Age 52 years, type 2 diabetes mellitus, a small blister on the right heel with no redness, warmth, or drainage, no invasive devices
options.rationale: Chronic illness is a risk factor, but the blister shows no sign of infection, and sepsis needs an infection to start.

questions.takeaway: Risk factors for sepsis: older adults, reduced immune function, chronic illness or serious wounds, invasive devices or recent procedures, and anyone whose infection is worsening. Risk rises as factors add up on top of an active infection.
questions.strategy: Sepsis starts with an infection. Remove the clients who have none, then compare an improving infection with a worsening one in a client with several risk factors.

steps.detail: MRSA colonization and an uninfected blister cannot lead to sepsis yet.
Cellulitis is shrinking on treatment; the urinary tract infection is worsening.
Chemotherapy, cancer, and a central port add reduced immunity, chronic illness, and a device.

elimination.verdict: The client receiving chemotherapy with a central venous port and a worsening urinary tract infection.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.scenario: A client, 76 years old, is on day 2 after surgery on the right hip. At 0700 the client was alert and oriented, heart rate 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, urine output 50 mL per hour. At 1100 the client is confused, heart rate 116 beats per minute, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, blood pressure 98/58 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 93% on room air, oral temperature 38.6 °C, and urine output 20 mL per hour. The hip incision is red with cloudy drainage. The client has an indwelling urinary catheter and a peripheral intravenous catheter in the left forearm. The nurse has activated the rapid response process, and the provider has ordered blood cultures and a serum lactate.
questions.stem: For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated for this client now.

rows.text: Trend vital signs, oxygen saturation, mental status, and hourly urine output against the 0700 values
rows.rationale: Sepsis assessment trends vital signs, oxygenation, mental status, and urine output. The 0700 values are the baseline that shows how far the client has moved.

rows.text: Inspect the hip incision, the urinary catheter, and the intravenous site for a likely source of infection
rows.rationale: The nurse assesses for a likely infection source. The cloudy drainage is a strong lead, but the catheter and the intravenous site are also possible sources.

rows.text: Prepare for the ordered blood cultures and serum lactate, and check that the intravenous access works
rows.rationale: The nurse anticipates ordered cultures and lactate testing, obtains ordered specimens, and assesses intravenous access so treatment is not delayed.

rows.text: Hold further assessments until the lactate result shows whether the client has sepsis
rows.rationale: Clinical assessment remains essential alongside diagnostic information. No single test confirms sepsis, and the findings are already changing.

rows.text: Treat a single lactate result that is not elevated as ruling out sepsis
rows.rationale: No single test confirms or rules out sepsis, and a lactate result is interpreted with the assessment, not instead of it. New confusion, a respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute, and low urine output remain signs of organ dysfunction.

rows.text: Wait for organisms to grow in the blood cultures before treating the condition as sepsis
rows.rationale: An organism does not need to be found in the bloodstream for sepsis to be present. The diagnosis is clinical, based on signs of organ dysfunction.

questions.takeaway: In suspected sepsis, trend vital signs, oxygenation, mental status, and urine output; look for the source; anticipate cultures and lactate. Tests support the clinical assessment and never replace it.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each action by whether it keeps the clinical assessment going or waits on a test result. Waiting on a lactate or a culture is the trap.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Trending against 0700 and searching for the source are indicated.
Ordered cultures, lactate, and working intravenous access are indicated.
Holding assessment for a lactate, trusting one lactate value, or waiting for culture growth are not indicated.

elimination.verdict: Indicated: trend against 0700, find the source, prepare for cultures and lactate. Not indicated: holding assessment, trusting one lactate value, waiting for culture growth.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: A client, 45 years old, is admitted with a cough for 6 weeks, night sweats, and weight loss of 5 kg. The provider documents suspected pulmonary tuberculosis and orders sputum specimens. The client coughs often and is waiting in a private room with the door closed. Which precautions does the nurse prepare?

options.text: Move the client to an airborne infection isolation room, and wear a fitted respirator to enter
options.rationale: Tuberculosis spreads by particles that stay suspended in the air, so an airborne infection isolation room and respiratory protection are needed, along with standard precautions.

options.text: Keep the private room with the door closed, and wear a surgical mask within 1 meter of the client
options.rationale: A mask and placement in a private room fit droplet precautions, where large droplets reach nearby mucous membranes. The suspected tuberculosis is the cue: its particles remain in the air, so a closed door and a surgical mask are not enough.

options.text: Keep the private room, and wear a gown and gloves for all contact with the client
options.rationale: Gown and gloves interrupt contact spread from wounds or shared equipment. They do not protect against particles in the air.

options.text: Wait for the sputum results, and use standard precautions until tuberculosis is confirmed
options.rationale: Precautions start when the infection is suspected. Waiting for results leaves staff and other clients exposed to the air in the room.

questions.takeaway: Droplet precautions use a mask and patient placement; airborne precautions use an airborne infection isolation room and respiratory protection. Choose by how the organism travels, and start them when infection is suspected.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Both a mask and a respirator protect the airway. Decide by the route: particles that stay suspended in the air need an airborne room.

steps.detail: Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis spreads by particles suspended in air.
Droplet precautions use a mask; airborne precautions use a special room and a respirator.
Precautions begin on suspicion, so waiting for results is out.

elimination.verdict: A. Airborne infection isolation room and a fitted respirator.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: A nurse is assigned a client, 77 years old, transferred from another hospital this morning. The transfer record shows a urine culture positive for CRE 5 days ago. The nurse cared for a client with MRSA yesterday using gown and gloves on contact precautions. Which action does the nurse take before entering the room?

options.text: Enter using yesterday's MRSA routine without checking, because all resistant organisms share one plan
options.rationale: Gown and gloves are likely part of the plan, but VRE and CRE require checking organism specific precautions before care; resistant organisms are not all handled identically.

options.text: Wait to start added precautions until this hospital repeats the urine culture and reports it
options.rationale: The positive culture from 5 days ago is enough to act on. Waiting leaves other clients exposed.

options.text: Wear a mask and eye protection, because resistant organisms spread through the air
options.rationale: CRE spreads by contact with the client and the environment, not through the air.

options.text: Check the facility guidance for CRE precautions, and add what it lists to standard precautions
options.rationale: VRE and CRE require checking organism specific precautions before care. For CRE this is typically contact precautions, gown and gloves, in addition to standard precautions.

questions.takeaway: MRSA, VRE, and CRE are resistant organisms, but VRE and CRE require checking the facility's organism specific precautions before care. Standard precautions continue for every client.
questions.strategy: Reusing a routine that worked yesterday sounds efficient. The cue is the organism named: CRE means check the specific guidance before care rather than copy the MRSA routine.

steps.detail: CRE, carbapenem resistant Enterobacterales.
Reusing the MRSA routine assumes the precautions are identical; checking the guidance confirms what to add to standard precautions.
Waiting for a new culture and airborne protection do not fit.

elimination.verdict: D. Check the facility guidance for CRE precautions and add what it lists to standard precautions.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: A client with confirmed C. difficile used a bedside commode, which will now go to the equipment room for another client. A client with MRSA used the same model of commode on another unit last week. The unit stocks a standard disinfectant wipe and a sporicidal cleaning agent. Which action does the nurse take with the commode?

options.text: Clean the commode with the sporicidal agent before it is used for another client
options.rationale: C. difficile spores persist in the environment and standard disinfectants may not kill them, so shared equipment is cleaned with a sporicidal agent.

options.text: Clean the commode with the standard disinfectant wipe, as for the commode used with MRSA
options.rationale: A standard disinfectant is appropriate for many organisms, including MRSA. The C. difficile diagnosis is the cue: its spores may survive standard disinfectants.

options.text: Rinse the commode with soap and water, because soap removes spores from hands
options.rationale: Soap and water is used for hand hygiene when facility policy indicates it. It does not replace sporicidal cleaning of equipment.

options.text: Clean the commode with alcohol based sanitizer, and let it dry before it is used
options.rationale: Alcohol does not reliably kill C. difficile spores, which is why sporicidal agents are used.

questions.takeaway: C. difficile spores persist in the environment and standard disinfectants may not be effective. Enhanced contact precautions include dedicated or appropriately cleaned equipment and sporicidal environmental cleaning.
questions.strategy: Both wipes are real cleaning products. The organism decides: spores need a sporicidal agent.

steps.detail: C. difficile forms spores.
A standard disinfectant may not kill spores; a sporicidal agent does.
Soap and alcohol sanitizer are hand hygiene, not equipment cleaning.

elimination.verdict: A. Clean the commode with the sporicidal agent.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: A client, 34 years old, is seen in the clinic with a sore throat, runny nose, and cough for 2 days. Oral temperature 37.6 °C, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. The provider diagnoses a viral upper respiratory infection and prescribes rest and fluids. The client says, "Last time I got an antibiotic and felt better in 3 days. Can I get one just to be safe?" Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "I will let the provider know you are concerned, since your temperature is slightly raised."
options.rationale: This sounds like advocacy, but a temperature of 37.6 °C fits a viral upper respiratory infection, the diagnosis is already made, and teaching why an antibiotic will not help is the nurse's role here.

options.text: "Your oxygen level and breathing rate are normal, so you do not need any treatment at all."
options.rationale: Rest and fluids are prescribed treatment. The response also dismisses the client's question instead of teaching.

options.text: "An antibiotic from last time would work if you have any left over at home."
options.rationale: Leftover antibiotics should not be used, and an antibiotic would not act on a viral infection.

options.text: "Antibiotics do not treat viruses, and using one without need helps resistant germs grow."
options.rationale: Antibiotics do not treat viral infections, and unnecessary use contributes to resistance. The response teaches the reason in plain language.

questions.takeaway: Antibiotics do not treat viral infections, and unnecessary use contributes to antimicrobial resistance. The nurse supports appropriate antimicrobial use through teaching.
questions.strategy: Passing the concern to the provider sounds like advocacy. The diagnosis in the stem decides: a viral infection is not treated with an antibiotic, so the nurse teaches instead.

steps.detail: Viral upper respiratory infection.

steps.action: Compare the two that answer the request
steps.detail: Relaying the concern defers a question the nurse can answer; explaining why an antibiotic will not help teaches the client.
Dismissing all treatment and using leftover pills are both wrong.

elimination.verdict: D. Explain that antibiotics do not treat viruses and unneeded use helps resistant germs grow.

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.stem: A client, 80 years old, had an indwelling urinary catheter placed on admission for a fracture of the left hip. On day 5 the client has cloudy urine, and the urine culture grows an organism from the client's own bowel. The family asks, "Since the germ came from the client's own body, did this infection have anything to do with the hospital care?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "No, because an organism from the client's own body is not a healthcare associated infection."
options.rationale: This is the common belief, but healthcare associated infections can come from the client's own organisms or from an outside source.

options.text: "Yes, because the germ must have been carried in on a caregiver's hands to cause the infection."
options.rationale: An outside source is possible, but the culture shows an organism from the client's own bowel.

options.text: "Yes, it developed during care, and the catheter gave the client's own germs a path in."
options.rationale: The infection developed on day 5 of care, after the catheter was placed. Organisms for a healthcare associated infection may come from the client, and the catheter bypasses natural barriers.

options.text: "No, because a urinary tract infection at this age comes from a weak immune system."
options.rationale: Age extremes raise risk, but the catheter placed in the hospital created a direct path for the organism.

questions.takeaway: A healthcare associated infection develops during healthcare delivery. The organism may come from the client or an outside source, and invasive devices such as urinary catheters create a path past natural barriers.
questions.strategy: The source of the organism sounds like it decides. The cue that decides is when and how the infection developed: on day 5, after a catheter placed during care.

steps.detail: The infection appeared on day 5, after the catheter was placed.

steps.action: Compare the yes and no answers
steps.detail: Healthcare associated infections can come from the client's own organisms.
The culture names the client's bowel organism, not a caregiver's hands; the catheter gave it a path.

elimination.verdict: C. Yes, it developed during care, and the catheter gave the client's own germs a path in.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.scenario: During a morning huddle on a medical unit, the nurse reviews findings and team comments about several clients and the unit as a whole.
questions.stem: For each finding or comment, indicate the term that best describes it.

rows.text: A rectal swab taken on admission grows VRE; the client has formed stools and an oral temperature of 36.9 °C
rows.rationale: The organism is present, but there is no sign of disease. Colonization differs from infection, and the client is still a source the team must contain.

rows.text: After 3 days of an antibiotic, the organisms that normally live in the client's bowel are reduced, and liquid stools begin
rows.rationale: The microbiome is the set of microorganisms normally living in and on the body. Antibiotics can disturb it, which changes how the bowel works.

rows.text: One case of influenza on the unit was followed by 6 more cases in clients and staff within 4 days
rows.rationale: Communicability is the ability to spread. Fast spread from one case to many describes how readily the organism moves between people.

rows.text: A small number of organisms entered a cut on the right hand and caused severe tissue damage within 24 hours
rows.rationale: Virulence is the ability to cause disease. Severe damage from few organisms in a short time describes a highly virulent organism, not how easily it spreads.

rows.text: The incision on the left knee is red and swollen with purulent drainage, and the culture grows Staphylococcus aureus
rows.rationale: Infection is invasion and growth of a pathogen in the body. Here the organism has invaded and is producing signs of disease at the site.

rows.text: Skin swabs of a client with no wounds or symptoms grow organisms that are always present on healthy skin
rows.rationale: These organisms normally live on the body and cause no harm. They are part of the microbiome, not colonization by a pathogen or an infection.

questions.takeaway: Infection is invasion and growth of a pathogen. Colonization is presence without disease. Virulence is how able an organism is to cause disease, communicability is how able it is to spread, and the microbiome is the organisms that normally live in and on the body.
questions.strategy: Ask what each statement is about: whether disease is present, how severe the disease is, how far it spread, or which organisms belong there normally.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Signs at the site mean infection; an organism with no signs means colonization.
Severe damage from few organisms is virulence; many cases from one is communicability.
Organisms that normally live on skin and in the bowel are the microbiome.

elimination.verdict: Colonization, microbiome, communicability, virulence, infection, microbiome.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.stem: A client, 69 years old, is admitted with dehydration. The nurse's admission assessment includes the findings below. Which findings point to a portal of entry that increases this client's risk for infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Both eyes are red and irritated from frequent rubbing
options.rationale: Damaged mucous membranes, including the conjunctiva, allow organisms to enter.

options.text: A scar on the right knee from surgery 6 years ago, with intact skin
options.rationale: A healed scar with intact skin is a barrier again. It does not provide a path for organisms.

options.text: A peripheral IV catheter in the left forearm, placed in the emergency department today
options.rationale: An invasive device breaks the skin and gives organisms a direct path into the body.

options.text: Wears glasses for reading and hearing aids in both ears
options.rationale: Glasses and hearing aids do not break skin or mucous membranes and are not invasive devices.

options.text: A colonoscopy with biopsy was done 2 days ago
options.rationale: Medical procedures in the GI tract are a route for gastrointestinal infection.

options.text: The lining of the throat is raw and cracked on inspection
options.rationale: Damaged mucous membranes in the throat allow organisms to enter.

questions.takeaway: Infections enter through mucous membrane lined tracts. Gastrointestinal infections can follow medical procedures, damaged membranes of the throat or conjunctiva let organisms in, and invasive devices such as IV catheters bypass natural barriers.
questions.strategy: For each finding, ask whether a barrier is broken, a device bypasses it, or a tract has been entered by a procedure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Red, irritated eyes and a raw, cracked throat lining.
A new IV catheter and a recent colonoscopy with biopsy.
A healed scar with intact skin; glasses and hearing aids.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Identify patient factors that increase infection risk

questions.stem: In a clinic waiting room, a client with a new cough coughs near other people without covering the mouth. No diagnosis has been made. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Wait until the provider diagnoses the cough before choosing any precautions
options.rationale: Standard precautions, including respiratory hygiene, apply to every client whether or not an infection has been diagnosed. Waiting leaves the others exposed.

options.text: Put on a gown and gloves for this client's care, as for contact spread
options.rationale: Contact spread comes from touching a person or a contaminated item, such as wound drainage or shared equipment. A cough near other people is a respiratory concern, and gown and gloves do nothing to contain it.

options.text: Put on a fitted respirator and move the client to an airborne isolation room
options.rationale: An airborne isolation room fits a suspected airborne infection. Nothing in the stem suggests one, and the first step is containing the cough at its source.

options.text: Begin respiratory hygiene now, as for any client, without a diagnosis
options.rationale: Standard precautions apply to every client whether or not an infection has been diagnosed, and respiratory hygiene is one of them. The uncovered cough near others is the reason to start it now.

questions.takeaway: Standard precautions apply to every client whether or not an infection has been diagnosed, and they include respiratory hygiene. In practice that means covering the cough, a mask if tolerated, and hand hygiene after coughing.
questions.strategy: No diagnosis is needed for standard precautions. Match the precaution to the concern in the stem: a cough near other people.

steps.detail: They apply before any diagnosis, so waiting is wrong.
A cough near others calls for respiratory hygiene, not contact gear.
An airborne isolation room has no supporting cue.

elimination.verdict: D. Begin respiratory hygiene now.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: A client is admitted with a respiratory infection spread by droplets and coughs often. Which plan for the room and precautions is correct?

options.text: Gown and gloves for all contact, with equipment kept only for this room
options.rationale: These are contact precautions, for spread by touching a person or a contaminated item. Droplets reach nearby mucous membranes, so a mask is the key protection.

options.text: An airborne isolation room, with a fitted respirator worn for every entry
options.rationale: These are airborne precautions, for particles that stay suspended in the air. Droplet spread needs a mask and placement, not an isolation room.

options.text: A mask for care, and placement so the client does not cough near others
options.rationale: Droplet precautions use a mask and appropriate placement. Droplets reach nearby mucous membranes, so the concern is coughing near another person. A private room is the usual way to meet this.

options.text: A mask for care, and a bed next to a client who had surgery yesterday
options.rationale: The mask is right, but placement is wrong. Coughing near another person is the concern with droplet spread, and a postoperative client is a susceptible host.

questions.takeaway: Droplet spread happens when respiratory droplets reach nearby mucous membranes, so coughing near another person is the concern. Droplet precautions are a mask and appropriate placement that keeps the client from coughing near others.
questions.strategy: Name the route first, then check both parts of the precaution: the protection and the placement.

steps.detail: The provider documents droplet spread.
Droplet means a mask and appropriate placement.
Only one places the client away from a susceptible roommate.

elimination.verdict: C. A mask and placement away from other clients.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: A client has confirmed COVID 19. The nurse puts on a gown, clean gloves, and a fitted respirator to collect a sputum specimen. Which protection does the nurse add?

options.text: Goggles or a face shield to protect the eyes
options.rationale: Precautions for COVID 19 call for appropriate respiratory protection and eye protection. The respirator covers the first; the eyes are still exposed to a cough at close range.

options.text: A second respirator worn over the first one
options.rationale: A second respirator adds nothing once the first is fitted. The gap in protection is the eyes.

options.text: Sterile gloves to keep the specimen sterile
options.rationale: Clean gloves are already on for contact with sputum. Sterile gloves add nothing to COVID 19 precautions; eye protection is the missing piece.

options.text: Nothing more, since the respirator is enough
options.rationale: The respirator alone leaves the eyes unprotected, and COVID 19 precautions include eye protection.

questions.takeaway: Precautions for COVID 19 combine appropriate respiratory protection with eye protection, with placement and other details per facility policy. Standard precautions continue alongside them.
questions.strategy: The nurse already has the respiratory protection. Ask which part of the COVID 19 precautions is still missing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Respiratory protection plus eye protection.
A gown and clean gloves cover contact with sputum; a fitted respirator covers the respiratory part.
The eyes are still exposed.

elimination.verdict: A. Goggles or a face shield.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: A nurse works a 12 hour shift on a medical unit. In which situations is alcohol based hand sanitizer the correct method of hand hygiene? Select all that apply.

options.text: Before counting the radial pulse at the right wrist, with hands not visibly soiled
options.rationale: Alcohol based sanitizer is preferred in most routine clinical situations when hands are not visibly soiled.

options.text: After using the restroom during a break
options.rationale: Soap and water is used after using the restroom.

options.text: Before eating lunch in the break room
options.rationale: Soap and water is used before eating.

options.text: After removing intact gloves used to empty a urinary drainage bag, with hands not visibly soiled
options.rationale: Hands are cleaned after removing gloves. With no visible soil, sanitizer is the preferred method.

options.text: In place of gloves when emptying a wound drain, if the hands are cleaned right after
options.rationale: Sanitizer does not replace appropriate protective equipment. Gloves are worn for expected contact with drainage.

options.text: After drainage from a wound soaks through the glove onto the left hand
options.rationale: Hands that are visibly soiled are washed with soap and water.

questions.takeaway: Use alcohol based sanitizer for routine care when hands are not visibly soiled. Use soap and water when hands are visibly soiled, before eating, and after using the restroom. Clean hands after removing gloves, and never use sanitizer in place of protective equipment.
questions.strategy: Sort each situation by two questions: are the hands visibly soiled, and is it eating or toileting? If neither, sanitizer is preferred.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Drainage on the left hand calls for soap and water.
Both call for soap and water.
Sanitizer never replaces gloves.
Before a pulse check and after glove removal with clean hands.

elimination.verdict: A, D.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: A client with an MRSA wound infection is on contact precautions. The client's adult child reads the sign on the door and says, "All this gear seems like a lot. I am family, so do I really need it?" Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "It is the hospital rule, so please follow the sign on the door before you go in."
options.rationale: The visitor asked why. Citing a rule without explaining it does not help the visitor follow the precautions correctly.

options.text: "This germ spreads by touch. Let me show you the hand cleaning, gown, and gloves first."
options.rationale: Precautions are explained in plain language, and visitors are taught the required hand hygiene and protective equipment before entering the care area.

options.text: "Family members are already exposed at home, so you can visit without a gown and gloves."
options.rationale: Contact precautions address contact with the client and the environment. Prior exposure does not remove the need for them.

options.text: "Go ahead in for now, and I will show you how to use the gown and gloves next time."
options.rationale: Teaching after entry leaves the visitor unprotected during this visit. Visitors are taught before entering.

questions.takeaway: Explain precautions to clients, visitors, and staff in plain language, and teach visitors the required hand hygiene and protective equipment before they enter the care area.
questions.strategy: The visitor's question asks why. Choose the response that explains in plain words and teaches before entry.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The visitor wants to know why.
Teaching happens before entering, not after.
Prior exposure at home does not waive contact precautions.

elimination.verdict: B. Explain in plain language and teach before entry.

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.stem: A client who lives alone is being discharged with an oral antibiotic for cellulitis, to take 4 times a day for 10 days. Which finding from the discharge assessment is most likely to interfere with treatment of the infection at home?

options.text: Oral temperature 37.1 °C, with the redness now inside the skin marking drawn on admission
options.rationale: A receding border and no fever show the infection is responding. This finding supports discharge.

options.text: The client says, "I like to take my pills with a glass of orange juice each morning."
options.rationale: The method of taking a pill is a minor teaching point. It does not stop the client from taking the doses.

options.text: Blood glucose 168 mg/dL before breakfast, close to the client's readings at home this month
options.rationale: Diabetes affects immune status and is part of the infection risk, but this value matches the client's usual readings. It does not by itself stop the antibiotic from working.

options.text: The client says, "I often forget whether I took my pills, so I skip a dose to be safe."
options.rationale: The nurse considers the client's ability to follow the care plan. Skipped doses of an antibiotic taken 4 times a day leave the infection undertreated.

questions.takeaway: The infection assessment considers the client's immune status and the ability to follow the care plan. A client who cannot follow the antibiotic schedule is at risk for an undertreated infection.
questions.strategy: Ask which finding directly stops the treatment from being carried out. A known, usual value is less urgent than a behavior that removes doses.

steps.detail: No fever and a receding border show response.
The glucose matches the client's usual readings.

steps.action: Find the threat to the plan
steps.detail: Skipped doses undercut the antibiotic course.

elimination.verdict: D. The client skips doses when unsure.

questions.objective: Assess for infection and recognize clinical deterioration

questions.stem: A client, 70 years old, is admitted with a cough and fever. Oral temperature 38.3 °C, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 92% on room air. The complete blood count with differential shows a white blood cell count of 8200 per mm3. A chest radiograph shows an infiltrate in the right lower lobe. A sputum culture is pending. Which statement by the nurse in report interprets these results accurately?

options.text: "The radiograph locates the likely source, and the breathing findings show its effect."
options.rationale: Imaging helps locate the infection, and results are read together with the assessment. The fast breathing and low saturation show the infection's effect even though the cell count is not raised.

options.text: "The white blood cell count is not raised, so infection is unlikely and the radiograph can wait."
options.rationale: The blood count adds information about the immune response, but it is one piece. It does not outweigh the fever, the fast breathing, and the infiltrate.

options.text: "The pending culture must come back before any of these other results can guide the care."
options.rationale: The culture identifies the organism and guides the antimicrobial choice, but the other results and the assessment guide care now.

options.text: "The radiograph identifies the organism, so the pending sputum culture can be canceled."
options.rationale: Imaging locates the infection; it does not identify the organism. Culture and susceptibility does that.

questions.takeaway: Culture and susceptibility identifies the organism and guides treatment, the complete blood count with differential adds information about the immune response, and imaging helps locate the infection or its effects. Each result is interpreted together with the assessment.
questions.strategy: Match each test to what it can tell you, then check which statement reads the results with the assessment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Culture names the organism; the blood count shows the immune response; imaging locates the source.
Imaging cannot replace the culture.
Fast breathing and low saturation outweigh a cell count that is not raised.

elimination.verdict: A. The radiograph locates the source, read with the assessment.

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.stem: A client, 83 years old, is admitted with a urinary tract infection. Oral temperature 38.4 °C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, oral mucous membranes dry, and the client reports chills and body aches of 4 of 10. The urine culture has been collected, and the first dose of an intravenous antimicrobial is due now. Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give the first dose as ordered now that the urine culture is collected
options.rationale: The nurse treats the suspected cause as ordered. The culture is already collected, so nothing stands in the way of the dose.

options.text: Hold the antimicrobial until the oral temperature is below 38 °C
options.rationale: The antimicrobial treats the cause of the fever. Holding it delays treatment.

options.text: Offer oral fluids often, as allowed, and record intake and output
options.rationale: Supporting hydration is part of infection treatment, and dry mucous membranes with fever point to fluid loss.

options.text: Change damp linen and offer a light blanket while the chills last
options.rationale: Supporting comfort is part of treatment. Damp linen and chills add to the discomfort of fever.

options.text: Limit fluids so the client needs to urinate less often during the infection
options.rationale: Limiting fluids worsens dehydration. Hydration is supported, not restricted.

options.text: Check the drug, dose, and route against the order before starting it
options.rationale: Prescribed antimicrobials are given safely, which includes checking the order before the dose. Checking allergies before a first dose is part of the same check.

questions.takeaway: Treat the suspected or identified cause as ordered, give prescribed antimicrobials safely, and support hydration and comfort.
questions.strategy: Sort each action into treating the cause, giving the drug safely, supporting hydration, supporting comfort, or getting in the way of treatment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Give the ordered dose now, after checking the order.
Offer fluids and track intake and output.
Dry linen and a light blanket for chills.
Holding the dose and limiting fluids.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, F.

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.nursesNote: Day 3 of admission for an infected wound on the left foot, 1600. Dressing on the left foot dry and intact. Skin warm and flushed, heart rate 118 beats per minute, was 86 beats per minute at 1000. New pinpoint purple rash on both lower legs. Alert, oriented, and asking about dinner. Bowel sounds present in all 4 quadrants. Left foot pain 9 of 10, was 3 of 10 at 1000. Healed scar on the right knee. Oxygen saturation 91% on room air, was 96% at 1000.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that suggest sepsis.

segments.text: Dressing on the left foot dry and intact.
segments.rationale: A dry, intact dressing shows no new drainage. It is not a sign of sepsis.

segments.text: Skin warm and flushed, heart rate 118 beats per minute, was 86 beats per minute at 1000.
segments.rationale: A fast heart rate with warm skin is a sign of sepsis. Warm skin does not mean the client is doing well.

segments.text: New pinpoint purple rash on both lower legs.
segments.rationale: A new rash can be a sign of sepsis, especially away from the infected site.

segments.text: Alert, oriented, and asking about dinner.
segments.rationale: Mental status is at baseline. Sepsis can still be present, but this finding is not a cue of it.

segments.text: Bowel sounds present in all 4 quadrants.
segments.rationale: Bowel sounds in all quadrants are an expected finding.

segments.text: Left foot pain 9 of 10, was 3 of 10 at 1000.
segments.rationale: Extreme pain or discomfort is a sign of sepsis, and this is a sharp rise from 1000.

segments.text: Healed scar on the right knee.
segments.rationale: An old, healed scar is unrelated to the current infection.

segments.text: Oxygen saturation 91% on room air, was 96% at 1000.
segments.rationale: Decreased oxygen saturation shows the body may be struggling to meet its demands.

questions.takeaway: Signs of sepsis include a fast heart rate, warm or clammy skin, a rash, extreme pain or discomfort, and decreased oxygen saturation. Normal mental status does not rule sepsis out.
questions.strategy: Compare each finding with 1000 and ask whether it fits the whole body response to infection rather than the wound alone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Heart rate, pain, and saturation all moved.
A new rash on both legs.
Intact dressing, bowel sounds, the healed scar, and baseline mental status.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: A client, 67 years old, with sepsis from pneumonia has just finished the prescribed intravenous fluid bolus. Blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg, was 88/52 mm Hg before the bolus. Heart rate 124 beats per minute, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, both hands and feet cool and mottled, and urine output 10 mL per hour, was 25 mL per hour before the bolus. Which condition does the nurse recognize?

options.text: Sepsis that is responding to treatment, because the full bolus is in
options.rationale: Response is judged by the whole trend, not by finishing the fluids. Blood pressure and urine output are worse, and the skin shows poor perfusion.

options.text: An inflammatory response alone, since no organism is named in the blood
options.rationale: The client has pneumonia, a known infection, and an organism does not need to be found in the bloodstream for sepsis to be present.

options.text: Septic shock, because circulation keeps failing despite the fluids
options.rationale: Septic shock is the more severe form of sepsis, with significant circulatory and metabolic problems that can lead to organ failure and death. Blood pressure that falls despite fluids, cool mottled skin, and falling urine output show that circulation is failing.

options.text: Sepsis without shock, because the client is still making some urine
options.rationale: Some urine output does not rule out shock. 10 mL per hour with low blood pressure after fluids shows failing perfusion.

questions.takeaway: Septic shock is a more severe form of sepsis with significant circulatory and metabolic problems that can lead to organ failure and death. Low blood pressure that persists after fluids and signs of poor perfusion in the skin and urine output point to it, and persistent poor perfusion requires further escalation.
questions.strategy: Look at what the fluid bolus changed. When blood pressure, skin perfusion, and urine output all worsen after treatment, sepsis has progressed.

steps.detail: Blood pressure is lower than before the bolus.
Cool, mottled hands and feet and 10 mL per hour of urine.
Output fell from 25 to 10 mL per hour.

elimination.verdict: C. Septic shock.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

chapters.title: Acute Coronary Syndromes: Coronary Artery Disease

questions.stem: A client with hypertension and dyslipidemia asks how these conditions lead to coronary artery disease. The nurse explains that they injure the endothelium of the coronary artery, and that low density lipoprotein then enters the artery wall and is oxidized. Which event does the nurse describe next?

options.text: Macrophages are drawn into the wall and a fatty streak forms
options.rationale: Oxidized LDL attracts macrophages. They fill with lipid and form the fatty streak, the first visible lesion.

options.text: The fatty streak develops into a fibrous plaque in the wall
options.rationale: This is the right process one step too late. The fatty streak must form before it can mature into a fibrous plaque.

options.text: The narrowed coronary artery restricts blood flow to the heart
options.rationale: Narrowing comes after the plaque has formed and takes up room in the lumen.

options.text: Reduced oxygen delivery to the heart muscle causes ischemia
options.rationale: Ischemia is the end of the chain, after the artery has narrowed and flow is restricted.

questions.takeaway: Atherosclerosis becomes coronary artery disease in four steps: endothelial injury, plaque formation (LDL enters and is oxidized, macrophages form a fatty streak, then a fibrous plaque), narrowing of the coronary artery, and ischemia from reduced oxygen delivery.
questions.strategy: Build the plaque in the order it grows. Nothing can mature into a fibrous plaque until a fatty streak exists, and nothing narrows the artery until the plaque is there.

steps.detail: Endothelial injury, then LDL enters and is oxidized.
Fatty streak comes before fibrous plaque.
Narrowing and ischemia come after the plaque is formed.

elimination.verdict: A. Macrophages are drawn into the wall and a fatty streak forms.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.nursesNote: Client, 59 years old, seen for a wellness visit. Parent died of a myocardial infarction at 62 years old. Has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes per day for 30 years. Blood pressure 148/94 mm Hg. LDL cholesterol 172 mg/dL. Works at a desk and does not exercise. Body mass index 23 kg/m2. Fasting blood glucose 118 mg/dL. Eats fried food or fast food 5 days each week.
