questions.stem: Highlight the findings that are modifiable risk factors for coronary artery disease.

segments.text: Client, 59 years old
segments.rationale: Increasing age is a risk factor, but it is nonmodifiable. The client cannot change it.

segments.text: Parent died of a myocardial infarction at 62 years old
segments.rationale: Family history is a nonmodifiable risk factor. It raises risk but cannot be changed.

segments.text: Has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes per day for 30 years
segments.rationale: Cigarette smoking is a modifiable risk factor. It injures the endothelium, and the client can stop.

segments.text: Blood pressure 148/94 mm Hg
segments.rationale: 148/94 mm Hg is above the normal range of below 120/80 mm Hg. Hypertension is modifiable with lifestyle change and medication.

segments.text: LDL cholesterol 172 mg/dL
segments.rationale: 172 mg/dL is above the reference of below 100 mg/dL. Dyslipidemia is a modifiable risk factor.

segments.text: Works at a desk and does not exercise
segments.rationale: A sedentary lifestyle is a modifiable risk factor.

segments.text: Fasting blood glucose 118 mg/dL
segments.rationale: 118 mg/dL is above the reference of 70 to 99 mg/dL, which points to insulin resistance. Diabetes and insulin resistance are modifiable risk factors.

segments.text: Eats fried food or fast food 5 days each week
segments.rationale: An atherogenic diet, high in fat, is a modifiable risk factor.

segments.text: Body mass index 23 kg/m2
segments.rationale: A body mass index of 23 kg/m2 is inside the reference range of 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m2, so obesity is not present.

questions.takeaway: Modifiable risk factors for coronary artery disease are dyslipidemia, hypertension, cigarette smoking, diabetes and insulin resistance, obesity and a sedentary lifestyle, and an atherogenic diet. Age and family history raise risk but cannot be changed.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions of each finding: does it raise risk, and can the client change it? Age and family history pass the first test and fail the second. A value inside its range fails the first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Age 59 and a parent's myocardial infarction cannot be changed.

steps.action: Check each value against its range
steps.detail: Blood pressure, LDL, and glucose are above range. Body mass index 23 kg/m2 is inside 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m2.
Smoking, no exercise, and frequent fried or fast food are all changeable.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client, 52 years old, has blood pressure readings of 164/98 mm Hg and 160/96 mm Hg at two clinic visits. LDL cholesterol is 92 mg/dL, and the client has never smoked. The client asks, "My cholesterol is in range, so how could my blood pressure put plaque in my heart arteries?" Which response by the nurse answers the client's question?

options.text: "High pressure makes your heart work harder and need more oxygen, so plaque in your heart arteries starts to cause chest pressure."
options.rationale: This is true about hypertension and the heart, but it explains why existing plaque causes symptoms. The client asked how plaque forms.

options.text: "High pressure thickens the heart muscle until it presses on the coronary arteries and narrows them from the outside."
options.rationale: Hypertension can thicken the left ventricle, but plaque narrows a coronary artery from inside the wall, not by outside pressure.

options.text: "High pressure makes the artery walls thicken and stiffen over time, and that thickened wall is the plaque."
options.rationale: Hypertension does thicken arteriole walls (medial hyperplasia), but plaque is a buildup of lipid laden macrophages inside the wall that starts with endothelial injury, not the thickened muscle layer.

options.text: "High pressure damages the inner lining of your heart arteries, which lets cholesterol get into the wall and start plaque."
options.rationale: Endothelial injury from hypertension is the first step of atherosclerosis. Once the lining is injured, LDL enters the wall, is oxidized, and starts plaque.

questions.takeaway: Hypertension contributes to coronary artery disease two ways: it injures the endothelium, which starts plaque formation, and it raises myocardial oxygen demand. The question asked decides which one is the answer.
questions.strategy: Two options are true about hypertension and the heart. The deciding cue is the client's exact question: how pressure puts plaque in the arteries. Only the endothelial injury answer explains plaque.

steps.action: Read the question the client asked
steps.detail: The client asks how blood pressure causes plaque, not why chest pain happens.

steps.action: Set aside the true but off target option
steps.detail: Higher oxygen demand explains angina, not plaque formation.
Plaque grows inside the wall.
Medial thickening from hypertension is not plaque. Plaque starts with injury to the lining.
Endothelial injury lets LDL into the wall.

elimination.verdict: Hypertension injures the lining, which lets LDL enter the wall and start plaque.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: A client with coronary artery disease has chest pressure that starts after walking uphill for about 5 minutes and goes away within 3 minutes of sitting down. The client asks why it comes and goes. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: A plaque narrows the artery so that flow meets the heart's needs at rest but falls short during exertion
options.rationale: The narrowed artery restricts flow. At rest the supply is enough. Walking uphill raises demand, oxygen delivery falls short, and ischemia causes the pressure until rest lowers demand again.

options.text: A clot fully blocks the artery while the client walks and then dissolves each time the client sits down
options.rationale: Plaque rupture with a clot causes an acute coronary syndrome. A clot does not form and dissolve on a predictable schedule with each walk.

options.text: Walking sends blood to the leg muscles and away from the heart, and sitting returns the flow to the heart
options.rationale: Exertion raises the heart's own demand; it does not divert coronary flow to the legs. The pressure comes from a narrowed artery that cannot raise supply to match.

options.text: A spasm of the coronary artery closes it during walking, and the spasm relaxes once the client sits down
options.rationale: Vasospastic angina usually occurs at rest or in the early morning, not on a predictable exertion schedule. A fixed narrowing that cannot meet higher demand fits this pattern.

questions.takeaway: A fixed narrowing restricts coronary flow. When exertion raises oxygen demand beyond what the narrowed artery can supply, the muscle becomes ischemic, and rest ends the shortfall. That is the predictable pattern of chronic angina.
questions.strategy: Every option offers a mechanism for pressure that comes and goes. Choose the one that fits a predictable trigger and relief with rest: a fixed narrowing that cannot raise supply when demand rises.

steps.detail: Pressure with uphill walking that ends within 3 minutes of sitting.

steps.action: Match it to supply and demand
steps.detail: Narrowing limits supply, exertion raises demand, rest lowers it.
Exertion raises the heart's own demand; it does not divert coronary flow to the legs.
A clot is the acute event, not a predictable pattern.
Spasm angina comes at rest, not predictably with exertion.

elimination.verdict: Narrowed artery: supply meets demand at rest but not during exertion.

questions.stem: A client has had chronic angina for 2 years. The chest pressure has always started after climbing two flights of stairs and ended within 3 minutes of rest. Over the past 2 weeks, the same pressure starts after walking from the bedroom to the kitchen, and it still ends within 3 minutes of rest. No pressure now. Blood pressure 128/78 mm Hg, heart rate 82 beats per minute. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Reinforce the plan to rest at the first sign of pressure, because rest still ends it within 3 minutes
options.rationale: Relief with rest fits chronic angina, and teaching rest is reasonable. But the pressure now starts with far less exertion. That is a worsening pattern, and reinforcing the old plan leaves it unevaluated.

options.text: Teach the client to take sublingual nitroglycerin before walking to the kitchen to prevent the pressure
options.rationale: Taking nitroglycerin before a known trigger is reasonable teaching for a predictable pattern. This pattern is no longer predictable: the threshold has dropped from two flights of stairs to a short walk, and that change needs evaluation, not prevention.

options.text: Report the change in the pattern to the provider today for urgent evaluation
options.rationale: Angina that is new, worsening, or at rest is unstable and needs urgent evaluation. Pressure that once needed two flights of stairs and now comes with walking to the kitchen is worsening.

options.text: Document the episodes and review the pattern again at the routine clinic visit in 3 months
options.rationale: Documenting is part of care, but waiting 3 months delays evaluation of angina that is getting worse.

questions.takeaway: Chronic angina is predictable: the same trigger, the same relief. A change in the pattern, such as pressure that now starts with less exertion, means unstable angina and urgent evaluation, even when rest still relieves it.
questions.strategy: Relief with rest makes the old plan look right. The deciding cue is the trigger: two flights of stairs before, a walk to the kitchen now. A lower threshold is a worsening pattern.

steps.action: Compare the trigger then and now
steps.detail: Two flights of stairs, now bedroom to kitchen.
Worsening angina is unstable, even with relief by rest.
Reinforcing rest and waiting 3 months both leave the change unevaluated.

steps.action: Reject prevention of the old pattern
steps.detail: Nitroglycerin before exertion treats a predictable pattern. The pattern has changed.

elimination.verdict: Report the worsening pattern for urgent evaluation.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client, 74 years old, with coronary artery disease and type 2 diabetes mellitus calls the clinic to describe symptoms from the past week. Which reports may be manifestations of myocardial ischemia? Select all that apply.

options.text: An ache in the jaw that starts while raking leaves and stops with rest
options.rationale: Angina may radiate to the jaw. Onset with exertion and relief with rest fit ischemia.

options.text: Unusual fatigue and weakness while making the bed
options.rationale: Fatigue and weakness can accompany ischemia, and some clients have atypical symptoms rather than chest pain.

options.text: Shortness of breath and sweating while carrying groceries up the stairs
options.rationale: Dyspnea and diaphoresis can occur with ischemia, and they came on with exertion.

options.text: Cramping in the right calf after walking one block that stops when standing still
options.rationale: The exertion and rest pattern looks like angina, but the discomfort is in the right calf. Angina radiates to the jaw, neck, shoulder, arm, or back, not the leg.

options.text: Pressure across the upper back that comes on with exertion
options.rationale: Angina may radiate to the back, and pressure is a common description.

options.text: Pain in the left shoulder that began after lifting a heavy box and worsens when the arm moves
options.rationale: The shoulder is a site angina can reach, but this pain began with a lift and changes with arm movement, which points to the muscle or joint rather than the heart.

questions.takeaway: Angina is pressure, heaviness, squeezing, or pain that may radiate to the jaw, neck, shoulder, arm, or back, and it may come with dyspnea, diaphoresis, pallor, fatigue, or weakness. Some clients have atypical or silent ischemia, so ask about associated symptoms, not only chest pain.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options borrow one feature of angina: the exertion and rest pattern, or the shoulder location. Check every report for both a site angina reaches and a pattern ischemia follows.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Jaw, back, and shoulder are sites angina reaches. The calf is not.
Fatigue, weakness, dyspnea, and diaphoresis can all accompany ischemia.
Shoulder pain that started with a lift and changes with arm movement points to a muscle or joint.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client with chronic angina for 3 years, whose chest pressure has always come only with exertion, arrives at the emergency department with chest pressure that began 30 minutes ago while sitting at a desk. Pain 6 of 10. Blood pressure 150/90 mm Hg, heart rate 102 beats per minute. Which process best explains the change in the client's chest pressure?

options.text: The plaque has slowly grown, so flow now falls short only when exertion raises the heart's demand
options.rationale: Slow growth of a fixed plaque explains angina with exertion. This pressure began at rest, so exertion is not the trigger.

options.text: A plaque has likely ruptured and a clot has formed, cutting flow to the heart muscle even at rest
options.rationale: Plaque rupture with thrombosis turns chronic narrowing into an acute coronary syndrome. Pressure that starts at rest in a client whose pressure came only with exertion fits that change.

options.text: New LDL entered the artery wall today and formed a fatty streak that is now blocking the artery
options.rationale: A fatty streak is an early lesion that develops over time. It does not form in a day or block an artery.

options.text: The blood pressure of 150/90 mm Hg raised demand above what the narrowed artery can supply
options.rationale: Higher pressure does raise demand, but the client is sitting at a desk. A sudden change to pressure at rest points to rupture and a clot, not this blood pressure.

questions.takeaway: Plaque rupture and thrombosis are what turn chronic coronary artery disease into an acute coronary syndrome or acute myocardial infarction. Angina that changes to occurring at rest is the cue.
questions.strategy: Ask what changed. Angina with exertion is a narrowing problem. Pressure at rest in a client whose angina came only with exertion means something new happened in the artery: rupture and a clot.

steps.detail: Pressure has always come with exertion. Now it began at rest.
Gradual growth and a new fatty streak do not cause sudden pressure at rest.
150/90 mm Hg at a desk does not explain the abrupt change.
Rupture and a clot cut flow at rest.

elimination.verdict: Plaque rupture with a clot.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.scenario: A client with coronary artery disease diagnosed 6 months ago arrives at the emergency department. Chest pressure began 40 minutes ago while lying on the sofa. Pain 7 of 10, radiating to the left arm, with diaphoresis and shortness of breath. Blood pressure 156/92 mm Hg, heart rate 106 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Lungs are clear in both bases, and there is no edema in either ankle.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Draw blood for a troponin level as prescribed
options.rationale: Troponin T and I are the preferred biomarkers for acute myocardial infarction.

options.text: Obtain a chest X ray to look for pulmonary congestion
options.rationale: A chest X ray is a CAD diagnostic, but the lungs are clear in both bases, so it does not answer the question this presentation raises.

options.text: Teach a low sodium diet before discharge
options.rationale: Diet teaching is part of risk reduction, but it does not address pressure at rest happening now.

options.text: Obtain a 12 lead ECG
options.rationale: The 12 lead ECG is a core diagnostic test for coronary artery disease and acute coronary syndrome.

options.text: Draw a B type natriuretic peptide level to assess for heart failure
options.rationale: BNP points to ventricular stretch and fluid overload. Clear lungs and no edema do not suggest heart failure; ischemia is the problem.

options.text: Left sided heart failure
options.rationale: Left sided failure causes pulmonary congestion with crackles. The lungs are clear in both bases.

options.text: Acute coronary syndrome
options.rationale: Pressure at rest, 7 of 10, with diaphoresis and dyspnea in a client with known coronary artery disease fits an acute coronary syndrome.

options.text: Chronic angina with a predictable pattern
options.rationale: Predictable angina comes with exertion and ends with rest. This pressure began while lying on the sofa.

options.text: Hypertensive crisis
options.rationale: Hypertensive crisis is a blood pressure of 180/120 mm Hg or higher. This reading is 156/92 mm Hg.

options.text: Orthostatic blood pressure
options.rationale: Orthostatic checks are a hypertension and medication assessment. Standing a client with active ischemia raises demand and is not the priority.

options.text: Capillary blood glucose
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario points to a glucose problem; pain and rhythm show whether ischemia continues.

options.text: Heart rhythm on the cardiac monitor
options.rationale: Ischemic muscle is irritable, and a heart rate of 106 beats per minute is already above range.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: Daily weight tracks fluid in heart failure. Lungs are clear and there is no edema.

options.text: Chest pain intensity
options.rationale: Pain intensity shows whether ischemia is continuing or easing with treatment.

questions.takeaway: Chest pressure at rest with diaphoresis and dyspnea in a client with coronary artery disease is an acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise. Obtain a 12 lead ECG and a troponin, and watch pain intensity and heart rhythm.
questions.strategy: Rule out each condition with one stem fact: the pressure began at rest, the pressure is below 180/120 mm Hg, and the lungs are clear. Then choose the actions that diagnose the problem now and the parameters that show whether ischemia is continuing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pressure at rest with diaphoresis and dyspnea: acute coronary syndrome.
Not predictable angina, not 180/120 mm Hg or higher, lungs clear.
12 lead ECG and troponin.
Lungs clear, no edema.
Pain intensity and heart rhythm.

elimination.verdict: Actions: 12 lead ECG and troponin. Condition: acute coronary syndrome. Parameters: pain intensity and heart rhythm.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A nurse in the emergency department reviews the chest symptoms and test results of six clients with coronary artery disease. Which findings are consistent with an acute coronary syndrome rather than chronic angina with a predictable pattern? Select all that apply.

options.text: Chest heaviness when climbing two flights of stairs that ends after 3 minutes of rest, unchanged for 8 months
options.rationale: A predictable trigger and relief with rest, unchanged for months, is chronic angina.

options.text: Chest pressure that began while lying in bed reading
options.rationale: Angina at rest is unstable and needs urgent evaluation.

options.text: Jaw ache during yard work that ends with sitting down, in a pattern present for 1 year
options.rationale: Radiation to the jaw can occur with any angina. The trigger, relief, and 1 year pattern make this predictable.

options.text: A first episode of chest squeezing, which started yesterday
options.rationale: New angina is unstable. There is no established pattern to call predictable.

options.text: Chest pressure with a troponin I of 0.4 ng/mL
options.rationale: Troponin is the preferred biomarker for acute myocardial infarction. A value above range with chest pressure points to infarction.

options.text: Pressure with brisk walking that ends after a nitrate, in a pattern unchanged over the past year
options.rationale: Predictable angina is relieved by rest or nitrates.

questions.takeaway: Chronic angina is predictable with exertion or stress and relieved by rest or nitrates. Angina that is new, worsening, or at rest is unstable, and troponin above range points to myocardial infarction; both are acute coronary syndromes.
questions.strategy: Ignore how dramatic a symptom sounds. Jaw ache can be part of a predictable pattern. Sort each finding by trigger, relief, and whether the pattern is new or changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Look for rest or new onset
steps.detail: Pressure in bed and a first episode are unstable.
Troponin I above 0.03 ng/mL points to infarction.

steps.action: Look for the same trigger and relief over time
steps.detail: Stairs, yard work, and brisk walking with relief by rest or a nitrate are predictable.
Jaw ache does not by itself make angina unstable.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client arrives at the emergency department with chest pressure that began 45 minutes ago while watching television. Pain 5 of 10. The 12 lead ECG shows no ST elevation. The first troponin I is 0.01 ng/mL. The provider prescribes continuous cardiac monitoring and repeat troponin levels. The client says, "My heart tracing and blood test are normal, so can I go home now?" Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "These results point to unstable angina rather than a heart attack, so the repeat levels are a routine precaution."
options.rationale: Unstable angina does not raise troponin, so this sounds reasonable. But the pressure began only 45 minutes ago, too early for troponin to separate unstable angina from an infarction without ST elevation. The repeat levels are not a formality.

options.text: "Troponin can take hours to rise after heart muscle is damaged, so the repeat levels come first."
options.rationale: In infarction without ST elevation, troponin may be normal at first and rise over 3 to 12 hours. The pressure began 45 minutes ago, so the first value is too early to rule out infarction.

options.text: "You will need a treadmill stress test first, and if it shows no changes, you can go home later today."
options.rationale: A stress test is part of the workup, but it is done after the acute stage. Exercise now would raise demand while pressure from 45 minutes ago may still be an acute event.

options.text: "Your tracing shows no ST elevation, so this is not a heart attack, and the repeat test checks for other causes."
options.rationale: Infarction can occur without ST elevation, and in that case troponin rises over 3 to 12 hours.

questions.takeaway: Troponin T and I are the preferred markers for acute myocardial infarction, but they are drawn as a series. In infarction without ST elevation the first value may be normal and rise over 3 to 12 hours, so an early normal result does not rule out infarction.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stress test sounds like the logical next diagnostic step. The deciding cue is time: pressure began only 45 minutes ago, too early for troponin to have risen, and stress testing waits until after the acute stage.

steps.detail: The pressure began 45 minutes ago.
Troponin may rise over 3 to 12 hours, so one early normal value does not rule out infarction.
It comes after the acute stage, not during pressure at rest.
45 minutes is too early to call unstable angina or rule out infarction.

elimination.verdict: Explain that troponin can take hours to rise, so the repeat levels are needed.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client in the emergency department with chest pressure 7 of 10 has a prescription for sublingual nitroglycerin. Blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg, heart rate 98 beats per minute, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Which finding requires the nurse to clarify the prescription before giving the dose?

options.text: A blood pressure of 138/84 mm Hg, which is above the normal range
options.rationale: Checking blood pressure before a nitrate is right, but a reading of 138/84 mm Hg is well above the level at which nitroglycerin is withheld.

options.text: The client chewed aspirin 325 mg at home 30 minutes before arrival
options.rationale: Chewed aspirin is part of emergency care for new chest pressure. It does not interact dangerously with nitroglycerin.

options.text: The client took tadalafil for erectile dysfunction 14 hours ago
options.rationale: Nitroglycerin within 24 to 48 hours of a phosphodiesterase inhibitor such as tadalafil can cause profound hypotension. 14 hours is inside that window.

options.text: The client reports a mild headache that began this morning
options.rationale: A mild headache is not a reason to withhold nitroglycerin. Headache is a common nitrate effect, so the nurse expects it may worsen after the dose, but it does not make the dose unsafe.

questions.takeaway: Before giving nitroglycerin, ask about sildenafil, tadalafil, avanafil, or vardenafil in the past 24 to 48 hours. Together they can cause profound hypotension. Recheck pain and vital signs 5 minutes after each dose.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three findings are expected in chest pressure or its treatment. The one that makes the drug dangerous is an interaction, not a vital sign that is above range.

steps.detail: A reading of 138/84 mm Hg is well above the level at which nitroglycerin is withheld.
Chewed aspirin belongs in chest pain care.
A mild headache does not contraindicate nitroglycerin.
Tadalafil 14 hours ago is within 24 to 48 hours.

elimination.verdict: Tadalafil taken 14 hours ago.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client with coronary artery disease is due for oral metoprolol at 0900. At 0845, heart rate is 64 beats per minute and blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg. The client reports no chest pain, and the lungs are clear in both bases. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the dose, because both values are within their reference ranges
options.rationale: Both values sit inside the stated ranges, but a beta blocker is held for a systolic pressure below 100 mm Hg. 88 mm Hg is below that hold point.

options.text: Give the dose and recheck the blood pressure in 1 hour
options.rationale: The dose would lower an already low systolic pressure before the recheck.

options.text: Give half of the dose to limit the drop in blood pressure
options.rationale: Changing a prescribed dose is outside the nurse's scope, and any dose would lower the pressure further.

options.text: Hold the dose and report the blood pressure to the provider
options.rationale: Beta blockers lower heart rate and cardiac output. A systolic pressure below 100 mm Hg is a hold point even when the heart rate is acceptable.

questions.takeaway: Assess heart rate and blood pressure before every beta blocker dose. Hold and contact the provider for a pulse below 50 beats per minute or a systolic pressure below 100 mm Hg; either one alone is enough, and a value inside a general reference range can still be below a drug hold point.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Both values sit inside their stated reference ranges, which makes giving the dose look acceptable. The drug has its own hold point: a systolic pressure of 88 mm Hg is below 100 mm Hg, and that alone is reason to hold.

steps.detail: Heart rate 64 beats per minute is above the hold point. Systolic 88 mm Hg is below 100 mm Hg.
Either value below its hold point means hold.
The dose would lower the pressure further before the recheck.
The nurse does not change a prescribed dose.

elimination.verdict: Hold the dose and report the blood pressure.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: Which treatments in the plan of care for a client with coronary artery disease reduce myocardial oxygen demand? Select all that apply.

options.text: A beta blocker that slows the heart rate
options.rationale: A slower heart rate means less work for the heart muscle, so it needs less oxygen.

options.text: Percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent
options.rationale: PCI opens the narrowed artery. It improves coronary flow, the supply side, rather than lowering demand.

options.text: Rest periods between activities such as bathing and walking
options.rationale: Rest lowers the heart's workload and therefore its oxygen needs.

options.text: Lowering the blood pressure from 152/94 mm Hg toward the goal of below 130/80 mm Hg
options.rationale: The heart pumps against the blood pressure. Lowering it toward the goal of below 130/80 mm Hg reduces workload and oxygen demand.

options.text: Coronary artery bypass grafting
options.rationale: CABG routes blood around the blocked artery. It improves supply, not demand.

options.text: Antiplatelet therapy
options.rationale: Antiplatelet therapy helps keep a clot from forming on plaque. It protects flow, the supply side.

questions.takeaway: CAD treatment works on both sides of the balance: improve coronary flow (PCI or stent, CABG, antiplatelet therapy) and reduce myocardial oxygen demand (beta blockers, rest, blood pressure control), while preventing complications.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each treatment by side: does it bring more blood to the muscle, or make the muscle need less? Revascularization and antiplatelet therapy all work on supply.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Slower heart rate, rest, and lower blood pressure all cut workload.
PCI, CABG, and antiplatelet therapy all protect or restore flow.
A, C, D.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client is admitted with coronary artery disease. Cardiac catheterization shows long, calcified narrowings in three coronary arteries. Which treatment does the nurse prepare the client for, and why?

options.text: Percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent, because it opens the vessel without surgery
options.rationale: PCI works best for single or double vessel disease with discrete, noncalcified lesions. These narrowings are long, calcified and in three vessels.

options.text: Coronary artery bypass grafting, because it improves cardiac output in heart failure
options.rationale: Bypass grafting is the right procedure, but improving cardiac output is a heart failure goal. CAD treatment aims to improve flow, reduce myocardial oxygen demand, and prevent complications.

options.text: Coronary artery bypass grafting, because grafts carry blood around the diseased arteries
options.rationale: CABG bypasses occluded arteries with grafts. It is indicated for multivessel disease that PCI does not suit, such as long, calcified narrowings in three vessels.

options.text: Fibrinolytic therapy, because it dissolves the material that is narrowing the arteries
options.rationale: Fibrinolytics dissolve a fresh clot. They do not treat fixed calcified narrowing.

questions.takeaway: CAD treatment aims to improve coronary flow, reduce myocardial oxygen demand, and prevent complications, using risk factor reduction, nitrates, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, antiplatelet therapy, and revascularization by PCI or CABG.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask what each treatment does: opens a discrete lesion, bypasses disease a stent cannot treat, or dissolves a fresh clot. Then check that the reason matches a CAD goal, not a heart failure goal.

steps.action: Match the disease to the procedure
steps.detail: Long, calcified narrowings in three vessels do not suit PCI: CABG.
Fibrinolytics act on a fresh clot, not calcified plaque.
Only one gives the reason that fits CAD; improving cardiac output belongs to heart failure.

elimination.verdict: C. Coronary artery bypass grafting, because grafts carry blood around the diseased arteries.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A nurse evaluates discharge teaching on risk factor reduction with six clients who have coronary artery disease. Which client statements indicate a need for further teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: "My diabetes is a risk I can change, because keeping my glucose in my target range lowers it."
options.rationale: Diabetes and insulin resistance are modifiable risk factors, and glucose control lowers the risk.

options.text: "My LDL reached my target on the statin, so the fried food I eat most days no longer adds to my risk."
options.rationale: Reaching an LDL target is real progress, but an atherogenic diet is its own modifiable risk factor. The cue is fried food most days.

options.text: "Being 67 years old is a risk I cannot change, so I will put my effort into my weight and my walking."
options.rationale: The client correctly separates a nonmodifiable factor from modifiable ones and acts on the modifiable ones.

options.text: "My parent had a heart attack at 52, so my risk is already set and stopping smoking would not change much."
options.rationale: Family history is nonmodifiable, but it does not cancel the benefit of changing modifiable factors. Smoking is one of the most important to stop.

options.text: "My pressure is 126/78 mm Hg on my medicine, so I will keep taking it and keep my salt low."
options.rationale: Hypertension is controlled by both the drug and sodium reduction, and the client keeps both going.

options.text: "I lost 10 lb, so my weight is no longer a risk factor even though I stopped walking last month."
options.rationale: Weight loss lowers the obesity risk, but a sedentary lifestyle is a risk factor too. The cue is that the client stopped walking.

questions.takeaway: Modifiable CAD risk factors are dyslipidemia, hypertension, smoking, diabetes and insulin resistance, obesity and sedentary lifestyle, and atherogenic diet; age and family history are not modifiable. Progress on one factor never cancels another, and a nonmodifiable risk never makes the modifiable ones pointless.
questions.strategy: Each statement starts with something true. Read to the end for the cue that turns it wrong: fried food most days, would not change much, or stopped walking.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A statin target does not cancel diet; weight loss does not cancel inactivity.
Family history does not make quitting smoking pointless.
Glucose control, acting on modifiable factors at 67, and drug plus salt reduction are all correct.

elimination.verdict: B, D, F.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client had chest pressure that began at 0600 on day 1 and was diagnosed with an acute myocardial infarction. Percutaneous coronary intervention opened the blocked artery at 0900. Compared with a client whose artery stays blocked, this client's troponin I and creatine kinase MB levels peaked earlier, which reflects [[1]].

On day 6, troponin I is still elevated, while creatine kinase MB has returned to the client's baseline. This pattern is expected because [[2]].

The nurse explains that troponin T and I are the preferred markers for an acute myocardial infarction because [[3]].

options.text: A larger area of heart muscle damage than in a blocked artery
options.rationale: An earlier peak reflects the return of flow, not the size of the damage. Reperfusion is meant to limit damage.

options.text: A second infarction that occurred during the procedure
options.rationale: A second infarction would cause a new rise later. An early peak after flow returns is the expected pattern.

options.text: Washout of the markers from the heart muscle once blood flow returned
options.rationale: Restoring flow carries the markers out of the injured muscle into the blood quickly, so levels peak earlier after reperfusion.

options.text: Injury to the leg muscle where the catheter was inserted
options.rationale: Troponin T and I are specific to heart muscle, so a catheter site cannot explain an earlier troponin peak.

options.text: Troponin stays elevated for days longer than creatine kinase MB
options.rationale: Creatine kinase MB returns to baseline within a few days, while troponin remains elevated for more than a week after an infarction.

options.text: The infarction has healed by day 6, so creatine kinase MB is no longer released
options.rationale: Healing takes weeks. The difference reflects how long each marker stays in the blood, not completed healing.

options.text: Troponin rises again each day that ischemia continues
options.rationale: A persisting troponin after one infarction is expected. It does not mean new ischemia is happening each day.

options.text: They rise within minutes of reversible ischemia
options.rationale: Reversible ischemia, as in unstable angina, does not cause a detectable troponin rise. Troponin rises over hours after cell death.

options.text: They are released only from damaged heart muscle
options.rationale: Troponin T and I are specific to cardiac muscle, so an elevated level points to heart muscle injury.

options.text: They also rise with injury to skeletal muscle, which widens the time to detect damage
options.rationale: Troponin T and I are specific to cardiac muscle. Skeletal muscle injury does not raise them, which is why they are preferred over less specific markers.

questions.takeaway: Troponin T and I are the preferred markers for acute MI because they are specific to heart muscle, and they stay elevated for more than a week. Creatine kinase MB returns to baseline within a few days. Reperfusion makes both markers peak earlier.
questions.strategy: Read the graph in two parts: reperfusion changes when the markers peak, and each marker's lifespan in the blood explains the day 6 pattern.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Flow returned at 0900, so the markers wash out and peak early.
Creatine kinase MB clears in days; troponin lingers longer.
Troponin is specific to heart muscle.

elimination.verdict: Washout after flow returned; troponin stays elevated longer; troponin is released only from damaged heart muscle.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client is going home after a coronary stent on aspirin 81 mg and clopidogrel 75 mg, both once daily. Which statement by the client shows understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "I will call my provider if I have black stools, nosebleeds or bruises I cannot explain."
options.rationale: Bleeding is the major side effect of aspirin and clopidogrel taken together. Black stools, nosebleeds and unexplained bruising are signs to report.

options.text: "I can take an over the counter pain reliever with aspirin for my back, since aspirin protects my heart."
options.rationale: Products with added aspirin raise the dose and the bleeding risk. Over the counter pain relievers with aspirin are avoided.

options.text: "Once a month passes with no chest pain, I can stop the clopidogrel on my own."
options.rationale: Clopidogrel keeps platelets from clumping on the stent and is continued for up to 12 months. Stopping it without the provider raises the risk of a clot.

options.text: "I will take my aspirin on an empty stomach so that it starts working faster."
options.rationale: Aspirin is taken with food because it irritates the stomach. Taking it on an empty stomach raises that risk.

questions.takeaway: After a stent, dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor such as clopidogrel prevents clotting on the stent. Teach to report bleeding, avoid extra aspirin, take with food and never stop the drugs without the provider.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each wrong option sounds like a reasonable plan for the client. Ask which one matches the main risk of two antiplatelet drugs together: bleeding.

steps.detail: Two antiplatelet drugs together raise bleeding risk.
Extra aspirin adds to that risk.
Stopping clopidogrel early risks a clot in the new stent.
Aspirin is taken with food.

elimination.verdict: The client will report signs of bleeding.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client with coronary artery disease and a predictable pattern of angina calls the clinic from home. Chest pressure began 7 minutes ago while carrying laundry upstairs. The client sat down and placed 1 sublingual nitroglycerin tablet under the tongue 5 minutes ago. The pressure is 5 of 10, the same as before the tablet. The client adds, "The tablet did not tingle. That bottle was opened 8 months ago and I keep the pills in a plastic pill box. I have a new bottle in the cabinet." Which instruction does the nurse give?

options.text: "Your tablets have likely lost strength. Take one from the new bottle now, and call back if the pressure has not eased in 5 minutes."
options.rationale: The old tablets may well have lost potency, since they lose strength over 3 to 5 months and outside a glass container. But the rule is about time, not the tablet: no relief 5 minutes after 1 tablet means 911 now.

options.text: "Call 911 now. While you wait for the ambulance, take a tablet from the new bottle."
options.rationale: Chest pressure that has not eased 5 minutes after 1 tablet calls for 911 now, whatever the reason the tablet failed. The client may then take a fresh tablet while waiting.

options.text: "Lie down and rest 10 more minutes, because rest is what usually ends your pressure."
options.rationale: The client has already rested 7 minutes and taken a tablet with no relief. Pressure that does not respond is not the usual pattern.

options.text: "Have a neighbor drive you to the emergency department now, and bring the old bottle with you."
options.rationale: Emergency care is needed, but a private car cannot give care if the rhythm or pressure worsens on the way. Emergency services are called.

questions.takeaway: At home: stop, sit or lie down, take 1 nitroglycerin tablet, and wait 5 minutes. If there is no relief, call 911, then repeat the tablet every 5 minutes while waiting. Replace tablets every 3 to 5 months and keep them in a glass, light resistant container.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The old bottle is a real problem and makes A tempting. The deciding cue is the time: 5 minutes after 1 tablet with the pressure unchanged. The 911 call does not wait for a second try.

steps.detail: 5 minutes after 1 tablet, pressure unchanged at 5 of 10.
No relief at 5 minutes means call 911 now.
Lost potency explains the failure but does not change the rule; a fresh tablet is taken while waiting.
More rest delays care; a private car cannot give care on the way.

elimination.verdict: Call 911 now and take a fresh tablet while waiting.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a client with suspected coronary artery disease about the diagnostic tests the provider has prescribed. Which statements by the client indicate correct understanding? Select all that apply.

options.text: "The catheterization will show exactly where my heart arteries are narrowed and how much."
options.rationale: Cardiac catheterization shows the extent and exact location of coronary obstructions and helps decide between PCI and CABG.

options.text: "The treadmill stress test watches my heart tracing for signs of low oxygen while my heart works harder."
options.rationale: The exercise tolerance test looks for ECG changes of ischemia as exertion raises the heart's demand.

options.text: "The thallium scan shows cold spots where blood is not reaching my heart muscle."
options.rationale: Thallium imaging shows areas of reduced or absent perfusion, called cold spots, that mark ischemia or infarction.

options.text: "The echocardiogram measures how much troponin my heart muscle is releasing."
options.rationale: An echocardiogram is an ultrasound of heart structure and motion. Troponin is measured with a blood test.

options.text: "The chest x ray can show whether my heart is enlarged or fluid is building up in my lungs."
options.rationale: A chest x ray shows the size of the heart and congestion in the lungs. It does not show plaque inside the coronary arteries.

options.text: "The stress test is done while I have chest pressure so the tracing catches the problem."
options.rationale: A stress test is done after an acute episode has passed. Exercising during active chest pressure would worsen ischemia.

questions.takeaway: Catheterization maps the location and extent of narrowing; the stress test shows ischemia under exertion; thallium shows cold spots; echocardiography shows structure; troponin is a blood test; the chest x ray shows heart size and lung congestion, not plaque.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Match each test with what it actually measures. Wrong options pair a real test with a job that belongs to a different test.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Location and extent of narrowing: correct.
Ischemia under exertion and cold spots: correct.
Heart size and lung congestion: correct.
An echocardiogram does not measure troponin.
No stress test during active chest pressure.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client in a cardiac unit has chest pressure, 6 of 10, at 1400. Blood pressure is 136/82 mm Hg and heart rate is 88 beats per minute. The nurse has the client lie down and gives 1 sublingual nitroglycerin tablet, prescribed every 5 minutes for up to 3 tablets. At 1405, chest pressure is 4 of 10, blood pressure is 104/64 mm Hg, and heart rate is 94 beats per minute. The client is alert and denies dizziness. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the second tablet, because the pressure persists and the systolic pressure is above 100 mm Hg
options.rationale: The systolic is above 100 mm Hg, but it has fallen 32 mm Hg in 5 minutes. The textbook rule is to lower the head of the bed and notify the provider if the systolic is less than 100 mm Hg or 25 mm Hg lower than the previous reading.

options.text: Give the second tablet and recheck the pressure in 5 minutes, because the chest pressure is easing
options.rationale: Easing pain shows the drug is working, but it does not make another dose safe after a 32 mm Hg fall. A second tablet could drop the pressure further.

options.text: Sit the client upright and recheck the blood pressure in 5 minutes before deciding on the dose
options.rationale: Rechecking is reasonable, but sitting upright can lower the pressure further. The head of the bed is kept low after a nitrate causes a large drop.

options.text: Withhold the second tablet, keep the head of the bed low, and notify the provider
options.rationale: The systolic fell from 136 to 104 mm Hg, more than 25 mm Hg below the previous reading. The nurse holds the next dose, keeps the client low and reports for another plan.

questions.takeaway: Before repeating sublingual nitroglycerin, check the blood pressure 5 minutes after each dose. Hold the next dose, lower the head of the bed and notify the provider if the systolic is below 100 mm Hg or 25 mm Hg lower than the previous reading.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A tempts because the prescription allows up to 3 tablets and the systolic is still above 100 mm Hg. The deciding cue is the 32 mm Hg fall from 136 to 104 mm Hg in 5 minutes.

steps.detail: Systolic 104 mm Hg is above 100, but it fell 32 mm Hg.
A fall of more than 25 mm Hg means hold the next dose.
A and B both give the second tablet.
C raises the head when it should stay low.

elimination.verdict: Withhold the second tablet, keep the client low and notify the provider.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the history of a client, 58 years old, before teaching about atherosclerosis. Which findings are risk factors for atherosclerosis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Type 2 diabetes for 10 years
options.rationale: Diabetes is a listed risk factor for atherosclerosis and also injures the endothelium.

options.text: Rheumatoid arthritis treated for 6 years
options.rationale: Autoimmunity is a listed risk factor for atherosclerosis, even though the disease is best known for its joint effects.

options.text: Heartburn after large meals for 2 years
options.rationale: Heartburn can mimic chest discomfort, but a digestive problem is not a risk factor for plaque in the arteries.

options.text: Smokes half a pack of cigarettes a day
options.rationale: Smoking is a listed risk factor, and even a lower daily amount injures the endothelium.

options.text: Mitral valve prolapse found on an echocardiogram
options.rationale: This is a structural valve problem. It is a cardiac finding, but it does not cause plaque to form in the arterial wall.

options.text: Blood pressure averaging 148/92 mm Hg over 3 visits
options.rationale: Hypertension is a listed risk factor and a cause of endothelial injury.

questions.takeaway: Risk factors for atherosclerosis are diabetes, smoking, hyperlipidemia or dyslipidemia, hypertension, and autoimmunity. A cardiac or chest finding is not a risk factor unless it promotes plaque in the arterial wall.
questions.strategy: Check each finding against the five listed risk factors. Watch for the autoimmune disease that looks unrelated, and for cardiac sounding findings that do not build plaque.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Diabetes, smoking, and hypertension are listed.
Rheumatoid arthritis is autoimmune, and autoimmunity is listed.
Heartburn and a valve problem do not build plaque.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, F.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: A client, 62 years old, has had chest pressure only with brisk walking for 2 years, in a predictable pattern that ends with rest. The client was told the diagnosis is coronary artery disease and says, "My neighbor had a heart attack and was told it was coronary artery disease too. Do we have the same problem?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Both are coronary artery disease. Your angina is the chronic form, and the acute coronary syndromes are unstable angina and heart attack."
options.rationale: Coronary artery disease is any disorder that narrows or occludes the coronary arteries, leading to ischemia or infarction. It includes chronic angina with a predictable pattern and the acute coronary syndromes, unstable angina and myocardial infarction.

options.text: "Both are coronary artery disease. Your angina is the chronic form, and the acute coronary syndromes are unstable angina and heart failure."
options.rationale: The chronic form is correct, but heart failure is not an acute coronary syndrome. The acute coronary syndromes are unstable angina and myocardial infarction.

options.text: "Both are acute coronary syndromes, because any chest pressure from a narrowed heart artery belongs in that group."
options.rationale: Angina in a predictable pattern that ends with rest is the chronic form. Acute coronary syndromes are new, worsening, or at rest pain from unstable angina, or a myocardial infarction.

options.text: "No. Coronary artery disease means a heart attack has damaged the muscle, so your angina is a separate condition."
options.rationale: Coronary artery disease covers ischemia as well as infarction. The client's angina is coronary artery disease without an infarction.

questions.takeaway: Coronary artery disease is any vascular disorder that narrows or occludes the coronary arteries, causing ischemia or infarction. The spectrum runs from chronic angina in a predictable pattern to the acute coronary syndromes: unstable angina (reversible ischemia) and myocardial infarction.
questions.strategy: Two options share the same frame. Check what each places under the acute coronary syndromes: unstable angina and myocardial infarction, not heart failure.

steps.detail: Narrowing or occlusion of coronary arteries causing ischemia or infarction.
Predictable pattern that ends with rest: the chronic form.
Acute coronary syndromes are unstable angina and infarction, not heart failure.
Not every angina is acute, and the disease is not limited to infarction.

elimination.verdict: Both are coronary artery disease, at different points on the spectrum.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client with chronic angina in a predictable pattern started a calcium channel blocker 3 weeks ago. Episodes of angina are now 1 per week, were 4 per week before the drug. Today: blood pressure 116/72 mm Hg sitting, was 138/86 mm Hg before the drug, and heart rate 74 beats per minute; the client denies dizziness. There is new 2+ pitting edema in both ankles. Neck veins are flat with the head of the bed at 45 degrees, the lungs are clear in both bases, and weight is unchanged on the same scale for 3 weeks. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: New right sided heart failure, because the ankle edema shows blood backing up into the systemic veins
options.rationale: Dependent edema is a right sided finding, but flat neck veins, clear lungs, and an unchanged weight do not support venous congestion or fluid gain.

options.text: A desired effect of the drug, since the angina episodes have dropped and the edema shows better perfusion
options.rationale: Fewer episodes do show benefit, but edema is not a sign of better perfusion. It is an adverse effect that the nurse monitors.

options.text: Peripheral edema, a known adverse effect of the drug, to report to the provider
options.rationale: Calcium channel blockers cause vasodilation, and the nurse monitors for hypotension and peripheral edema. With flat neck veins, clear lungs, and no weight gain, the edema fits the drug rather than heart failure. The lower pressure without dizziness is the expected effect, not hypotension.

options.text: Fluid overload from sodium retention caused by the drug, so the client should restrict fluids
options.rationale: The weight is unchanged and the lungs are clear, so there is no evidence of fluid overload. Fluid restriction is not a nursing decision and does not address a drug effect.

questions.takeaway: Calcium channel blockers promote vasodilation and myocardial perfusion. Monitor for hypotension and peripheral edema, and review how often angina episodes occur to judge benefit.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ankle edema makes heart failure tempting. Look for the findings that would go with venous congestion or fluid gain; when JVD, crackles, and weight gain are all absent, the edema points to the drug.

steps.detail: Angina down from 4 to 1 episode per week: the drug is helping.
Flat neck veins, clear lungs, unchanged weight: no congestion or fluid gain.
Peripheral edema is a known adverse effect of a calcium channel blocker, and a lower pressure without dizziness is an expected effect.
Edema is not a benefit, and fluid restriction is not indicated.

elimination.verdict: Peripheral edema from the drug, reported to the provider; the lower pressure is an expected effect.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client with coronary artery disease had chest pressure that began at 0700 while sitting in a chair and ended at 0730. A 12 lead ECG at 0715 showed ST depression. Troponin I was 0.01 ng/mL at 0720 and 0.01 ng/mL at 1320. The client is most likely experiencing [[1]].

The finding that decides between the two acute coronary syndromes is [[2]].

The nurse explains that the heart muscle [[3]].

options.text: Chronic angina with a predictable pattern
options.rationale: Chronic angina in a predictable pattern comes with exertion and is relieved by rest or nitrates. Pressure that began while sitting is at rest, so it does not fit that pattern.

options.text: Unstable angina
options.rationale: Pressure at rest is an acute coronary syndrome, and troponin I that has not risen across draws 6 hours apart means no detectable muscle death. That fits unstable angina.

options.text: Acute myocardial infarction
options.rationale: Rest pain and ST depression make this tempting. An infarction releases troponin from dying muscle, and the troponin I did not rise between 0720 and 1320.

options.text: Chest pressure that began while sitting in a chair
options.rationale: Pressure at rest separates an acute coronary syndrome from chronic angina with a predictable pattern, but both unstable angina and infarction can begin at rest.

options.text: ST depression on the 0715 ECG
options.rationale: ST depression shows ischemia. It can appear with unstable angina and with an infarction, so it does not decide between them.

options.text: Troponin I unchanged between 0720 and 1320
options.rationale: Troponin is the preferred marker for myocardial infarction. A level that stays the same 6 hours later shows no detectable cell death, which separates unstable angina from infarction.

options.text: Had less oxygen than it needed, without detectable cell death, so the injury can reverse
options.rationale: Unstable angina is reversible myocardial ischemia: oxygen delivery fell short, but the muscle did not die.

options.text: Has a small area of permanent cell death that will form a scar
options.rationale: Permanent cell death describes an infarction, which would raise troponin.

options.text: Received all the oxygen it needed, so the pressure came from another cause
options.rationale: ST depression during the pressure shows ischemia. The muscle was short of oxygen.

questions.takeaway: Chronic angina is predictable with exertion. Unstable angina is new, worsening, or at rest and is reversible ischemia. Myocardial infarction is muscle death, and troponin T and I are the preferred markers that separate the two acute coronary syndromes.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Rest pain and ST depression narrow it to an acute coronary syndrome but cannot choose between the two. Read the two troponin values 6 hours apart: unchanged troponin means no detectable muscle death.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pressure while sitting rules out a predictable exertional pattern.
ST depression shows ischemia in either syndrome.
0.01 ng/mL at 0720 and at 1320: no rise.
Reversible ischemia without cell death.

elimination.verdict: Unstable angina; troponin I unchanged between 0720 and 1320; less oxygen without detectable cell death, so the injury can reverse.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client, 77 years old, has coronary artery disease and type 2 diabetes. At 1300 the client walked the length of the hallway without shortness of breath. At 1400, while sitting in a chair, the client becomes tired, sweaty, and short of breath, and denies any chest pain or pressure. Heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 146/88 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 94% on room air. Capillary blood glucose 138 mg/dL. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Gives 15 g of fast acting carbohydrate, since sweating and fatigue in diabetes point to a low blood glucose.
options.rationale: Sweating and fatigue in a client with diabetes do raise concern for low glucose, which makes this tempting. The capillary blood glucose of 138 mg/dL rules it out.

options.text: Obtains a 12 lead ECG, since these findings at rest may be ischemia without chest pain.
options.rationale: The deciding cue is the glucose of 138 mg/dL, which removes the other explanation. Some clients have atypical or silent ischemia, with dyspnea, sweating, and fatigue instead of chest pain, and older adults with diabetes are among them. A 12 lead ECG looks for ischemia.

options.text: Has the client rest for 30 minutes and then reassesses, since there is no chest pain or pressure.
options.rationale: Waiting assumes ischemia always causes chest pain. New symptoms at rest need evaluation now.

options.text: Coaches slow, deep breathing for anxiety and stays with the client until the symptoms pass.
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem points to anxiety. Attributing new dyspnea, sweating, and tachycardia to anxiety delays evaluation for ischemia.

questions.takeaway: Chest discomfort may come with dyspnea, diaphoresis, pallor, fatigue, or weakness, and some clients have atypical or silent ischemia. New findings at rest in a client with coronary artery disease are evaluated with a 12 lead ECG even without chest pain.
questions.strategy: Two options explain sweating and fatigue in an older adult with diabetes: low glucose or ischemia. The glucose value in the stem decides it.

steps.detail: No dyspnea walking at 1300; dyspnea, sweating, and fatigue at rest at 1400.
Glucose 138 mg/dL rules out low glucose.
Ischemia without chest pain.
Waiting and coaching for anxiety both postpone evaluation.

elimination.verdict: Obtain a 12 lead ECG; glucose 138 mg/dL rules out the other explanation.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client with suspected coronary artery disease had a 12 lead ECG, a chest x ray and a troponin level today, and an echocardiogram is scheduled for tomorrow. The client asks, "What will the echocardiogram tell my provider that today's tests did not?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "It measures whether a protein from damaged heart muscle is in your blood."
options.rationale: This describes troponin, the preferred biomarker for acute myocardial infarction. It was drawn today and is a blood test, not imaging.

options.text: "It shows the heart's structure and how much blood it pumps out with each beat."
options.rationale: An echocardiogram shows the heart's structure and the ejection fraction. None of today's tests measures how well the ventricle pumps.

options.text: "It records the electrical tracing of your heart to look for signs of low oxygen."
options.rationale: This describes the 12 lead ECG, which was done today.

options.text: "It shows on a film whether the heart is enlarged or fluid is in your lungs."
options.rationale: This describes the chest x ray, which shows cardiomegaly and congestion. It was done today.

questions.takeaway: Diagnostic tests for coronary artery disease include troponin, chest x ray, thallium scans, cardiovascular magnetic resonance, echocardiography, CT coronary angiography, the 12 lead ECG, stress testing and cardiac catheterization. The echocardiogram shows structure and ejection fraction.
questions.strategy: Match each option to the test it describes. Three describe tests already done today, so only one can be news from the echocardiogram.

steps.detail: Troponin, echocardiogram, ECG, chest x ray.
ECG, chest x ray and troponin were done today.
Structure and ejection fraction.

elimination.verdict: B. Structure and ejection fraction.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client, 68 years old, had surgery on the right hip under general anesthesia. The client last voided 300 mL at 0600, before surgery, and has not voided since. At 1400 the client reports lower abdominal pressure, 5 of 10. Intravenous intake since 0600 has been 1,400 mL. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Insert a straight catheter to drain the bladder and measure the volume
options.rationale: Catheterization may be needed, but it is an invasive intervention taken before the nurse knows whether the bladder is full. A catheter is used only after the indication is confirmed and alternatives are considered.

options.text: Palpate above the symphysis pubis and obtain a bladder scan
options.rationale: The client has not voided for 8 hours after anesthesia and reports lower abdominal pressure. The nurse assesses bladder fullness and obtains a bladder scan to find out how much urine the bladder holds before choosing an intervention.

options.text: Give 480 mL of oral fluid over the next hour to stimulate voiding
options.rationale: The client has already received 1,400 mL of fluid. Lack of fluid is not the problem, and more volume adds to a bladder that may not be emptying.

options.text: Report urinary retention to the provider and request an indwelling catheter
options.rationale: Retention has not been confirmed yet. An indwelling catheter also carries a risk of catheter associated infection, so the nurse gathers bladder data first.

questions.takeaway: When retention is suspected, the nurse assesses the last void, symptoms, and output, then obtains a bladder scan when indicated. Assessment comes before catheterization or a report.
questions.strategy: Three options act on retention as if it were confirmed. Find the option that confirms it first.

steps.detail: No void for 8 hours after anesthesia, with lower abdominal pressure.
Catheterizing, adding fluid, and reporting retention all act before the bladder volume is known.
Palpate the bladder and obtain a bladder scan.

elimination.verdict: B. Palpate above the symphysis pubis and obtain a bladder scan.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.stem: A client, 68 years old, had surgery on the right hip under general anesthesia 9 hours ago. A bladder scan at 1500 shows 650 mL of urine. The client says, "I feel like I have to go, but nothing comes out. Why is that happening?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "The kidneys slow urine production for a day after anesthesia, so your bladder is nearly empty."
options.rationale: The bladder scan shows 650 mL, so the bladder is not empty. The kidneys filter blood and produce urine; the problem here is emptying, not production.

options.text: "The tubes from your kidneys swell after surgery and hold the urine back before it reaches the bladder."
options.rationale: The ureters carry urine to the bladder, and the scan shows 650 mL already in the bladder. The urine has arrived; it is not leaving.

options.text: "Your bladder muscle is weak after surgery, so the sphincter has to tighten to push the urine out."
options.rationale: The bladder muscle does contract to empty the bladder, but the sphincter relaxes to let urine leave. A sphincter that tightens holds urine in.

options.text: "Anesthesia can slow the nerve signals that make the bladder muscle contract and the sphincter relax."
options.rationale: Urination depends on nerve signals about bladder fullness, contraction of the bladder muscle, and relaxation of the sphincter. Anesthesia is a non obstructive cause of retention because it interferes with that coordinated nerve and muscle function.

questions.takeaway: Urine collects in the bladder, nerve signals report fullness, the bladder muscle contracts, and the sphincter relaxes. Anesthesia can disrupt this nerve and muscle coordination and cause non obstructive retention.
questions.strategy: Two options name the bladder muscle and the sphincter. Check what each structure actually does during voiding.

steps.detail: 650 mL in the bladder rules out low production and a ureter blockage.
The sphincter must relax, not tighten, for urine to leave.
Anesthesia slows the nerve signals that coordinate contraction and relaxation.

elimination.verdict: D. Anesthesia can slow the nerve signals that make the bladder muscle contract and the sphincter relax.

questions.objective: Explain urinary system functions

questions.stem: A client, 70 years old, had surgery on the right hip 2 days ago. The order reads: perform straight catheterization if the postvoid residual is greater than 300 mL. The assistive personnel helped the client void 150 mL at 1000 and performed a bladder scan at 1045, which showed 380 mL. The client reports no abdominal pressure. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: Perform the straight catheterization, because the residual is greater than 300 mL
options.rationale: The order would apply to a residual of 380 mL. The cue is the timing: the scan was done 45 minutes after the void, so the kidneys kept filling the bladder and the number does not reflect what was left after voiding.

options.text: Record 380 mL as the postvoid residual and plan the next scan for 1400
options.rationale: Recording the value treats the scan as valid. A scan done 45 minutes after voiding does not measure the residual, so it cannot be recorded as one.

options.text: Have the client void again and repeat the scan within 5 to 15 minutes after that void
options.rationale: A postvoid residual is accurate only when it is measured within 5 to 15 minutes after the client voids. The 1045 scan was done 45 minutes after the void, so the nurse obtains a valid measurement before acting on the order.

options.text: Report a postvoid residual of 380 mL to the provider and request an indwelling catheter
options.rationale: This treats the 380 mL as a true residual, and an indwelling catheter adds infection risk. The measurement must be repeated at the correct time first.

questions.takeaway: Measure a postvoid residual within 5 to 15 minutes after the client voids. A scan done later includes newly produced urine and overstates what the bladder failed to empty.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options act on the order. Before using a number, check whether it was measured correctly: the 45 minute delay decides.

steps.detail: Void at 1000, scan at 1045: 45 minutes apart.
A scan that late includes new urine, so 380 mL is not a valid residual.
Repeat the void and scan within 5 to 15 minutes, then apply the order.

elimination.verdict: C. Have the client void again and repeat the scan within 5 to 15 minutes after that void.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.stem: As the nurse injects sterile water into the balloon port of a newly inserted indwelling urinary catheter, the client cries out with sudden pain and the nurse feels resistance. Which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Stop, let the water return, advance the catheter farther, and reinflate
options.rationale: Sudden pain and resistance mean the balloon may be inflating in the urethra. The nurse stops, lets the fluid return, advances the catheter farther into the bladder, and reinflates.

options.text: Finish injecting the full volume quickly so the balloon seats inside the bladder
options.rationale: Continuing to inflate a balloon that may be in the urethra can injure the urethra. Pain and resistance are signals to stop.

options.text: Leave the balloon partly inflated and secure the catheter to the upper thigh
options.rationale: An underinflated balloon can become distorted and damage the bladder, and the catheter may still sit in the urethra.

options.text: Remove the catheter now and report the sudden pain to the provider
options.rationale: Removal and a report are the steps if pain continues after the catheter is repositioned. The first step is to deflate, advance, and reinflate.

questions.takeaway: If the client reports sudden pain or the nurse feels resistance during balloon inflation, stop, let the fluid return, advance the catheter, and reinflate. If pain continues, remove the catheter and notify the provider.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options stop inflating. Ask which one corrects the likely cause before giving up on the catheter.

steps.detail: Sudden pain and resistance during inflation suggest the balloon is in the urethra.
Finishing the injection or leaving it partly inflated both risk injury.
Removal is for pain that continues; repositioning comes first.

elimination.verdict: A. Stop, let the water return, advance the catheter farther, and reinflate.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: An assistive personnel cares for a client with an indwelling urinary catheter. Which actions by the assistive personnel require the nurse to intervene? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hangs the drainage bag on the bed frame below the level of the bladder
options.rationale: Keeping the bag below the bladder lets urine drain by gravity and prevents backflow. No correction is needed.

options.text: Sets the drainage bag on the floor while repositioning the client
options.rationale: The bag must stay off the floor. Contact with the floor contaminates the bag and its emptying spout.

options.text: Disconnects the catheter from the tubing to empty the bag faster
options.rationale: Separating the catheter from the tubing opens the closed drainage system and lets organisms in. The bag is emptied through its spout.

options.text: Places the drainage bag on the client's lap during the transfer to a chair
options.rationale: On the lap, the bag sits above the bladder, so urine can flow back into the bladder.

options.text: Coils the extra tubing on the mattress so that it has no kinks
options.rationale: Tubing free of kinks keeps urine flowing. No correction is needed.

options.text: Leaves the tubing under the client's right thigh after turning the client
options.rationale: Lying on the tubing compresses it and blocks drainage. The tubing must stay free of kinks and pressure.

questions.takeaway: Routine indwelling catheter care: hand hygiene before all care, a closed drainage system, tubing free of kinks, and the bag below the bladder and off the floor.
questions.strategy: Test each action against the four routine care rules: hand hygiene, closed system, no kinks, bag below the bladder and off the floor.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Bed frame below the bladder is correct; the floor and the lap are not.
Disconnecting the catheter breaks the closed system.
Coiled tubing with no kinks is correct; tubing under the thigh is compressed.

elimination.verdict: B, C, D, F.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.scenario: A client, 66 years old, had an indwelling urinary catheter removed at 0600 after 3 days. The nurse reviews the findings recorded between 0600 and 1400.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is expected after catheter removal or requires follow up.

rows.text: Mild burning with the first void at 0930
rows.rationale: Mild burning or discomfort with the first voids after removal comes from urethral irritation and soon subsides.

rows.text: Voided 320 mL of clear, pale yellow urine at 0930
rows.rationale: A void of 320 mL of clear urine within a few hours shows the bladder is filling and emptying after removal.

rows.text: Voids of 40 mL at 1130, 1200, and 1230, with a feeling of incomplete emptying
rows.rationale: Small, frequent voids with a sensation of incomplete emptying can mean retention. The nurse assesses for bladder distention and obtains a bladder scan.

rows.text: Oral temperature 38.5 °C at 1300, was 36.8 °C at 0600, with pain in the right flank
rows.rationale: Any client whose catheter was recently removed is at risk for urinary tract infection. A new fever with flank pain may mean an upper urinary tract infection.

rows.text: Burning with every void through 1400, rated 6 of 10
rows.rationale: Burning with the first few voids is expected, but burning that continues with every void may mean infection.

rows.text: Drinking 240 mL of fluid every 2 hours as taught
rows.rationale: Maintaining fluid intake after removal is part of the teaching, and it supports normal urine output.

questions.takeaway: After catheter removal, expect mild burning with the first voids. Evaluate for retention (small, frequent voids, incomplete emptying) and for infection (fever, flank pain, continued painful voiding).
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Separate the first void from the pattern. A brief symptom at the first void is expected; the same symptom that persists, or a new systemic sign, needs follow up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Burning at the first void is expected; burning with every void through 1400 is not.
Three voids of 40 mL with incomplete emptying need a bladder assessment.
A new temperature of 38.5 °C with right flank pain needs follow up.
A 320 mL clear void and intake as taught show the plan working.

elimination.verdict: Expected: rows 1, 2, 6. Requires follow up: rows 3, 4, 5.

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: A client, 31 years old, comes to the clinic and reports that urine has leaked twice in 2 days before the client reached the toilet. The client also reports burning with each void, voiding every 30 to 45 minutes, and lower abdominal discomfort, 4 of 10. The bladder is not palpable above the symphysis pubis.
