The urine in the collection cup is cloudy with a strong odor. Which problem do these findings most likely indicate?

options.text: Urgency incontinence from a bladder that contracts without warning
options.rationale: Leakage with a sudden urge fits urgency incontinence. The burning, the cloudy urine with a strong odor, and the frequency point to an infection as the cause.

options.text: A urinary tract infection causing urgency and frequent voiding
options.rationale: Burning with urination, urgency, frequent voiding, lower abdominal discomfort, and a change in urine appearance are the signs of a urinary tract infection. The urgency explains the leakage.

options.text: Stress incontinence from weak pelvic floor muscles
options.rationale: Stress incontinence is leakage with coughing, sneezing, or activity. The client leaks with urgency, not with effort.

options.text: Chronic urinary retention with leakage from an overfull bladder
options.rationale: Retention can cause small voids and leakage, but the bladder is not palpable, and the client reports no feeling of incomplete emptying.

questions.takeaway: A urinary tract infection presents with burning or pain with urination, urgency or frequency, lower abdominal discomfort, and possible changes in urine appearance.
questions.strategy: Leakage pulls toward an incontinence type. Ask which problem explains every finding, including the burning and the cloudy urine.

steps.detail: Burning, urgency with leakage, frequency, lower abdominal discomfort, cloudy urine with odor.
Urgency incontinence explains the leakage but not the burning or the urine change; stress incontinence has the wrong trigger.
No palpable bladder and no incomplete emptying.
A urinary tract infection explains all the findings.

elimination.verdict: B. A urinary tract infection causing urgency and frequent voiding.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client how to collect a clean voided urine specimen for culture. Which statement by the client indicates correct understanding?

options.text: "I will start my stream in the toilet and then move the cup into the stream."
options.rationale: The first part of the stream flushes organisms from the urethral opening. The specimen is caught from the middle of the stream, and the cup is removed before the flow stops.

options.text: "I will catch the very first part of the stream, because that urine has been in the bladder longest."
options.rationale: The first urine carries organisms from the urethral opening and contaminates the culture. The first part goes into the toilet.

options.text: "I will clean the area with the towelette, void into the toilet hat, and pour it into the cup."
options.rationale: Cleansing is correct, but a toilet hat is not sterile. Pouring from it contaminates the specimen.

options.text: "I will hold the lid by its inside surface so that my fingers stay off the outside of the cup."
options.rationale: The inside of the lid and the cup must not be touched. The client handles only the outside surfaces.

questions.takeaway: For a clean voided specimen, cleanse the urethral opening, start the stream into the toilet, collect from the middle of the stream, and touch only the outside of the cup and lid.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Find the step each wrong statement contaminates: the first stream, a nonsterile container, or the inside of the lid.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The first urine flushes the opening, so it is not collected.
A toilet hat is not sterile.
Only outside surfaces are touched.
Start in the toilet, then move the cup into the stream.

elimination.verdict: A. Start the stream in the toilet and then move the cup into the stream.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: A client in long term care can walk with help but needs assistance to reach the bathroom and has had urine leakage. Which actions by the nurse support the client's dignity and independence? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask the client about the usual times of voiding at home
options.rationale: Asking about the usual routine lets the plan follow the client's own pattern.

options.text: Explain each step of perineal care before uncovering the client
options.rationale: Explaining care before exposing or touching the client respects the client's privacy and gives the client control.

options.text: Place an absorbent product on the client at all times so staff can change it on rounds
options.rationale: This replaces toileting with containment for staff convenience. The client can walk with help and needs access to the toilet, not a product worn at all times.

options.text: Use a bedpan at night instead of the commode the client prefers, to save staff time
options.rationale: The client's preferred toileting method is supported when it is safe. Saving staff time is not a reason to override it.

options.text: Ask the client to pull up the pants as able after toileting
options.rationale: Encouraging participation in self care supports independence.

questions.takeaway: Dignity in elimination care: ask about the usual routine, explain before exposing or touching, provide privacy and respectful language, support the preferred toileting method when safe, and encourage self care.
questions.strategy: Mark each action true or false by asking whose need it serves: the client's routine, privacy, and independence, or staff convenience.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Asking about home voiding times and explaining before uncovering are correct.
Having the client pull up the pants encourages self care.
A product worn at all times and a bedpan in place of the preferred commode serve staff, not the client.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E.

questions.objective: Select dignity supporting interventions

questions.stem: A client, 79 years old, has weakness of the left arm and leg after a stroke. The client uses the call light as soon as the urge to void begins. Urine leaks while the client waits 10 to 15 minutes for help walking to the bathroom. When staff help the client onto the toilet within 5 minutes of the urge, no leakage occurs and each void is 250 to 300 mL. Which intervention best addresses the cause of the leakage?

options.text: Begin bladder training to lengthen the time between voids
options.rationale: Bladder training fits urgency incontinence, and leakage after an urge looks like that pattern. The cue is that no leakage occurs when the client reaches the toilet within 5 minutes; the bladder holds urine, but the trip takes too long.

options.text: Teach pelvic floor muscle exercises to strengthen control of urine flow
options.rationale: Pelvic floor training fits stress incontinence, which is leakage with coughing, sneezing, or activity. That is not this client's pattern.

options.text: Insert an indwelling catheter to keep the perineal skin dry
options.rationale: A catheter adds infection risk and does not address the cause. The client recognizes the urge and voids normal volumes.

options.text: Place a commode on the right side of the bed and schedule toileting
options.rationale: The client recognizes the urge but leaks while waiting for help to walk, which is functional incontinence. A commode on the stronger right side and scheduled toileting improve access to the toilet.

questions.takeaway: Functional incontinence is leakage because the client has difficulty reaching or using the toilet. Care improves access, such as a bedside commode, and schedules regular toileting assistance.
questions.strategy: Leakage after an urge points to two types. Decide by what happens when the toilet is reached quickly: no leakage within 5 minutes means the barrier is access, not the bladder.

steps.detail: The client feels the urge and calls, then leaks while waiting for help to walk.
No leakage when on the toilet within 5 minutes, with voids of 250 to 300 mL, rules out a bladder that cannot hold urine.

steps.action: Match the care to the cause
steps.detail: Functional incontinence needs better access and scheduled toileting.

elimination.verdict: D. Place a commode on the right side of the bed and schedule toileting.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: A client, 66 years old, had abdominal surgery this morning and has an indwelling urinary catheter with hourly output measurement. Urine output was 55 mL at 1000, 22 mL at 1100, and 18 mL at 1200. Heart rate is 108 beats per minute, was 84 beats per minute at 1000. Blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg, was 126/78 mm Hg at 1000. The nurse finds the tubing straight, with no kinks, and the bag below the bladder. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Irrigate the catheter with sterile saline to clear a possible blockage
options.rationale: The tubing has been checked and drains freely. Irrigation is done only when it is indicated and ordered, and there is no order. The falling heart rate and blood pressure trend points away from a blocked catheter.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids and recheck the hourly output again in 2 hours
options.rationale: Waiting 2 more hours delays the report of a significant drop in output while the heart rate rises and the blood pressure falls.

options.text: Report the falling output with the heart rate and blood pressure trends
options.rationale: Output has dropped from 55 mL to 18 mL per hour over 2 hours while the heart rate rose and the blood pressure fell. The nurse has already ruled out a drainage problem, so a significant decrease in output is reported promptly with the trends that go with it.

options.text: Document the output and continue hourly measurement as ordered
options.rationale: Documenting is required, but recording the trend without reporting it leaves a significant decrease in output untreated.

questions.takeaway: Compare output with the trend and the clinical situation. Once the drainage system is checked, a significant decrease or absent output is reported promptly, together with the vital sign changes.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you the assessment of the drainage system is already done. Pick the action that moves the problem forward without waiting.

steps.detail: 55 mL, then 22 mL, then 18 mL per hour, with heart rate up and blood pressure down.
Tubing straight, bag below the bladder, so drainage is not the cause.
Rechecking in 2 hours and only documenting both postpone the report.
Irrigation needs an indication and an order.

elimination.verdict: C. Report the falling output with the heart rate and blood pressure trends.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.stem: A client on intake and output measurement walks to the bathroom independently and receives intravenous fluid. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place the urine collection device in the client's toilet before the next void
options.rationale: Using the correct collection device lets each void be caught and measured while the client keeps privacy in the bathroom.

options.text: Record oral fluids only, since the pump records the intravenous fluid
options.rationale: Intake is recorded from every source, including intravenous fluid. Leaving it out makes the comparison with output inaccurate.

options.text: Compare the output trend with the total intake at the end of each shift
options.rationale: Trends are compared with intake and the clinical situation, so a drop in output relative to intake is recognized early.

options.text: Document the amount and the time of each void on the record
options.rationale: Amount and time are both documented so trends can be compared.

options.text: Estimate the volume of each void from how full the device looks
options.rationale: An estimate is not an accurate measurement. Output is measured.

options.text: Total the output from memory at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Output is documented with the amount and time of each void, not reconstructed later from memory.

questions.takeaway: Accurate intake and output means the correct collection device, measured output, every source of intake recorded, the amount and time of each entry, and trends compared with intake.
questions.strategy: Ask of each option whether it makes the numbers more accurate or less accurate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The correct device is in place before the next void.
Measured, never estimated or remembered.
All intake sources; amount and time for each void.
Output trend against intake.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.stem: A client, 79 years old, has vomited for 2 days and has not voided for 9 hours. Oral mucosa is dry, heart rate is 112 beats per minute, and the client reports no lower abdominal pressure. The bladder is not palpable above the symphysis pubis, and a bladder scan shows 45 mL of urine. Which interpretation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: The kidneys are producing little urine, so the problem is not bladder emptying
options.rationale: The kidneys filter blood and produce urine, and the bladder only stores what reaches it. A bladder holding 45 mL after 9 hours with no fullness means little urine is being made, which fits the fluid loss from vomiting. Retention would show a full bladder.

options.text: The sphincter is not relaxing, so urine is held in the bladder
options.rationale: Failure of the sphincter to relax would trap urine in the bladder. The scan shows only 45 mL, so the bladder is not holding urine back.

options.text: The urethra is blocked, so urine cannot leave the body
options.rationale: A blocked urethra would leave urine in the bladder, and the bladder would be full and palpable. Neither is present.

options.text: The bladder muscle is not contracting, so the bladder cannot empty
options.rationale: Weak contraction causes retention with a full bladder. A bladder with 45 mL has little to empty.

questions.takeaway: Low output and retention look alike at first because the client is not voiding. A bladder scan separates them: retention means urine is stored and not emptied, while a nearly empty bladder points to the kidneys making little urine.
questions.strategy: Three options describe a bladder that holds urine. The scan says the bladder holds very little.

steps.detail: 45 mL after 9 hours, bladder not palpable, no pressure.
Sphincter, urethra, and bladder muscle problems all leave a full bladder.
Little urine is being produced by the kidneys.

elimination.verdict: A. The kidneys are producing little urine, so the problem is not bladder emptying.

questions.objective: Explain urinary system functions

questions.stem: A nurse receives report on four clients at 0700. Which client should the nurse assess first?

options.text: A client, 71 years old, with chronic incomplete emptying and a postvoid residual of 120 mL, the same as yesterday
options.rationale: This is ongoing incomplete emptying that has not changed. It needs follow up but is not a sudden change.

options.text: A client, 48 years old, who has leaked small amounts of urine when coughing for the past 3 years
options.rationale: Leakage with coughing is a long standing pattern of stress incontinence. It affects quality of life but is not urgent.

options.text: A client, 35 years old, on the second day of an antibiotic for a urinary tract infection, with burning on voiding, 3 of 10
options.rationale: Burning on the second day of treatment is expected to ease as the antibiotic works. The client is being treated.

options.text: A client, 62 years old, who has not voided since 2300 and has lower abdominal pain, 8 of 10, with a palpable bladder
options.rationale: Sudden inability to void with severe pain and a palpable bladder is acute retention. A sudden inability to void needs urgent attention.

questions.takeaway: Acute retention is a sudden inability to urinate and needs urgent attention. Chronic retention and long standing incontinence patterns are ongoing problems that can wait for the acute one.
questions.strategy: Sort acute from chronic. A new, sudden problem with severe pain outranks problems that are unchanged or already treated.

steps.detail: No void for 8 hours with pain 8 of 10 and a palpable bladder.
Residual the same as yesterday; leakage for 3 years.
Infection on day 2 of an antibiotic.
The client with acute retention.

elimination.verdict: D. The client who has not voided since 2300 with pain 8 of 10 and a palpable bladder.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: A client, 63 years old, had surgery on the left knee 6 hours ago and has an order for activity as tolerated with assistance. The client feels the urge to void but has been unable to void on a bedpan in bed for 15 minutes. The curtain is partly open, and visitors are talking with the roommate. A bladder scan shows 380 mL. Which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Insert a straight catheter to empty the bladder and measure the volume
options.rationale: Catheterization is considered only after measures that promote normal voiding are tried. The client has an urge and has not yet tried a usual position with privacy.

options.text: Close the curtain, help the client sit on a bedside commode, and allow time
options.rationale: The client feels the urge but cannot void lying on a bedpan with no privacy. A usual sitting position, privacy, and adequate time help the bladder empty, and the nurse then reassesses with the void amount or a repeat scan.

options.text: Leave the client on the bedpan and return in 1 hour to check for a void
options.rationale: Staying in the same position without privacy does not change what is keeping the client from voiding, and the bladder keeps filling.

options.text: Give 480 mL of oral fluid to increase the urge to void
options.rationale: The bladder already holds 380 mL and the client has an urge. More fluid adds volume without helping the bladder empty.

questions.takeaway: For suspected retention, provide safe positioning, privacy, and time before an invasive step, and reassess after each intervention.
questions.strategy: The stem names the barriers: lying on a bedpan, an open curtain, visitors. Pick the option that removes them safely.

steps.detail: Supine on a bedpan, no privacy, little time.
The order allows activity with assistance.
A catheter comes after normal voiding measures.
Neither removes a barrier.

elimination.verdict: B. Close the curtain, help the client sit on a bedside commode, and allow time.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews the histories of six clients who each have urinary retention.
questions.stem: For each history, indicate whether it points to obstructive or non obstructive retention.

rows.text: Spinal anesthesia for surgery 5 hours ago
rows.rationale: Anesthesia interferes with the nerve signals and muscle function that empty the bladder. Nothing blocks the outflow.

rows.text: A stone lodged at the outlet of the bladder
rows.rationale: A bladder stone at the outlet physically blocks urine from leaving the bladder.

rows.text: Nerve damage from diabetes for 20 years
rows.rationale: Nerve damage weakens the signals that tell the bladder it is full and trigger contraction.

rows.text: A new medication that slows bladder muscle contraction
rows.rationale: Medications can cause retention by reducing bladder contraction. The outflow path is open.

rows.text: A tumor that narrows the urethra
rows.rationale: A tumor narrowing the urethra blocks the path urine takes out of the body.

rows.text: A spinal cord injury at the level of the waist
rows.rationale: Spinal cord injury interrupts the nerve pathways that coordinate bladder contraction and sphincter relaxation.

questions.takeaway: Obstructive retention comes from something blocking the outflow, such as stones, tumors, an enlarged prostate, or pelvic organ prolapse. Non obstructive retention comes from nerve damage, spinal cord injury, medications, or anesthesia that interfere with the signals and muscles of emptying.
questions.strategy: Ask one question for each row: is something in the way, or are the nerves and muscle not working?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The stone at the bladder outlet and the tumor narrowing the urethra.

steps.action: Find the signal and muscle problems
steps.detail: Anesthesia, diabetic nerve damage, the medication, and spinal cord injury.

elimination.verdict: Obstructive: rows 2 and 5. Non obstructive: rows 1, 3, 4, and 6.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: A client, 46 years old, reports leaking small amounts of urine when sneezing, laughing, or lifting groceries for 1 year. The client voids every 3 to 4 hours, about 300 mL each time, with no burning and no sudden urges. A postvoid residual is 20 mL. Which intervention should the nurse plan?

options.text: Teach pelvic floor muscle exercises to strengthen control of urine flow
options.rationale: Leakage with sneezing, laughing, and lifting is stress incontinence. Pelvic floor muscle training strengthens the muscles around the urethra so that they hold urine when abdominal pressure rises.

options.text: Schedule toileting every 2 hours to keep the bladder from filling
options.rationale: Scheduled toileting addresses functional or urgency patterns. This client leaks with pressure, not with a full bladder or difficulty reaching the toilet.

options.text: Repeat the bladder scan after each void to check for retention
options.rationale: A postvoid residual of 20 mL shows that the bladder empties. Repeated scans do not address leakage with pressure.

options.text: Advise the client to drink less fluid so that less urine is available to leak
options.rationale: Restricting fluid concentrates the urine and irritates the bladder. It does not strengthen the muscles that fail under pressure.

questions.takeaway: Stress incontinence is leakage with coughing, sneezing, or activity. Match care to the cause: pelvic floor muscle training for stress leakage.
questions.strategy: Name the incontinence type from the trigger first, then pick the intervention that treats that cause.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sneezing, laughing, lifting: rises in abdominal pressure.
No urgency, normal voids, residual 20 mL.
Pelvic floor muscle training.

elimination.verdict: A. Teach pelvic floor muscle exercises.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: A client, 72 years old, has had diabetes for 25 years. The client reports dribbling urine throughout the day and night and voids 30 to 60 mL at a time. After a void, the bladder is palpable above the symphysis pubis, and a bladder scan shows 410 mL. The client denies burning and has no strong urges. Which problem do these findings most likely indicate?

options.text: Urgency incontinence from sudden bladder contractions
options.rationale: Urgency incontinence follows a sudden strong urge. The client has no strong urges, and the bladder does not empty.

options.text: Stress incontinence from weak pelvic floor muscles
options.rationale: Stress leakage follows coughing, sneezing, or activity, and the bladder empties normally between episodes.

options.text: Overflow incontinence from incomplete bladder emptying
options.rationale: Constant dribbling, small voids, a palpable bladder after voiding, and 410 mL left behind show leakage from a bladder that does not empty. Long standing diabetes can damage the nerves that signal fullness.

options.text: Functional incontinence from difficulty reaching the toilet
options.rationale: Functional incontinence happens when the client cannot get to or use the toilet in time. Nothing in the stem describes a barrier to the toilet.

questions.takeaway: Overflow incontinence is leakage with incomplete emptying. Small voids or leakage can occur with retention, so a palpable bladder and a high residual after voiding point to overflow.
questions.strategy: Look for the finding that only one type explains: urine left in the bladder after voiding.

steps.detail: Palpable bladder and 410 mL after a void.
No strong urges and no pressure trigger.
No barrier to the toilet is described.

elimination.verdict: C. Overflow incontinence from incomplete bladder emptying.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: A client, 67 years old, walks independently without a device and reports a sudden strong urge to void that comes on so quickly that urine leaks before the client reaches the bathroom 3 meters away. The client voids every 60 minutes, 100 to 150 mL each time. Urine is clear, with no burning, and the postvoid residual is 25 mL. Which intervention best addresses the cause of the leakage?

options.text: Place a bedside commode next to the bed to shorten the distance
options.rationale: A commode helps when reaching the toilet is the problem. This client walks independently and the bathroom is 3 meters away; the leakage starts with the urge itself.

options.text: Limit total fluid intake to 1,000 mL per day to reduce urine volume
options.rationale: Restricting fluid concentrates urine, which irritates the bladder and can worsen urgency.

options.text: Apply an absorbent product and change it every 4 hours
options.rationale: An absorbent product contains leakage but does not treat its cause, and leaves the skin wet between changes.

options.text: Begin bladder training that gradually lengthens the time between voids
options.rationale: A sudden strong urge with leakage is urgency incontinence. Bladder training teaches the client to delay voiding and gradually lengthen the interval, which reduces urgency and leakage.

questions.takeaway: Urgency incontinence is a sudden strong urge followed by leakage. Bladder training lengthens the time between voids and treats the cause.
questions.strategy: The cue is that the client is independent and close to the bathroom, so access is not the problem. The urge is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sudden strong urge, then leakage: urgency incontinence.
Walks independently, bathroom 3 meters away.
Absorbent products and fluid limits do not treat the urge.
Bladder training.

elimination.verdict: D. Begin bladder training.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: A client, 86 years old, has 4 to 5 episodes of urinary incontinence each day. The nurse inspects the perineal skin and finds redness over both buttocks with no open areas. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wash the area with soap and a washcloth, using firm strokes to remove all urine
options.rationale: Firm scrubbing and soap residue damage skin that is already red. Cleansing after incontinence is gentle.

options.text: Cleanse the skin gently after each episode and pat it dry
options.rationale: Gentle cleansing removes urine without friction, and patting dry avoids rubbing the reddened skin.

options.text: Leave each pad in place until it is fully soaked to limit handling of the skin
options.rationale: A soaked pad keeps urine against the skin and worsens the moisture damage.

options.text: Apply a barrier cream to the reddened area after cleansing
options.rationale: A barrier cream protects the skin from urine between episodes.

options.text: Request an indwelling catheter to keep the perineal skin dry
options.rationale: A catheter is used only when indicated and carries a risk of infection. Incontinence alone is not an indication.

options.text: Inspect the perineal skin each time incontinence care is given
options.rationale: Inspecting the perineal skin is indicated with ongoing incontinence, so early damage is found and the plan can change.

questions.takeaway: Incontinence care includes gentle cleansing, skin protection with a barrier cream, and regular inspection of the perineal skin. A catheter is not a skin care measure.
questions.strategy: Judge each option by whether it shortens contact between urine and skin without adding friction or risk.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gentle cleansing, patting dry, barrier cream.
Inspect the skin with each episode of care.
Scrubbing, soaked pads, and a catheter without an indication.

elimination.verdict: B, D, F.

questions.objective: Select dignity supporting interventions

questions.nursesNote: Clinic visit. Client is 81 years old, 2 weeks after starting a plan for functional incontinence with a bedside commode and toileting every 2 hours. Leakage 1 time this week, was 6 times in the week before the plan. Uses the commode at night without help. Perineal skin red with a 2 cm open area on the left buttock. Pain with voiding 0 of 10. Says, "If my urine turns cloudy or I get a fever, I will wait for my next visit." Drinks 1,800 mL of fluid per day as planned. A family member reports that toileting at 1400 is skipped when the client naps.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that show the plan of care needs revision.

segments.text: Leakage 1 time this week, was 6 times in the week before the plan
segments.rationale: Leakage has dropped from 6 episodes to 1, which shows the plan is working on this outcome.

segments.text: Uses the commode at night without help
segments.rationale: Independent use of the commode meets the goal of greater independence.

segments.text: Perineal skin red with a 2 cm open area on the left buttock
segments.rationale: The outcome is intact skin. An open area means skin protection in the plan needs revision.

segments.text: Pain with voiding 0 of 10
segments.rationale: No pain with voiding meets the comfort outcome.

segments.text: Says, "If my urine turns cloudy or I get a fever, I will wait for my next visit."
segments.rationale: Cloudy urine and fever are reportable changes. The client does not know to report them, so teaching needs revision.

segments.text: Drinks 1,800 mL of fluid per day as planned
segments.rationale: Fluid intake matches the plan.

segments.text: A family member reports that toileting at 1400 is skipped when the client naps
segments.rationale: A missed scheduled toileting time means the client cannot fully manage the plan as written. The schedule needs to be revised with the client and family.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation asks whether the pattern is better, the client has comfort, the skin is intact, the client can manage the plan, and the client knows reportable changes. A no to any of these means the plan needs revision.
questions.strategy: Hold each finding against one evaluation question. Findings that meet their outcome are not the cues.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Leakage down from 6 to 1, uses the commode alone: met.
Open area on the left buttock: not met.
Would wait with fever and cloudy urine; 1400 toileting skipped: not met.
Pain 0 of 10 and 1,800 mL per day: met.

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: A urine specimen for culture is ordered for a client with an indwelling urinary catheter. Which action should the nurse take to collect the specimen?

options.text: Drain urine from the bag spout into a sterile cup and label it at the bedside
options.rationale: Urine in the bag has been standing and can grow bacteria, so a specimen from the bag gives an inaccurate culture. A specimen is never collected from the drainage bag.

options.text: Clamp below the sampling port, cleanse the port, and aspirate with a sterile syringe
options.rationale: Clamping below the port lets fresh urine collect. Cleansing the port and using a sterile syringe and container avoids contaminating the specimen and keeps the drainage system closed.

options.text: Disconnect the catheter from the tubing and let urine drip into a sterile cup
options.rationale: Disconnecting opens the closed drainage system, which lets bacteria enter and raises the risk of infection.

options.text: Withdraw urine through the balloon inflation port with a sterile syringe
options.rationale: The balloon port leads to the balloon, not the bladder. It holds sterile water, not urine.

questions.takeaway: Avoid contaminating a specimen. With an indwelling catheter, collect urine from the sampling port with sterile technique, never from the bag, and never by opening the closed system.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options open the system or use old urine. One uses the wrong port. Choose the one that gets fresh urine with the system closed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Urine in the bag has been standing.
Disconnecting invites infection.
The balloon port holds water.
Sampling port after clamping below it.

elimination.verdict: B. Clamp below the sampling port, cleanse the port, and aspirate with a sterile syringe.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: A nurse is collecting urine specimens for urinalysis from three clients. Which actions by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Collect all three specimens and label them together in the utility room
options.rationale: Labeling away from the client after collecting several specimens risks switching them. Each specimen is labeled at the bedside.

options.text: Verify each order and check each client's identity with two identifiers before collecting
options.rationale: The nurse verifies the order and the client's identity before collection so that the right test is done on the right client.

options.text: Label each container with the client's identifiers before leaving the bedside
options.rationale: Specimens are labeled according to requirements so the laboratory can match the result to the right client. Labels usually include the name, date, time, and type of collection.

options.text: Leave the specimens at the bedside until the next laboratory pickup
options.rationale: Specimens are transported according to requirements. Urine left standing at the bedside grows bacteria and changes the results.

options.text: Fill each cup from urine that has stood in the client's bedpan since the last void
options.rationale: Urinalysis needs fresh urine. Urine left standing grows bacteria and changes the results.

options.text: Explain the collection method to each client before the specimen is collected
options.rationale: The nurse explains the collection method so the client can help collect the specimen correctly and without contamination.

questions.takeaway: Specimen collection: verify the order and identity, explain the collection method, use the correct container and technique, avoid contamination, and label and transport according to requirements.
questions.strategy: Look at each step from order to laboratory and ask whether it keeps the right specimen with the right client and the result accurate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Verify the order and two identifiers; explain the method.
Fresh urine, not urine that has stood in a bedpan.
Label at the bedside; transport, do not leave it waiting.

elimination.verdict: B, C, F.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.scenario: A nurse observes the urine of six clients during the morning assessment and reviews each client's history.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is expected or requires follow up.

rows.text: Dark amber urine in a client who drank 600 mL in the past 24 hours and has a dry mouth
rows.rationale: Dark urine sits at the concentrated end of the urine color chart. With low intake and a dry mouth, the finding points to a fluid deficit that needs follow up.

rows.text: Cloudy, foul smelling urine with burning and urgency on voiding
rows.rationale: A change in urine appearance with burning and urgency fits a urinary tract infection.

rows.text: Pale yellow, clear urine in a client who drinks 2,000 mL per day
rows.rationale: Pale, clear urine fits the dilute end of the color chart and the client's intake.

rows.text: Dark yellow first morning void that lightens to pale yellow after the client drinks 720 mL
rows.rationale: Urine held overnight is more concentrated. It lightens as intake increases, and the trend matches the history.

rows.text: Urine output of 120 mL in 8 hours with an intake of 1,600 mL
rows.rationale: Output far below intake is a significant decrease that is compared with intake and reported promptly.

rows.text: Light yellow urine with a mild odor, 250 to 300 mL every 3 to 4 hours
rows.rationale: Light color, mild odor, and regular voids of this size are an expected pattern.

questions.takeaway: Observe color, clarity, and odor, measure output, and combine the findings with symptoms and history. Dark urine with low intake, cloudy foul urine with burning, and output well below intake need follow up.
questions.strategy: For each finding, ask whether the history explains it. If the history makes it worse rather than explains it, follow up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Use the color chart with the history
steps.detail: Dark with low intake: follow up. Dark in the morning that lightens with fluid: expected.
Cloudy and foul with burning and urgency: follow up.
120 mL out against 1,600 mL in: follow up.

elimination.verdict: Requires follow up: rows 1, 2, and 5. Expected: rows 3, 4, and 6.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.stem: A client with burning on voiding has orders for a urinalysis and a urine culture. After the nurse explains each test, which client statement indicates understanding?

options.text: "The urinalysis will tell which antibiotic works best against my infection."
options.rationale: Identifying the organism and the antibiotic it responds to is the purpose of the culture, not the urinalysis.

options.text: "The culture is a quick screen, so I will have the full result in about an hour."
options.rationale: A culture needs time for bacteria to grow. A preliminary report takes about 24 hours and the full result usually 48 to 72 hours.

options.text: "Both tests check the same thing, so the second one just confirms the first."
options.rationale: The tests answer different questions. One screens the urine; the other identifies bacteria and the antibiotics they respond to.

options.text: "The culture shows which germ is growing and which antibiotic it responds to."
options.rationale: A culture and sensitivity test identifies the bacteria present and the antibiotics they are sensitive to. The urinalysis is a broader screen of the urine.

questions.takeaway: Explain the purpose of each test. A urinalysis screens urine for signs of infection, blood, and other problems; a culture identifies the bacteria and the antibiotics they respond to, and results take 48 to 72 hours.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Match each test to the question it answers before reading the statements.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Urinalysis screens; culture identifies bacteria and sensitivity.
Culture results take 48 to 72 hours.
The statement that gives the culture its correct purpose.

elimination.verdict: D. "The culture shows which germ is growing and which antibiotic it responds to."

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: A client is scheduled tomorrow for an imaging study of the urinary tract. Which finding should the nurse address before the test?

options.text: The signed consent form for the study is on the chart
options.rationale: A signed consent on the chart is expected preparation. It does not need action.

options.text: Blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg and heart rate is 80 beats per minute
options.rationale: These values give no reason to delay or change the preparation for the study.

options.text: The client says, "Nobody has told me why I need this test or what it involves."
options.rationale: The nurse explains the purpose of each test. The client does not know why the study is ordered or what will happen, so the nurse explains the purpose and the procedure before the test.

options.text: The client plans to walk to the bathroom with the urine collection device in place
options.rationale: Using the collection device in the bathroom supports privacy and independence. It does not need correction.

questions.takeaway: For laboratory and diagnostic tests, the nurse explains the purpose so the client understands what is being done and why.
questions.strategy: Three options describe preparation that is already in place. Find the cue that shows a need the nurse can meet now.

steps.detail: Consent signed, vital signs give no concern.
Using the device in the bathroom is correct.
The client does not know the purpose of the test.

elimination.verdict: C. The client says nobody has told them why the test is needed or what it involves.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse matches three clients to the catheter each needs.

A client who needs continuous irrigation after bladder surgery to keep blood clots from forming needs a [[1]] catheter.

A client whose urethra is blocked by scar tissue and who needs long term drainage is expected to have a [[2]] catheter.

A client with a postvoid residual of 450 mL and an order to drain the bladder one time needs a [[3]] catheter.

options.text: three way
options.rationale: A three way catheter includes a separate channel for irrigation, which allows continuous irrigation through a closed system.

options.text: straight
options.rationale: A straight catheter is inserted briefly for drainage and removed. It cannot deliver continuous irrigation.

options.text: suprapubic
options.rationale: A suprapubic catheter drains the bladder through the abdominal wall. It is not chosen for continuous irrigation.

options.text: indwelling urethral
options.rationale: An indwelling urethral catheter passes through the urethra, which is blocked in this client.

options.text: suprapubic
options.rationale: A suprapubic catheter enters the bladder through the abdomen, so it drains urine when the urethra is blocked.

options.text: straight
options.rationale: A straight catheter also passes through the urethra and is removed after one drainage.

options.text: straight
options.rationale: A straight catheter is inserted briefly to drain the bladder and then removed, which fits a one time order.

options.text: three way
options.rationale: A three way catheter stays in place for irrigation. Nothing here calls for irrigation.

options.text: indwelling
options.rationale: An indwelling catheter remains in the bladder and adds infection risk when only one drainage is ordered.

questions.takeaway: Straight catheters drain once and are removed, indwelling catheters remain in the bladder, three way catheters add an irrigation channel, suprapubic catheters enter through the abdomen, and external devices collect urine outside the urethra.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions for each client: does the catheter stay or come out, and which path can it take?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Continuous irrigation needs an irrigation channel: three way.
A blocked urethra needs a path through the abdomen: suprapubic.
One drainage needs a catheter that is removed: straight.

elimination.verdict: Three way; suprapubic; straight.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to insert an indwelling urinary catheter for a client who needs hourly output measurement after major surgery. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use clean gloves for insertion, since the perineum is not sterile
options.rationale: Catheter insertion uses aseptic technique with sterile gloves and sterile equipment to keep bacteria out of the bladder.

options.text: Check the record and ask the client about an allergy to latex
options.rationale: Catheters and gloves can contain latex. The nurse checks for relevant allergies before insertion.

options.text: Select a larger catheter so that urine does not leak around it
options.rationale: The smallest appropriate catheter is used. A larger catheter increases trauma to the urethra and the risk of infection.

options.text: Confirm that the reason for the catheter is documented in a current order
options.rationale: The nurse confirms the indication before insertion. Hourly output after major surgery is the indication here.

options.text: Secure the catheter to the client's upper thigh after insertion
options.rationale: Securing the catheter prevents movement and pulling that injure the urethra and raise infection risk.

options.text: Leave the catheter unsecured so it can move freely with position changes
options.rationale: An unsecured catheter moves and pulls with each position change, which causes trauma.

questions.takeaway: Catheter safety: confirm the indication, consider an alternative, check allergies, use aseptic technique and sterile equipment, use the smallest appropriate catheter, and secure it after insertion.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option is the opposite of a safety step. Find the pairs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sterile, not clean.
Smallest appropriate, not larger.
Secured to the thigh, not left free.
Indication and latex allergy.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: A client, 64 years old, is on day 3 after abdominal surgery. An indwelling urinary catheter was placed for hourly output during surgery and the first 24 hours. The client now walks in the hall with assistance, is alert and oriented, and the hourly output order ended yesterday. The agency has a nurse driven catheter removal protocol. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Keep the catheter in place until discharge to avoid urinary retention at home
options.rationale: Each day a catheter remains raises the risk of a catheter associated infection. The risk of retention is managed by monitoring voiding after removal.

options.text: Change the catheter today, since it has been in place for 3 days
options.rationale: Routine catheter changes do not prevent infection. The question is whether the catheter is still needed.

options.text: Review the indication and remove the catheter per the removal protocol
options.rationale: The reason for the catheter, hourly output, no longer exists. Catheters are removed promptly when no longer indicated, per order or protocol, and voiding is monitored after removal.

options.text: Send a urine culture before removal to screen for infection
options.rationale: The client has no signs of infection. A culture without symptoms does not decide whether the catheter stays.

questions.takeaway: Prevent CAUTI: use a catheter only when needed, review the indication regularly, and remove it promptly when no longer indicated.
questions.strategy: Ask why the catheter was placed and whether that reason still exists.

steps.detail: Hourly output, which ended yesterday.
Walks with assistance, alert, no output order.
Review the indication and remove per protocol.

elimination.verdict: C. Review the indication and remove the catheter per the removal protocol.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: A client, 77 years old, has a long term indwelling urinary catheter. No urine has drained in 2 hours. The nurse finds the tubing straight with no kinks, the bag below the bladder, and gritty sediment in the tubing. A bladder scan shows 420 mL, and the client reports lower abdominal pressure, 5 of 10. There is no order for irrigation. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Report the findings and obtain an order to irrigate or change the catheter
options.rationale: The catheter is likely blocked by sediment, and the bladder is filling. Irrigation is done only when indicated and ordered, and changing a blocked catheter is often safer than flushing debris into the bladder. The provider needs the findings to decide.

options.text: Irrigate the catheter with sterile saline through a closed system now
options.rationale: Closed irrigation is the right technique, but irrigation is done only when it is ordered, and there is no order.

options.text: Reposition the client and recheck the drainage again in 2 hours
options.rationale: The tubing and bag have been checked, and the bladder holds 420 mL with pressure. Waiting 2 more hours lets the bladder keep filling.

options.text: Disconnect the tubing and flush the catheter with a syringe of water
options.rationale: Disconnecting opens the closed drainage system, and flushing without an order risks pushing debris into the bladder.

questions.takeaway: Irrigate only when indicated and ordered, and follow the approved procedure. When a catheter is blocked and there is no order, report the findings so the provider can order irrigation or a change.
questions.strategy: One option uses the right technique without the order. The cue that decides is the last sentence of the stem.

steps.detail: Tubing straight, bag low, sediment present, 420 mL in the bladder.
No order for irrigation.

steps.action: Reject delay and opening the system
steps.detail: Waiting 2 hours; disconnecting to flush.
Report and obtain an order.

elimination.verdict: A. Report the findings and obtain an order to irrigate or change the catheter.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: The nurse evaluates discharge teaching for a client with a new continent urinary reservoir and stoma. Which statement by the client indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "My spouse will take over the device care so I never have to look at the stoma."
options.rationale: Self management support aims for the client to take part in device care. Avoiding the stoma also means the client cannot check drainage and skin.

options.text: "I will call if the skin around my stoma gets red and sore or my urine changes."
options.rationale: The client names reportable changes in skin and drainage, which shows the client knows what to watch for and can manage the plan.

options.text: "If the skin around my stoma breaks down, I will wait for my next visit in a month."
options.rationale: Skin breakdown is a reportable change. Waiting a month leaves it untreated.

options.text: "I do not need to check the drainage since the reservoir is inside my body."
options.rationale: Drainage and skin are assessed with every urinary diversion, including a continent reservoir.

questions.takeaway: With a urinary diversion, care includes assessing drainage and skin, supporting device care and self management, and individualized teaching. Evaluation checks whether the client can manage the plan and knows reportable changes.
questions.strategy: Use the evaluation questions: can the client manage the care, and does the client know what to report?

steps.detail: Handing all care to a spouse and never looking at the stoma.
Waiting a month with skin breakdown.
Drainage is checked with every diversion.
Reports skin and urine changes.

elimination.verdict: B. "I will call if the skin around my stoma gets red and sore or my urine changes."

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: On day 3 after creation of an ileal conduit, which finding requires follow up by the nurse?

options.text: Urine in the pouch clear and pale yellow, 900 mL in 8 hours
options.rationale: Clear, pale urine with this output is an expected drainage finding.

options.text: Pouch emptied and output recorded every 4 hours
options.rationale: Emptying the pouch and recording output supports device care and accurate intake and output.

options.text: Client watched the pouch change and asks to try the next one
options.rationale: Asking to take part in device care shows readiness for self management.

options.text: Skin around the stoma red and weeping where urine leaked
options.rationale: Assessing drainage and skin is part of continuing care, and the outcome is intact skin. Red, weeping skin where urine leaked needs follow up.

questions.takeaway: With an ileal conduit, assess drainage and skin, support device care, and support self management. Skin damage from leaking urine needs follow up.
questions.strategy: Three options describe care and drainage that are on track. Find the one that describes harm.

steps.detail: Clear, pale urine and output recorded: on track.
Asks to try the next change: on track.
Red and weeping under the wafer: requires follow up.

elimination.verdict: D. Skin around the stoma red and weeping where urine leaked.

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: A client is admitted with new episodes of urine leakage at night. Which admission findings can affect the client's urinary elimination? Select all that apply.

options.text: Started a diuretic 1 week ago, taken at 2000 each evening
options.rationale: Medications affect urinary elimination. A diuretic increases urine output, and an evening dose produces more urine overnight.

options.text: Has an allergy to penicillin
options.rationale: A drug allergy does not change how the client stores or empties urine.

options.text: Has arthritis in both hands and wears pants with small buttons
options.rationale: Clothing management is a factor. Stiff hands and small buttons slow undressing once the client reaches the toilet.

options.text: Reads large print books each afternoon
options.rationale: Reading habits do not affect urinary elimination.

options.text: Says it is hard to void with the roommate behind the curtain
options.rationale: Privacy affects the ability to void. A shared room can make the client hold urine or not empty fully.

options.text: Drinks 4 cups of coffee each evening
options.rationale: Fluid intake and habits are factors. A large volume of a caffeinated drink in the evening adds to urine overnight.

questions.takeaway: Factors that influence urinary elimination include fluid intake and habits, growth and development, illness and medications, mobility and clothing management, privacy and culture, and toilet access.
questions.strategy: For each finding, ask whether it changes how much urine is made, how fast the client can get to and use the toilet, or how easily the client can void.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Evening diuretic and evening coffee add overnight urine.
Small buttons with arthritis; a roommate behind the curtain.
Penicillin allergy and reading habits.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.stem: During a nursing history, a client, 69 years old, reports a delay before the urine stream starts and a feeling that the bladder does not empty. Both began 4 days ago. The client denies burning, walks independently, and drinks about 2,000 mL of fluid per day. Which question should the nurse ask next?

options.text: "Do you leak urine when you cough, sneeze, laugh, or lift something heavy?"
options.rationale: This question screens for stress incontinence. The client reports trouble starting and emptying, not leakage.

options.text: "How many cups of coffee or tea do you usually drink each day?"
options.rationale: Fluid habits matter, but the client's intake is already known, and caffeine does not explain a new delay in starting the stream.

options.text: "Which medicines, prescribed or not, have you started in the last few days?"
options.rationale: Hesitancy and incomplete emptying that began suddenly 4 days ago suggest retention. Medications are a common non obstructive cause, so a recent medication history is the most useful next question.

options.text: "Do you need help getting to the bathroom during the night?"
options.rationale: The client walks independently. Toilet access does not explain hesitancy or incomplete emptying.

questions.takeaway: The nursing history covers pain, urgency, hesitancy, leakage, the feeling of incomplete emptying, fluid intake, and medication history. A new onset of hesitancy and incomplete emptying calls for the medication history.
questions.strategy: Use what the stem has already answered to remove options, then ask what could have changed 4 days ago.

steps.detail: Fluid intake is known; mobility is independent.
Leakage with coughing is not the complaint.

steps.action: Find the cause of a new change
steps.detail: A recently started medication.

elimination.verdict: C. Ask which medicines, prescribed or not, were started in the last few days.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.stem: At 0300 a nurse finds that a client, 77 years old, has been incontinent of urine in bed. The client is awake, alert, and looks away from the nurse. The roommate is awake. Which statement by the nurse best supports the client's dignity?

options.text: "Let's get your diaper changed so you won't wet the bed again tonight."
options.rationale: "Diaper" and "wet the bed" are childlike terms that shame an adult. Respectful language uses neutral words.

options.text: "I'll close the curtain and help you into dry clothes, explaining each step first."
options.rationale: Closing the curtain gives privacy from the awake roommate, neutral words respect the client, and explaining each step before touching supports dignity.

options.text: "Next time, please call before you have an accident so we can prevent this."
options.rationale: This places blame on the client. The client may have been unable to call in time, and blame increases embarrassment.

options.text: "Don't worry about it, this happens to everyone who is your age."
options.rationale: This minimizes the client's feelings and is not true of every older adult. It does not provide privacy or explain care.

questions.takeaway: Support dignity with privacy, respectful language, and an explanation of care before exposing or touching the client.
questions.strategy: Eliminate the options that shame, blame, or dismiss. Then confirm the remaining option includes privacy.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Diaper and wet the bed.
Calling before an accident.
Happens to everyone your age.
Curtain, dry clothes, each step explained.

elimination.verdict: B. "I'll close the curtain and help you into dry clothes, explaining each step first."

questions.objective: Select dignity supporting interventions

questions.stem: A client, 83 years old, in a rehabilitation unit has functional incontinence after hip surgery and needs help to transfer to a commode. The client says, "I want to stop leaking so I can go to the dining room for meals." The nurse and client plan care together. Which outcome is most appropriate?

options.text: Client will use the commode with help and have 1 or fewer leakage episodes per day within 1 week
options.rationale: This outcome is set with the client's goal in mind, is measurable by the number of episodes, includes a time frame, and is realistic for a client who still needs help to transfer.

options.text: Client will understand the importance of the toileting schedule before discharge
options.rationale: Understanding cannot be measured as written. It names no observable behavior.

options.text: Nurse will offer toileting assistance every 2 hours while the client is awake each day
options.rationale: This is a nursing intervention, not a client outcome. Outcomes describe what the client will do or experience.

options.text: Client will never leak urine again once the toileting plan has started on the unit
options.rationale: Never is absolute and unrealistic for a client who still needs help to reach the commode.

questions.takeaway: Set priorities with the client and choose measurable outcomes: a client behavior, a number, and a time frame, realistic for the client's situation.
questions.strategy: Check each option for three parts: the client as the subject, something you can count or observe, and a time frame.

steps.detail: Offering toileting is an intervention.
Understand names no behavior.
Never is unrealistic.
Commode with help, 1 episode per day or fewer, within 1 week.

elimination.verdict: A. Client will use the commode with help and have 1 or fewer leakage episodes per day within 1 week.

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: A client, 81 years old, lives alone and reports wetting the underwear on the way to the bathroom 2 or 3 times a week. The client drinks about 600 mL of fluid a day "so I do not have accidents," and the urine is dark amber. The last bowel movement was 4 days ago. The bathroom is at the end of a dim hallway with a rug and stacked boxes along the wall. The client walks with a cane in the right hand. Which recommendations support normal urinary elimination for this client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wear absorbent briefs during the day in place of walking to the bathroom
options.rationale: Briefs used in place of toileting leave urine against the skin and do nothing to remove the contributors named. The client can still walk to the bathroom with a cane once the path is safe.

options.text: Spread fluid intake through the day, aiming for urine that is light yellow
options.rationale: The kidneys need enough fluid to produce dilute urine. Dark amber urine at 600 mL a day is concentrated, and concentrated urine irritates the bladder and raises the risk of infection. Restricting fluid does not prevent leakage.

options.text: Wait until the urge is strong before walking to the bathroom
options.rationale: Waiting for a strong urge leaves less time to reach the toilet. With a long walk and a cane, the client needs more time, not less.

options.text: Light the hallway and clear the rug and boxes from the path
options.rationale: Poor lighting, clutter and an inaccessible bathroom are environmental barriers to reaching the toilet in time, and they add fall risk for a client who walks with a cane.

options.text: Stop drinking fluids after the noon meal to prevent leakage
options.rationale: Fluid is limited only in the 2 to 4 hours before bed, not for the whole afternoon. The client is already taking in too little fluid for dilute urine.

options.text: Add fiber and fluid to reestablish regular bowel movements
options.rationale: Constipation places pressure on the bladder and urethra and contributes to incontinence. No bowel movement for 4 days is a reversible contributor.

questions.takeaway: Normal elimination depends on enough fluid for dilute urine, regular bowel movements, and a safe, short path to the toilet. Fluid restriction, constipation, limited mobility and environmental barriers all work against continence.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each option by whether it removes a contributor named in the stem: low fluid, constipation, or a long dim cluttered path.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dark amber urine, no bowel movement for 4 days, a dim cluttered hallway and a cane are each a contributor.
Fluid spread through the day, bowel regularity, and a clear lit path.
Waiting for a strong urge, briefs in place of toileting, and stopping fluid at noon add risk.

elimination.verdict: B, D, F.

questions.objective: Explain urinary system functions and factors that support normal elimination

questions.stem: A resident with moderate dementia does not recognize the need to void, cannot follow instructions to delay voiding, and walks to the bathroom with the help of 1 staff member. A bladder diary shows voiding about every 2 hours while awake. Which toileting program does the nurse place in the plan of care?

options.text: Bladder training, with voiding every 45 minutes and the urge suppressed between intervals
options.rationale: Bladder training depends on a client who is alert, aware of bladder fullness and able to resist the urge. This resident cannot follow instructions to delay voiding.

options.text: Scheduled toileting, with staff assisting the resident to the toilet every 2 hours
options.rationale: Scheduled toileting relies on a time schedule set from the voiding pattern and does not require the resident to sense fullness or delay voiding. The diary supports a 2 hour interval, and the goal is to reach the toilet before leakage.

options.text: Absorbent briefs changed every 2 hours, so the resident is not walked to the bathroom
options.rationale: Briefs used in place of timed toileting undermine the program and leave urine on the skin. They also lead residents to get up alone, a common cause of falls.

options.text: Prompted voiding alone, with the resident expected to ask staff for help when the urge comes
options.rationale: Prompted voiding supplements scheduled toileting by prompting the resident to ask for help. Used alone, it fails for a resident who does not recognize the need to void.

questions.takeaway: Match the toileting program to cognition. Bladder training needs an alert client who can suppress the urge. Scheduled toileting works on a timed interval set from the voiding diary and suits cognitive impairment, with prompted voiding added as a supplement.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Prompted voiding is the right idea with one thing off: it depends on the resident asking. The cue that decides is that the resident does not recognize the need to void.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The resident does not sense fullness and cannot delay voiding.
It requires suppressing the urge between intervals.
It depends on the resident asking for help.
Briefs replace toileting and harm skin and safety.

elimination.verdict: B. Scheduled toileting every 2 hours with staff assistance.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.scenario: A client, 74 years old, has urge incontinence. The provider is choosing between an antimuscarinic drug, oxybutynin, and mirabegron. The nurse prepares teaching and monitoring points for each drug.
questions.stem: For each item, indicate the drug it applies to.

rows.text: Reduces involuntary bladder contractions
rows.rationale: Antimuscarinics block the nerve signals that trigger involuntary contractions of the bladder.

rows.text: Relaxes the detrusor muscle by stimulating beta 3 receptors
rows.rationale: Mirabegron relaxes the bladder muscle while urine is stored, which increases bladder capacity.

rows.text: Report new forgetfulness or confusion
rows.rationale: Cognitive effects are an antimuscarinic side effect and are a particular concern in older adults, so they are monitored closely.

rows.text: Report straining to void or a feeling that the bladder is not empty
rows.rationale: Antimuscarinics can cause urinary retention, which shows as straining or incomplete emptying.

rows.text: Check the blood pressure at follow up visits
rows.rationale: Mirabegron can raise blood pressure, so blood pressure is monitored while the client takes it.

rows.text: Use sugarless hard candy for dry mouth and add fiber for constipation
rows.rationale: Dry mouth and constipation are expected antimuscarinic side effects managed with these measures.

questions.takeaway: Antimuscarinics reduce involuntary bladder contractions and cause dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention and cognitive effects. Mirabegron relaxes the bladder during storage and requires blood pressure monitoring.
questions.strategy: Learn one unique point for mirabegron, blood pressure. Antimuscarinic side effects follow the drying, slowing pattern: dry mouth, constipation, retention, confusion.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Beta 3 relaxation of the detrusor and blood pressure.
Fewer involuntary contractions with dry mouth, constipation, retention and cognitive effects.
Every drying or slowing side effect belongs to the antimuscarinic.

elimination.verdict: Mirabegron: beta 3 relaxation of the detrusor and blood pressure. Antimuscarinic: involuntary contractions, confusion, retention, dry mouth and constipation.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: The nurse evaluates a client's understanding of pelvic floor muscle training. Which client statement shows the exercises are being performed correctly?

options.text: "I hold the squeeze as long as I can and try not to let the muscles relax between squeezes."
options.rationale: Training is a controlled contraction followed by complete relaxation. Holding without relaxing fatigues the muscle and is not the method.

options.text: "I do the squeezes only on days when the leaking is worse, so the muscles get a rest."
options.rationale: Pelvic floor training needs consistent, regular practice over time. Practicing only on bad days does not build strength.

options.text: "I tighten the muscles that stop my stream, relax them fully, and practice when not urinating."
options.rationale: Correct muscle identification is essential, and stopping the stream once helps find the muscles. Each controlled contraction is followed by complete relaxation, and practice happens outside of urination.

options.text: "I practice by stopping and starting my stream every time I urinate, so I never forget to do them."
options.rationale: Stopping the stream is a way to identify the muscles, not the exercise itself. Practice is done outside of urination.

questions.takeaway: Pelvic floor training: identify the correct muscles, contract with control, relax completely, practice outside of urination, and keep practicing regularly over time on an individualized plan.
questions.strategy: Option D is the right idea with one thing off: stopping the stream identifies the muscles, but practice happens outside of urination.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Option A skips complete relaxation.
Option B practices only on bad days.
Option D practices during urination.
Option C identifies, contracts, relaxes and practices outside of urination.

elimination.verdict: C. Tighten the identified muscles, relax fully, and practice while not urinating.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: A client, 70 years old, with diabetic neuropathy reports leaking small amounts of urine many times a day and night for 3 weeks, with a weak stream and a feeling of urgency. The client began a new antimuscarinic drug for urgency 4 weeks ago. Intake over the last 24 hours was 2000 mL, and the measured voided output was 700 mL. The lower abdomen is firm above the pubic bone. A bladder scan right after the client voided shows 450 mL. Which conclusion does the nurse draw?

options.text: The leakage is urge incontinence from involuntary bladder contractions, so the antimuscarinic dose needs to increase
options.rationale: Urgency and frequent leakage fit urge incontinence, and that is the reason the drug was started. The postvoid volume of 450 mL shows the bladder is not emptying, and an antimuscarinic adds to retention.

options.text: The leakage is from a weak pelvic floor, so pelvic floor muscle training is the first step
options.rationale: Pelvic floor weakness causes leakage with coughing or lifting. It does not explain 450 mL left in the bladder after voiding.

options.text: The low output reflects reduced kidney production, so oral fluid intake needs to increase
options.rationale: The urine is being made; it is staying in the bladder, as the firm lower abdomen and 450 mL scan show. More fluid adds to a bladder that is not emptying.

options.text: The leakage is from incomplete emptying, with urinary retention that the antimuscarinic may be worsening
options.rationale: Leakage can occur with incomplete emptying. A postvoid volume of 450 mL, output far below intake, and a firm suprapubic area point to retention. Diabetic neuropathy and the antimuscarinic are both contributors.

questions.takeaway: Leakage does not always mean an overactive bladder. When output is well below intake and the bladder holds a large volume right after voiding, the leakage comes from incomplete emptying, and antimuscarinics, which cause retention, can make it worse.
questions.strategy: Urge incontinence and retention are both defensible from the reported urgency and frequent leakage. The cue that decides is the 450 mL bladder scan taken right after voiding.

steps.detail: 450 mL remains in the bladder right after voiding.
Involuntary contractions empty the bladder; a full bladder after voiding means it is not emptying.
Diabetic neuropathy and an antimuscarinic both promote retention.
Pelvic floor weakness and low kidney output do not explain a full bladder.

elimination.verdict: D. Leakage from incomplete emptying, with retention the antimuscarinic may be worsening.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.nursesNote: 1015. Client is 34 years old. Oral temperature 37.0 °C. Has type 1 diabetes. Denies flank pain and denies chills. Reports burning during voiding since yesterday. Drank 1800 mL of fluid yesterday. Voids small amounts every 30 to 45 minutes and feels a sudden need to void. Reports no change in vision. Urine is pink tinged. Reports aching above the pubic bone, 4 of 10.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that are cues for a lower urinary tract infection, including risk factors.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.0 °C
segments.rationale: The temperature is within the expected range. Fever would suggest spread beyond the bladder.

segments.text: Has type 1 diabetes
segments.rationale: Diabetes and reduced immunity are risk factors for urinary infection.

segments.text: Denies flank pain and denies chills
segments.rationale: Flank pain and chills point to the kidney. Their absence fits a lower urinary infection.

segments.text: Reports burning during voiding since yesterday
segments.rationale: Dysuria, a stinging or burning pain during voiding, is a hallmark of cystitis.

segments.text: Drank 1800 mL of fluid yesterday
segments.rationale: This intake is adequate and is not a cue for infection.

segments.text: Voids small amounts every 30 to 45 minutes and feels a sudden need to void
segments.rationale: Frequency and urgency, often with small amounts, are signs of cystitis.

segments.text: Reports no change in vision
segments.rationale: Vision is unrelated to the urinary findings.

segments.text: Urine is pink tinged
segments.rationale: Hematuria, with pink, red or tea colored urine, warrants evaluation and occurs with cystitis.

segments.text: Reports aching above the pubic bone, 4 of 10
segments.rationale: Suprapubic discomfort is a sign of bladder inflammation.

questions.takeaway: Cystitis presents with dysuria, urgency and frequency in small amounts, suprapubic discomfort and hematuria. Diabetes raises infection risk. Fever, chills and flank pain suggest the infection has spread to the kidney.
questions.strategy: Read each phrase against the cystitis signs and the infection risk factors. Leave expected and absent findings unhighlighted.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Type 1 diabetes.
Burning, small frequent voids with urgency, pink urine, suprapubic aching.
Normal temperature, no flank pain or chills, adequate intake and normal vision.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: A client, 41 years old, was seen in the clinic yesterday for dysuria and urgency. The urinalysis showed nitrites and white blood cells, a clean catch specimen was sent for culture and susceptibility, and the client started an oral antibiotic at 1600 yesterday. Today at 1100 the culture reports Escherichia coli resistant to the prescribed antibiotic and susceptible to 2 other antibiotics. The client reports dysuria 5 of 10, was 6 of 10 yesterday at 1500. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Report the susceptibility result to the provider so the antibiotic can be matched to the organism
options.rationale: Culture identifies the organism, and susceptibility testing guides the antibiotic choice. An organism resistant to the current drug will not be treated by it, so the result is reported.

options.text: Tell the client that dysuria has decreased, so the current antibiotic is working and is continued
options.rationale: Pain dropping from 6 of 10 to 5 of 10 in less than a day is not evidence that the drug works. The culture shows the organism is resistant to it.

options.text: Repeat the urinalysis to confirm the infection before any change in the antibiotic is considered
options.rationale: The infection is already supported by symptoms, urinalysis and culture. Repeating the urinalysis delays effective treatment.

options.text: Request phenazopyridine for the dysuria and continue the current antibiotic until the course ends
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine relieves discomfort but does not treat infection. Continuing a drug the organism resists leaves the infection untreated.

questions.takeaway: Urinalysis suggests infection; culture identifies the organism; susceptibility testing guides antibiotic choice. Results are interpreted together with the symptoms, and a resistant organism means the antibiotic needs to change.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A small drop in pain is tempting evidence. The culture result outweighs it because it shows the drug cannot kill this organism.

steps.detail: The organism is resistant to the current antibiotic.
A 1 point drop in pain does not override resistance.
Repeating the urinalysis adds no new information.
Phenazopyridine treats discomfort, not infection.

elimination.verdict: A. Report the susceptibility result so the antibiotic can be changed.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings

questions.stem: A client with cystitis is prescribed an oral antibiotic and phenazopyridine and has no fluid restriction. Which actions does the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Confirm the client's drug allergies before the first antibiotic dose
options.rationale: Allergies are checked before any antibiotic, because antibiotic allergies are common and change the drug choice.

options.text: Teach the client to expect orange or red urine while taking phenazopyridine
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine turns the urine orange or red. Knowing this ahead prevents alarm.

options.text: Teach the client to stop the antibiotic once the burning has ended
