options.rationale: The full course is taken exactly as prescribed even when symptoms end early, to prevent recurrence and resistance. Adverse effects are reported rather than handled by stopping the drug.

options.text: Teach the client to report fever, flank pain or vomiting right away
options.rationale: Fever, flank pain, vomiting or worsening symptoms suggest the infection is spreading upward and need immediate reporting.

options.text: Explain that phenazopyridine treats the infection while the antibiotic eases the pain
options.rationale: The roles are reversed. Phenazopyridine relieves discomfort but does not treat infection; the antibiotic treats the infection.

options.text: Encourage regular fluid intake and emptying the bladder regularly
options.rationale: With no fluid restriction, appropriate hydration and regular bladder emptying flush bacteria from the bladder.

questions.takeaway: Cystitis care: check allergies before antibiotics, monitor for improvement and adverse effects, encourage fluids within limits, and give ordered pain relief. Teach the full course, report adverse effects rather than stop, and report fever, flank pain, vomiting or worsening at once. Phenazopyridine turns urine orange or red and does not treat infection.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option has the client stopping a drug or misreading what phenazopyridine does. Keep the options that complete treatment and report danger signs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Allergy check before the antibiotic.
Orange or red urine with phenazopyridine; complete the antibiotic course.
Fever, flank pain or vomiting are reported right away.
Stopping when the burning ends, and calling phenazopyridine a treatment, are errors.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, F.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: A client, 84 years old, was admitted 3 days ago and has an indwelling urinary catheter placed in the emergency department for accurate output measurement. The client now drinks fluids well and walks to the chair with assistance. The perineal skin is red with no open areas. The provider has ordered a urine culture. Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Review with the provider today whether the catheter is still indicated
options.rationale: Necessity is reviewed daily and the catheter is removed promptly. The original reason, accurate output measurement, may no longer apply.

options.text: Collect the culture specimen from the sampling port using aseptic technique
options.rationale: A proper specimen comes from the sampling port without opening the closed system, so the result reflects the bladder and not the bag.

options.text: Pour the culture specimen from the drainage bag into a sterile container
options.rationale: Urine in the bag has been standing and is not a proper specimen. Specimens are collected properly so they can be interpreted.

options.text: Disconnect the catheter from the tubing to obtain a fresh specimen
options.rationale: The closed drainage system is maintained. Disconnecting opens a route for bacteria.

options.text: Hang the drainage bag below the bladder and off the floor during walks
options.rationale: The bag stays below the bladder and off the floor so urine drains away from the bladder and the bag is not contaminated.

options.text: Cleanse the reddened perineal skin gently and keep it dry, with privacy during care
options.rationale: Skin protection and dignity are part of catheter care: gentle cleansing keeps the irritated skin intact, and privacy preserves dignity.

questions.takeaway: CAUTI prevention: use an indwelling catheter only for an appropriate indication, keep the drainage system closed and the tubing unobstructed, keep the bag below the bladder and off the floor, and review necessity daily and remove promptly. Collect specimens properly and protect skin and dignity.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The specimen options test the closed system. Keep the port with aseptic technique; reject the bag and the disconnection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The reason for the catheter may have ended, so review it today.
Port with aseptic technique, not the bag or a disconnection.
Bag below the bladder and off the floor.
Gentle cleansing, dry skin and privacy.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E, F.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: A resident of a long term care facility, 88 years old, became confused this morning, was alert and oriented to person and place at 2000 yesterday. A new sleeping medication was started at 2100 yesterday. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, and blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg. The resident has no dysuria, no new urgency or frequency, and no suprapubic or flank pain. A urine culture sent 2 days ago grew bacteria. A family member asks the nurse to request an antibiotic for a urinary infection. Which response does the nurse make?

options.text: "A culture alone does not show infection, so I will check other causes, like the new sleeping medication."
options.rationale: Bacteria in urine without attributable infection symptoms is asymptomatic bacteriuria, and confusion alone does not establish a urinary infection. The nurse assesses other causes; a sleeping medication started the night before is a likely one.

options.text: "Confusion is a common sign of urinary infection in older adults, so I will ask the provider for the antibiotic now."
options.rationale: Confusion can accompany infection in older adults, which makes this tempting. A positive culture with no urinary or systemic findings does not establish infection, and most asymptomatic bacteriuria in older adults does not require antibiotics.

options.text: "The culture result means an infection is present, so the provider will order an antibiotic."
options.rationale: A positive culture alone does not establish symptomatic infection. Results are matched with clinical findings.

options.text: "I will repeat the urine culture, and if it grows bacteria again, an antibiotic will be started."
options.rationale: A second positive culture still shows only bacteria in the urine. Treatment depends on infection symptoms, not on culture results.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, bacteria in the urine without urinary or systemic findings is asymptomatic bacteriuria and usually is not treated. Confusion or falls alone do not establish a urinary infection; assess other causes and look for urinary or systemic findings.
questions.strategy: Both the antibiotic request and the search for other causes are defensible, because confusion can signal infection in older adults. The cue that decides is the absence of any urinary or systemic findings, with a sleeping medication started the night before.

steps.detail: New confusion, normal vital signs, no urinary symptoms, positive culture.
A positive culture plus confusion alone is not a urinary infection.
A new sleeping medication started at 2100 yesterday.
Treating or repeating the culture ignores the missing symptoms.

elimination.verdict: A. The culture alone does not show infection; assess other causes, including the new sleeping medication.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.scenario: A nurse on a medical unit reviews urinary findings recorded today for several clients.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate the term that describes it.

rows.text: Voids 15 times while awake, 50 to 80 mL each time, with a 24 hour output of 1400 mL
rows.rationale: Urinating more often than usual is frequency. The voids are small, but the 24 hour output of 1400 mL shows the total output is not decreased, so this is not oliguria.

rows.text: Sleeps from 2200 to 0600 and is woken 3 times by the need to void
rows.rationale: Waking from sleep to urinate is nocturia. The problem is the timing during sleep, not the number of voids while awake.

rows.text: Total urine output 300 mL over 24 hours, with 3 voids
rows.rationale: Oliguria is decreased urine output. Few voids with a low 24 hour total point to less urine, not to a voiding pattern problem.

rows.text: Reports a sudden, compelling need to void while in the shower and rushes out to reach the toilet
rows.rationale: A sudden, compelling need to urinate is urgency. One episode with a rush to the toilet describes the sensation, not how often voiding occurs.

rows.text: Indwelling catheter has drained 18 mL per hour for 4 hours, was 60 mL per hour yesterday
rows.rationale: A falling hourly output through a draining catheter is decreased urine output, oliguria. Urgency, frequency and nocturia do not apply to a client whose urine drains through a catheter.

rows.text: Wakes at 0200 and 0430 each night to void 250 mL, with 6 voids while awake
rows.rationale: Six voids while awake is not more often than usual. The finding that stands out is waking from sleep to void: nocturia.

questions.takeaway: Each term names one thing: nocturia is waking from sleep to urinate, frequency is urinating more often than usual, urgency is a sudden compelling need, and oliguria is decreased urine output. Small voids are not oliguria when the 24 hour total is not decreased.
questions.strategy: Ask which part of the pattern is off for each finding: the time of night, the number of voids, the sensation, or the total amount.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 300 mL in 24 hours and 18 mL per hour are decreased output: oliguria. 1400 mL is not.
15 voids while awake: frequency.
Woken from sleep to void: nocturia. Sudden compelling need: urgency.

elimination.verdict: Frequency, nocturia, oliguria, urgency, oliguria, nocturia.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings

questions.stem: A client, 72 years old, is seen in the clinic for urine leakage that began 4 months ago. History: pelvic surgery 2 years ago, a stroke 8 months ago with weakness of the right arm and leg, and a urethral stricture with a weak stream. A bladder scan right after voiding shows 300 mL. For 3 days the client has had burning with voiding and urgency, and the urinalysis is positive for nitrites. The client takes levothyroxine each morning, drinks 2000 mL of fluid spread through the day, and has a soft bowel movement daily. Which findings does the nurse identify as risk factors or contributors for this client's incontinence? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pelvic surgery 2 years ago
options.rationale: Pelvic surgery is a cause of pelvic floor weakness, a patient factor for incontinence. Aging adds to the weakness.

options.text: Levothyroxine taken each morning
options.rationale: The medications that contribute are those affecting awareness, urine production or emptying, such as diuretics, sedatives and anticholinergics. Levothyroxine is not one of them.

options.text: Stroke 8 months ago with right arm and leg weakness
options.rationale: Neurologic conditions such as stroke impair bladder control, and the weakness limits mobility to reach the toilet.

options.text: Fluid intake of 2000 mL spread through the day
options.rationale: Adequate fluid spread through the day supports dilute urine and normal elimination. It does not contribute to leakage.

options.text: Urethral stricture with 300 mL left after voiding
options.rationale: Obstruction causes incomplete emptying, and leakage can occur when the bladder does not empty.

options.text: Burning, urgency and nitrites for 3 days
options.rationale: Urinary infection is a clinical contributor to incontinence and is reversible with treatment.

questions.takeaway: Incontinence risk factors: pelvic floor weakness from childbirth, pelvic surgery or aging; neurologic disease such as stroke, spinal cord injury or diabetic neuropathy; obstruction with incomplete emptying; urinary infection; constipation; medications affecting awareness, production or emptying; and limited mobility or environmental barriers.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into a known category of contributor. A drug counts only when it changes awareness, urine production or emptying.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pelvic surgery and stroke.
Stricture with incomplete emptying, and urinary infection.
Levothyroxine, adequate fluid and a daily bowel movement are not contributors.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: A resident of an assisted living facility, 79 years old, has woken wet with urine between 0100 and 0400 on each of the last 5 nights and does not recall feeling the urge to void. A sedative at bedtime was started 6 days ago. The resident has taken a diuretic at 0800 each day for 3 years. Urine is light yellow, with no dysuria, urgency or frequency. Oral temperature 36.7 °C. Bowel movements are soft and daily. The resident does not leak when coughing or lifting. Which contributor does the nurse identify as most likely?

options.text: The morning diuretic, which increases urine production during the night
options.rationale: Diuretics raise urine production, but this one is taken at 0800 and has been taken for 3 years without nighttime leakage. Its effect is greatest during the day.

options.text: A urinary infection, which irritates the bladder and causes leakage
options.rationale: Infection is a reversible contributor, but there is no dysuria, urgency, frequency or fever to support it.

options.text: The bedtime sedative, which reduces awareness of a full bladder
options.rationale: Sedatives affect awareness. The leakage began the night after the sedative started, occurs during sleep, and the resident does not sense the urge.

options.text: Pelvic floor weakness from aging, which lets urine leak with pressure
options.rationale: Pelvic floor weakness causes leakage with coughing or lifting, which the resident denies.

questions.takeaway: Medications contribute to incontinence by changing awareness (sedatives), urine production (diuretics) or emptying (anticholinergics). Timing points to the cause: the new drug whose start matches the onset is the first to consider.
questions.strategy: The diuretic is the right idea with one thing off: it raises production, but it is old and taken in the morning. The cue that decides is the sedative starting the day before the leakage began.

steps.detail: Leakage started 5 nights ago; the sedative started 6 days ago.
No sensation of the urge during sleep fits reduced awareness.
The diuretic is long standing and taken at 0800, infection has no signs, and no stress leakage is present.

elimination.verdict: C. The bedtime sedative.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: A client, 77 years old, on bed rest after a fall, has urge incontinence, and an external urine collection device was applied 2 days ago. In the last 12 hours the device has come loose twice, and the linens were wet 3 times. The skin under the edge of the device is red, with no open areas. The device collected 400 mL in 24 hours, and intake was 1800 mL. Which conclusion does the nurse draw?

options.text: The device is not effective, and its fit and skin contact need to be reassessed
options.rationale: External devices are evaluated for fit, skin contact and effectiveness. Repeated loosening, wet linens and red skin show the device fails on all three.

options.text: The device is effective because it collected 400 mL, so the plan continues
options.rationale: Collecting some urine is not the measure. Most of the output is leaking onto the linens, and the skin is red.

options.text: The device has failed, so an indwelling catheter is needed to protect the skin
options.rationale: Indwelling catheters are used only for an appropriate indication. Incontinence is not one, and the skin has no open areas.

options.text: The device is loose, so it needs to be applied more tightly to stay in place
options.rationale: A tighter fit adds pressure to skin that is already red. The fit itself needs to be reassessed, with another size or device considered.

questions.takeaway: External collection devices are evaluated on 3 points: fit, skin contact and effectiveness. Wet linens and red skin mean the device is failing, and the answer is to reassess the device, not to switch to an indwelling catheter.
questions.strategy: Options C and D both accept that the device failed but choose a fix that adds risk. The global option names all 3 evaluation points.

steps.detail: Wet linens 3 times and loosening twice.
Red skin under the edge.
An indwelling catheter lacks an indication; a tighter fit adds pressure.

elimination.verdict: A. Reassess the fit and skin contact of a device that is not effective.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: A client, 68 years old, has urge incontinence. An antimuscarinic was stopped because of new confusion, and the client now has an onabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) injection into the bladder muscle. Ten days after the injection, the client reports straining to void and passing small amounts. A bladder scan right after voiding shows 420 mL. Oral temperature 36.8 °C, and there is no dysuria. The client has full use of both hands and says, "The leaking has stopped." Which plan does the nurse expect?

options.text: Restart the antimuscarinic to combine it with the injection
options.rationale: Combining approaches is reasonable in some clients, but antimuscarinics cause retention and caused confusion in this client. Adding one now worsens the problem.

options.text: Insert an indwelling catheter to drain the bladder until the leaking returns
options.rationale: Indwelling catheters are used only for an appropriate indication and removed promptly, and device therapy includes intermittent catheterization for incomplete emptying.

options.text: Arrange an artificial sphincter so the bladder empties completely
options.rationale: An artificial sphincter controls leakage at the urethra; it does not empty the bladder. Surgical options are individualized and do not treat retention.

options.text: Teach intermittent self catheterization to empty the bladder
options.rationale: Botox relaxes the bladder muscle, which stops the leakage, and the straining with 420 mL left after voiding shows incomplete emptying. Self catheterization is a device therapy that empties the bladder, and the client has the hand use to perform it. The retention after Botox is usually temporary.

questions.takeaway: Botox relaxes the bladder muscle and relieves urge incontinence. When the bladder then does not empty, device therapy with intermittent self catheterization empties it. Treatment is individualized, and approaches are combined only when they do not add to the problem, as an antimuscarinic adds retention.
questions.strategy: The cue that decides is the 420 mL left in the bladder after voiding. Treat the retention with the device therapy that empties the bladder.

steps.detail: Leakage stopped, but 420 mL remains after voiding: retention.
Botox relaxes the bladder muscle.

steps.action: Choose the fix that empties the bladder
steps.detail: Intermittent self catheterization; the client has full use of both hands.
The antimuscarinic adds retention, an indwelling catheter needs an appropriate indication and prompt removal, and a sphincter does not empty the bladder.

elimination.verdict: D. Intermittent self catheterization.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: A client, 58 years old, is at a clinic visit for hypertension in a private exam room. The urinary questions on the intake form are blank. The nurse sees an absorbent pad in the client's bag. When asked about bladder control, the client looks away and says, "It is normal for my age, I just deal with it." The client's adult child is in the waiting room. Which response does the nurse make?

options.text: "Leaking is common and often treatable. How often does it happen, and when?"
options.rationale: Urinary concerns are assessed directly and with dignity. Normalizing the topic and asking specific questions about frequency and triggers starts identifying the type and cause.

options.text: "Leaking is part of getting older, so pads are a good way to manage it."
options.rationale: Incontinence is not a normal part of aging, and accepting pads without assessment skips identifying a cause that may be reversible.

options.text: "I will note that you have no urinary concerns, and we can move on to your blood pressure."
options.rationale: Recording no concerns when there are cues of leakage denies the problem and leaves it unassessed.

options.text: "Your child in the waiting room may know how often it happens, so I can ask for you."
options.rationale: Asking a family member without consent breaks privacy and dignity. The client is the source of this history.

questions.takeaway: Assess urinary concerns directly, in private, and with dignity. Clients often hide leakage from embarrassment or the belief that it is normal with age. Specific questions about how often and when it happens identify the type and cause.
questions.strategy: Options B and C both close the topic. The patient centered option keeps the client talking and gathers data.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Blank form, a pad in the bag, and looking away.
Calling it normal for age, or noting no concerns, ends the assessment.
Asking the adult child without consent.
Normalize, then ask how often and when.

elimination.verdict: A. Normalize the concern and ask direct questions about the leakage.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: A client, 55 years old, has received radiation therapy to the pelvis for 3 weeks. For 4 days the client has had burning with voiding, urgency and frequency. Oral temperature 36.9 °C, heart rate 82 beats per minute. The urinalysis is negative for nitrites, and the urine culture shows no growth at 48 hours. The client asks for an antibiotic. Which interpretation does the nurse make?

options.text: The symptoms show a lower urinary tract infection, so an antibiotic is needed even without growth
options.rationale: Symptoms alone do not establish infection. Urine tests are matched with the clinical findings, and here they show no organism.

options.text: The bladder is inflamed without an infection, so an antibiotic would not treat it
options.rationale: Bladder inflammation can occur without infection, from irritation by other sources. Cystitis symptoms with no nitrites and no organism on culture fit inflammation without infection. Pelvic radiation is one such irritant.

options.text: The findings show asymptomatic bacteriuria, which does not need an antibiotic
options.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is bacteria in the urine without symptoms. This client has symptoms and no bacteria, the opposite pattern.

options.text: The culture was likely contaminated, so a repeat specimen is needed before treating
options.rationale: A contaminated specimen grows mixed organisms. No growth with a negative urinalysis does not suggest contamination.

questions.takeaway: Cystitis is inflammation of the bladder, and bladder inflammation can occur without infection. Urine tests are interpreted with the symptoms: the culture identifies organisms, and symptoms with no organism point away from infection. Radiation, drugs and chemicals are examples of irritants.
questions.strategy: Options B and C are an opposite pair. Asymptomatic bacteriuria is bacteria without symptoms; this client has symptoms without bacteria.

steps.detail: Classic symptoms, but no nitrites and no growth.
No organism identified, so there is no infection to treat.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria needs bacteria and no symptoms.

elimination.verdict: B. Bladder inflammation without infection.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: A client with recurrent cystitis often holds urine for an entire work shift. After teaching on prevention, which statement shows the client understands how the infection developed?

options.text: "The bacteria reached my bladder through my blood, so the best thing I can do is take vitamins."
options.rationale: Spread through the blood is uncommon. Bacteria most often ascend through the urethra to the bladder.

options.text: "I will drink less during my shift so I do not need to stop work to use the bathroom."
options.rationale: Less fluid concentrates the urine and means fewer voids to flush bacteria, adding to the risk.

options.text: "Bacteria move up the urethra, so I will void every few hours instead of holding it all shift."
options.rationale: Upward migration through the urethra is the most frequent route. Regular voiding flushes bacteria out before they multiply in the bladder.

options.text: "I will scrub the area with a strong antiseptic soap several times a day to kill the bacteria."
options.rationale: Perineal hygiene is gentle. Harsh, repeated scrubbing goes against that teaching.

questions.takeaway: Bacteria most commonly ascend through the urethra to the bladder. Prevention follows from the route: adequate hydration, emptying the bladder regularly, and gentle perineal hygiene.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option is a prevention idea with one thing off: the wrong route, too little fluid, or harsh hygiene. Match the teaching to the ascending route.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Upward through the urethra.

steps.action: Check the habit in the stem
steps.detail: Holding urine for a whole shift.

steps.action: Keep the statement that fixes it
steps.detail: Voiding every few hours flushes bacteria.

elimination.verdict: C. Bacteria ascend through the urethra, so void regularly.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: A client, 60 years old, has had 4 episodes of cystitis this year, and each resolved with a full antibiotic course. The client has a urethral stricture and reports a weak stream. A bladder scan right after voiding shows 280 mL. Fluid intake is 2200 mL a day. Fasting blood glucose today is 92 mg/dL. The client has never had a urinary catheter. Which factor does the nurse identify as most likely to explain the repeated infections?

options.text: Urine left in the bladder from the stricture, which lets bacteria multiply
options.rationale: Obstruction and incomplete emptying cause stasis, and bacteria multiply in urine that stays in the bladder. The stricture and 280 mL after voiding fit this.

options.text: Low fluid intake, which concentrates urine and lowers flushing of bacteria
options.rationale: Intake of 2200 mL a day is adequate and does not explain the repeated infections.

options.text: Resistance to antibiotics from the repeated courses of treatment
options.rationale: Each episode resolved with treatment, so the drugs are working. The problem is that the infections keep returning.

options.text: Reduced immunity from diabetes, which lets bacteria invade more easily
options.rationale: Diabetes is a risk factor, but the fasting glucose of 92 mg/dL does not support it.

questions.takeaway: Incomplete emptying and obstruction, such as strictures, tumors, stones or reflux, cause stasis that lets bacteria multiply. Recurrent infection plus a high volume after voiding points to the obstruction.
questions.strategy: Each option is a real risk factor; the stem rules out all but one. Use the data given to test each.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 2200 mL a day is adequate.
Glucose 92 mg/dL.
Each episode resolved.
Stricture and 280 mL after voiding.

elimination.verdict: A. Stasis from the stricture.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: A client, 26 years old, is receiving chemotherapy, takes a corticosteroid daily, and is on day 2 of an oral antibiotic for cystitis. The client calls the clinic at 0900 and reports that the burning with voiding is worse than yesterday and that the client vomited twice since waking. Oral temperature at home is 37.2 °C, and there is no flank pain. The client says, "I will drink extra water and wait until my clinic visit in 10 days." Which response does the nurse give?

options.text: "Without a fever or side pain, waiting until your visit is reasonable."
options.rationale: Fever and flank pain are only two of the findings to report. Vomiting and worsening symptoms are reported immediately on their own.

options.text: "Extra water will flush the bladder, so call back if a fever starts."
options.rationale: Fluids are encouraged, but they do not replace evaluation, and waiting for fever ignores vomiting and worsening burning.

options.text: "Stop the antibiotic, since it may be causing the vomiting, and rest today."
options.rationale: Adverse effects are reported rather than managed by stopping. Stopping also leaves the infection untreated.

options.text: "Vomiting and worse burning need checking now, so let us see you today."
options.rationale: Vomiting and worsening symptoms are reported immediately. Reduced immunity from chemotherapy and a corticosteroid raises the risk of infection, so these signs need evaluation now.

questions.takeaway: Teach clients with cystitis to report fever, flank pain, vomiting or worsening symptoms immediately. Any one of them is enough. Reduced immunity is a risk factor for urinary infection, which makes prompt reporting matter more.
questions.strategy: Options A and B wait for fever, which is the trap: the findings to report are fever, flank pain, vomiting or worsening, and this client has two of the four.

steps.detail: Chemotherapy plus a daily corticosteroid: reduced immunity.
Vomiting twice and burning worse than yesterday.
Waiting 10 days, waiting for fever, or stopping the antibiotic.
Arrange a visit today.

elimination.verdict: D. Arrange prompt evaluation today.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: Which actions by the nurse follow measures to prevent catheter associated urinary tract infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Declines a request to insert an indwelling catheter in a client who is incontinent so the linens stay dry
options.rationale: An indwelling catheter is used only for an appropriate indication. Keeping linens dry is staff convenience, not an indication.

options.text: Clamps the drainage tubing while the client walks so urine does not flow back into the bladder
options.rationale: Tubing is kept unobstructed. Backflow is prevented by keeping the bag below the bladder, not by clamping.

options.text: Separates the catheter from the tubing to flush a slow draining catheter
options.rationale: Opening the connection breaks the closed drainage system and lets bacteria enter.

options.text: Performs hand hygiene and uses aseptic technique to insert a catheter for acute retention
options.rationale: Acute retention is an appropriate indication, and hand hygiene with aseptic insertion keeps bacteria out of the bladder.

options.text: Straightens tubing found kinked under a client's right thigh
options.rationale: A kink obstructs flow and causes urine to pool. Keeping tubing unobstructed is a prevention step.

options.text: Leaves a catheter in place the night after surgery in case the client has trouble voiding
options.rationale: Necessity is reviewed daily and the catheter is removed promptly. In case is not an indication.

questions.takeaway: CAUTI prevention: use an indwelling catheter only for an appropriate indication, perform hand hygiene and insert aseptically, keep the drainage system closed and the tubing unobstructed, keep the bag below the bladder and off the floor, and review necessity daily and remove promptly.
questions.strategy: Test each action against the 6 prevention steps. Any action that breaks the system, blocks flow, or keeps a catheter without an indication is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Incontinence and in case are not indications; acute retention is.
Separating the connection breaks closed drainage.
Clamping blocks flow; straightening a kink restores it.

elimination.verdict: A, D, E.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: A client with heart failure and a prescribed fluid limit of 1500 mL a day is prescribed an oral antibiotic for cystitis. Which statement by the client indicates a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I will keep my fluids at 1500 mL a day and spread them out over the day."
options.rationale: Fluids are encouraged within prescribed limits. Spreading the allowed amount through the day supports regular voiding without exceeding the limit.

options.text: "I will drink as much water as I can to flush the infection out of my bladder."
options.rationale: Fluids are encouraged only within prescribed limits. Drinking without limit can overload a client with heart failure.

options.text: "If the antibiotic gives me diarrhea, I will call the clinic instead of just stopping it."
options.rationale: Clients report adverse effects rather than stopping the antibiotic, so the provider can adjust treatment.

options.text: "I will call right away if I get a fever, pain in my side, or start vomiting."
options.rationale: Fever, flank pain, vomiting or worsening symptoms are reported immediately because they suggest the infection is spreading.

questions.takeaway: Encourage fluids within prescribed limits. For a client with a fluid restriction, the limit wins over the usual advice to drink more. Teach the client to report adverse effects instead of stopping the antibiotic.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the wrong statement. The fluid limit in the stem is the cue that turns usual advice into an error.

steps.detail: Find the statement that is incorrect.
Heart failure with 1500 mL a day.
A, C and D follow the plan; B ignores the limit.

elimination.verdict: B. Drinking as much as possible ignores the fluid limit.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client, 45 years old, is on day 3 of a 5 day oral antibiotic and a 2 day course of phenazopyridine for cystitis. Today: dysuria 1 of 10, was 6 of 10 on day 1; voids every 3 hours, was every 30 minutes on day 1; urine is orange; oral temperature 36.8 °C; 4 watery stools since 0600, with none before today.

The orange urine is [[1]].

The change in dysuria and voiding shows [[2]].

The nurse [[3]].

options.text: a sign of new hematuria that needs a culture
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine explains the color, and the other findings are moving the right way.

options.text: an expected effect of phenazopyridine
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine turns urine orange or red. It is expected and not a sign of bleeding.

options.text: a sign of dehydration from the stools
options.rationale: Concentrated urine is dark yellow or amber. Orange urine on phenazopyridine is a drug effect.

options.text: an allergic reaction to the antibiotic
options.rationale: Urine color is not a sign of allergy.

options.text: a response to treatment, with the full course still to be finished
options.rationale: Symptoms are decreasing, which is the expected improvement. The full course is completed even when symptoms ease.

options.text: a cure, so the remaining antibiotic doses can be stopped
options.rationale: Stopping early leaves bacteria behind. The full course is completed.

options.text: masking by phenazopyridine, so the antibiotic is failing
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine eases pain, but the voiding interval has also returned toward normal, which is an antibiotic effect.

options.text: spread of infection toward the kidney
options.rationale: Spread brings fever, flank pain or vomiting. The temperature is 36.8 °C and symptoms are easing.

options.text: tells the client to stop the antibiotic until the stools end
options.rationale: Clients report adverse effects rather than stopping. The provider decides on a change.

options.text: tells the client that watery stools are expected and need no follow up
options.rationale: Four new watery stools in a few hours are an adverse effect to report.

options.text: asks the provider to extend the phenazopyridine course
options.rationale: Pain is 1 of 10, and phenazopyridine does not treat infection.

options.text: reports the watery stools to the provider as a possible adverse effect
options.rationale: Monitoring includes adverse effects. New watery stools after starting an antibiotic are reported rather than ignored or managed by stopping the drug.

questions.takeaway: During cystitis treatment, monitor both improvement and adverse effects. Decreasing dysuria and frequency show response, but the full course is completed. Orange urine on phenazopyridine is expected. New adverse effects are reported, not managed by stopping the drug.
questions.strategy: Evaluate each finding separately: expected drug effect, treatment response, or adverse effect.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Orange urine from phenazopyridine.
Pain 6 to 1 and voids every 30 minutes to every 3 hours, with the course unfinished.
4 new watery stools today: report.

elimination.verdict: 1: expected effect of phenazopyridine. 2: response to treatment, finish the course. 3: report the watery stools.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: A client, 34 years old, reports burning with urination and urgency for 4 days. Today the client has shaking chills, nausea, and pain in the right flank rated 7 of 10. Oral temperature 39.1 °C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. Light percussion over the right costovertebral angle reproduces the pain. Which interpretation of these findings by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Cystitis, because burning and urgency place the infection in the bladder
options.rationale: Burning and urgency are lower tract symptoms and can be present in pyelonephritis too. Cystitis does not explain shaking chills, a temperature of 39.1 °C, and right flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness.

options.text: Pyelonephritis, because the fever, chills, and right flank tenderness show kidney spread
options.rationale: Fever and shaking chills signal that infection has spread beyond the lower tract, and flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness is the hallmark of kidney involvement. Nausea, tachycardia, and tachypnea are associated findings, and dysuria and urgency may still be present.

options.text: Acute glomerulonephritis, because the kidney is involved and the heart rate is elevated
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis presents with cola colored urine, facial and peripheral edema, elevated blood pressure, and decreased urine output. None of those findings are described, and fever with flank tenderness points to infection.

options.text: Urinary retention, because urgency with flank pain points to a bladder that is not emptying
options.rationale: Retention causes a distended bladder and incomplete emptying. It does not explain fever, shaking chills, and costovertebral angle tenderness.

questions.takeaway: Lower tract symptoms (dysuria, urgency) can occur in both cystitis and pyelonephritis. Fever with chills and flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness are what move the infection up to the kidney.
questions.strategy: Sort the findings into local bladder symptoms and systemic or kidney findings. The option that accounts for every finding wins.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Burning and urgency are lower tract; chills, 39.1 °C, and right flank tenderness are systemic and kidney findings.
Costovertebral angle tenderness points to the kidney.
Cystitis explains only the burning and urgency.
Glomerulonephritis needs edema, high blood pressure, and cola colored urine, which are absent.

elimination.verdict: Pyelonephritis.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: A client, 46 years old, is admitted with right flank pain rated 8 of 10, right costovertebral angle tenderness, oral temperature 39.3 °C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, and blood pressure 104/64 mm Hg. A stone in the right ureter was removed 2 months ago. Which diagnostic tests does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.

options.text: A 24 hour urine collection for total protein
options.rationale: Measuring urine protein levels belongs to the workup for glomerulonephritis, where damaged glomeruli leak protein. It does not identify the organism or the spread of a kidney infection.

options.text: Urinalysis and urine culture with susceptibility testing
options.rationale: Urinalysis shows findings such as white blood cells and nitrites, and the culture identifies the organism. Susceptibility testing guides the antibiotic choice.

options.text: Blood cultures
options.rationale: Blood cultures are drawn when sepsis is a risk. A temperature of 39.3 °C, a heart rate of 116 beats per minute, and a blood pressure of 104/64 mm Hg raise that risk.

options.text: Imaging of the kidneys and ureters
options.rationale: Imaging is used when obstruction or complications are suspected. A stone removed from the right ureter 2 months ago makes obstruction on the painful side a real concern.

options.text: Serum creatinine and electrolytes
options.rationale: Kidney function tests and electrolytes show whether the infection is affecting kidney function and give a baseline to trend.

questions.takeaway: The pyelonephritis workup has four parts: urinalysis and urine culture, blood cultures when sepsis is a risk, kidney function tests and electrolytes, and imaging when obstruction or a complication is suspected.
questions.strategy: Match each test to a question the nurse needs answered: which organism, has it reached the blood, how are the kidneys working, and is something blocking flow. A test that answers none of these is out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Urinalysis and culture with susceptibility testing.
Fever, tachycardia, and a blood pressure of 104/64 mm Hg justify blood cultures.
Creatinine and electrolytes.
The recent ureteral stone justifies imaging.
Urine protein measurement is a glomerulonephritis test.

elimination.verdict: B, C, D, E.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings.

questions.stem: A client with pyelonephritis is going home with a 10 day course of an oral antibiotic and feels better by day 3. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will drink the amount of fluid you told me to drink each day."
options.rationale: Taking the prescribed fluid intake is part of the plan. This statement is correct.

options.text: "I will keep my appointment for a repeat urine test after I finish all the pills."
options.rationale: Follow up testing confirms the infection has cleared. This statement is correct.

options.text: "If the pills upset my stomach, I will stop them and call if the fever returns."
options.rationale: Adverse effects are reported to the provider rather than handled by stopping the drug, and the full course is completed even when the client feels better on day 3. Stopping early risks a return of the kidney infection.

options.text: "If I get chills or the pain in my side comes back, I will call right away."
options.rationale: Fever, chills, or worsening symptoms are reported promptly. This statement is correct.

questions.takeaway: Pyelonephritis teaching: complete the full antibiotic course, report adverse effects instead of stopping, report fever, chills, or worsening, take the prescribed fluids, and keep follow up testing.
questions.strategy: In a need for further teaching item, look for the statement with one wrong step hidden inside a correct one. Calling about fever is right; stopping the drug on its own is not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that is wrong.
Fluids, follow up testing, and calling about chills or pain are all correct.
Stopping the antibiotic for stomach upset abandons the full course.
Adverse effects are reported, not treated by stopping.

elimination.verdict: The client who plans to stop the antibiotic for stomach upset needs more teaching.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan.

questions.scenario: A client, 67 years old, weighing 70 kg, was admitted at 0800 with pyelonephritis and started on IV antibiotics. The nurse reassesses the client at 1600.
questions.stem: For each finding at 1600, indicate whether it is expected with pyelonephritis or signals progression toward sepsis.

rows.text: Confused about the date and place, was oriented at 0800
rows.rationale: New confusion is the first warning sign in the progression from urinary infection to sepsis.

rows.text: Right flank pain 6 of 10 with right costovertebral angle tenderness, was 7 of 10 at 0800
rows.rationale: Flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness is the hallmark of pyelonephritis, and the pain has not grown worse since 0800.

rows.text: Blood pressure 88/52 mm Hg, was 126/78 mm Hg at 0800
rows.rationale: Hypotension with poor perfusion is the next stage of the progression to sepsis.

rows.text: Respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, was 20 at 0800, and urine output 60 mL over the past 4 hours
rows.rationale: Rapid breathing and decreased urine output are late signs of sepsis. An output of 60 mL in 4 hours in a client weighing 70 kg is about 0.2 mL/kg per hour.

rows.text: Burning and urgency with each void
rows.rationale: Dysuria and urgency may be present with pyelonephritis because the infection usually ascends from the bladder.

rows.text: Nausea with one episode of vomiting
rows.rationale: Nausea and vomiting are associated findings in pyelonephritis.

questions.takeaway: The progression from urinary infection to sepsis runs from new confusion, to hypotension and poor perfusion, to rapid breathing and decreased urine output. Flank pain, dysuria, and nausea belong to the kidney infection itself.
questions.strategy: Ask whether each finding is the kidney infection itself or a sign that the infection is now affecting the brain, circulation, lungs, or kidney output. Changes from the 0800 baseline are the cues.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, dysuria, urgency, and nausea are pyelonephritis findings.
New confusion, a fall in blood pressure from 126/78 to 88/52 mm Hg, a respiratory rate rising to 30, and 60 mL of urine in 4 hours.
Confusion, then hypotension and poor perfusion, then rapid breathing and low urine output.

elimination.verdict: Expected: flank pain with tenderness, burning and urgency, nausea. Sepsis progression: new confusion, hypotension, rapid breathing with low urine output.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.stem: A client, 72 years old, weighing 80 kg, is on day 2 of IV antibiotics for pyelonephritis. Serum creatinine 2.2 mg/dL, was 1.1 mg/dL on admission. BUN 40 mg/dL, was 20 mg/dL on admission. Urine output 100 mL over the past 6 hours. Lungs are clear and there is no edema. Which interpretation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: Kidney function is declining, because creatinine and BUN both doubled as urine output fell
options.rationale: Creatinine is excreted only by the kidneys, so a creatinine that doubles reflects about a 50% loss of filtration. When BUN and creatinine rise together and output falls to about 0.2 mL/kg per hour, the kidneys themselves are failing to clear waste.

options.text: Fluid volume deficit is the cause, because the BUN rises when a client is dehydrated
options.rationale: Dehydration does raise the BUN, but it raises the BUN faster than the creatinine. Here both values doubled at the same rate, which points to kidney dysfunction rather than low blood volume.

options.text: The infection is resolving, because a lower urine output means less fluid lost by the kidneys
options.rationale: Falling urine output on day 2 is a warning sign, not a sign of recovery. Response to treatment is judged by fever, pain, and kidney function trends.

options.text: Fluid overload has developed, because low urine output always produces crackles and edema
options.rationale: The lungs are clear and there is no edema. Low output can lead to fluid retention, but it does not always produce it, and the creatinine trend is the cue being tested.

questions.takeaway: Rising creatinine with falling urine output means kidney dysfunction. When BUN and creatinine rise together, the cause is the kidney itself, not dehydration.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Use creatinine as the kidney specific value. Then check whether the BUN rose alone or alongside the creatinine.

steps.detail: 2.2 mg/dL from 1.1 mg/dL is a doubling.
BUN also doubled, so the ratio is unchanged.
100 mL over 6 hours in 80 kg is about 0.2 mL/kg per hour.
An absolute about edema and a claim of recovery do not fit the data.

elimination.verdict: Kidney function is declining.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.stem: A client, 58 years old, with pyelonephritis has vomited 6 times in 2 days and has dry oral mucosa. BUN 36 mg/dL, was 15 mg/dL on admission 2 days ago. Serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, was 0.9 mg/dL on admission. Urine is dark amber, 180 mL over the past 8 hours. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Reduced blood volume is raising the BUN, because the creatinine has not changed
options.rationale: Dehydration concentrates the blood and raises the BUN faster than the creatinine. Creatinine is excreted only by the kidneys, and an unchanged value of 0.9 mg/dL shows filtration has not fallen. Vomiting, dry mucosa, and dark amber urine fit fluid loss.

options.text: Kidney tissue damage from the infection is raising the BUN and lowering urine output
options.rationale: Pyelonephritis can damage the kidney, and the output is low. But kidney damage raises creatinine along with BUN, and the creatinine is unchanged at 0.9 mg/dL.

options.text: Fever is breaking down muscle, so the creatinine will rise to match the BUN within a day
options.rationale: No fever is described, and nothing in the data predicts a creatinine rise. The pattern of a high BUN with unchanged creatinine fits fluid loss.

options.text: Kidney function cannot be judged until a 24 hour urine protein result is available
options.rationale: Serum creatinine already gives a kidney function value. Urine protein measurement is used in glomerulonephritis and is not needed to interpret this pattern.

questions.takeaway: BUN rises with dehydration as well as with kidney dysfunction. Creatinine is the kidney specific value: a high BUN with an unchanged creatinine points to low blood volume, while both rising together points to the kidney.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options explain the high BUN and low output. The unchanged creatinine decides it, because kidney damage would raise creatinine too.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: BUN 15 to 36 mg/dL; creatinine 0.9 to 0.9 mg/dL.

steps.action: Use creatinine as the kidney marker
steps.detail: No change means filtration has not fallen.
Vomiting 6 times, dry mucosa, and dark amber urine fit fluid loss.
No fever is described, and urine protein is not needed.

elimination.verdict: Reduced blood volume is raising the BUN.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings.

questions.stem: A client, 19 years old, was treated for a sore throat 2 weeks ago. Today the client reports puffy eyelids each morning and urine the color of cola. Blood pressure 164/98 mm Hg, was 118/72 mm Hg at a clinic visit 1 month ago. Oral temperature 37.1 °C. Urine output 400 mL over the past 24 hours. There is no flank pain and no costovertebral angle tenderness. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Pyelonephritis, because blood in the urine shows infection has reached the kidneys
options.rationale: Pyelonephritis is a kidney infection with fever, chills, and flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness. The temperature is 37.1 °C and there is no flank tenderness.

options.text: Cystitis, because dark urine and reduced voiding point to inflammation of the bladder
options.rationale: Cystitis causes dysuria, urgency, frequency, and suprapubic discomfort. It does not cause facial edema, a new blood pressure of 164/98 mm Hg, or a fall in urine output.

options.text: Urinary retention, because low output with swelling shows urine held in the bladder
options.rationale: Retention holds urine in the bladder but does not cause cola colored urine, eyelid edema, or hypertension.

options.text: Acute glomerulonephritis, because injured glomeruli leak blood and retain fluid
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis may follow a bacterial infection. Damaged glomeruli leak blood into the urine, giving cola or tea colored urine, and reduced filtration causes fluid retention with facial edema, elevated blood pressure, and decreased urine output.

questions.takeaway: Glomerulonephritis cues: cola or tea colored urine, facial and peripheral edema, elevated blood pressure, and decreased urine output, often after a recent infection. Fever and flank pain point instead to pyelonephritis.
questions.strategy: Two options name the kidney. Decide between them by asking whether the picture is infection (fever, flank pain) or fluid retention with blood in the urine (edema, hypertension, low output).

steps.detail: A sore throat 2 weeks ago can precede glomerulonephritis.
Cola colored urine, eyelid edema, new hypertension, and 400 mL in 24 hours.

steps.action: Rule out infection of the kidney
steps.detail: Temperature 37.1 °C and no costovertebral angle tenderness.
Cystitis and retention do not cause edema or hypertension.

elimination.verdict: Acute glomerulonephritis.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: A client has acute glomerulonephritis. Which results does the nurse interpret as evidence of glomerular injury or reduced kidney filtration? Select all that apply.

options.text: Protein 3+ in the urine
options.rationale: Damaged glomeruli leak protein into the urine, so protein on the urinalysis is a direct sign of glomerular injury.

options.text: Negative nitrites in the urine
options.rationale: Nitrites point to bacteria in the urine. A negative result says nothing about the glomeruli.

options.text: Serum creatinine 2.0 mg/dL, was 0.8 mg/dL 2 weeks ago
options.rationale: Creatinine is cleared by the kidneys, so a rise from 0.8 to 2.0 mg/dL shows reduced filtration.

options.text: Hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL
options.rationale: This value does not reflect glomerular leakage or filtration.

options.text: Many red blood cells in the urine
options.rationale: Damaged glomeruli also leak blood, which is why the urine can look cola or tea colored.

options.text: Serum potassium 5.8 mEq/L
options.rationale: When filtration and urine output fall, the kidneys excrete less potassium, so the serum level rises. Electrolytes are checked for this reason.

questions.takeaway: The glomerulonephritis workup is urinalysis for protein and blood, urine protein levels, creatinine, and electrolytes. Protein and blood show leaky glomeruli; creatinine and potassium show reduced filtration.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: For each result ask two questions: is it abnormal, and does it come from the glomerulus leaking or from the kidney filtering less? Only results that answer yes to both are selected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Protein 3+ and many red blood cells.
Creatinine up from 0.8 to 2.0 mg/dL and potassium 5.8 mEq/L.
Negative nitrites relate to bacteria, not the glomerulus.
Hemoglobin does not measure kidney filtration.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings.

questions.stem: A client, 52 years old, with acute glomerulonephritis is on a prescribed fluid and sodium restriction. Findings at 1200: blood pressure 166/100 mm Hg, was 168/102 mm Hg at 0800; urine output 25 mL per hour, was 25 mL per hour at 0800 when it was reported to the provider; weight 74.2 kg, was 73.9 kg yesterday; crackles in both lower lobes with a respiratory rate of 28 breaths per minute, lungs were clear with a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute at 0800. Which finding does the nurse report to the provider immediately?

options.text: Blood pressure 166/100 mm Hg, was 168/102 mm Hg at 0800
options.rationale: Elevated blood pressure is an expected cue in glomerulonephritis, and it has not risen since 0800.

options.text: Crackles in both lower lobes, respirations 28 breaths per minute
options.rationale: Reduced filtration causes fluid retention, and fluid in the lungs is the dangerous form of it. Crackles and a respiratory rate rising from 18 to 28 since 0800 are new and show respiratory distress, which is reported immediately.

options.text: Urine output 25 mL per hour, unchanged since it was reported at 0800
options.rationale: Decreased urine output signals kidney dysfunction and is a serious finding, but it is unchanged since 0800 and the provider already knows it.

options.text: Weight 74.2 kg this morning, was 73.9 kg yesterday morning
options.rationale: Daily weight tracks fluid retention, and the trend is documented. A gain of 0.3 kg in a day is not the most urgent change here.

questions.takeaway: Report respiratory distress or worsening kidney function immediately. A finding that is new since the last assessment outranks a serious finding that is unchanged and already reported.
questions.strategy: Both the low urine output and the crackles are reportable. The cue that decides is the 0800 comparison: output is unchanged and the provider already knows; the crackles are new and affect breathing.

steps.detail: Blood pressure and urine output are unchanged; the lungs have changed.
Urine output was reported at 0800.
New crackles with a rising respiratory rate threaten oxygenation.
A 0.3 kg gain is documented for the trend.

elimination.verdict: New crackles with a respiratory rate of 28.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.stem: A client with acute glomerulonephritis is going home on a prescribed sodium and fluid restriction. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding of the care plan?

options.text: "I will weigh myself once a week and call if my weight goes up."
options.rationale: Weight is the right measure, but it is checked daily, not weekly. A weekly weight misses fluid gained over a few days.

options.text: "I will drink extra water to flush out my kidneys while they heal."
options.rationale: Reduced filtration causes fluid retention, so the prescribed fluid limit is followed. Extra water adds to the fluid overload.

options.text: "I will call right away if I am short of breath or need more pillows to sleep."
options.rationale: Respiratory distress signals fluid in the lungs and is reported immediately. Needing more pillows to breathe while lying down is a practical sign the client can recognize.

options.text: "I can go back to using regular salt once the puffiness around my eyes is gone."
options.rationale: The sodium restriction is part of the prescribed plan and is not stopped on the client's own judgment when the edema goes down.

questions.takeaway: Glomerulonephritis home care: follow the prescribed fluid, sodium, and dietary limits, weigh daily, take medications as ordered, and report respiratory distress or worsening kidney function immediately.
questions.strategy: Check each statement against the plan. The weekly weight option is the right idea with the wrong frequency.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fluid and sodium limits, daily weight, report breathing changes.
Weighing is correct, but weekly is not daily.
Extra water and resuming salt break the restrictions.
Shortness of breath is reported right away.

elimination.verdict: The client who will call right away for shortness of breath understands the plan.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan.

questions.stem: A client is admitted with pyelonephritis and left flank pain. Which findings in the health history does the nurse recognize as increasing this client's risk for pyelonephritis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Daily fluid intake of about 2500 mL
options.rationale: A steady fluid intake keeps urine moving through the tract. It does not cause obstruction, reflux, or stasis.

options.text: A stone in the left ureter seen on imaging last month
options.rationale: A ureteral stone obstructs urine flow. Obstruction lets bacteria multiply above the blockage, and the stone sits on the same side as the flank pain.

options.text: Post void residual of 20 mL measured by bladder scan
options.rationale: This is the right idea with one thing off: incomplete emptying is a risk, but a residual of 20 mL means the bladder is emptying, so urine is not pooling.

options.text: Vesicoureteral reflux diagnosed in childhood
options.rationale: Reflux carries bladder urine back up the ureter toward the kidney, giving bacteria a route from the bladder to the renal pelvis.

options.text: A spinal cord injury that leaves urine sitting in the bladder for long periods
options.rationale: Urine held in the bladder is urinary stasis. Stagnant urine lets bacteria multiply and ascend to the kidney.

options.text: Hypertension treated with one daily medication
options.rationale: Treated hypertension does not block urine flow, reverse it, or cause it to pool, so it does not raise the risk of an ascending kidney infection.

questions.takeaway: The three pyelonephritis risk factors are urinary obstruction, vesicoureteral reflux, and urinary stasis. Each one lets bacteria multiply or travel upward toward the kidney.
questions.strategy: Ask of every history item: does it block urine, push it backward, or let it sit? Only those three raise the risk of an ascending kidney infection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pyelonephritis usually starts as an ascending urinary infection.
The left ureteral stone blocks flow.
Vesicoureteral reflux carries urine back toward the kidney.
The spinal cord injury leaves urine sitting in the bladder.
A residual of 20 mL shows the bladder empties, so there is no stasis.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: A client, 41 years old, with vesicoureteral reflux is admitted with a third episode of pyelonephritis in 12 months. Each earlier episode cleared with antibiotics. Serum creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, was 1.0 mg/dL one year ago. Urine output 1500 mL over the past 24 hours. Which long term complication does the nurse recognize this client is at greatest risk for?

options.text: Acute glomerulonephritis triggered by the repeated bacterial infections
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis can follow a bacterial infection, so this option sounds connected. It presents with cola colored urine, edema, and high blood pressure, none of which are described, and repeated pyelonephritis damages the kidney through scarring instead.

options.text: Urinary incontinence from weakness of the pelvic floor muscles
options.rationale: Pelvic floor weakness is an incontinence risk factor. Nothing in the stem describes leakage, and reflux with repeated kidney infections threatens the kidney rather than bladder control.

options.text: Kidney scarring that leads to a permanent loss of kidney function
options.rationale: Recurrent kidney infections can scar the kidney and cause permanent impairment. A creatinine that rose from 1.0 to 1.6 mg/dL over the year of repeated infections suggests that loss has already begun.

options.text: Asymptomatic bacteriuria that will need antibiotics for the rest of life
options.rationale: Most asymptomatic bacteriuria does not need antibiotics. Each episode here caused symptoms and cleared with treatment, so this is not the long term threat.

questions.takeaway: Recurrent pyelonephritis can scar the kidney and cause permanent kidney impairment. A creatinine that climbs across repeated episodes is the cue that damage is accumulating.
questions.strategy: The cues are a repeated kidney infection plus a creatinine trend over a year. Pick the complication that explains a slow rise in creatinine; the others describe different organs or different diseases.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Creatinine rose from 1.0 to 1.6 mg/dL across 3 kidney infections.
Repeated infection of the kidney leads to scarring.
Glomerulonephritis needs edema, high blood pressure, and cola colored urine.
Incontinence and bacteriuria do not explain a rising creatinine.

elimination.verdict: Kidney scarring with permanent loss of function.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: A client admitted with pyelonephritis has right flank pain of 7 of 10 and prescriptions for an IV antibiotic, an analgesic as needed for pain, and IV fluids at 100 mL per hour. Which actions does the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask about drug allergies before giving the first antibiotic dose
options.rationale: Antibiotics are given after an allergy check. Asking before the first dose is the step that prevents an allergic reaction to a drug the client has never received in this admission.

options.text: Hold all oral fluids so the kidneys can rest during treatment
options.rationale: Fluids are encouraged within prescribed limits during pyelonephritis treatment. Withholding oral fluids is not part of the prescriptions and does not rest an infected kidney.

options.text: Give the ordered analgesic for the right flank pain of 7 of 10
options.rationale: Ordered analgesics are part of pyelonephritis treatment, and the client reports flank pain of 7 of 10.

options.text: Measure intake and output every shift
options.rationale: Intake and output are monitored to track hydration and to catch a fall in urine output, which can signal worsening infection or kidney dysfunction.

options.text: Teach that phenazopyridine will clear the kidney infection faster
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine relieves urinary discomfort and turns urine orange or red, but it does not treat infection. The antibiotic treats the kidney infection.

options.text: Recheck temperature, pulse, and respirations and report new confusion
options.rationale: Vital signs and response to treatment are monitored to watch for worsening. New confusion is the first warning sign of progression toward sepsis.

questions.takeaway: Pyelonephritis care: antibiotics after an allergy check, ordered analgesics, fluids within prescribed limits, vital signs and intake and output, and a watch for worsening or adverse effects.
questions.strategy: Sort each option by whether it treats the infection, relieves pain, supports fluid balance, or monitors for worsening. An option that misstates what a drug does or invents a restriction is out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The allergy check comes before the first antibiotic dose.
The analgesic is ordered and the pain is 7 of 10.
Intake and output, vital signs, and mental status catch worsening.
Fluids are encouraged within limits, not withheld.
Phenazopyridine relieves discomfort only.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, F.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan.

questions.scenario: A client, 74 years old, was admitted 48 hours ago with pyelonephritis and has received IV antibiotics since admission. The nurse compares the findings now with the findings on admission.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it shows an effective response to treatment or a response that is not effective.

rows.text: Oral temperature 37.2 °C, was 39.2 °C on admission
rows.rationale: The fever that signaled spread of infection to the kidney has resolved, which shows the antibiotic is working.

rows.text: Right flank pain 2 of 10, was 8 of 10 on admission
rows.rationale: Flank pain is the hallmark of kidney infection. A drop from 8 of 10 to 2 of 10 shows the inflammation is settling.

rows.text: Urine output 140 mL over the past 8 hours, was 520 mL over 8 hours on admission
rows.rationale: Falling urine output is a warning sign of progression toward sepsis or of kidney dysfunction. It needs follow up even though other findings are better.

rows.text: Heart rate 84 beats per minute, was 118 beats per minute on admission
rows.rationale: Tachycardia is an associated finding of pyelonephritis. A return to 84 beats per minute shows the systemic response is easing.

rows.text: Asking repeatedly where the client is, was oriented on admission
rows.rationale: New confusion is the first warning sign in the progression from urinary infection to sepsis. It cannot be dismissed as age related because it is new since admission.

rows.text: Eating breakfast with no nausea, was vomiting on admission
rows.rationale: Nausea and vomiting are associated findings of pyelonephritis. Eating without nausea shows the systemic illness is resolving.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate each finding against its own baseline. Resolving fever, flank pain, tachycardia, and nausea show response to treatment, but new confusion or falling urine output means worsening even when the other numbers look better.
questions.strategy: Read each row as now versus admission. A finding that moved toward normal is effective; a finding that is new or moving the wrong way is not, regardless of how the rest of the picture looks.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Temperature, pain, heart rate, and nausea all moved toward normal.
Confusion is new since admission.
Urine output fell from 520 mL to 140 mL over 8 hours.
Several good findings do not cancel two warning signs.

elimination.verdict: Effective: temperature, flank pain, heart rate, nausea. Not effective: urine output and new confusion.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan.

questions.stem: A client, 33 years old, with an immune mediated disease diagnosed 2 years ago reports puffy eyelids and urine the color of tea for 1 week. The client has had no sore throat, skin infection, or fever. Blood pressure 158/96 mm Hg, urine output 500 mL over the past 24 hours, urinalysis with protein 3+ and many red blood cells. The client says, "My cousin had kidney inflammation after a bacterial throat infection and was back to normal in a few weeks. Will mine clear up the same way?" Which response by the nurse reflects an accurate analysis of the client's condition?

options.text: "Yes, this kind of kidney inflammation almost always clears up completely within a few weeks."
options.rationale: This is false reassurance. Recovery from glomerulonephritis varies by cause, and the client's cause is different from the cousin's.

options.text: "This cannot be kidney inflammation, because you have not had a sore throat or other infection."
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis can occur with immune mediated disease as well as after a bacterial infection. Tea colored urine, edema, high blood pressure, low output, and protein with blood in the urine fit glomerulonephritis.

options.text: "No, when an immune disease affects the kidneys, it always leads to permanent kidney failure."
options.rationale: The absolute word always makes this inaccurate. Severity and recovery vary, so the nurse does not promise either a full recovery or a permanent loss.

options.text: "Recovery depends on the cause, and yours differs from your cousin's, so we will follow your tests."
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis may follow an infection or occur with immune mediated disease, as it does for this client, and severity and recovery vary by cause. This response is honest and keeps the focus on monitoring.

questions.takeaway: Glomerulonephritis can follow a bacterial infection or occur with an immune mediated disease, and severity and recovery vary by cause. A missing infection history does not rule it out.
questions.strategy: Two options promise an outcome in opposite directions, and one denies the diagnosis. The accurate answer names the cause and avoids predicting the outcome.

steps.detail: Tea colored urine, edema, high blood pressure, low output, protein, and blood fit glomerulonephritis.
The client has an immune mediated disease and no recent infection.
Almost always clears and always leads to failure are absolutes in opposite directions.
Glomerulonephritis does not require a preceding infection.

elimination.verdict: Recovery depends on the cause, so the nurse explains that and monitors kidney tests.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: A client with acute glomerulonephritis has followed a prescribed fluid and sodium restriction and taken prescribed medications for 3 days. Which set of findings best shows that the plan of care is achieving its goal?

options.text: Weight 70.6 kg, was 73.0 kg 3 days ago; output 1400 mL per 24 hours, was 450 mL; lungs clear
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis causes fluid retention. A 2.4 kg weight loss with rising urine output and clear lungs shows retained fluid is leaving, which is the goal of the fluid and sodium restriction and medications.

options.text: Took every dose on time and drank no more than the prescribed fluid allowance on each of the 3 days
options.rationale: This shows the client is following the plan, which matters, but adherence is not an outcome. The nurse evaluates the client's response, not the client's actions.

options.text: Blood pressure 154/94 mm Hg, was 160/98 mm Hg 3 days ago; new crackles in both lower lobes
options.rationale: The small drop in blood pressure is outweighed by new crackles, a sign of fluid overload and possible respiratory distress that is reported immediately.

options.text: Facial puffiness looks smaller to the client; urine output 380 mL over 24 hours, was 450 mL
options.rationale: A subjective report of less swelling is not a measured trend, and urine output has fallen, which suggests worsening kidney function.

questions.takeaway: Glomerulonephritis outcomes are judged by documented trends: daily weight, blood pressure, intake and output, and lung sounds. Falling weight with rising output and clear lungs means retained fluid is leaving.
questions.strategy: Evaluate outcomes with measured trends in the client, not with adherence or impressions. Any option that contains a new warning sign is out even if one value moved the right way.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Remove retained fluid and protect kidney function.
Taking doses and limiting fluid are actions, not outcomes.
New crackles signal fluid overload despite a small blood pressure drop.
Puffiness looking smaller is an impression, and output fell.
Weight down, output up, lungs clear: every value moved toward the goal.

elimination.verdict: Weight loss with rising urine output and clear lungs.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan.

questions.stem: A client, 82 years old, is seen in the clinic for fatigue that has lasted 3 months. The client eats red meat 4 times a week, eats fruit and vegetables daily, and takes no medications. Laboratory results today: hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL, serum vitamin B12 140 pg/mL, serum iron 38 mcg/dL. Heart rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg. Which age related change in the gastrointestinal system best explains these findings?

options.text: Slower peristalsis with dulled nerve impulses in the colon
options.rationale: Slower peristalsis and dulled nerve impulses decrease the sensation to defecate and lead to constipation and impaction. They do not explain low iron and vitamin B12.

options.text: Atrophy of the gastric mucosa, which lowers absorption in the stomach
options.rationale: Gastric mucosal atrophy decreases absorption of iron and vitamin B12. Low levels in a client whose intake includes red meat point to poor absorption rather than poor intake, and the low hemoglobin follows.

options.text: Dilation of the pancreatic ducts, which lowers lipase production
options.rationale: Lower lipase reduces fat digestion and absorption and causes steatorrhea. It does not account for low iron and vitamin B12.

options.text: Fewer and smaller liver cells, which slows the metabolism of drugs
options.rationale: Fewer and smaller hepatic cells depress drug metabolism and raise the risk of drug toxicity. The client takes no drugs, and this change does not explain poor absorption of iron and vitamin B12.

questions.takeaway: Atrophy of the gastric mucosa in older adults decreases absorption of iron and vitamin B12 and allows bacteria to proliferate, which can cause atrophic gastritis. Low levels with adequate intake point to an absorption problem.
questions.strategy: Match the nutrient to the change that affects its absorption. The diet history rules out poor intake, so look for the change that blocks absorption of iron and vitamin B12.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Red meat 4 times a week supplies iron and vitamin B12.

steps.action: Name the effect of each change
steps.detail: Peristalsis causes constipation, lipase causes steatorrhea, liver cells cause drug toxicity.
Gastric mucosal atrophy decreases iron and vitamin B12 absorption.
