elimination.verdict: B. Atrophy of the gastric mucosa.

questions.objective: Describe age related changes in the GI system and their impact on digestion, absorption, and elimination

questions.stem: A client, 78 years old, reports stools that are pale, greasy and foul smelling and that float in the toilet bowl. This began 2 months ago. The client has lost 2.3 kg in the 2 months without trying, has a bowel movement every day, and denies black or bloody stools. The client started no new medications this year. Which explanation does the nurse consider most likely?

options.text: Slower drug metabolism from fewer and smaller liver cells
options.rationale: This change leads to accumulation of drugs, possibly to toxic levels. The client has started no new medications, and drug accumulation does not produce fatty stools.

options.text: Less sensation to defecate from dulled nerve impulses
options.rationale: Dulled nerve impulses lead to postponed bowel movements, constipation and impaction. The client has a bowel movement every day.

options.text: Bacterial overgrowth from atrophy of the gastric mucosa
options.rationale: Gastric mucosal atrophy causes bacterial overgrowth, atrophic gastritis and poor absorption of iron and vitamin B12. It is not the source of fatty stools.

options.text: Poor fat digestion from age related pancreatic duct changes
options.rationale: Distention and dilation of the pancreatic ducts lower lipase, so fat is poorly digested and absorbed. The result is steatorrhea, fatty stools that are pale, greasy and float, with weight loss from lost calories.

questions.takeaway: Distention and dilation of the pancreatic ducts with aging decrease lipase. Fat is poorly digested and absorbed, which produces steatorrhea and can cause unintended weight loss.
questions.strategy: Name the stool first. Pale, greasy, floating stool is fatty stool, and fat digestion depends on lipase from the pancreas.

steps.detail: Pale, greasy, foul smelling, floating stool is steatorrhea.
Fat digestion depends on lipase.
Age related pancreatic duct changes lower lipase.

elimination.verdict: D. Poor fat digestion from pancreatic duct changes.

questions.objective: Describe age related changes in the GI system and their impact on digestion, absorption, and elimination

questions.stem: An older adult with constipation says, "I never feel the urge anymore, so I just wait until I do." The nurse teaches about age related changes in bowel elimination. Which client statement shows understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "I will sit on the toilet after breakfast daily, even with no urge."
options.rationale: With age, peristalsis slows and nerve impulses are dulled, so the urge to defecate is weaker. Waiting for the urge postpones bowel movements and leads to constipation and impaction. A set daily time does not depend on a sensation the client no longer feels.

options.text: "I will wait for a strong urge, so that I do not strain the bowel."
options.rationale: Waiting for the urge is the behavior causing the problem. The client reports the urge rarely comes, and postponement leads to constipation and impaction.

options.text: "I will drink less during the day so that my stools do not get loose."
options.rationale: Less fluid makes stool harder and worsens constipation. The client's stools are already hard.

options.text: "I will take a laxative every night so the urge does not matter."
options.rationale: Nightly laxative use does not address the cause and builds dependence on the drug. A regular toileting time works with the slowed bowel instead.

questions.takeaway: Decreased peristalsis and dulled nerve impulses in older adults weaken the sensation to defecate. Postponing bowel movements leads to constipation and impaction, so teaching focuses on a regular toileting time that does not rely on the urge.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The client's own words name the problem: waiting for an urge that no longer comes. The right statement removes the waiting.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the cause in the stem
steps.detail: The client waits for an urge that has weakened with age.

steps.action: Reject options that keep the cause
steps.detail: Waiting for a strong urge repeats the problem.
Less fluid hardens stool; nightly laxatives build dependence.

elimination.verdict: A. Sit on the toilet at a set time each day.

questions.objective: Describe age related changes in the GI system and their impact on digestion, absorption, and elimination

questions.stem: The nurse begins a focused gastrointestinal health history for a client with watery diarrhea for 4 days. Which questions does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: "What have you taken for the diarrhea, and did it help?"
options.rationale: The history includes actions taken to relieve diarrhea or constipation and whether they were successful.

options.text: "Is your tetanus immunization up to date?"
options.rationale: Tetanus status does not describe the diarrhea, its cause, or its effect on nutrition and elimination.

options.text: "What color are the stools, and have you seen any blood?"
options.rationale: Color and consistency of the feces and the presence of frank blood or tarry stools are part of the bowel history.

options.text: "Would you rather use a stool softener or a fiber supplement?"
options.rationale: Choosing a treatment comes after assessment, and a stool softener does not fit watery diarrhea.

options.text: "Have you had nausea or vomiting along with the diarrhea?"
options.rationale: Nausea and vomiting are common GI symptoms included in the nutrition and current health history.

options.text: "Have you lost weight since this started, without trying?"
options.rationale: Unintentional weight gain or loss is part of the assessment of changes in bowel habits.

questions.takeaway: A focused GI history covers the pattern, color and consistency of stool, blood or tarry stools, what the client did for the symptom and whether it worked, associated symptoms such as nausea and vomiting, and unintentional weight change.
questions.strategy: Keep each question that describes the symptom, its associated symptoms, or its effect on nutrition. Reject questions about unrelated systems or treatment choices.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stool color and blood.
Actions taken and whether they worked.
Nausea, vomiting and unintentional weight loss.
Tetanus status is unrelated; a treatment choice skips assessment.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Obtain a focused GI health history, including nutritional habits, bowel patterns, and common GI symptoms

questions.stem: A client, 61 years old, with a history of peptic ulcer disease calls the clinic. The client reports 2 stools since yesterday that are black, sticky and shiny, with a strong odor. The client takes no iron supplements and has eaten no black licorice or blueberries. The client reports a heart rate of 104 beats per minute on a home monitor, and the heart rate was 78 beats per minute at the clinic visit 1 month ago. How does the nurse interpret the stool report?

options.text: Hematochezia, which suggests bleeding near the rectum or anus
options.rationale: Hematochezia is bright red blood in the stool and usually comes from the lower bowel. Black, sticky stool is digested blood.

options.text: Steatorrhea, which suggests poor fat digestion from low lipase
options.rationale: Steatorrhea is pale, greasy, floating stool. It is not black or tarry.

options.text: Melena, which suggests bleeding high in the gastrointestinal tract
options.rationale: Black, sticky, tarry stool is melena, blood that has been digested on its way through the bowel. With a history of peptic ulcer disease and a rising heart rate, it points to upper GI bleeding.

options.text: Acholic stool, which suggests that bile is not reaching the bowel
options.rationale: Acholic stool is pale or clay colored because bile pigment is missing. It is the opposite of black stool.

questions.takeaway: Melena is black, tarry stool from digested blood and points to bleeding high in the GI tract. Hematochezia is bright red blood from lower in the tract. Both are reported findings in the bowel history.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Color and texture decide. Black and sticky means the blood has been digested, so the source is high in the tract; the ulcer history and rising heart rate fit.

steps.detail: Black, sticky and shiny is tarry stool.
Melena is black and from high in the tract; hematochezia is red and from low in the tract.
Steatorrhea and acholic stool are pale.

elimination.verdict: C. Melena from upper GI bleeding.

questions.objective: Obtain a focused GI health history, including nutritional habits, bowel patterns, and common GI symptoms

questions.scenario: A client, 52 years old, is admitted with abdominal pain. The nurse uses the PQRST approach to organize the pain assessment and records the client's statements.
questions.stem: For each client statement, indicate the part of the pain assessment it describes.

rows.text: "It feels like a deep burning, like acid."
rows.rationale: Quality describes how the pain feels, such as burning, sharp, dull or crushing.

rows.text: "It began 3 days ago, and each episode lasts about 2 hours."
rows.rationale: Timing covers onset, duration and frequency: when the pain started and how long each episode lasts.

rows.text: "Lying still with my knees pulled up makes it ease off a little."
rows.rationale: Palliative factors are what make the pain better or worse.

rows.text: "It starts under my ribs on the right and spreads to my right shoulder blade."
rows.rationale: Region is where the pain is, and radiation is where it spreads.

rows.text: "At its worst it is 8 of 10, and it makes me stop and sit down."
rows.rationale: Severity covers the rating, how bad it is at its worst, and whether it forces the client to sit, lie down or slow down.

rows.text: "It came on after a big fried dinner."
rows.rationale: Precipitating factors are what brings the pain on.

questions.takeaway: PQRST organizes a pain assessment: P is what brings it on or relieves it, Q is how it feels, R is where it is and where it spreads, S is how severe it is and how it limits activity, and T is onset, duration and frequency.
questions.strategy: Ask what question each statement answers: what causes or eases it, what it feels like, where it is, how bad it is, or when it happens.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The fried dinner brings it on; lying still with knees up eases it.
Burning is quality; right ribs to shoulder blade is region and radiation.
8 of 10 and having to sit is severity; began 3 days ago with 2 hour episodes is timing.

elimination.verdict: Quality, timing, palliative, region, severity, precipitating.

questions.objective: Assess abdominal pain using the PQRSTU framework and recognize associated GI symptoms

questions.stem: A client, 57 years old, reports a dull ache in the right upper quadrant, 4 of 10, for 2 weeks and says, "My eyes look a little yellow in the mirror." The nurse plans the next questions to identify skin changes linked to GI disorders. Which questions does the nurse ask? Select all that apply.

options.text: "Have you had itching anywhere on your body?"
options.rationale: Itching is a skin change that can result from liver and biliary obstruction.

options.text: "Do your fingers turn white and then blue in cold weather?"
options.rationale: Color change of the fingers with cold is a vascular finding, not a skin change from a GI disorder.

options.text: "Do you bruise more easily or bleed longer from small cuts?"
options.rationale: Increased bruising or a tendency to bleed is a skin change linked to GI disorders. The liver makes clotting proteins.

options.text: "Have you noticed any rashes or changes in your skin color?"
options.rationale: Skin discolorations, including jaundice, and rashes are skin changes the nurse asks about.

options.text: "Have you had a sunburn in the past 2 weeks?"
options.rationale: Sunburn does not explain yellow eyes or a right upper quadrant ache.

options.text: "Do you get blisters on your feet when you wear new shoes?"
options.rationale: Friction blisters from footwear are not linked to GI or liver disorders.

questions.takeaway: Skin changes linked to GI disorders such as liver and biliary obstruction are discoloration or rashes, itching, jaundice, and increased bruising or a tendency to bleed.
questions.strategy: Yellow eyes and right upper quadrant pain point to the liver and biliary tract. Keep the questions that match the 4 skin changes linked to that system.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Yellow eyes with a right upper quadrant ache points to the liver and biliary tract.
Discoloration or rash, itching, jaundice, bruising or bleeding.
Cold induced finger color change, sunburn and friction blisters from shoes do not fit.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D.

questions.objective: Assess abdominal pain using the PQRSTU framework and recognize associated GI symptoms

questions.stem: A client, 49 years old, reports epigastric pain that goes through to the back, 7 of 10, with nausea. The pain began 6 days ago, and the client did not seek care until today. The serum amylase drawn today is within the expected range for the laboratory. The urine amylase collected today is elevated. How does the nurse interpret these results?

options.text: Pancreatitis is unlikely, because the serum amylase is within the expected range
options.rationale: This would be a reasonable reading in the first days of symptoms, when serum amylase is elevated. After 6 days, a normal serum level does not rule out pancreatitis.

options.text: The urine result is likely a collection error, because the serum level is normal
options.rationale: Normal serum and elevated urine amylase together are an expected pattern later in pancreatitis, not a sign of error.

options.text: The results fit pancreatitis, because urine amylase stays elevated longer than serum
options.rationale: Renal clearance of amylase increases in acute pancreatitis. Urine amylase stays elevated 5 to 7 days after onset, even after the serum level returns to normal. With symptoms for 6 days, this pattern supports pancreatitis.

options.text: The results fit liver disease, because amylase is cleared from the blood by the liver
options.rationale: Amylase is cleared through the kidneys into the urine, and elevated amylase points to the pancreas, not the liver.

questions.takeaway: In acute pancreatitis, serum amylase rises early and falls within days, while urine amylase stays elevated for 5 to 7 days after onset. Urine amylase matters for a client who has had symptoms for several days.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two readings are defensible: a normal serum amylase seems to rule out pancreatitis. The cue that decides is the 6 days since onset, which is when the urine level is still high and the serum level has already fallen.

steps.detail: Symptoms began 6 days ago.
Serum amylase falls within days; urine amylase stays high 5 to 7 days.
A normal serum level late in the illness does not rule out pancreatitis.

elimination.verdict: C. The results fit pancreatitis.

questions.objective: Identify common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate GI function and disorders

questions.stem: The nurse has finished inspecting all 4 quadrants of a client's abdomen. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Lightly palpate each quadrant, beginning in the right upper quadrant
options.rationale: Palpation before auscultation stimulates the bowel and changes the bowel sounds. Auscultation comes before palpation.

options.text: Percuss over the liver and spleen to estimate the size of each organ
options.rationale: Percussion to size solid organs may be performed by the health care provider, and it would also alter bowel sounds if done before auscultation.

options.text: Place the bell of the stethoscope firmly over the left upper quadrant first
options.rationale: Bowel sounds are high pitched and are heard with the diaphragm, not the bell. Listening begins in the right lower quadrant.

options.text: Place the diaphragm of the stethoscope lightly over the right lower quadrant
options.rationale: Auscultation follows inspection. Bowel sounds are high pitched, so the diaphragm is used, and listening begins in the right lower quadrant over the ileocecal valve, where sounds are normally present.

questions.takeaway: The nurse assesses the abdomen by inspection, then auscultation, then light palpation, so that touch does not change bowel sounds. Auscultation uses the diaphragm and begins in the right lower quadrant.
questions.strategy: Two decisions in one option: what comes after inspection, and how to listen. Only one option gets both right.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Auscultation follows inspection.
The diaphragm picks up high pitched bowel sounds.
Begin in the right lower quadrant.

elimination.verdict: D. Diaphragm, right lower quadrant.

questions.objective: Demonstrate the correct sequence and techniques for abdominal assessment, including inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation

questions.stem: A nursing student performs an abdominal assessment under the supervision of the nurse. Which actions by the student require the nurse to intervene? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspects all 4 quadrants before using the stethoscope
options.rationale: Inspection comes first in the abdominal assessment.

options.text: Presses the fingers about 5 cm into each quadrant to outline the organs
options.rationale: Pressing more than 1 inch is deep palpation, which determines organ size and shape. Deep palpation is performed by the health care provider, not the nurse generalist.

options.text: Uses the diaphragm and begins listening in the right lower quadrant
options.rationale: Bowel sounds are heard with the diaphragm, starting in the right lower quadrant.

options.text: Taps over the right upper quadrant to estimate the size of the liver
options.rationale: Percussion to determine the size of solid organs may be performed by the health care provider. The nurse generalist performs inspection, auscultation and light palpation.

options.text: Presses the fingers about 2 cm into each quadrant to check for tenderness
options.rationale: Light palpation, 0.5 to 1 inch deep, detects large masses and tenderness and is within the nurse generalist's role.

questions.takeaway: The nurse generalist performs inspection, auscultation and light palpation of 0.5 to 1 inch to detect large masses and tenderness. Deep palpation of more than 1 inch and percussion to size the liver and spleen are performed by the health care provider.
questions.strategy: Sort each action by depth and technique. Anything deeper than 1 inch or any percussion falls outside the nurse generalist's role.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Inspection, then auscultation with the diaphragm from the right lower quadrant, is correct.
About 2 cm is light palpation; 5 cm is deep palpation.
Percussion to size the liver belongs to the provider.

elimination.verdict: B, D.

questions.objective: Demonstrate the correct sequence and techniques for abdominal assessment, including inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation

questions.nursesNote: 0900. Client is 70 years old and reports nausea since last night. Abdomen rises and falls with each breath. No flatus or stool for 2 days. Umbilicus midline. Abdomen distended, with taut, glistening skin. Skin warm and dry, with no scars. Lungs clear in all lobes. Visible waves moving across the left upper quadrant toward the right. Oral temperature 37.1 °C. Loud, high pitched gurgling sounds heard in the upper quadrants. Oriented to person, place and time. Vomited 300 mL of green fluid at 0700.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require further evaluation.

segments.text: Abdomen rises and falls with each breath
segments.rationale: Rising and falling with breathing is a normal abdominal movement.

segments.text: No flatus or stool for 2 days
segments.rationale: No passage of flatus or stool suggests that bowel contents are not moving forward.

segments.text: Umbilicus midline
segments.rationale: A midline umbilicus is an expected finding.

segments.text: Abdomen distended, with taut, glistening skin
segments.rationale: Distention with taut, glistening skin is an abnormal inspection finding that suggests trapped gas or fluid.

segments.text: Skin warm and dry, with no scars
segments.rationale: Warm, dry, intact skin is an expected finding.

segments.text: Lungs clear in all lobes
segments.rationale: Clear lungs are an expected finding.

segments.text: Visible waves moving across the left upper quadrant toward the right
segments.rationale: Peristaltic movements are rarely seen. Visible waves are reported with the quadrant of origin and direction because they may indicate an intestinal obstruction.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.1 °C
segments.rationale: The temperature is within the expected range.

segments.text: Loud, high pitched gurgling sounds heard in the upper quadrants
segments.rationale: Loud, high pitched gurgling sounds (borborygmus) can be heard above a complete intestinal obstruction.

segments.text: Oriented to person, place and time
segments.rationale: Orientation is an expected finding.

segments.text: Vomited 300 mL of green fluid at 0700
segments.rationale: Vomiting with nausea and no stool or flatus fits a bowel that is not moving contents forward.

questions.takeaway: Visible peristaltic waves, distention with taut glistening skin, loud high pitched bowel sounds above a blockage, vomiting and no flatus or stool together point to a possible intestinal obstruction and need further evaluation.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Read each phrase as normal or abnormal for the abdomen. Then check whether the abnormal ones form one picture.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Distention with taut skin and visible peristaltic waves.
Loud, high pitched gurgling in the upper quadrants.
No flatus or stool for 2 days and green vomit.
Breathing movement, midline umbilicus, warm dry skin, normal temperature and orientation.

questions.objective: Differentiate normal and abnormal GI assessment findings and identify findings that require further evaluation

questions.stem: A nurse inspects the abdomen of a client, 74 years old, with a history of hypertension who reports a vague ache in the lower back, 3 of 10. Blood pressure 162/94 mm Hg, heart rate 88 beats per minute. The nurse sees a bulging mass just above the umbilicus that pulses with each heartbeat. The nurse has not yet auscultated. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Listen over the mass with the stethoscope for a bruit, then report the findings
options.rationale: Listening for a bruit seems to gather useful data, but the nurse does not auscultate or palpate a pulsating abdominal mass. A bulging, pulsating mass may be an abdominal aortic aneurysm.

options.text: Continue the assessment in order, with auscultation and then light palpation
options.rationale: This would fit a faint aortic pulsation that can be visible in some clients. A bulging mass that pulses is not that finding, and routine auscultation and palpation would place hands and stethoscope over it.

options.text: Avoid touching or listening over the mass, and report the finding immediately
options.rationale: A bulging, pulsating mass may be an abdominal aortic aneurysm, a life threatening problem. The nurse does not touch the area with hands or a stethoscope and notifies the health care provider immediately.

options.text: Palpate the mass lightly with the fingertips to estimate its size and borders
options.rationale: Palpation of a pulsating abdominal mass can be dangerous if it is an aneurysm, and sizing a mass is not the nurse's role.

questions.takeaway: A bulging, pulsating abdominal mass may be an abdominal aortic aneurysm. The nurse does not auscultate, palpate or percuss it and notifies the health care provider immediately.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options are defensible: a visible aortic pulsation can be a normal finding, so continuing the examination seems reasonable. The cue that decides is that the mass is bulging, which makes it a possible aneurysm.

steps.detail: The mass bulges and pulses with each heartbeat.
A possible abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Listening, palpating and continuing the routine all place hands or a stethoscope on the mass.

elimination.verdict: C. Avoid the mass and report it immediately.

questions.objective: Differentiate normal and abnormal GI assessment findings and identify findings that require further evaluation

questions.stem: A client, 66 years old, is 2 days after surgery to remove part of the colon. At 1400: no bowel sounds heard after listening for 5 minutes in each quadrant, abdomen distended and held tense when touched lightly, pain 8 of 10, was 4 of 10 at 0800. Oral temperature 38.8 °C. Heart rate 122 beats per minute, was 84 beats per minute at 0800. Respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Peritonitis, an inflammation of the lining of the abdominal cavity
options.rationale: Absent bowel sounds occur with peritonitis. Fever, a heart rate that rose from 84 to 122 beats per minute, rising pain and a tense abdomen point to inflammation of the peritoneum, not just a slowed bowel.

options.text: Paralytic ileus, from slowed bowel activity after surgery
options.rationale: Absent bowel sounds and distention fit paralytic ileus, but ileus does not explain a temperature of 38.8 °C, a heart rate of 122 beats per minute and pain that doubled since 0800.

options.text: Gastroenteritis, with increased motility of the bowel
options.rationale: Gastroenteritis increases motility and produces loud, gurgling bowel sounds. This client has no bowel sounds.

options.text: Bowel obstruction, with loud sounds heard above the blockage
options.rationale: Loud, high pitched sounds are heard above a complete obstruction. This client has no bowel sounds in any quadrant.

questions.takeaway: Bowel sounds are diminished or absent after abdominal surgery and with paralytic ileus or peritonitis. Fever, a rising heart rate, worsening pain and a tense abdomen separate peritonitis from an ileus.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Absent bowel sounds fit two conditions here. The systemic signs, fever and a rising heart rate, are what separate inflammation from a slowed bowel.

steps.detail: Absent sounds rule out gastroenteritis and the loud sounds of obstruction.
Ileus and peritonitis both have absent sounds.
Fever, heart rate 122 beats per minute and rising pain point to peritonitis.

elimination.verdict: A. Peritonitis.

questions.objective: Differentiate normal and abnormal GI assessment findings and identify findings that require further evaluation

questions.stem: A client, 19 years old, is admitted with pain in the right lower quadrant, 8 of 10, that began around the umbilicus 12 hours ago. Oral temperature 38.3 °C, heart rate 106 beats per minute. The provider's admission note states that appendicitis is suspected and a CT scan is pending. The nurse has inspected and auscultated the abdomen. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Lightly palpate the right lower quadrant first to find the most painful point
options.rationale: Light palpation is within the nurse's role, but a painful area is assessed last, never first, so the client does not tense the abdomen. When appendicitis is suspected, palpation is not done at all.

options.text: Omit palpation and document the inspection and auscultation findings
options.rationale: Palpation is not done when appendicitis is suspected. The nurse has completed the parts of the assessment that are safe for this client and records them.

options.text: Palpate deeply in the right lower quadrant to check for tenderness
options.rationale: Deep palpation is performed by the health care provider, and palpation is avoided when appendicitis is suspected.

options.text: Percuss each quadrant to locate the areas of tympany and dullness
options.rationale: Percussion may be performed by the health care provider and is not part of the nurse generalist's assessment.

questions.takeaway: The nurse generalist inspects, auscultates and lightly palpates the abdomen, assessing painful areas last. If appendicitis or an abdominal aneurysm is suspected, palpation is not done.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options are defensible: light palpation is part of the nurse generalist's assessment, so palpating seems reasonable. The cue that decides is the documented suspicion of appendicitis, which removes palpation from the assessment.

steps.detail: Appendicitis is suspected.
Palpation is not done when appendicitis is suspected, and a painful area is never palpated first.
Deep palpation and percussion belong to the provider.

elimination.verdict: B. Omit palpation.

questions.objective: Demonstrate the correct sequence and techniques for abdominal assessment, including inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation

questions.stem: A client, 58 years old, is scheduled for an abdominal CT scan with IV contrast at 1300 to evaluate a mass seen on an abdominal radiograph. At 0900 the nurse reviews the client's data. Which finding is the priority for the nurse to report before the scan?

options.text: Ate a breakfast of toast and juice at 0700
options.rationale: The client must be NPO for at least 4 hours before a contrast CT. A meal at 0700 is 6 hours before the 1300 scan.

options.text: Has a peripheral IV in the left forearm placed at 0800
options.rationale: IV access is required for the contrast injection, so this is expected preparation.

options.text: Had hives and wheezing after IV contrast 3 years ago
options.rationale: The nurse asks about past contrast reactions and severe allergies before a contrast CT. Hives and wheezing are an allergic reaction, and the team needs this before contrast is given again.

options.text: Had a metallic taste with IV contrast for a CT 3 years ago
options.rationale: A warm, flushed feeling or a metallic taste during the injection is expected. The nurse explains it, but it is not a reaction.

questions.takeaway: Before an abdominal CT with contrast, the nurse asks about past contrast reactions and severe allergies, keeps the client NPO for at least 4 hours, establishes IV access, and explains that a warm, flushed feeling or metallic taste is expected.
questions.strategy: Two options describe past contrast experiences. Separate an expected sensation from a reaction that involves the skin and airway.

steps.detail: 0700 to 1300 is 6 hours, more than 4.
An IV is required, so it is expected.
A metallic taste is expected; hives and wheezing are a reaction.

elimination.verdict: C. Hives and wheezing after contrast.

questions.objective: Identify common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate GI function and disorders

questions.stem: A client at average risk for colorectal cancer has a negative result on a multitargeted stool DNA home kit. Which client statement shows understanding of the screening plan?

options.text: "I will do the stool DNA kit again 1 year from now."
options.rationale: Yearly screening is the interval for the fecal immunochemical test and the guaiac based fecal occult blood test, not the stool DNA test.

options.text: "I will do the stool DNA kit again 3 years from now."
options.rationale: The multitargeted stool DNA test is performed every 3 years.

options.text: "I will not need more screening since this result was negative."
options.rationale: Screening for colorectal cancer continues at regular intervals. A single negative result does not end screening.

options.text: "I will send a stool sample for parasites next year instead."
options.rationale: A stool test for ova and parasites looks for parasitic infection. It does not screen for colorectal cancer.

questions.takeaway: Stool screening for colorectal cancer is an annual fecal immunochemical test, an annual guaiac based fecal occult blood test, or a multitargeted stool DNA home test every 3 years.
questions.strategy: Two options differ only in the interval. Match the interval to the test the client used.

steps.detail: Multitargeted stool DNA.
Every 3 years.
Yearly is for the other stool tests; parasite testing is not cancer screening.

elimination.verdict: B. Repeat in 3 years.

questions.objective: Identify common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate GI function and disorders

questions.scenario: A client, 55 years old, had an endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with removal of a gallstone at 0900. The gag reflex returned at 1000. At 1500 the client reports severe pain in the upper abdomen that goes through to the back, 8 of 10, and has vomited twice. Blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg, was 124/78 mm Hg at 1000. Heart rate 112 beats per minute. Oral temperature 37.9 °C. Serum lipase 1250 units/L.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Withhold oral food and fluids
options.rationale: Severe pain with vomiting after ERCP suggests a complication, so oral intake is withheld.

options.text: Offer clear liquids to replace the fluid lost with vomiting
options.rationale: Oral intake is withheld while a post procedure complication with vomiting is being evaluated.

options.text: Encourage walking to help pass the air instilled during the test
options.rationale: Gas pain is colicky, not severe pain through to the back with vomiting, a rising heart rate and a high lipase.

options.text: Report the findings to the provider
options.rationale: Pancreatitis is a severe post ERCP complication that needs prompt treatment.

options.text: Prepare the client for discharge with a driver as planned
options.rationale: Severe pain, vomiting and falling blood pressure are not findings that allow discharge.

options.text: Expected gas pain from air instilled during the test
options.rationale: Gas pain is colicky and mild. It does not raise the lipase or the heart rate.

options.text: Aspiration from an absent gag reflex
options.rationale: The gag reflex returned at 1000, and the findings are abdominal, not respiratory.

options.text: Acute pancreatitis
options.rationale: Severe upper abdominal pain through to the back, vomiting and an elevated lipase after ERCP point to pancreatitis, the complication the nurse observes for.

options.text: Respiratory depression from sedation
options.rationale: The findings are severe pain and vomiting 6 hours after the test, not slowed breathing.

options.text: Return of the gag reflex
options.rationale: The gag reflex returned at 1000.

options.text: Serum amylase and lipase levels
options.rationale: Amylase and lipase elevate in acute pancreatitis and are trended.

options.text: Passage of a capsule in the stool
options.rationale: Capsule passage applies to small bowel capsule endoscopy, not ERCP.

options.text: Abdominal pain severity and location
options.rationale: Severe abdominal pain is the key sign of pancreatitis after ERCP and is reassessed.

questions.takeaway: After ERCP, the nurse observes for pancreatitis, shown by severe abdominal pain, and monitors for bleeding, sedation effects and respiratory depression. Elevated amylase and lipase support pancreatitis.
questions.strategy: Start with the condition: severe pain through to the back, vomiting and a high lipase after ERCP. Then choose actions and parameters that fit that condition.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Severe pain to the back, vomiting and lipase 1250 units/L point to pancreatitis.
Withhold oral intake and report the findings.
Amylase and lipase levels and abdominal pain.

elimination.verdict: Actions: withhold oral intake, report the findings. Condition: acute pancreatitis. Parameters: amylase and lipase, abdominal pain.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: A client, 63 years old, had an esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with moderate sedation using midazolam and fentanyl 20 minutes ago. The client opens the eyes to a loud voice and falls back asleep. Respiratory rate 8 breaths per minute and shallow, was 16 breaths per minute before the procedure. Oxygen saturation 90% on room air. Blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg, heart rate 64 beats per minute. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Check the gag reflex first and then offer the client small sips of water
options.rationale: Fluids are withheld until the gag reflex returns and the client is alert. A drowsy client breathing 8 times a minute is at risk for aspiration and needs breathing support first.

options.text: Lower the side rails so the client can be turned onto the right side
options.rationale: Side rails stay raised while sedation wears off. Lowering them adds fall risk without improving breathing.

options.text: Record the vital signs and plan to recheck them again in 30 minutes
options.rationale: A respiratory rate of 8 breaths per minute with an oxygen saturation of 90% needs action now, not a recheck in 30 minutes.

options.text: Call the client by name, gently shake the shoulder, coach deep breaths
options.rationale: Sedation drugs depress the rate and depth of breathing. When the respiratory rate falls below 10 breaths per minute, the nurse stimulates the client to encourage deeper, faster breathing. This client opens the eyes to a loud voice, so a verbal and light touch stimulus is enough to rouse the client and coach deep breaths.

questions.takeaway: After endoscopy with moderate sedation, the nurse monitors respiratory rate and depth, oxygen saturation and capnography. A respiratory rate below 10 breaths per minute calls for a stimulus that rouses the client, matched to how the client responds, to promote deeper, faster breaths.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Apply the ABCs. Breathing is failing, so the first action supports breathing.

steps.detail: Respiratory rate 8 breaths per minute, shallow, with saturation 90%.
The client rouses to voice, so call the name, touch the shoulder and coach deep breaths.
Fluids, lowered rails and a delayed recheck do not support breathing.

elimination.verdict: D. Rouse the client and coach deep breaths.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: A client, 50 years old, lives alone and is scheduled for an outpatient colonoscopy at 0800 tomorrow. The client has type 2 diabetes treated with an oral medication. Which instructions does the nurse include in the teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: "You may drive yourself home once you feel awake after the test."
options.rationale: Moderate sedation impairs judgment and reaction time. Another person drives the client home, and the client does not drive for the rest of the day.

options.text: "Drink only clear liquids today, and avoid red, orange or purple drinks."
options.rationale: A clear liquid diet the day before helps empty the colon. Red, orange and purple drinks and gelatin can look like blood or residue in the colon.

options.text: "Call your primary provider about your diabetes medicine for tomorrow."
options.rationale: The client is NPO before the test, so the primary provider decides how to adjust diabetes medication that day.

options.text: "Eat a full meal tonight to keep your blood sugar up during the prep."
options.rationale: A full meal leaves residue in the colon. Poor bowel preparation decreases visualization and can lead to an unsuccessful colonoscopy.

options.text: "Drink fluids after the test to replace what you lost with the prep."
options.rationale: The bowel prep causes watery diarrhea and fluid loss, so the nurse encourages fluid intake to rehydrate after the procedure.

questions.takeaway: Colonoscopy teaching covers the bowel prep and a clear liquid diet the day before without red, orange or purple drinks, a plan for diabetes medication while NPO, a driver home because of sedation, and fluids afterward to rehydrate.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Check each instruction against two goals: a clean colon for viewing and safety around sedation and fluid loss.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clear liquids without red, orange or purple; no full meal.
A driver home; a plan for diabetes medicine while NPO.
Fluids after the test.

elimination.verdict: B, C, E.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: A client, 68 years old, had a colonoscopy with removal of 2 polyps at 1000. At 1230 the client is awake and alert, lying on the left side, and reports cramping 3 of 10 with passage of flatus. The first stool after the procedure has a small streak of red blood. Blood pressure 126/78 mm Hg, was 130/80 mm Hg at 1030. Heart rate 84 beats per minute, was 80 beats per minute at 1030. How does the nurse evaluate these findings?

options.text: Expected after polyp removal, so the nurse continues to monitor and offers fluids
options.rationale: A small amount of blood in the first stool is expected after polyp removal. Cramping and flatus are expected for several hours, and fluids are permitted once flatus shows peristalsis has returned. Blood pressure and heart rate are near their 1030 values.

options.text: A sign of hemorrhage, so the nurse reports the bleeding to the provider now
options.rationale: Any blood after a colonoscopy seems worth reporting, and excessive bleeding is reported immediately. A small streak after polyp removal, with blood pressure and heart rate near baseline, is not excessive.

options.text: A sign of perforation, so the nurse keeps the client NPO and prepares for imaging
options.rationale: Perforation causes severe pain and guarding. Cramping of 3 of 10 with flatus is expected.

options.text: Expected after any colonoscopy, so the client is discharged with no teaching
options.rationale: Blood is expected only when a polyp is removed or a biopsy is taken. The client still needs teaching on what to report and someone to drive home.

questions.takeaway: After colonoscopy, fullness, cramping and flatus are expected for several hours, and a small amount of blood in the first stool is expected if a polyp was removed or a biopsy taken. Excessive bleeding, severe pain or a rapid drop in blood pressure is reported.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options are defensible: blood after a colonoscopy can be a sign of hemorrhage. The cue that decides is the removal of 2 polyps, which makes a small streak of blood an expected finding.

steps.detail: 2 polyps were removed.
A small streak, with blood pressure and heart rate near the 1030 values.
Cramping 3 of 10 with flatus is expected, not perforation.

elimination.verdict: A. Expected after polyp removal.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: A client, 81 years old, is admitted with nausea and is prescribed a new medication for the gastrointestinal tract at the usual adult dose. Laboratory results today: serum albumin 3.1 g/dL, ALT 52 units/L. The client takes 2 other daily medications and has no known kidney disease. Which plan does the nurse include for the new medication?

options.text: Ask the provider to raise the dose, because older adults absorb drugs more slowly
options.rationale: A higher than usual dose is never the starting point in an older adult. Age related changes in the liver make toxic levels more likely, not less.

options.text: Watch closely for adverse effects, because slower metabolism can raise drug levels
options.rationale: Fewer and smaller hepatic cells lower protein synthesis and enzyme activity, which depresses drug metabolism. Drugs can accumulate to toxic levels even at a usual dose, so the nurse monitors closely.

options.text: Ask the provider to halve the dose, because older adults always need lower doses
options.rationale: Older adults do not always need lower doses. The word always is the cue; the safe plan is close monitoring at the prescribed dose.

options.text: Hold the dose if nausea occurs, because nausea is an expected side effect at this age
options.rationale: Nausea is not an expected effect of a correctly dosed medication in an older adult. New nausea after a medication starts is a possible sign of toxicity to report, not a routine reason to hold.

questions.takeaway: A decrease in the number and size of hepatic cells lowers liver mass, protein synthesis and enzyme activity. Drug metabolism slows, so an older adult can reach toxic drug levels at a usual dose and needs close monitoring.
questions.strategy: Link the low albumin and the liver enzyme change to the aging liver, then ask what slower drug metabolism means for a usual dose.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low albumin and a changed ALT fit fewer and smaller liver cells with less protein synthesis.
Slower metabolism lets drugs build up toward toxic levels.
Raising the dose adds risk, and always lowering the dose is an absolute.
Close monitoring for adverse effects at the prescribed dose.

elimination.verdict: B. Watch closely for adverse effects.

questions.objective: Describe age related changes in the GI system and their impact on digestion, absorption, and elimination

questions.stem: A client, 86 years old, lives in a long term care facility and has eaten about 40% of each meal for 6 weeks. Weight is 51.2 kg now, was 53.4 kg 6 weeks ago. The client says, "I just do not feel hungry." Dentures fit, chewing and swallowing cause no pain or coughing, and mood is unchanged per staff. The client has a soft, formed stool every day with no fatty or pale stools. Hemoglobin is 13.6 g/dL. Which age related change does the nurse consider most likely?

options.text: Atrophy of the gastric mucosa, which lowers absorption of iron and vitamin B12
options.rationale: Gastric mucosal atrophy lowers iron and vitamin B12 absorption and can lead to anemia. The hemoglobin does not suggest that picture, and it does not explain the loss of appetite.

options.text: Slower peristalsis with dulled nerve impulses in the colon
options.rationale: Slower peristalsis lowers the sensation to defecate and leads to constipation. The client has a formed stool every day.

options.text: Dilation of the pancreatic ducts, which lowers lipase production
options.rationale: Lower lipase causes steatorrhea and weight loss from poorly absorbed fat. The client denies fatty or pale stools.

options.text: Disruption of the microbial balance in the gut, which can dull the appetite
options.rationale: Disrupted intestinal microbial balance in older adults contributes to anorexia and the undernutrition that follows. Poor appetite with weight loss and no other GI finding fits this change.

questions.takeaway: Disruption of microbial balance in the aging gut contributes to anorexia and then undernutrition. Rule out the other changes by their own signs: anemia, constipation and steatorrhea.
questions.strategy: Each age related change has its own signature. Match the one finding left, poor appetite, to the change that explains it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A hemoglobin of 13.6 g/dL does not suggest poor iron or vitamin B12 absorption.
A formed stool every day argues against slowed peristalsis.
No fatty or pale stools argues against low lipase.
Disrupted microbial balance explains anorexia and the weight loss.

elimination.verdict: D. Disruption of the microbial balance in the gut.

questions.objective: Describe age related changes in the GI system and their impact on digestion, absorption, and elimination

questions.stem: The nurse gathers the nutrition and family history for a client with bloating and loose stools after meals. Which questions does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: "Do the symptoms follow meals with milk, cheese or ice cream?"
options.rationale: Lactose intolerance is part of the nutrition history. Bloating, gas and loose stools after dairy point toward it.

options.text: "Has anyone in your family had colon cancer, polyps or other bowel disorders?"
options.rationale: Family history of GI disorders matters because some GI problems carry a genetic predisposition.

options.text: "Would you like a referral to a dietitian before you leave today?"
options.rationale: A referral may come later, but it is an intervention, not a history question. The nurse finishes collecting data first.

options.text: "How many drinks with alcohol or caffeine do you have in a usual week?"
options.rationale: Alcohol and caffeine intake belong in the nutrition history and can contribute to GI symptoms.

options.text: "Have you received an influenza vaccine this season?"
options.rationale: Immunization status is general health data, not part of a focused GI nutrition and family history.

options.text: "Has the taste of food changed, or do you have trouble swallowing?"
options.rationale: Changes in taste and dysphagia are listed nutrition history items and may reveal another GI problem.

questions.takeaway: A focused GI history covers the nutrition history (special diets, food allergies, lactose intolerance, anorexia, taste change, dysphagia, pain with eating, nausea, dyspepsia, weight loss, alcohol and caffeine) and family history with genetic risk.
questions.strategy: Sort each option into history data or something else. Keep questions that gather nutrition or family data; drop interventions and unrelated health data.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dairy, alcohol and caffeine, taste and swallowing.
Colon cancer, polyps and bowel disorders in relatives.
A referral is a next step, not data collection.
Vaccination status is not part of this focused history.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, F.

questions.objective: Obtain a focused GI health history, including nutritional habits, bowel patterns, and common GI symptoms

questions.stem: A client, 67 years old, is seen in the clinic for fatigue for 1 month. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL, was 13.2 g/dL 6 months ago. During the GI history the client makes four statements. Which statement requires further assessment by the nurse first?

options.text: "I take ibuprofen 3 or 4 times a day for my arthritis."
options.rationale: Regular use of NSAIDs such as ibuprofen predisposes the client to peptic ulcer disease and GI bleeding. With a falling hemoglobin, this is the statement to explore: dose, duration, and any black or bloody stools.

options.text: "I have worn dentures for 10 years, and they still fit well."
options.rationale: Well fitting dentures support chewing and nutrition. Nothing here needs follow up.

options.text: "I eat a bran cereal most mornings to keep myself regular."
options.rationale: Fiber supports regular bowel movements. This is a healthy habit, not a concern.

options.text: "I stay away from hot peppers, because they are not to my taste."
options.rationale: Avoiding spicy food is a preference. It does not suggest a GI problem.

questions.takeaway: Regular NSAID use, such as ibuprofen, predisposes clients to peptic ulcer disease and GI bleeding. A medication history is part of a focused GI history, and a falling hemoglobin makes it urgent.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that could explain the abnormal data in the stem. The others describe healthy habits or preferences.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hemoglobin fell from 13.2 to 10.8 g/dL with fatigue.
Frequent ibuprofen can cause ulcers and GI bleeding.
Fitting dentures, fiber and a taste preference are not concerns.

elimination.verdict: A. The ibuprofen statement.

questions.objective: Obtain a focused GI health history, including nutritional habits, bowel patterns, and common GI symptoms

questions.scenario: A nurse in a GI clinic reviews the bowel histories that clients gave during intake today.
questions.stem: For each stool description, indicate the stool finding it describes.

rows.text: "My stools have been pale, almost like clay, for a week, and my urine is dark."
rows.rationale: Acholic stool is pale or clay colored because bile is not reaching the bowel. Dark urine often comes with it.

rows.text: "I pass small, hard, separate lumps every 4 days, and I have to strain."
rows.rationale: Small, hard, separate lumps passed with straining are pebble stools, a sign of constipation.

rows.text: "There is bright red blood on the outside of my stool."
rows.rationale: Bright red blood in or on the stool is hematochezia and points to bleeding low in the GI tract.

rows.text: "My stools are bulky and greasy, they float, and they are hard to flush."
rows.rationale: Bulky, greasy, floating stools are steatorrhea, caused by poor fat digestion or absorption.

rows.text: "My stools look gray, my skin itches, and my eyes have turned yellow."
rows.rationale: Gray stool with itching and jaundice suggests that bile is blocked from the bowel, producing acholic stool.

rows.text: "My stools are black and sticky, like tar, with a very strong odor."
rows.rationale: Black, tarry stool is melena, from digested blood high in the GI tract.

questions.takeaway: Name the stool: acholic (pale, clay colored, no bile), pebble (small hard lumps, constipation), hematochezia (bright red blood, lower GI), melena (black and tarry, upper GI), steatorrhea (greasy, floating, fat). Each name points to a different problem to explore.
questions.strategy: Use color first, then consistency. Pale or gray means bile, red means low bleeding, black means high bleeding, greasy means fat, and hard lumps mean constipation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clay and gray are acholic; bright red is hematochezia; black and tarry is melena.
Greasy and floating is steatorrhea; small hard lumps are pebble stool.
Dark urine, itching and yellow eyes support blocked bile.

elimination.verdict: Acholic, pebble, hematochezia, steatorrhea, acholic, melena.

questions.objective: Obtain a focused GI health history, including nutritional habits, bowel patterns, and common GI symptoms

questions.stem: A client, 38 years old, has had cramping and diarrhea 4 to 5 times a day for 3 weeks. When the nurse asks about bowel habits, the client looks away, speaks quietly and says, "Do we have to talk about this?" The client mentions starting a new job and moving to a new city last month. A family member who came to the visit is in the waiting room. The door to the exam room is open. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Move on to the physical examination and plan to return to the bowel history at the next visit
options.rationale: Skipping the history delays data the nurse needs now. Avoiding the topic also tells the client the subject is too awkward to discuss.

options.text: Close the door, say that many people find this awkward, and ask about recent stressful events
options.rationale: Elimination topics are often embarrassing, so the nurse provides privacy and acknowledges the feeling. Recent stress is linked to the onset or flare of some GI disorders, so asking about the job and move is relevant data.

options.text: Ask the family member in the waiting room to describe the client's bowel pattern instead
options.rationale: Asking a family member breaks confidentiality and bypasses the client, who is able to answer and is the primary source.

options.text: Explain that diarrhea from stress is common and should go away once the client settles in
options.rationale: This reassurance assumes a cause before assessment is complete and dismisses 3 weeks of diarrhea, which needs evaluation.

questions.takeaway: GI and elimination topics can feel embarrassing. Provide privacy, acknowledge the feeling, ask about recent stressful events, and refer for ongoing support when needed.
questions.strategy: Choose the option that keeps the client as the source, protects privacy and still gathers the data. Eliminate options that avoid, bypass or dismiss.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Looking away and a quiet voice show embarrassment; the door is open.
A new job and a move are recent stressful events worth exploring.
Postponing, asking family and premature reassurance all fail the client.
Privacy, acknowledgment and a stress question.

elimination.verdict: B. Close the door, acknowledge, ask about stress.

questions.objective: Obtain a focused GI health history, including nutritional habits, bowel patterns, and common GI symptoms

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to assess the abdomen of a client, 50 years old, admitted with abdominal discomfort, 3 of 10. The client is lying supine with the legs straight and the arms folded behind the head. The client last voided 4 hours ago and says the bladder feels full. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Have the client empty the bladder, then lie supine with knees bent and arms at the sides
options.rationale: Emptying the bladder and lying supine with knees bent and arms at the sides relaxes the abdominal muscles. A full bladder and tensed muscles distort the findings.

options.text: Begin inspection now, then have the client void before the nurse listens for bowel sounds
options.rationale: Stopping halfway interrupts the sequence. Preparation, including voiding, comes before inspection begins.

options.text: Turn the client onto the left side with the knees drawn up to relax the abdominal wall
options.rationale: The side lying position is used for some procedures, such as colonoscopy. The abdomen is assessed with the client supine.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees so that the abdominal muscles can relax fully
options.rationale: Sitting upright folds and tenses the abdomen. The supine position with knees bent relaxes it.

questions.takeaway: Prepare for abdominal assessment by having the client empty the bladder and lie supine with knees bent and arms at the sides to keep the abdominal muscles relaxed.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Preparation comes before the first step of the assessment. Pick the option that fixes both problems in the stem: the full bladder and the tensed position.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A full bladder and arms behind the head with straight legs.
Supine, knees bent, arms at the sides.
Voiding happens before inspection, not midway.

elimination.verdict: A. Empty the bladder, then supine with knees bent.

questions.objective: Demonstrate the correct sequence and techniques for abdominal assessment, including inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation

questions.stem: A client has had 8 watery stools since yesterday. On auscultation the nurse hears loud, frequent, high pitched gurgling in all 4 quadrants. How does the nurse interpret the bowel sounds?

options.text: Diminished bowel sounds, as heard with a paralytic ileus
options.rationale: Diminished or absent sounds occur after surgery and with paralytic ileus or peritonitis. These sounds are loud and frequent, the opposite of diminished.

options.text: Normal bowel sounds, because gurgling is heard in each quadrant
options.rationale: Gurgling in each quadrant alone would be normal, but loud, frequent, high pitched gurgling is more than normal activity.

options.text: Hyperactive bowel sounds that point to peritonitis
options.rationale: Peritonitis makes bowel sounds diminished or absent, not hyperactive. The soft, flat abdomen also argues against it.

options.text: Hyperactive bowel sounds, called borborygmus
options.rationale: Bowel sounds are graded hypoactive, normal or hyperactive. Loud, frequent, high pitched gurgling is hyperactive, the gurgling called borborygmus, which matches a bowel moving fast enough to cause 8 watery stools.

questions.takeaway: Grade bowel sounds as hypoactive, normal or hyperactive. Diminished or absent sounds follow surgery and occur with paralytic ileus or peritonitis; loud, frequent gurgling is hyperactive (borborygmus), as with diarrhea.
questions.strategy: Grade the sound first, then check each option's condition against that grade. Ileus and peritonitis quiet the bowel; they do not make it loud.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Loud, frequent, high pitched gurgling is hyperactive.
Loud and frequent is more than normal gurgling.
Both give diminished or absent sounds.
Hyperactive sounds, borborygmus.

elimination.verdict: D. Hyperactive bowel sounds, borborygmus.

questions.objective: Differentiate normal and abnormal GI assessment findings and identify findings that require further evaluation

questions.stem: A client, 45 years old, reports bloating and has passed no flatus for 24 hours. The abdomen is distended and soft. The health care provider percusses the abdomen and documents loud, high pitched, musical notes over all 4 quadrants and a soft, thudlike note over the right upper quadrant that does not extend past the rib margin. Which conclusion does the nurse draw from the percussion findings?

options.text: The musical notes show fluid filling the abdominal cavity
options.rationale: Fluid gives a dull note. Loud, high pitched musical notes are tympany from air.

options.text: The thudlike note over the right upper quadrant shows hepatomegaly
options.rationale: A dull note over the liver is expected. The note stays within the rib margin, so it does not suggest an enlarged liver.

options.text: The musical notes show air in the bowel, and the liver note is expected
options.rationale: Tympany is the high pitched, musical sound of an air filled intestine and fits the bloating. Dullness over a normal sized liver is expected.

options.text: The musical notes show a solid mass, because tympany occurs over solid tissue
options.rationale: Solid tissue such as an organ or mass gives a dull, thudlike note, not tympany.

questions.takeaway: Percussion, often done by the health care provider, sizes solid organs. Tympany is a high pitched, air filled sound; dullness is a thudlike sound over a solid organ such as the liver.
questions.strategy: Match each note to what lies beneath: air sounds musical and high pitched, solid tissue and fluid sound dull. Then ask whether the dull area is the expected size.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Musical and high pitched is tympany; thudlike is dullness.
Air in a distended bowel, which fits no flatus and bloating.
Dullness confined within the rib margin is an expected liver size.

elimination.verdict: C. Air in the bowel, expected liver dullness.

questions.objective: Demonstrate the correct sequence and techniques for abdominal assessment, including inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation

questions.stem: A client is 1 day after abdominal surgery and has hypoactive bowel sounds. Which finding best shows that peristalsis is returning?

options.text: The client reports feeling hungry and asks for breakfast
options.rationale: Hunger is welcome, but it does not show that the bowel is moving contents forward.

options.text: One bowel sound heard in the right lower quadrant after 2 minutes
options.rationale: A single faint sound still fits hypoactive bowel sounds and does not confirm that contents are moving.

options.text: The client reports passing flatus twice since 0600
options.rationale: Passing flatus is a favorable indicator that peristalsis is returning after surgery. Gas is moving through the whole bowel.

options.text: The abdomen is soft, and there has been no nausea since 0600
options.rationale: A soft abdomen without nausea is reassuring, but neither shows forward movement of bowel contents.

questions.takeaway: After abdominal surgery, bowel sounds are diminished or absent. The client's report of passing flatus is a favorable indicator that peristalsis is returning, so ask about it first.
questions.strategy: Choose the finding that proves contents are moving all the way through, not one that is only reassuring.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hypoactive bowel sounds are expected after surgery.
Hunger, one faint sound and a soft abdomen do not show movement through the bowel.
Flatus has traveled the length of the bowel.

elimination.verdict: C. Passing flatus.

questions.objective: Differentiate normal and abnormal GI assessment findings and identify findings that require further evaluation

questions.stem: A client, 62 years old, with cirrhosis is scheduled for an esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with possible biopsy at 1300. The client reports bruising easily and bleeding gums when brushing the teeth. At 0800 the nurse reviews the client's data. Which finding is the priority for the nurse to report before the procedure?

options.text: Prothrombin time 19 seconds
options.rationale: A prolonged prothrombin time means blood takes longer to clot, which fits the easy bruising and bleeding gums. Bleeding is a known challenge of EGD, especially with a biopsy, so this is reported before the procedure.

options.text: Potassium 4.1 mEq/L
options.rationale: This potassium value is within the expected range and does not change the plan.

options.text: Nothing by mouth since 2400
options.rationale: Being NPO for more than 6 to 8 hours is the expected preparation for EGD.

options.text: Blood glucose 104 mg/dL
options.rationale: A glucose of 104 mg/dL after fasting since midnight does not threaten the procedure.

questions.takeaway: Prothrombin time is a serum test of clotting. Before EGD, bleeding risk matters: bleeding is a challenge of the procedure, and anticoagulants are avoided. Increased bruising or a tendency to bleed is a skin change linked to GI disorders such as liver disease, where the liver makes fewer clotting proteins.
questions.strategy: Ask which value changes safety for the planned procedure. A biopsy cuts tissue, so the clotting value matters most.

steps.detail: Easy bruising and bleeding gums show a tendency to bleed.
A prothrombin time of 19 seconds is prolonged.
Potassium, glucose and NPO status are expected for this procedure.

elimination.verdict: A. Prothrombin time 19 seconds.

questions.objective: Identify common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate GI function and disorders

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client, 58 years old, with cirrhosis is newly confused and slow to answer questions, and the sclera are yellow. The nurse expects the confusion to be linked to an elevated serum [[1]].

The nurse expects the yellow sclera to be linked to an elevated serum [[2]].

Today the AST and ALT are both several times higher than at the last visit. The nurse interprets this as [[3]].

options.text: ammonia
options.rationale: The liver converts ammonia to urea. Hepatocellular injury, such as cirrhosis, raises serum ammonia, which is linked to hepatic encephalopathy and confusion.

options.text: amylase
options.rationale: Amylase rises with acute pancreatitis. It does not explain confusion in liver disease.

options.text: carcinoembryonic antigen
options.rationale: This oncofetal antigen monitors GI cancer therapy and recurrence. It does not cause confusion.

options.text: lipase
options.rationale: Lipase rises with pancreatitis, not with jaundice from liver disease.

options.text: bilirubin
options.rationale: Bilirubin is the main pigment in bile. Impaired excretion by the liver raises serum bilirubin and produces jaundice.

options.text: potassium
options.rationale: Potassium shifts with vomiting and diarrhea. It does not cause yellow sclera.

options.text: ongoing injury to liver cells, which releases these enzymes into the blood
options.rationale: AST and ALT are liver enzymes. Injured liver cells release them into the blood, so a sharp rise points to ongoing liver cell injury, highest with necrosis such as hepatitis and cirrhosis.

options.text: recovery of liver function, because a healing liver makes more enzymes
options.rationale: Rising AST and ALT reflect enzymes leaking from damaged cells, not a healing liver. Recovery would bring the levels down.

options.text: a pancreatic problem, because these enzymes reflect pancreatic function
options.rationale: AST and ALT are liver enzymes. Amylase and lipase reflect the pancreas.

questions.takeaway: Liver tests: ammonia rises with hepatocellular injury and is linked to confusion, bilirubin rises with impaired excretion and causes jaundice, and AST and ALT rise when injured liver cells release them.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Match each finding to the substance the failing liver can no longer process: ammonia for the brain, bilirubin for the color, enzymes for the damaged cells.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Confusion in cirrhosis points to ammonia that the liver cannot convert to urea.
Yellow sclera point to bilirubin that the liver cannot excrete.
A sharp rise in AST and ALT means liver cells are still being injured and releasing enzymes.

elimination.verdict: Ammonia; bilirubin; ongoing injury to liver cells.

questions.objective: Identify common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate GI function and disorders

questions.stem: A client, 70 years old, has had vomiting and diarrhea for 3 days. Laboratory results today: potassium 2.9 mEq/L, sodium 132 mEq/L, hemoglobin 16.2 g/dL, hematocrit 50%. Heart rate 108 beats per minute and irregular. Blood pressure 98/58 mm Hg. Which plan does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Restrict fluids, because the high hematocrit shows fluid overload
options.rationale: A high hematocrit with vomiting, diarrhea and low blood pressure suggests hemoconcentration from fluid loss, not overload. Restricting fluid worsens it.

options.text: Replace potassium and fluids as prescribed, and recheck the electrolytes
options.rationale: Excessive vomiting or diarrhea depletes sodium and potassium and requires replacement. Rechecking the results evaluates the response.

options.text: Give potassium by IV push, so that the level corrects as quickly as possible
options.rationale: Potassium is never given by IV push; a rapid rise can cause a fatal dysrhythmia. Replacement is diluted and given slowly as prescribed.

options.text: Offer high fiber foods, so that the stools firm and the potassium rises
options.rationale: Fiber does not correct a potassium of 2.9 mEq/L, and food is not the first step with active vomiting.

questions.takeaway: Electrolytes are altered in GI dysfunction; excessive vomiting or diarrhea causes sodium and potassium depletion that requires replacement. A high hemoglobin and hematocrit with fluid loss reflect hemoconcentration.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Read the labs as one picture of fluid and electrolyte loss, then pick the safe replacement plan.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low potassium and sodium follow vomiting and diarrhea.
High hemoglobin and hematocrit with low blood pressure mean fluid loss.
Potassium is never given by IV push.
Prescribed replacement with a recheck.

elimination.verdict: B. Replace potassium and fluids, recheck.

questions.objective: Identify common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate GI function and disorders

questions.stem: A client who had surgery for colon cancer has a rising carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level, and the provider plans more testing. Which client statement shows understanding of the purpose of the test?

options.text: "Since this blood test is followed, I can stop having colonoscopies."
options.rationale: CEA does not replace other monitoring. The provider is already planning more testing because a blood value alone is not enough.

options.text: "This blood test is how they first found out I had colon cancer."
options.rationale: CEA and CA 19 9 are used to monitor therapy and recurrence, not to make the first diagnosis.

options.text: "A rising level proves that my cancer has come back."
options.rationale: These antigens can also rise in benign GI conditions, so a rising level calls for further testing rather than proving recurrence.

options.text: "This test tracks how well treatment worked and whether cancer may return."
options.rationale: Oncofetal antigens such as CEA and CA 19 9 monitor the efficacy of cancer therapy and assess for recurrence of GI cancer.

questions.takeaway: Oncofetal antigens (CA 19 9 and CEA) monitor how well GI cancer therapy is working and screen for recurrence. They can rise in benign GI conditions, so a rise leads to more testing.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Find the statement that matches the purpose of the test without overstating it. Words like proves and stop are the warning signs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Monitor therapy and recurrence.
A rise does not prove recurrence; benign conditions can raise it.
It is not the initial diagnostic test and does not replace colonoscopy.

elimination.verdict: D. Tracks treatment and possible recurrence.

questions.objective: Identify common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate GI function and disorders

questions.stem: A client, 30 years old, returned 2 weeks ago from a camping trip where the client drank untreated stream water. The client finished a 10 day course of an oral antibiotic for a dental infection 3 days ago. The client now has cramping, bloating and greasy, foul smelling stools that float, with 6 loose stools in 24 hours. Weight is 64.0 kg, was 66.3 kg 2 weeks ago. Which stool tests does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ova and parasites
options.rationale: Drinking untreated water followed by diarrhea suggests a parasitic infection. A stool sample for ova and parasites aids the diagnosis.

options.text: Fecal fats
options.rationale: Greasy, floating stools are steatorrhea. Fecal fat testing is done when steatorrhea or malabsorption is suspected.

options.text: Multitargeted stool DNA kit
options.rationale: This home kit screens average risk adults for colorectal cancer every 3 years. It is not used to diagnose acute diarrhea.

options.text: Annual fecal immunochemical test
options.rationale: The FIT screens for hidden blood as a colorectal cancer screening option. It does not identify the cause of acute diarrhea.

options.text: Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile)
options.rationale: Recent antibiotic therapy is a risk factor for Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile), a common infectious cause of diarrhea. The stool is tested for it.

questions.takeaway: Stool studies for diarrhea include ova and parasites for parasitic infection, fecal fats for steatorrhea or malabsorption, and C. difficile after antibiotic therapy. FIT, gFOBT and stool DNA kits are screening tests for colorectal cancer.
questions.strategy: Tie each test to a cue in the stem. Screening tests are for people without symptoms, not for working up acute diarrhea.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Untreated stream water points to ova and parasites.
Greasy, floating stools point to fecal fats.
A recent antibiotic points to C. difficile.
FIT and stool DNA screen for colorectal cancer.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E.

questions.objective: Identify common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate GI function and disorders

questions.stem: A client, 58 years old, with type 1 diabetes is scheduled for an abdominal radiograph at 0900 and an abdominal MRI at 1400. The client wears an insulin pump on the left side of the abdomen, a wedding ring and a leather belt with a metal buckle. Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Have the client wear a hospital gown and remove the belt and ring for the radiograph
options.rationale: No preparation is needed for an abdominal radiograph except a hospital gown and removal of jewelry and belts that can interfere with the film.

options.text: Keep the client NPO from midnight for the radiograph
options.rationale: An abdominal radiograph needs no preparation, so fasting is not required for it.

options.text: Report the insulin pump to the MRI team so that it is screened before the scan
options.rationale: MRI uses powerful magnets. The nurse screens for metal implants and devices such as insulin pumps, pacemakers and aneurysm clips.

options.text: Explain that the MRI takes longer than a CT scan and that lying still is needed
options.rationale: The MRI takes longer than a CT, and the client must lie still for clear images.

options.text: Explain that the MRI gives a small dose of radiation, about the same as a radiograph
options.rationale: MRI uses magnets and gives no radiation exposure.

options.text: Tell the client that the radiograph will be taken while seated upright in a chair
options.rationale: The abdominal radiograph is taken with the client lying supine.

questions.takeaway: Abdominal radiograph: no preparation, hospital gown, remove jewelry and belts, taken supine. MRI: screen for metal implants and devices such as insulin pumps, remove all metal, longer than CT, lie still, no radiation.
questions.strategy: Sort each statement by test, then check it against that test's preparation. The radiograph needs almost nothing; the MRI needs metal screening.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gown and removal of metal; no fasting; supine.
Screen the insulin pump; lie still; longer than CT.
MRI uses magnets, not radiation.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D.
