questions.stem: A client had an esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with moderate sedation and an anesthetic throat spray 40 minutes ago. The client is awake and oriented and says, "My throat still feels numb and thick. Can I have some water?" Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give 30 mL of water by mouth, because the client is awake and oriented now
options.rationale: Being awake does not mean the gag reflex has returned. A numb throat after anesthetic spray means swallowing is not yet safe.

options.text: Stop the IV infusion, because the client is awake and is asking to drink
options.rationale: The IV fluid is discontinued only when the client tolerates oral fluids without nausea or vomiting, which has not happened yet.

options.text: Check the gag reflex before any food or fluid is given by mouth
options.rationale: The priority after EGD is preventing aspiration. The client stays NPO until the gag reflex returns, usually in 30 to 60 minutes.

options.text: Lower the side rails, because the effects of the sedation have worn off
options.rationale: The side rails stay raised while sedation wears off. Orientation 40 minutes after the procedure does not show that sedation has fully cleared.

questions.takeaway: After EGD, keep the client NPO until the gag reflex returns (usually 30 to 60 minutes), check vital signs every 30 minutes until sedation wears off, keep the side rails raised, and stop IV fluids once oral fluids are tolerated without nausea or vomiting.
questions.strategy: The client's own words give the cue: a numb throat means the gag reflex may not be back. Assess it before anything goes by mouth.

steps.detail: "My throat still feels numb and thick."
Aspiration if fluids are given before the gag reflex returns.
The IV and side rails stay until fluids are tolerated and sedation clears.
Check the gag reflex first.

elimination.verdict: C. Check the gag reflex.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: A client, 55 years old, is scheduled for an outpatient esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) at 0800 tomorrow. The client takes a prescribed anticoagulant every morning. The provider has not given the client any special instructions about this drug. The nurse reviews the teaching. Which client statement indicates a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I will not eat or drink anything for 6 to 8 hours before the test."
options.rationale: NPO for 6 to 8 hours before EGD is correct and lowers the risk of aspiration.

options.text: "I will take my anticoagulant tomorrow morning as usual before the test."
options.rationale: Anticoagulants are usually avoided before EGD because of the bleeding risk, unless the provider says otherwise. The client needs to clarify this drug with the provider before the test.

options.text: "My throat will be sprayed, so swallowing will feel hard for a while."
options.rationale: An anesthetic spray inactivates the gag reflex, and swallowing will be difficult until it wears off. This is correct.

options.text: "A block will be placed between my teeth to protect them during the test."
options.rationale: A bite block keeps the client from biting the scope and protects the teeth. This is correct.

questions.takeaway: Before EGD: avoid anticoagulants unless told otherwise, NPO 6 to 8 hours, moderate sedation, anesthetic throat spray that inactivates the gag reflex, atropine to dry secretions, and a bite block.
questions.strategy: Negative polarity: look for the wrong statement. Bleeding risk is the safety issue the client has missed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that is unsafe.
NPO, throat spray and bite block are correct.
Taking the anticoagulant as usual raises bleeding risk.

elimination.verdict: B. Taking the anticoagulant as usual.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.nursesNote: 1500. Client, 61 years old, had an EGD with dilation of an esophageal stricture at 1100. Gag reflex returned at 1200. Took sips of water at 1230 without nausea. Reports new pain behind the sternum, 7 of 10, was 0 of 10 at 1200. Respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. Oral temperature 37.0 °C, was 36.9 °C at 1100. Alert and oriented to person, place and time. Heart rate 118 beats per minute, was 82 beats per minute at 1100. SpO2 97% on room air. Spit up saliva streaked with bright red blood at 1445. IV fluid infusing at 75 mL per hour as prescribed.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require further evaluation.

segments.text: Gag reflex returned at 1200
segments.rationale: Return of the gag reflex within 30 to 60 minutes is expected after EGD.

segments.text: Took sips of water at 1230 without nausea
segments.rationale: Tolerating fluids after the gag reflex returns is an expected finding.

segments.text: Reports new pain behind the sternum, 7 of 10, was 0 of 10 at 1200
segments.rationale: After endoscopy the nurse monitors for perforation and assesses pain. New, severe pain after dilation of a stricture suggests perforation.

segments.text: Respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute
segments.rationale: This respiratory rate is within the expected range.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.0 °C, was 36.9 °C at 1100
segments.rationale: The temperature is essentially unchanged and within the expected range.

segments.text: Alert and oriented to person, place and time
segments.rationale: Orientation shows the sedation has worn off, an expected finding.

segments.text: Heart rate 118 beats per minute, was 82 beats per minute at 1100
segments.rationale: A rising heart rate supports a developing complication such as perforation or bleeding.

segments.text: SpO2 97% on room air
segments.rationale: Oxygen saturation is within the expected range.

segments.text: Spit up saliva streaked with bright red blood at 1445
segments.rationale: After endoscopy the nurse monitors for bleeding, a known challenge of EGD. Fresh blood with new pain needs evaluation.

segments.text: IV fluid infusing at 75 mL per hour as prescribed
segments.rationale: An infusion running as prescribed is expected.

questions.takeaway: After endoscopy, monitor for perforation, bleeding and aspiration, and assess pain. Esophageal stricture and bleeding are challenges of EGD. Expected findings are a returned gag reflex and tolerated fluids.
questions.strategy: Compare each finding with its earlier value and with what is expected after EGD. Changes that point to one complication need follow up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pain 0 to 7 of 10 and heart rate 82 to 118; temperature barely changed.
Blood streaked saliva.
New pain, a rising heart rate and bleeding after stricture dilation point to perforation or bleeding.
Gag reflex, fluids tolerated, temperature, orientation, respiratory rate, SpO2, IV.

questions.stem: A client, 47 years old, with GI bleeding of unknown source is scheduled for small bowel capsule endoscopy. The nurse has taught the client about the test. Which client statement shows understanding?

options.text: "I will look for the capsule in my stool and call if I do not see it pass."
options.rationale: The capsule passes naturally in the stool. The client observes stools for its passage and reports if it does not pass.

options.text: "I will come back after the test so the capsule can be removed with a scope."
options.rationale: The capsule is a single use device that is excreted naturally. No scope is needed to remove it.

options.text: "I can eat my usual dinner tonight, since this test needs no preparation."
options.rationale: A clear liquid diet is required the day before, with NPO status as ordered.

options.text: "I will stay in the hospital until an x ray shows that the capsule is gone."
options.rationale: The client goes home during the test. Passage is confirmed by stool observation, not a hospital stay.

questions.takeaway: Small bowel capsule endoscopy: clear liquid diet the day before and NPO as ordered, swallow the capsule, then watch the stool for capsule passage and report if it does not pass.
questions.strategy: Picture the capsule's path. It is swallowed and leaves in the stool, so the teaching centers on preparation and on watching for it to pass.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A clear liquid diet the day before rules out the usual dinner.
The capsule is excreted, not retrieved.
Watching the stool for passage.

elimination.verdict: A. Look for the capsule in the stool.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: A client, 52 years old, had a flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsy at 1000. At 1300 the client has passed 3 stools of bright red blood with clots since 1100 and reports lightheadedness when sitting up. Blood pressure 96/60 mm Hg, was 128/80 mm Hg at 1000. Heart rate 118 beats per minute, was 76 beats per minute at 1000. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Have the client walk in the hall to ease the mild cramping expected after the test
options.rationale: Mild cramping is expected after sigmoidoscopy, but this client is lightheaded with falling blood pressure and is at risk for falling.

options.text: Explain that some bleeding after biopsy is expected and recheck in 1 hour
options.rationale: A small amount of blood is expected after biopsy, but repeated clots with falling blood pressure and a rising heart rate are excessive.

options.text: Report the bleeding and the vital sign changes to the provider now
options.rationale: After sigmoidoscopy the nurse monitors for bleeding, especially after a biopsy, and excessive bleeding is reported. Falling blood pressure and a rising heart rate make it urgent.

options.text: Give a cleansing enema to clear the blood from the rectum before reassessing
options.rationale: An enema is part of the preparation before sigmoidoscopy, not a treatment for bleeding afterward. It delays reporting the bleeding.

questions.takeaway: After sigmoidoscopy, mild cramping and gas pain are expected, and a small amount of bleeding may follow a biopsy. Monitor for bleeding and report excessive bleeding immediately.
questions.strategy: Separate expected from excessive. A small streak is expected after biopsy; repeated clots with a drop in blood pressure and a rise in heart rate are not.

steps.detail: Blood pressure 128/80 to 96/60 mm Hg and heart rate 76 to 118.
3 stools of blood with clots is excessive.
Report now; do not wait or walk the client.

elimination.verdict: C. Report the bleeding now.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.scenario: A client, 54 years old, is scheduled for an abdominal ultrasound in the morning and a liver spleen scan in the afternoon. The nurse plans the teaching.
questions.stem: For each statement, indicate whether the teaching is appropriate or not appropriate.

rows.text: "A gel will be placed on your skin, and the ultrasound uses no needles or radiation."
rows.rationale: Ultrasonography uses gel on the skin and is noninvasive, with no radiation.

rows.text: "You may need to fast before the ultrasound, depending on the organs being viewed."
rows.rationale: Ultrasonography may require fasting, depending on the organ, such as NPO for an abdominal ultrasound.

rows.text: "After the liver spleen scan, limit fluids so the tracer stays in your body longer."
rows.rationale: Hydration is encouraged after a liver spleen scan to help eliminate the radionuclide.

rows.text: "The scan uses a small amount of radioactive material, and the exposure is minimal."
rows.rationale: A small amount of radioactive material is used, and the exposure is minimal and safe.

rows.text: "You will need to stay on bed rest for 6 hours after the ultrasound."
rows.rationale: After ultrasonography there are no specific requirements; clients resume normal activities right away.

rows.text: "For the liver spleen scan, you will swallow the tracer with a cup of water."
rows.rationale: The radionuclide for a liver spleen scan is injected through IV access, not swallowed.

questions.takeaway: Ultrasonography: possible fasting, gel, noninvasive, no follow up care. Liver spleen scan: IV radionuclide, minimal and safe exposure, then fluids to help eliminate it.
questions.strategy: Check each statement against the test it names. Ultrasound needs almost no aftercare; the scan needs IV access and fluids afterward.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gel, fasting as ordered, normal activity afterward.
IV radionuclide, minimal exposure, encourage fluids.
Limiting fluids, bed rest and a swallowed tracer.

elimination.verdict: Appropriate, appropriate, not appropriate, appropriate, not appropriate, not appropriate.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: A client, 63 years old, is scheduled for endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) at 0800 tomorrow to evaluate a mass in the pancreas. A biopsy may be taken. Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tell the client that eating can resume as soon as the client is awake
options.rationale: After EUS the nurse confirms that the gag reflex has returned before any oral intake.

options.text: Tell the client that driving home is safe once the client feels awake
options.rationale: EUS uses sedation, so the client needs a driver. Feeling awake does not mean sedation has cleared.

options.text: Explain that a sore throat may occur for a short time after the procedure
options.rationale: The scope passes through the throat, so a sore throat is a possible side effect.

options.text: Teach the client to take nothing by mouth for 6 to 8 hours before the procedure
options.rationale: EUS requires NPO status for 6 to 8 hours before the procedure.

options.text: Confirm that informed consent is signed before any sedation is given
options.rationale: EUS is an invasive procedure that requires informed consent, obtained before sedation.

options.text: Explain that a biopsy cannot be taken during this procedure
options.rationale: EUS can include biopsy collection, and the nurse prepares for it.

questions.takeaway: EUS: NPO 6 to 8 hours, informed consent, sedation with possible biopsy, possible sore throat, and gag reflex return before oral intake, with monitoring for bleeding or perforation.
questions.strategy: EUS is an endoscopy, so apply the endoscopy rules: NPO, consent, sedation precautions and gag reflex before eating.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NPO 6 to 8 hours and informed consent.
Sore throat is possible; gag reflex before food or fluid.
Driving after sedation, early eating, and denying biopsy.

elimination.verdict: C, D, E.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: A client, 74 years old, is on day 3 after a stroke that caused weakness of the right arm and leg. During a swallow screen the client coughs and the voice sounds wet after each sip of water. Bowel sounds are active in all four quadrants, the abdomen is soft, and the client passed a formed stool this morning. Weight is 58 kg now, was 63 kg one month ago. The team discusses nutrition support. Which interpretation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: Parenteral nutrition fits, because the client cannot swallow safely
options.rationale: Unsafe swallowing makes oral intake unsafe, but parenteral nutrition is used when the GI tract cannot be adequately used. This client's GI tract works.

options.text: An oral diet should continue, because the bowel is working normally
options.rationale: A working bowel does not make swallowing safe. Coughing and a wet voice after sips signal a high risk of aspiration with oral intake.

options.text: Enteral nutrition fits, because the bowel works and swallowing is unsafe
options.rationale: Enteral nutrition is indicated when the GI tract functions but oral intake is unsafe or inadequate. Active bowel sounds and a formed stool show function; coughing with sips shows unsafe swallowing.

options.text: Parenteral nutrition fits, because the weight loss shows the bowel is not absorbing
options.rationale: The 5 kg loss fits inadequate intake, which is undernutrition. Bowel sounds and a formed stool point to a working GI tract, so the route stays enteral.

questions.takeaway: Choose the route by asking two questions: does the GI tract work, and is oral intake safe and adequate? A working gut with unsafe swallowing means enteral nutrition; a gut that cannot be adequately used means parenteral nutrition.
questions.strategy: Two options choose parenteral nutrition for different reasons. Check the bowel findings first: if the gut works, the intravenous route is not needed.

steps.detail: Coughing and a wet voice with sips: oral intake is unsafe. Bowel sounds and a formed stool: the GI tract works.
A working bowel does not protect the airway.
Weight loss reflects intake, not a gut that cannot absorb.
Enteral nutrition fits a working gut with unsafe swallowing.

elimination.verdict: C. Enteral nutrition fits, because the bowel works and swallowing is unsafe.

questions.objective: Compare enteral and parenteral nutrition and identify who needs enteral feeding

questions.stem: The provider prescribes a nasogastric tube for 2 to 3 weeks of feeding and medications for a client with dysphagia. The client has no nausea, vomiting, or abdominal distention. Which tube should the nurse anticipate using?

options.text: The 16 Fr double lumen tube, because a wider lumen clogs less often during feeding
options.rationale: A wider lumen does clog less, but large bore double lumen tubes are used for gastric decompression, lavage, and medications. A tube chosen for feeding is small bore.

options.text: The 10 Fr single lumen tube, because this size is meant for feeding and medications
options.rationale: Small bore tubes of 8 to 12 Fr are single lumen and are used for enteral feeding and medication administration. This client needs feeding, not decompression.

options.text: The 16 Fr double lumen tube, because medications can only pass through a large bore tube
options.rationale: Small bore feeding tubes are also used to give medications, with flushes. Medications do not require a large bore tube.

options.text: The 10 Fr single lumen tube, because it can also be attached to suction for decompression
options.rationale: The size is right, but the reason is wrong. Decompression is a use of large bore double lumen tubes, and this client has no distention or vomiting.

questions.takeaway: Large bore nasogastric tubes (14 to 18 Fr, double lumen) are used for decompression, lavage, and medications. Small bore tubes (8 to 12 Fr, single lumen) are used for feeding and medications.
questions.strategy: Two options pick each tube. Match the purpose of the order, feeding and medications with no distention, to the tube built for it.

steps.detail: Feeding and medications; no nausea, vomiting, or distention, so no decompression is needed.
Feeding is the use of a small bore single lumen tube.
The other small bore option gives a decompression reason, which belongs to the large bore tube.
The 10 Fr single lumen tube for feeding and medications.

elimination.verdict: B. The 10 Fr single lumen tube, because this size is meant for feeding and medications.

questions.objective: Describe feeding tube types and the factors that guide route selection

questions.stem: A small bore nasogastric feeding tube was inserted at the bedside without imaging guidance at 1000 for a client, 74 years old, with dysphagia after a stroke. The nurse marked the tube at 55 cm at the left naris. At 1030 the formula arrives, and the nurse aspirates fluid with a pH of 4. The prescribed x ray was taken at 1015, and no result is documented yet. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Hold formula, water, and medications until the x ray result is documented
options.rationale: A blindly inserted tube needs x ray confirmation before first use, and the nurse reviews the documented result before giving anything through the tube.

options.text: Start the feeding at the ordered rate, because a pH of 4 shows gastric placement
options.rationale: An acidic aspirate supports gastric placement, but pH alone cannot guarantee it. A blindly inserted tube still needs x ray confirmation before first use.

options.text: Inject 10 mL of air while listening over the stomach, then start the feeding
options.rationale: Air bolus auscultation does not reliably verify placement. A sound over the stomach can be heard even when the tube sits in the airway or esophagus.

options.text: Flush the tube with 30 mL of water to confirm it is open, then start the feeding
options.rationale: Water is held until placement is confirmed, the same as formula and medications. Water given through a tube in the airway enters the lungs.

questions.takeaway: A blindly inserted feeding tube is confirmed by x ray before first use. Formula, water, and medications all wait for the documented result; pH and air bolus checks do not replace it.
questions.strategy: Three options put something into the tube before confirmation. Ask what the tube must have before anything goes in.

steps.detail: Blind bedside insertion, and the x ray result is not documented.
pH alone cannot guarantee placement; air bolus auscultation is not reliable.
Water is a substance given through the tube, so it also waits.
Hold all tube use until the documented x ray result confirms placement.

elimination.verdict: A. Hold formula, water, and medications until the x ray result is documented.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding and verify tube placement

questions.stem: A client, 76 years old, receives bolus feedings through a small bore nasogastric tube. After x ray confirmation 2 days ago, the tube was marked and documented at 55 cm at the left naris. At 1200, before the bolus feeding, the nurse finds the mark at 49 cm at the naris and the tape loose. The client has no cough, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, and SpO2 is 96% on room air. The aspirate has a pH of 4. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Give the feeding, because an acidic aspirate with no breathing distress confirms gastric placement
options.rationale: An acidic aspirate and quiet breathing make this tempting, but aspirate pH alone cannot guarantee placement. The cue is the mark: 6 cm of tube has come out since the confirmed baseline.

options.text: Push the tube in 6 cm to the documented mark, retape it, and give the feeding
options.rationale: Advancing the tube does not prove where the tip now lies. A tube that has moved needs verification, not a blind adjustment followed by a feeding.

options.text: Give the feeding with the head of the bed raised to 45 degrees, then retape the tube
options.rationale: Raising the head of the bed reduces aspiration risk, but it does not address a tube that may be displaced. Placement comes before feeding.

options.text: Hold tube use, secure the tube, and obtain further verification per policy
options.rationale: The external length differs from the documented baseline, a sign of displacement. When placement is uncertain, the nurse holds tube use and obtains further verification.

questions.takeaway: Before each feeding and medication, compare the external tube length with the documented baseline. If the length has changed, hold tube use and obtain further verification, even when the aspirate is acidic.
questions.strategy: Two options rest on a defensible check: the acidic pH and the length mark. The mark decides, because pH alone cannot guarantee placement and the mark shows the tube has moved 6 cm.

steps.detail: Mark at 49 cm now, documented at 55 cm, with loose tape.
An acidic aspirate supports gastric placement but cannot guarantee it.
Pushing the tube back or raising the bed does not confirm the tip.
Hold tube use and obtain further verification.

elimination.verdict: D. Hold tube use, secure the tube, and obtain further verification per policy.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding and verify tube placement

questions.stem: Which actions by the nurse reduce the risk of aspiration for a client receiving continuous feeding through a small bore nasogastric tube? Select all that apply.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed flat for linen changes while the pump continues to run
options.rationale: Lying flat while formula runs lets it reflux toward the airway. The head of the bed stays raised during feeding.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed raised 30 to 45 degrees while the feeding runs
options.rationale: Elevating the head of the bed 30 to 45 degrees during feeding reduces reflux and aspiration.

options.text: Check the external tube mark and the securement device at each assessment
options.rationale: A tube that moves out of place can deliver formula into the esophagus or airway. Verifying placement and keeping the tube secured prevents aspiration.

options.text: Increase the rate to finish the daily volume sooner so the client can lie flat overnight
options.rationale: Continuous feeding rates are advanced only as ordered, and a faster rate raises the risk of reflux and vomiting.

options.text: Watch for reflux, vomiting, and abdominal distention during the feeding
options.rationale: Reflux, vomiting, and feeding intolerance come before aspiration. Monitoring them lets the nurse act early.

options.text: Plan to move the tube into the small intestine so aspiration can no longer happen
options.rationale: Small intestine feeding may reduce aspiration risk, but it does not eliminate it.

questions.takeaway: Aspiration prevention during enteral feeding: head of bed 30 to 45 degrees, verified and secured tube, and monitoring for reflux, vomiting, and intolerance. Small intestine feeding lowers the risk but never removes it.
questions.strategy: Keep the options that keep formula moving down, keep the tube in place, and catch reflux early.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Raised 30 to 45 degrees during feeding; never flat while the pump runs.
Check the mark and securement each assessment.
Reflux, vomiting, and distention.
Rate changes need an order, and small intestine feeding does not eliminate the risk.

elimination.verdict: B, C, E.

questions.objective: Prevent aspiration during enteral feeding

questions.nursesNote: 1400: Client, 66 years old, receiving continuous feeding through a small bore nasogastric tube at 55 mL per hour. Head of bed at 40 degrees. Coughing during the last hour, was not coughing at 1000. External tube mark at 60 cm at the right naris, matches the documented baseline. One soft formed stool at 1200. SpO2 90% on room air, was 96% at 1000. Oral temperature 37.0 °C. Abdomen firm and distended, was soft at 1000. Abdominal pain 0 of 10. Respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, was 18 breaths per minute at 1000.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: Head of bed at 40 degrees
segments.rationale: A head of bed angle of 40 degrees is within the 30 to 45 degrees used during feeding.

segments.text: Coughing during the last hour, was not coughing at 1000
segments.rationale: New coughing during feeding can signal aspiration of formula.

segments.text: External tube mark at 60 cm at the right naris, matches the documented baseline
segments.rationale: A mark that matches the baseline does not suggest displacement.

segments.text: One soft formed stool at 1200
segments.rationale: A soft formed stool does not suggest diarrhea or intolerance.

segments.text: SpO2 90% on room air, was 96% at 1000
segments.rationale: Oxygen desaturation during feeding can signal aspiration.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.0 °C
segments.rationale: No fever is present at this time.

segments.text: Abdomen firm and distended, was soft at 1000
segments.rationale: New distention is a sign of feeding intolerance and raises the risk of vomiting and aspiration.

segments.text: Abdominal pain 0 of 10
segments.rationale: No abdominal pain is reported.

segments.text: Respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, was 18 breaths per minute at 1000
segments.rationale: A rising respiratory rate with coughing and desaturation points to a breathing problem during feeding.

questions.takeaway: Monitor tolerance with the abdomen (fullness, nausea, distention), the stool, and the lungs (coughing, dyspnea, oxygen desaturation). Compare each finding with its earlier value.
questions.strategy: Look for what changed since 1000. Findings that match a baseline or a target are not the cues.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Coughing, SpO2, abdomen, and respiratory rate all changed since 1000.
Head of bed 40 degrees and the matching tube mark meet the plan.
A formed stool, no pain, and 37.0 °C need no follow up.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.scenario: A client, 70 years old, receives continuous feeding through a small bore nasogastric tube at 60 mL per hour. At 0300 the client vomits formula and begins coughing. Respiratory rate is 30 breaths per minute, was 18 breaths per minute at 2400. SpO2 is 87% on room air, was 95% at 2400. Crackles are heard in the right lower lobe. Oral temperature is 37.2 °C.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Stop the feeding pump
options.rationale: With suspected aspiration, the first priority is to stop the feeding so no more formula reaches the airway.

options.text: Check the gastric residual volume before deciding whether to stop the feeding
options.rationale: Residual volume does not reliably predict aspiration, and checking it delays stopping the formula.

options.text: Lower the rate to 30 mL per hour and recheck the SpO2 in 1 hour
options.rationale: A lower rate still delivers formula, and an hour is too long with SpO2 87%.

options.text: Flush the tube with 30 mL of water to clear the formula
options.rationale: More fluid through the tube adds to the risk while aspiration is suspected.

options.text: Assess the airway and breathing and call for help
options.rationale: After stopping the feeding, the nurse assesses the airway and breathing and obtains help.

options.text: Feeding intolerance from too high a rate
options.rationale: Vomiting can reflect intolerance, but coughing, desaturation, and new right lower lobe crackles point to formula in the lungs.

options.text: Refeeding syndrome
options.rationale: Refeeding syndrome is an electrolyte shift after nutrition restarts, not a sudden breathing change after vomiting.

options.text: Aspiration of formula
options.rationale: Vomiting followed by coughing, SpO2 87%, a respiratory rate of 30, and new crackles in the right lower lobe fit aspiration.

options.text: Clogged feeding tube
options.rationale: A clogged tube stops delivery; it does not cause vomiting with desaturation and crackles.

options.text: SpO2
options.rationale: Shows whether oxygenation recovers after the feeding is stopped.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: Weight tracks fluid and nutrition over days, not the airway now.

options.text: Respiratory rate and lung sounds
options.rationale: Show whether the breathing problem and the right lower lobe crackles are worsening or clearing.

options.text: Stool frequency
options.rationale: Stool pattern tracks tolerance of the gut, not the lungs.

options.text: Serum phosphate
options.rationale: Phosphate is monitored for refeeding syndrome, which is not the problem here.

questions.takeaway: Suspected aspiration during feeding: stop the feeding, assess the airway and breathing, and obtain help. Watch the SpO2, respiratory rate, and lung sounds.
questions.strategy: Name the problem from the sequence: vomiting, then coughing, desaturation, and new crackles. Then pick actions that stop more formula and protect the airway now.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vomiting followed by respiratory changes and right lower lobe crackles: aspiration.
Stop the pump; assess airway and breathing and call for help.
Residual checks, rate changes, and flushes delay or add fluid.
SpO2, respiratory rate, and lung sounds change within minutes.

elimination.verdict: Stop the feeding pump and assess the airway and breathing and call for help; aspiration of formula; SpO2 and respiratory rate with lung sounds.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: A client, 68 years old, receives continuous feeding through a small bore nasogastric tube at 50 mL per hour. Facility policy is to check gastric residual volume every 4 hours and to hold the feeding for a residual greater than 500 mL. The residual is 240 mL at 1200, was 160 mL at 0800. The abdomen is soft and not distended, bowel sounds are present, the client denies nausea, and the client has not vomited. The head of the bed is at 35 degrees. The nurse evaluates the client's response to the feeding. Which conclusion and action are most appropriate?

options.text: The rising residual shows intolerance, so hold the feeding for 1 hour and recheck
options.rationale: A rise from 160 mL to 240 mL looks like a warning. The cue is that the residual alone does not predict aspiration, it is below the policy limit, and there is no vomiting, distention, or nausea.

options.text: The residual predicts aspiration, so lower the head of the bed to help the stomach empty
options.rationale: Residual volume alone does not reliably predict aspiration, and lowering the head of the bed increases aspiration risk.

options.text: The feeding is tolerated, so continue the rate and keep watching for vomiting and distention
options.rationale: Residual volume is interpreted with vomiting, distention, and other intolerance findings. None are present and the value is below the policy limit, so the feeding continues with monitoring.

options.text: The residual shows delayed emptying, so ask the provider for feeding into the small intestine
options.rationale: There are no other signs of intolerance, so a change of route is not indicated by this number.

questions.takeaway: Gastric residual volume alone does not reliably predict aspiration. Follow facility policy and interpret the residual with vomiting, distention, nausea, and other intolerance findings.
questions.strategy: Two options read the rising number differently. Decide by the rest of the picture: no vomiting, no distention, no nausea, and a value under the policy limit.

steps.detail: No vomiting, distention, or nausea, and 240 mL is under the 500 mL policy limit.
A rising residual alone does not predict aspiration.
Lowering the head of the bed raises the risk.
Continue the feeding and keep monitoring for intolerance.

elimination.verdict: C. The feeding is tolerated, so continue the rate and keep watching for vomiting and distention.

questions.objective: Prevent aspiration during enteral feeding

questions.stem: The nurse reviews a client's findings documented this week. Which findings indicate undernutrition? Select all that apply.

options.text: Weight 52 kg now, was 57 kg two months ago, with no attempt to lose weight
options.rationale: Unintentional weight loss is a key assessment finding of undernutrition.

options.text: Blood pressure 126/78 mm Hg while sitting in a chair
options.rationale: This blood pressure does not reflect nutrient intake or absorption.

options.text: A stage 2 pressure injury on the sacrum that has not healed in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Poor wound healing is an assessment finding of undernutrition, because healing needs protein and calories.

options.text: Weak grip in both hands and naps three times a day because of fatigue
options.rationale: Muscle weakness and fatigue are assessment findings of undernutrition.

options.text: Urine output 1,500 mL in 24 hours
options.rationale: This output does not suggest a nutrient deficit.

options.text: Eats 30% of each meal and leaves the supplement drink untouched
options.rationale: Undernutrition is inadequate intake to meet the body's needs, and poor appetite is a risk factor. This intake does not meet needs.

questions.takeaway: Undernutrition shows as unintentional weight loss, muscle weakness, fatigue, and poor wound healing, often with poor intake. Identify deficits early so nutrition support can start.
questions.strategy: Ask whether each finding reflects intake, muscle, energy, or healing. Normal vital signs and output do not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A 5 kg loss without trying is unintentional.
A sacral injury not healing in 4 weeks, weak grip, and fatigue.
30% of meals with the supplement untouched.
Blood pressure and urine output do not reflect nutrition here.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, F.

questions.objective: Compare enteral and parenteral nutrition and identify who needs enteral feeding

questions.stem: A client, 81 years old, with advanced cancer of the tongue can no longer swallow safely. The GI tract works. The client is alert and oriented, accurately explains the risks and benefits of a gastrostomy tube, and has a written advance directive declining artificial nutrition. The client again declines the tube today. The client's adult child, who is the durable power of attorney for health care, insists that the tube be placed. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: Ask the durable power of attorney to sign the consent, since the family must agree
options.rationale: A durable power of attorney makes health decisions only when the client cannot make them. This client is alert and able to decide.

options.text: Support the client's decision, document it, and inform the provider of the refusal
options.rationale: The client has decision making capacity and an advance directive that matches the spoken choice. The nurse honors the client's preference, documents it, and communicates it to the provider.

options.text: Request an ethics committee review and delay any decision until consensus is reached
options.rationale: An ethics committee helps when a client cannot express wishes and no directive exists. The cue is that this client is alert, explains the choice, and has a directive, so the decision belongs to the client.

options.text: Prepare the client for the procedure, because the bowel works and feeding is indicated
options.rationale: A working GI tract makes enteral feeding possible, but patient preferences and treatment goals also guide the decision.

questions.takeaway: A working gut makes enteral feeding possible, not required. A client with decision making capacity decides, and an advance directive guides care; the durable power of attorney and ethics committee step in when the client cannot express wishes.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options bring in others to decide. Ask whether the client can decide now: alert, oriented, and explaining the risks means yes.

steps.detail: Alert, oriented, accurately explains risks and benefits, with a directive declining artificial nutrition.
The durable power of attorney acts only when the client cannot decide.
Ethics review fits when wishes cannot be known.
Honor and document the client's decision and inform the provider.

elimination.verdict: B. Support the client's decision, document it, and inform the provider of the refusal.

questions.objective: Compare enteral and parenteral nutrition and identify who needs enteral feeding

questions.stem: A client, 45 years old, weighed 41 kg on admission after eating very little for 4 weeks. Continuous enteral feeding started 36 hours ago. At 0800 the client reports weakness in both legs. Heart rate is 114 beats per minute and irregular, was 88 beats per minute and regular on admission. Serum phosphorus is 1.5 mg/dL, potassium 3.0 mEq/L, and magnesium 1.2 mEq/L. Lungs are clear, and there is no edema. Which problem do these findings most likely indicate?

options.text: Refeeding syndrome from electrolyte shifts as nutrition restarts
options.rationale: Severe undernutrition, a recent restart of feeding, and low phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium with weakness and a new irregular rhythm fit refeeding syndrome.

options.text: Fluid overload from the volume of formula and water flushes
options.rationale: Fluid overload would bring edema, crackles, or a rising weight. The lungs are clear and there is no edema.

options.text: Dehydration from concentrated formula that draws water into the bowel
options.rationale: No diarrhea, dry mucous membranes, or low output is reported, and dehydration does not explain three low electrolytes.

options.text: Aspiration of formula causing a fast and irregular heart rate
options.rationale: Aspiration presents with coughing, dyspnea, or desaturation. The lungs are clear, and the findings are electrolyte findings.

questions.takeaway: Refeeding syndrome is a dangerous electrolyte shift after nutrition restarts in a severely undernourished client. Watch potassium, magnesium, and phosphate, with I&O and daily weights.
questions.strategy: Each option is a real complication of enteral feeding. Choose the one that explains the history and all three low electrolytes.

steps.detail: 41 kg after 4 weeks of little intake, feeding restarted 36 hours ago.
Low phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium; weakness; a new irregular rhythm.
Clear lungs and no edema rule out overload and aspiration.
Refeeding syndrome.

elimination.verdict: A. Refeeding syndrome from electrolyte shifts as nutrition restarts.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: A client at risk for refeeding syndrome receives continuous enteral feeding by pump, as ordered. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Weigh the client daily on the same scale
options.rationale: Daily weights track fluid balance and the response to feeding.

options.text: Increase the rate by 10 mL per hour every 4 hours to reach the goal sooner
options.rationale: Continuous feeding rates are advanced only as ordered. Faster advancement raises the risk of dangerous electrolyte shifts.

options.text: Review the ordered potassium, magnesium, and phosphate results
options.rationale: Refeeding syndrome shifts potassium, magnesium, and phosphate, so the nurse monitors the ordered values.

options.text: Record the water flush volumes as part of the total fluid intake
options.rationale: Flushes are included in total fluid intake, so I&O is accurate.

options.text: Hold water flushes to keep the fluid intake as low as possible
options.rationale: Flushes keep the tube open and are given as ordered. Holding them risks a clogged tube and does not prevent refeeding syndrome.

questions.takeaway: For a client at risk for refeeding syndrome, monitor I&O (including flushes), daily weights, and ordered potassium, magnesium, and phosphate values, and advance feeding only as ordered.
questions.strategy: Keep the monitoring actions; reject anything that changes the plan without an order.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Daily weight and the ordered electrolytes.
Flushes count in total fluid intake.
Rate increases need an order; holding flushes risks clogging.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: A client has had a small bore nasogastric feeding tube taped to the nose for 6 days. The nurse finds a 0.5 cm area of red, nonblanching skin on the naris where the tube presses, and the lips are dry and cracked. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Remove the tape and let the tube hang loose so nothing presses on the naris
options.rationale: An unsecured tube can be pulled and displaced. The tube stays secured, but away from the injured skin.

options.text: Apply a thicker layer of tape directly over the red area to cushion the naris
options.rationale: More tape over the area keeps the pressure on injured skin and hides it from inspection.

options.text: Document the red area as expected and recheck the naris at the next 24 hour check
options.rationale: Nonblanching redness is a pressure injury, not an expected finding, and waiting lets it worsen.

options.text: Resecure the tube off the red area, give oral and lip care, and document
options.rationale: The nurse inspects the nares for pressure injury, secures the tube to reduce pressure, provides oral and lip care, and documents the site condition.

questions.takeaway: For a nasal feeding tube, inspect the nares and securement for pressure injury, secure the tube to reduce pulling and pressure, give frequent oral and lip care, and document the site.
questions.strategy: Two options act on the naris. Keep the tube secured and move the pressure, rather than removing securement or adding more tape.

steps.detail: Nonblanching redness where the tube presses; dry, cracked lips.
An unsecured tube risks displacement.
A pressure injury is not expected.
Resecure off the area, give oral and lip care, and document.

elimination.verdict: D. Resecure the tube off the red area, give oral and lip care, and document.

questions.objective: Provide oral, nasal and site care, teach the patient and document

questions.stem: A client who will need tube feeding for at least 6 months asks, "Why can't they just put the feeding tube in through my nose?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "A tube through the nose would have to be swapped for a wider one to carry formula that long."
options.rationale: Nasal feeding tubes are small bore by design. The reason for a different route is the expected duration, not the tube width.

options.text: "A tube into the stomach through the abdomen removes any chance of formula reaching your lungs."
options.rationale: Gastric feeding still carries aspiration risk; even small intestine feeding does not eliminate it.

options.text: "Nose tubes are meant for short periods; a tube through the abdomen suits months of feeding."
options.rationale: Expected feeding duration guides the route: nasal tubes for short term feeding, gastrostomy and jejunostomy tubes for prolonged support.

options.text: "A tube through the abdomen is placed without any sedation, so it is the simpler procedure."
options.rationale: A gastrostomy is created under sedation. The nasal route is the less invasive one.

questions.takeaway: Nasoenteric tubes are for short term feeding; enterostomal tubes (gastrostomy, PEG, jejunostomy) are for long term feeding. Duration, GI anatomy, and gastric emptying guide the route.
questions.strategy: Each option gives a reason for the abdominal tube. Keep the one whose reason is true: duration.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: At least 6 months of feeding.
Width is not the issue; aspiration risk remains; sedation is used.
Duration guides the route.

elimination.verdict: C. Nose tubes are meant for short periods; a tube through the abdomen suits months of feeding.

questions.objective: Describe feeding tube types and the factors that guide route selection

questions.stem: The nurse assesses the site of a client's percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube. Which findings require follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Skin around the tube is dry, intact, and the same color as the surrounding abdomen
options.rationale: Dry, intact skin with no color change is the expected site condition.

options.text: Formula leaks around the tube and has soaked the gauze since 0700
options.rationale: Leakage at the site irritates the skin and can signal a problem with the tube or stoma, so it is assessed and reported.

options.text: The external length mark at the skin matches the documented mark
options.rationale: A matching mark shows the tube has not moved.

options.text: Pain at the site is 7 of 10 when the tube is touched, was 2 of 10 yesterday
options.rationale: New or rising pain at the site needs follow up for infection or tube problems.

options.text: Tubing is secured to the abdomen with no tension on the site
options.rationale: Securing the tubing to reduce pulling and pressure is the goal of site care.

questions.takeaway: Assess gastrostomy and jejunostomy sites for redness, pain, drainage, leakage, and swelling. Keep the site clean and dry and secure the tubing to reduce pulling.
questions.strategy: Separate findings that meet the goals of site care from findings on the list of warning signs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Leakage soaking the gauze; pain rising from 2 to 7 of 10.
Intact skin, a matching mark, and secured tubing.

elimination.verdict: B, D.

questions.objective: Provide oral, nasal and site care, teach the patient and document

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client's spouse how to give bolus feedings through a gastrostomy tube at home. Which statement by the spouse indicates a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I will keep the head raised 30 to 45 degrees during the feeding, as you showed me."
options.rationale: This is correct. Elevation during feeding reduces aspiration risk.

options.text: "If coughing or trouble breathing starts during a feeding, I will slow it and finish."
options.rationale: Coughing or trouble breathing during a feeding can mean aspiration. The caregiver stops the feeding and seeks help, so this statement needs more teaching.

options.text: "I will flush the tube with water before and after each feeding, as I showed you."
options.rationale: This is correct. Flushes before and after intermittent feedings keep the tube open.

options.text: "I will call the clinic if the skin around the tube becomes red, swollen, or leaks."
options.rationale: This is correct. Redness, swelling, and leakage at the site need follow up.

questions.takeaway: Teach when to stop a feeding and seek help, and confirm understanding with teach back and return demonstration. Coughing or trouble breathing means stop, not slow down.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that keeps the feeding going when it should stop.

steps.detail: A need for more teaching means find the unsafe statement.
Elevation, flushes, and reporting site changes are correct.
Slowing and finishing a feeding during coughing or trouble breathing is unsafe.

elimination.verdict: B. If coughing or trouble breathing starts during a feeding, I will slow it and finish.

questions.objective: Provide oral, nasal and site care, teach the patient and document

questions.stem: The nurse prepares to hang a new container of formula for a continuous gastrostomy tube feeding by pump. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Compare the formula, route, volume, rate, and expiration date with the order
options.rationale: The nurse verifies formula, route, volume, rate, and expiration date before hanging formula.

options.text: Connect the feeding set to the gastrostomy tube with an ENFit connector
options.rationale: ENFit connections fit only enteral devices, which prevents wrong route administration such as formula entering an intravenous line.

options.text: Use a Luer slip adapter to make the connection if the ENFit set does not fit
options.rationale: Luer connectors also fit intravenous devices, which defeats the protection against wrong route administration.

options.text: Label the formula and the administration set
options.rationale: Labeling the formula and equipment supports safe hang times and correct identification.

options.text: Pour the new formula into the bag on top of the formula still hanging
options.rationale: Adding fresh formula to old formula breaks hang time limits and increases handling and contamination.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene and handle the formula and set as little as possible
options.rationale: Hand hygiene and minimal handling reduce contamination of the formula.

questions.takeaway: Before hanging formula, verify it against the order, perform hand hygiene, minimize handling, label the formula and set, follow hang time limits, and use ENFit connections to prevent wrong route administration.
questions.strategy: Treat each option as true or false against two goals: the right formula by the right route, and no contamination.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Verify against the order; ENFit, never a Luer adapter.
Hand hygiene, minimal handling, labeling; never top off old formula.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, F.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: A client, 63 years old, receives continuous feeding through a gastrostomy tube. Two liquid medications are due at 0900. The pharmacist has confirmed that both are appropriate for the tube and the delivery site and that neither requires a longer feeding interruption. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Give the second medication
options.rationale: The second medication follows the flush that cleared the first, so the two never mix in the tube.

options.text: Flush with 30 mL of water to clear the first medication from the tube
options.rationale: A 30 mL flush between medications keeps them separate and prevents clogging.

options.text: Pause the pump and check the tube placement
options.rationale: Placement is checked before medications, and the feeding is paused so medications are given separately from formula.

options.text: Flush with 30 mL of water and restart the feeding at the ordered rate
options.rationale: A final 30 mL flush clears the last medication; the feeding then resumes as ordered.

options.text: Give the first medication
options.rationale: The first medication goes in after the tube has been flushed.

options.text: Flush with 30 mL of water before any medication enters the tube
options.rationale: A 30 mL flush before medications clears formula from the tube.

questions.takeaway: Give each medication separately with a 30 mL water flush before, between, and after, after checking placement. Include the flushes in total fluid intake.
questions.strategy: Start with the check that makes the tube safe to use, then alternate flush and medication, and end with a flush before the feeding restarts.

steps.detail: Pause the pump and check placement.
Flush, first medication, flush, second medication.
Flush and restart the feeding.

elimination.verdict: Pause and check placement; flush; first medication; flush; second medication; flush and restart.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: A client, 63 years old, receives feeding through a gastrostomy tube and takes nothing by mouth. At 0900 the nurse prepares a blood pressure medication prescribed as one tablet by gastrostomy tube daily. The tablet is labeled "extended release." Tube placement was checked at 0855, and the tube flushes with no resistance. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Hold the tablet and contact the pharmacist about a form that is safe for the tube
options.rationale: Each medication must be appropriate for the tube. Crushing an extended release tablet releases the full dose at once, so the nurse holds it and asks the pharmacist about another form.

options.text: Crush the tablet finely, dissolve it in warm water, and give it with 30 mL flushes
options.rationale: This is the correct method for a tablet that can be crushed, which makes it tempting. The cue is the extended release label: this tablet must not be crushed.

options.text: Crush the tablet and mix it into the formula so the dose is delivered slowly
options.rationale: Medications are not mixed with formula, and crushing the tablet still destroys the extended release design.

options.text: Give the tablet whole through the tube, followed by a 60 mL water flush
options.rationale: A whole tablet cannot pass through a feeding tube and will clog it.

questions.takeaway: Verify that each medication is appropriate for the tube before giving it. Extended release tablets are not crushed; ask the pharmacist about a liquid or other safe form.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options handle a tablet correctly in general. The extended release label decides which one is safe for this tablet.

steps.detail: The tablet is labeled extended release.
Correct for most tablets, unsafe for an extended release one.
Medications are not mixed with formula; whole tablets clog the tube.
Hold the tablet and ask the pharmacist about another form.

elimination.verdict: A. Hold the tablet and contact the pharmacist about a form that is safe for the tube.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: During a continuous gastrostomy tube feeding, the pump alarms for an occlusion, and a 30 mL water flush meets resistance. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Instill 30 mL of cola and clamp the tube so the bubbles loosen the clog
options.rationale: Carbonated beverages and juice are avoided when unclogging tubes, because their acid can make formula proteins clump and worsen the clog.

options.text: Switch to a 10 mL syringe to push the water through with more force
options.rationale: A clogged tube is never forced. A small syringe creates high pressure that can rupture the tube.

options.text: Keep the pump running at the ordered rate so its pressure clears the clog
options.rationale: The pump cannot clear the clog, and the client receives no formula while the tube is blocked.

options.text: Attempt a gentle water flush again and follow policy if it stays blocked
options.rationale: For a clogged tube, the nurse attempts gentle water flushing, never forces it, and follows policy if the clog remains.

questions.takeaway: For a clogged feeding tube, attempt gentle water flushing and never force it. Do not use carbonated beverages or juice. Prevent clogs with 30 mL flushes before, between, and after medications.
questions.strategy: Three options apply force or the wrong fluid. Find the option that uses water gently.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Occlusion alarm and resistance to a water flush.
A 10 mL syringe or pump pressure forces the tube.
Carbonated drinks and juice worsen clogs.
Gentle water flushing, then policy.

elimination.verdict: D. Attempt a gentle water flush again and follow policy if it stays blocked.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: A client, 57 years old, is 6 days after bowel surgery and has a paralytic ileus. The client has been NPO since surgery. A nasogastric tube to low suction drained 900 mL in the past 24 hours. No bowel sounds are heard after 5 minutes in each quadrant, and the abdomen is distended. Weight is 68.0 kg now, was 72.5 kg before surgery. The client is alert and swallows saliva without coughing. Which nutrition plan does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Enteral feeding through the existing nasogastric tube, since a tube is already in place
options.rationale: A tube already in place is convenient, but enteral nutrition needs a functional GI tract. Formula put into a bowel that is not moving adds to the distention and drainage.

options.text: An oral diet started slowly, since the client swallows without coughing
options.rationale: Safe swallowing does not help when the bowel cannot move or absorb food. Oral intake would worsen the ileus.

options.text: Parenteral nutrition, peripheral or total, since the GI tract cannot be used
options.rationale: Parenteral nutrition delivers nutrients intravenously when the GI tract cannot be adequately used. Peripheral (PPN) and total parenteral nutrition (TPN) are its two types.

options.text: Enteral feeding through a new small bore tube, since small tubes clog less often
options.rationale: Tube size does not solve the problem. Any enteral route still relies on a working bowel.

questions.takeaway: Enteral nutrition delivers nutrients into a functional GI tract. Parenteral nutrition, peripheral or total, delivers nutrients intravenously when the GI tract cannot be adequately used.
questions.strategy: Ask first whether the gut works. Absent bowel sounds, distention and heavy drainage mean it does not, whatever the swallowing or tube situation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Ileus, absent bowel sounds and 900 mL of drainage: the GI tract cannot be used.
Three options feed into the GI tract; only one bypasses it.
Parenteral nutrition.

elimination.verdict: C. Parenteral nutrition.

questions.objective: Compare enteral and parenteral nutrition and identify who needs enteral feeding

questions.stem: The nurse assesses a client, 76 years old, who lives alone. Which findings place the client at risk for undernutrition? Select all that apply.

options.text: Walks for 20 minutes each morning with a neighbor
options.rationale: Regular activity with social contact is a healthy habit, not a risk factor.

options.text: Has had heart failure for 5 years and kidney disease for 2 years
options.rationale: Chronic illness is a risk factor for undernutrition.

options.text: Has had a poor appetite since a spouse died 3 months ago
options.rationale: Poor appetite is a risk factor for undernutrition, whatever its cause.

options.text: Coughs and clears the throat when drinking thin liquids
options.rationale: Coughing with liquids suggests difficulty swallowing, a risk factor for undernutrition and for aspiration.

options.text: Stopped driving, and the nearest grocery store is 8 km away with no bus
options.rationale: Limited access to food is a risk factor for undernutrition.

options.text: Takes a daily multivitamin with breakfast
options.rationale: A multivitamin does not create risk, and it does not replace adequate intake.

questions.takeaway: Risk factors for undernutrition are poor appetite, difficulty swallowing, chronic illness and limited food access. The nursing priority is to identify deficits early.
questions.strategy: Test each finding against the four risk factors: appetite, swallowing, chronic illness and access to food.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Grief has reduced the appetite.
Coughing with thin liquids.
Heart failure and kidney disease.
No car and no bus to a store 8 km away.

elimination.verdict: B, C, D, E.

questions.objective: Compare enteral and parenteral nutrition and identify who needs enteral feeding

questions.stem: A client, 60 years old, has delayed gastric emptying and has had 2 episodes of vomiting and aspiration pneumonia while receiving feedings through a nasogastric tube. The team expects tube feeding to be needed for at least 6 months. The provider also wants a way to drain the stomach when it is distended. Which tube does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: A dual access gastrojejunostomy tube, with a gastric port and a jejunal feeding port
options.rationale: Long term feeding calls for an enterostomal tube. Delayed gastric emptying and aspiration point to feeding into the small intestine, and the gastric port allows the stomach to be drained.

options.text: A large bore nasogastric tube, because a wider double lumen tube carries formula faster
options.rationale: Large bore tubes are for decompression and lavage, and nasal tubes are for short term use. Feeding into a slow stomach keeps the aspiration risk.

options.text: A gastrostomy tube, because feeding through the abdominal wall removes the aspiration risk
options.rationale: A gastrostomy is long term, but it still feeds a stomach that empties slowly. No route removes aspiration risk completely.

options.text: A nasojejunal tube, because nasal tubes into the jejunum suit feeding that lasts for months
options.rationale: Feeding into the jejunum fits the delayed emptying, but nasal tubes are for short term feeding, not 6 months.

questions.takeaway: Route selection depends on expected duration (nasal tubes for short term; G and J tubes for long term) and on GI anatomy and gastric emptying. Small intestine feeding may lower aspiration risk but does not eliminate it.
questions.strategy: Apply two filters in order: duration first (months means an enterostomal tube), then gastric emptying (a slow stomach means feeding beyond it).

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 6 months rules out the nasal tubes.
Delayed emptying and aspiration point past the stomach.
Removes the aspiration risk is never true.
A gastrojejunostomy tube that feeds the jejunum and drains the stomach.

elimination.verdict: A. A dual access gastrojejunostomy tube.

questions.objective: Describe feeding tube types and the factors that guide route selection

questions.stem: A client with dysphagia has a new gastrostomy tube. Which actions does the nurse take before starting the first intermittent feeding? Select all that apply.

options.text: Review the weight, intake and output, and the ordered laboratory results
options.rationale: Weight, hydration, intake and output, and laboratory results give the baseline for monitoring the response to feeding.

options.text: Offer 30 mL of water by mouth to see whether the client can swallow
options.rationale: The client has dysphagia. Testing with water by mouth risks aspiration; the swallow is evaluated, not challenged.

options.text: Verify the feeding order and identify the client with 2 identifiers
options.rationale: Verifying the order and identifying the client come first before any feeding.

options.text: Assess level of consciousness and the ability to protect the airway
options.rationale: Swallowing, consciousness and airway protection affect aspiration risk during feeding.

options.text: Send a stool culture to rule out infection before the first feeding
options.rationale: A stool culture is not part of the routine assessment before feeding. The nurse assesses bowel patterns.

options.text: Record the baseline respiratory rate, lung sounds and SpO2
options.rationale: A baseline respiratory status lets the nurse recognize aspiration if it occurs.

questions.takeaway: Before feeding: verify the order and identify the client; assess weight, hydration, I&O and labs; assess the abdomen, nausea, vomiting and bowel pattern; evaluate swallowing, consciousness and airway protection; and establish baseline respiratory status.
questions.strategy: Each correct option gives a baseline or confirms safety. Reject any option that puts the client at risk or is not part of the routine assessment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Order and identity.
Weight, I&O, labs and respiratory status.
Consciousness and airway protection.
Water by mouth with dysphagia; a stool culture.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, F.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding and verify tube placement

questions.stem: A client, 69 years old, receives bolus feedings through a small bore nasogastric tube. After x ray confirmation 3 days ago, the tube was documented at 62 cm at the right naris. At 0800, before the feeding, the mark is at 62 cm and the securement is intact. The client has no cough, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97% on room air. The aspirate has a pH of 6. The client receives an acid suppressing medication every morning. Which explanation for the pH does the nurse consider most likely?

options.text: The tube has moved into the airway, because fluid from the lungs is not acidic
options.rationale: Airway placement is the dangerous possibility, but the length matches, the securement is intact and the client has no respiratory signs.

options.text: The tube has moved into the esophagus, because any pH above 5 rules out the stomach
options.rationale: A pH above 5 does not rule out gastric placement. Acid suppressing medication can raise gastric pH.

options.text: The pH test strip is faulty, because fluid from the stomach always tests acidic
options.rationale: Gastric fluid is usually acidic, not always. The word always is the cue that this is wrong.

options.text: The daily acid suppressing medication has raised the pH of the gastric fluid
options.rationale: Acid suppressing medications can raise gastric pH. The matching length, intact securement and lack of respiratory signs support this, and pH is read with the overall assessment.

questions.takeaway: Gastric aspirate is usually acidic (pH 5 or less), but acid suppressing medications and formula change the result. pH alone cannot confirm or rule out placement; interpret it with length, securement and the client's condition, and hold use if placement is uncertain.
questions.strategy: Weigh the single abnormal value against all the other placement data before deciding what it means.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Length matches, securement intact, no respiratory signs.
A daily acid suppressing medication.
Any pH above 5 and always acidic are not true.
The medication raised the gastric pH.

elimination.verdict: D. The medication raised the gastric pH.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding and verify tube placement

questions.stem: A client, 80 years old, receives bolus feedings through a gastrostomy tube 4 times a day. The facility protocol directs that the head of the bed remain raised 30 to 45 degrees for 1 hour after each bolus feeding. A 240 mL bolus finished at 1215, and the head of the bed is at 40 degrees. At 1225 the client asks to lie flat for a nap. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Lower the head of the bed flat, since the feeding has already finished
options.rationale: Aspiration risk continues after the formula is in. The protocol requires upright positioning for 1 hour after the feeding.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed at 30 to 45 degrees until 1315, then lower it
options.rationale: Upright positioning after intermittent feeding is maintained as directed. The 1 hour protocol ends at 1315.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed and turn the client onto the left side
options.rationale: Side lying does not replace head elevation. Lying flat soon after a bolus still allows reflux and aspiration.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 30 degrees for 15 minutes, then lower it
options.rationale: The angle is right, but 15 minutes falls short of the 1 hour that the protocol directs.

questions.takeaway: Prevent aspiration by keeping the head of the bed at 30 to 45 degrees during feeding and maintaining upright positioning after intermittent feedings as directed.
questions.strategy: The protocol in the stem sets both the angle and the time. Pick the option that meets both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 30 to 45 degrees for 1 hour after each bolus.
1215 plus 1 hour is 1315.
15 minutes meets the angle but not the time.

elimination.verdict: B. Keep upright until 1315.

questions.objective: Prevent aspiration during enteral feeding

questions.scenario: A nurse on a rehabilitation unit reviews the feeding plans of several clients who receive enteral nutrition.
questions.stem: For each feeding plan, indicate the feeding method.

rows.text: A client wants the daytime free for therapy; formula runs by pump at 80 mL per hour from 2000 to 0600.
rows.rationale: Cyclic feeding runs by pump over a designated period, such as overnight, leaving the rest of the day free.

rows.text: A client receives 240 mL by syringe over 10 minutes every 4 hours while awake.
rows.rationale: A larger volume given over a short period is a bolus feeding.

rows.text: A client receives formula at 55 mL per hour by pump around the clock.
rows.rationale: A prescribed hourly rate by pump, without a planned stop, is continuous feeding.

rows.text: A client at home gives 200 mL by syringe over 15 minutes at 5 scheduled times a day.
rows.rationale: A larger volume over a short period, even at scheduled times, is a bolus feeding.

rows.text: A client receives formula by pump only during sleep, from 2200 to 0600.
rows.rationale: Pump feeding limited to a designated period each day is cyclic feeding.

questions.takeaway: Bolus: a larger volume over a short period. Continuous: a prescribed hourly rate by pump, advanced only as ordered. Cyclic: pump feeding over a designated period, such as overnight.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions: is a pump used, and does it stop? Short syringe feedings are bolus; pump all day is continuous; pump for part of the day is cyclic.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 240 mL over 10 minutes is a bolus.

steps.action: Find the round the clock pump
steps.detail: 55 mL per hour with no planned stop is continuous.
2000 to 0600 and 2200 to 0600 are cyclic.

elimination.verdict: Cyclic, bolus, continuous, bolus, cyclic.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: A client, 66 years old, receives continuous feeding through a gastrostomy tube at 60 mL per hour. A medication is due at 0900. The pharmacist's note in the record states that formula reduces absorption of this drug, so the order directs holding the feeding 1 hour before and 1 hour after each dose. At 0900 the nurse finds that the feeding was not paused at 0800. Placement was checked at 0855. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the medication now with 30 mL flushes and leave the feeding running
options.rationale: Flushes are correct, but giving the drug with formula running ignores the interaction and lowers absorption.

options.text: Add the medication to the formula bag so that it is absorbed slowly over time
options.rationale: Medications are never added to formula. They are given separately, and this drug interacts with the formula.

options.text: Pause the feeding and contact the pharmacist or provider about when to give the dose
options.rationale: Medication and feeding interactions and required interruptions are assessed before giving the drug. The required hold was missed, so the nurse pauses and clarifies the timing.

options.text: Give the medication now and hold the feeding for 2 hours afterward to make up for it
options.rationale: Extending the hold after the dose does not remove formula already in the stomach. The nurse does not change the schedule without clarification.

questions.takeaway: Verify that each medication suits the tube and site, give medications separately with ordered flushes, and assess medication and feeding interactions and any required feeding interruptions.
questions.strategy: The order's hold was missed, so the drug cannot be given as ordered. Choose the option that stops the interaction and gets direction rather than inventing a new schedule.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The 1 hour hold before the dose did not happen.
Formula is in the stomach and lowers absorption.
Mixing in formula or extending the hold changes the order.
Pause and clarify the timing.

elimination.verdict: C. Pause the feeding and clarify the timing.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: A client, 63 years old, receives continuous feeding through a gastrostomy tube at 60 mL per hour. The facility policy sets an 8 hour hang time limit for formula poured into an open feeding bag. At 1600 the nurse finds that the bag label reads "hung at 0600," and 150 mL of formula remains. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Discard the remaining formula, and hang fresh formula labeled with the date and time
options.rationale: The formula has hung for 10 hours, past the 8 hour limit. Old formula grows bacteria, so it is discarded and fresh formula is hung and labeled.

options.text: Pour a new can of formula into the bag so that the feeding is not interrupted
options.rationale: Adding fresh formula to formula past its hang time contaminates the new formula as well.

options.text: Let the remaining 150 mL finish, and then hang a new bag of formula
options.rationale: Running the last 150 mL delivers formula that is already past the hang time limit.

options.text: Leave the bag running, and relabel it with the current time and the nurse's initials
options.rationale: Relabeling hides the true hang time and leaves expired formula running.

questions.takeaway: Follow manufacturer and facility hang time limits. Label the formula and equipment, minimize handling, and never add new formula to formula already hanging.
questions.strategy: Count the hours: 0600 to 1600 is 10 hours, past the limit. Every option that keeps the old formula running is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 10 hours exceeds the 8 hour limit.
New formula on old formula is contaminated.
Finishing or relabeling still gives expired formula.
Discard and hang fresh, labeled formula.

elimination.verdict: A. Discard and hang fresh formula.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: A client, 72 years old, has a continuous feeding prescribed at 60 mL per hour for 24 hours, a total of 1,440 mL. Over the past 24 hours the feeding was paused for a CT scan, 2 baths, physical therapy and medications. The pump history shows 960 mL delivered. Weight is 53.8 kg, was 55.0 kg 1 week ago. The abdomen is soft, and there has been no nausea or vomiting. How does the nurse evaluate the feeding?

options.text: The client is tolerating the feeding and is meeting the prescribed intake
options.rationale: The client is tolerating the formula, but 960 mL is not the 1,440 mL prescribed.

options.text: The rate should be raised to 90 mL per hour so that the volume is made up
options.rationale: Continuous feeding rates are advanced only as ordered. The nurse does not change the rate to catch up.

options.text: The weight loss shows intolerance, so the feeding should be held for now
options.rationale: There are no signs of intolerance. Holding the feeding would widen the shortfall.

options.text: Formula is tolerated, but delivery falls short, so the nurse reports the gap
options.rationale: Tracking formula delivered against the prescribed amount shows about two thirds was given. With weight loss, the shortfall is reported so the plan can be adjusted.

questions.takeaway: Monitoring tolerance includes tracking formula delivered against the prescribed amount, along with intake and output, weight and ordered laboratory values. Interruptions add up.
questions.strategy: Separate two questions: is the formula tolerated, and is enough being delivered? The stem answers yes to the first and no to the second.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Soft abdomen, no nausea or vomiting.
960 of 1,440 mL is about two thirds.
Rates are advanced only as ordered.
Report the delivery gap with the weight loss.
